papers.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
papers.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. papers.intro:
Segmentation turns images into quantitative measurements such as organ volumes, tumour burden or cell counts. Dedicated models segment the structures they were trained on; everything else is delineated by people, increasingly with the help of promptable models. nnInteractive [4], for example, predicts a full 3D mask from points, scribbles, boxes or lassos placed in single slices and was trained on more than 120 volumetric datasets spanning CT, MRI, PET and 3D microscopy. Such a model makes every prompt count, but the annotation process itself remains with a human: deciding what the target is and where it lies, placing prompts, judging the 3D result, correcting it, and revising it when someone asks for changes.

papers.title: The XMM-Newton view of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
papers.abstract: We present the first multi-wavelength analysis of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud. We compare the DEM L36 superbubble with other Galactic and Magellanic Cloud superbubbles. We use data from XMM-Newton, supplemented by data from the Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Dark Energy Camera Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and the Australia Telescope Compact Array. We perform a multi-wavelength morphological analysis to understand the shape and structure of the superbubble and X-ray spectral analysis to derive physical parameters of the hot gas. We find significant X-ray emission in DEM L36, dominated by a central bubble region mostly confined by a thin H$α$ filamentary shell. This has two distinct blowout regions to the east and west, with a possible smaller blowout in the south. Spectral analysis shows the X-ray emission is well fit with a thermal plasma model in collisional ionisation equilibrium with a temperature of $kT=0.17~(0.16-0.18)$ keV and unabsorbed luminosity $L_{X~(0.5-7.0~\mathrm{keV})}=3.62\times 10^{35} $erg s$^{-1}$. Unlike other LMC superbubbles, we find no clear powering cluster at the centre, though relatively small clusters near the edge are likely supplying the mechanical input at the present epoch. We use photometric data of these clusters to estimate cluster masses, ages, and mechanical inputs to compare with the energy stored in the superbubble. We find that these clusters have supplied more energy over their lifetime than is currently observed in the superbubble, indicative of the so-called growth rate discrepancy problem. It is likely the DEM L36 superbubble was initially shaped by a central massive stellar population that has since dispersed and largely lost to supernovae, with smaller clusters at the edges of the swept-up shell being currently supplying the energy input.

papers.intro:
The evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM) is dominated by feedback from massive stars and later by supernovae and their remnants, regulating star formation efficiency, driving turbulence, and triggering or suppressing subsequent star formation on multiple scales. Winds and SNRs of OB stars in massive stellar clusters drive the evolution of massive star forming regions (MSFRs) and often form ‘superbubbles’ (SBs) - huge cavity regions within the ISM with diameters of 100-1000 pc which are filled with a hot, shock-heated X-ray emitting gas with temperatures of ∼106\sim 10^{6} K (see Kavanagh 2020, for a review). This hot gas is surrounded by a ‘supershell’ of swept-up ISM which is bright in optical emission, primarily powered by photoionisation from the intense UV radiation from the massive stars. These objects were initially described by the analytical models of Mac Low and McCray (1988) and Chu and Mac Low (1990), extensions of the wind-blown bubble model of Weaver et al. (1977), which assumed a continuous stellar input and uniform ambient interstellar medium (ISM).

However, observations of SBs and constraints on the mechanical input by their powering stellar populations deviate significantly from model predictions with the observed SBs being smaller than expected (Oey 1996, e.g.). This is known as the ‘growth rate discrepancy’. Various resolutions to this issue have been proposed such as a correction to ambient pressure (Oey and García-Segura 2004), blowouts (Breitschwerdt and de Avillez 2006, e.g.), radiative cooling (Kim et al. 2017, e.g.), and losses to cosmic ray acceleration (Butt and Bykov 2008). Another observed deviation from the models is that X-ray bright superbubbles have higher supershell expansion velocities than predicted (Oey 1996), which likely results from the time variability of the mechanical input due to interior supernovae (Oey and García-Segura 2004). To further our understanding of SB evolution and the contributions to the growth rate discrepancy, the identification and analysis of new objects is essential to provide empirical constraints on both analytical and numerical models. This not only broadens statistics on SBs and their properties but also reveals the diversity of feedback outcomes.

(2004). We present an analysis using X-ray data from XMM-Newton, optical data from the Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey (MCELS), infrared data from Spitzer and 21 cm radio data from the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA). These data enable us to gain insights into the physical characteristics and processes of the SB, assess the magnitude of the growth rate discrepancy problem for this object, and allow us to compare it to other known SBs.

papers.title: Reducing Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Forecast Error through Tree-Anchored Expert Combination
papers.abstract: A strong direct tree model may remain the best standalone photovoltaic forecaster, yet a weighted combination can reduce its residual errors. We examine whether complementary temporal predictors can lower the tree's mean absolute error (MAE) over 15--240 minutes without weaker ensemble members degrading performance. The candidate bank contains LightGBM and seven neural implementations with different temporal representations. A combiner fitted to MAE has nonnegative weights that sum to one. Unhelpful candidates can receive zero weight, while the tree anchors the combination and provides a development-stage fallback. The main design shares weights across horizons; horizon-specific weights and alternative losses test whether further complexity is needed. On 56,078 windows from two co-located public PVDAQ systems, the historical shared-MAE policy reduces scaled MAE by 3.21\% relative to the tree. The latest bounded neural correction does not reduce MAE further than this static combination. The results support selective combination of complementary predictions in this bank rather than equal averaging or indiscriminate addition of modules. Both analyses reuse a previously inspected evaluation period. They do not establish independent replication, weather-specific causation or universal gains from eight experts.

Related photovoltaic studies examine both temporal representations and how their predictions are combined. Costa (2022) compares convolutional, LSTM, and convolutional–LSTM networks at different forecast horizons and studies transfer from geographically aggregated training data to individual household systems. Zheng et al. (2025) combines kernel-clustering-based learner selection, joint feature and hyperparameter optimization, and adaptive weighted stacking for small-sample photovoltaic forecasting. Yang et al. (2025) couples numerical-weather-prediction-based time-series clustering with lag-enhanced gradient-boosting ensembles for day-ahead forecasting. These studies motivate testing temporal representations and fitted aggregation, but their datasets, information sets, and horizons differ from those used here. We do not compare their published error values directly with ours. The present study isolates a narrower question: whether MAE-fitted static weights can extract useful corrections to a strong direct tree, without adding a weather clustering or joint feature-search module.

papers.title: The Bayesian Learning Rule Beyond KL Geometry
papers.abstract: The Bayesian learning rule (BLR) exploits the relation between Bayesian updating and the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) to derive efficient additive updates for exponential family variational posteriors. The KL geometry is powerful but restrictive: combined with posterior families with parameter-dependent support it can lead to undefined objectives. We ask which non-KL geometries preserve the additive BLR computation. Previous works that use $f$-divergences suggest that this is only possible with the KLD. Here, we show that this is not true. We show that additive information-geometric optimization algorithms can be derived for the class of mixed-space Bregman or Fenchel-Young discrepancies. These discrepancies induce generalized maximum-entropy families, dual coordinates, and generalized-BLR canonical gradient updates, recovering the classical BLR. The generalized BLR leads to new algorithms that \textit{cannot} be derived from the KL-based BLR. For the Tsallis negentropy with quadratic statistics, the generalized BLR yields bounded-support and heavy-tailed $q$-Gaussian posteriors and an easy Newton-like implementation. Experiments up to CIFAR-100 illustrate controllable support and tail behavior and competitive performance.

papers.intro:
There is substantial work on generalizing Bayesian inference from the perspective of optimization: the variational posterior strikes a balance between information from the observations and adherence to the prior. Recently, Knoblauch et al. [2022] exploit the “modularity” of this optimization perspective, treating the variational family in which the posterior is sought, the loss connecting the posterior to the observations, and the divergence between the posterior and prior as independent design choices, ignoring formal interactions of these objects. In contrast, Khan and Rue [2023]’s Bayesian learning rule (BLR) is an iterated, conjugate inference extension of classical Bayes, preserving the standard couplings between the prior and entropic regularizer, and between prior and posterior families (Sec. 2). In the BLR, the updates stem from the interaction of Shannon entropy, KL geometry, and exponential-family posteriors, which is computationally powerful but restrictive: it ties the BLR to standard fixed-support exponential families. Posterior families with variable support or adaptive tail behavior fall outside the scope of the KL-based BLR. Here, we focus on a structural question raised by the BLR: are there generalizations of the KL-based variational objective that preserve the additive canonical-coordinate updates that free the BLR from its KL restriction?

By KL or mixed-space Bregman geometry we mean the convex-analytic structure defined by a reference score and convex function, which induce a mixed Bregman divergence: the score family and convex function determine the maxent posterior family whose convex conjugate determines dual coordinates, and a Hessian metric. Our terminology is motivated by the fact that a mixed Bregman divergence is the slack in a Fenchel-Young inequality.11 1 We use Fenchel rather than Legendre deliberately. In convex analysis, the Legendre transform is the differentiable special case of the Fenchel conjugate [Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004, Touchette, 2005]. Closest to our generalized BLR is Alquier [2021]’s mirror-descent update that optimizes the sum of an expected loss and a ff-divergence. Only when the ff-divergence coincides with the KLD is it possible to separate the ff-divergence ratio into a difference of linear expectations. Uniquely, the KLD belongs both to the classes of ff- and Bregman divergences [Amari, 2009]. The mixed-space Bregman divergence that we use recovers the KLD and BLR, but encompasses other divergences corresponding to generalized entropies. We optimize a generalized variational objective using dual coordinates of a relaxed class of reference scores in place of normalized priors, and generalized Fenchel posteriors in place of Gibbs posteriors. The resulting information-geometric algorithm has the same additive computation as the BLR, and admits a dual-space analogue of Bissiri et al. [2016]’s sequential coherence, unlike ff-divergence updates.

Parameter-dependent bounded-support qq-Gaussian posteriors allow the posterior mean to closely track MAP solutions (Figs. 1 and 2). By contrast, Gaussian variational means are far enough away from the MAP to avoid sampling parameter-space regions with high-loss. The heavy-tailed qq-Gaussian posterior updates we derive are reparametrizations of Student-tt distributions studied in robust Bayesian inference. Various aspects of robust Bayes can be reinterpreted in our framework, with the benefit of easy conjugate priors, but drawing these connections is beyond the scope of this paper; as is demonstrating state-of-the-art or scale. We develop the theoretical framework and check that the proposed algorithms for variational training with controllable support and tail behaviors are competitive with their Gaussian IVON counterpart [Khan et al., 2018, Osawa et al., 2019, Shen et al., 2024], without additional tuning.

papers.title: Atomic limits of empirical measures of interacting particle systems with self-duality
papers.abstract: We study the fixed-particle limit of empirical measures for a unified self-dual family of conservative particle systems on $\mathbb{Z}^d$: independent random walkers, the symmetric exclusion process, and the symmetric inclusion process. For a fixed number of particles $k$, under diffusive space-time scaling parametrised by $n$, we prove that as $n\to\infty$ the normalised empirical measure converges in $D([0,T],\mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R}^d))$ to an atomic empirical measure carried by $k$ independent diffusions, with constant covariance determined by the microscopic jump kernel. Equivalently, the limit is the unique atomic solution of the Dean-Kawasaki martingale problem with mass quantisation $1/k$. In particular, exclusion and inclusion have the same fixed-$k$ atomic limit as independent walkers: the interaction contributes only through microscopic near-collisions, whose rescaled occupation time vanishes. The proof combines self-duality, consistency-based reduction to two particles, and Green-function estimates for finite perturbations of symmetric random walks.

papers.intro:
The large-scale behaviour of conservative interacting particle systems is classically encoded in their empirical measure. Depending on the normalisation, however, this empirical measure may lead to rather different macroscopic objects. In the usual hydrodynamic regime one typically considers O⁡(nd)O(n^{d}) particles in a macroscopic box, normalises the empirical measure by n−dn^{-d}, and rescales diffusively. Self-averaging then takes place: the empirical density converges to an absolutely continuous measure whose density is the deterministic solution of a diffusion equation [12, 22, 2], and its n−d/2n^{-d/2} fluctuations converge to a Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type field [22, 12, 4]. A different formal object is suggested by fluctuating hydrodynamics, where the density field itself is kept stochastic and carries multiplicative noise, leading formally to the Dean-Kawasaki equation [13, 21]. These two viewpoints are often close in spirit, but they are structurally different: in fluctuation theory the drift is linearised around the hydrodynamic profile, by means of the Boltzmann-Gibbs principle [28], [8], [22, Chapter 11], and the noise is evaluated at that deterministic profile, hence the limit is Gaussian; in fluctuating hydrodynamics both the drift and the noise amplitude are evaluated at the random density itself. For the self-dual family considered here, self-duality makes the drift linear in the occupation variables, hence the two pictures differ only through the noise; for non-linear gradient systems, such as zero-range processes, they differ also in the drift. For the self-dual family, a quantitative version of the Boltzmann-Gibbs principle, with the order of every term made explicit, is obtained by means of orthogonal polynomial duality [3], and the terms of higher order are the subject of the second-order Boltzmann-Gibbs principle [20]. Quantitative central limit theorems for the density fluctuations of the simple symmetric exclusion process, first at fixed times and then on path space with higher-order lattice corrections, are obtained in [17, 16].

papers.title: In-Browser Human-AI Co-Writing for Counterspeech: An Exploratory User Study of Agency, Perceived Response Quality, and Time
papers.abstract: Writing counterspeech that challenges online hate speech can be cognitively and emotionally demanding, whereas fully automated generation may weaken users' sense of voice and responsibility. We present an in-browser AI-assisted co-writing tool that enables users to contribute their own ideas and offers three editable suggestions generated by a large language model using dynamically retrieved hate speech-counterspeech examples from the Multitarget CONAN dataset. We evaluated the tool in an exploratory within-subject study with ten participants, complemented by think-aloud observations and semi-structured interviews with half of the participants. Participants wrote responses to three self-selected hate speech instances without assistance and then repeated the task with the tool. Final responses were subsequently peer-rated for empathy, non-toxicity, relevance, specificity, and persuasiveness. Participants evaluated the interface positively, and qualitative accounts linked user input, selection among alternatives, and small edits to perceived agency and responsibility. Assisted responses received higher descriptive mean ratings across all five proxies, with the largest difference for empathy. Mean composition time increased from 2.52 to 3.88 minutes. Qualitative findings further revealed a tension between empathy-oriented outputs and users' desire to express legitimate anger or direct disagreement. We contribute exploratory design guidance for treating AI-assisted counterspeech as deliberative co-writing rather than automated text production.

papers.intro:
Online hate speech (HS) is a persistent feature of digital communication that can harm both its direct targets and the wider communities exposed to it. Prior research links exposure to HS to psychological distress, reduced feelings of safety, and the normalization of hostile discourse (Cohen-Almagor, 2011; Amnesty Global Insights, 2017; Hinduja and Patchin, 2010). Platforms commonly respond through content removal or account sanctions, but such measures remain contested and do not enable users to participate constructively in addressing harmful content. Counterspeech (CS) offers an alternative by challenging hateful narratives through non-aggressive responses that support targets, encourage reflection, and model more civil forms of online interaction for bystanders Benesch (2014); Schieb and Preuss (2016); Baider (2023). However, many users refrain from engaging because composing a response can be time-consuming, emotionally demanding, and rhetorically difficult Mun et al. (2024); Ping et al. (2025).

The interface requires user input, presents three editable LLM-generated CS suggestions, and leaves selection, revision, and posting entirely with the user. papers.title: Spectral Properties of X-Ray Flares in Gamma-Ray Bursts
papers.abstract: We conducted a systematic spectral analysis of the X-ray flares of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed by Swift/X-ray Telescope from 2005 April to 2015 March. The sample includes 521 flares from 206 GRBs. The GRBs cover the three subtypes: X-ray flashes (XRFs), X-ray-rich GRBs (XRRs), and classical GRBs (C-GRBs). We used a simple power-law model to fit the spectra during the flares, as well as to fit the preflare and postflare afterglow emissions, and obtained the parameters such as photon index and intrinsic hydrogen column density ($N_{\rm H}$). By comparing the spectral characteristics of flares, prompt emission, and afterglow emission, and analyzing the temporal evolution of the X-ray flare spectra, we obtained the following main conclusions. (1) The spectrum during the flare phase is significantly harder than that of the preflare and postflare phases, while there is no obvious difference in the spectrum between the preflare and postflare phases. (2) The intrinsic $N_{\rm H}$ shows no significant change between the preflare and flare phases, but significantly decreases after the flare. (3) The overall X-ray flare spectra are softer than those of the prompt emission. (4) For GRBs with multiple flares, the photon index softens with increasing flare peak time. (5) The X-ray flare spectra in XRFs are softer than those in C-GRBs. These results support the origin of X-ray flares being from the internal shock radiation driven by the late activity of the GRB central engine.

The physical origin of X-ray flares remains debated. Due to the similar curves of light variation and characteristics of the spectral evolution of X-ray flares to prompt emission pulses, many researchers generally believe that X-ray flares and prompt emission may have the same physical origin, and both are related to prolonged activity of the central engine of GRBs [6, 49, 38, 44, 13, 12, 15, 33, e.g.,]. Therefore, X-ray flares are regarded as an important probe for exploring the physical properties of the central engine of GRBs.

In this paper, based on the X-ray observation data from Swift/XRT, we use a simple power-law model to fit the spectra of X-ray flares and construct a comprehensive spectral data sample of these flares. By comparing and analyzing the spectral properties of X-ray flares with afterglow emission and with prompt emission, we can test and restrict some physical models of GRBs. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is the sample selection and spectral fitting of X-ray flares. Section 3 is the statistical analysis of the spectra of X-ray flares. papers.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

papers.intro:
How a language model acquires its depth can shape the computations it learns. Depth growing trains an initially shallow network and progressively duplicates blocks of layers, allowing later training stages to reuse computations learned earlier. Looping instead repeatedly applies a shared block within each forward pass. Originally motivated by training efficiency (Fahlman and Lebiere, 1989) and parameter efficiency, respectively, both approaches have attracted renewed interest for their reasoning capabilities (Saunshi et al., 2024; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). Although grown layers become independent after duplication, whereas looped layers remain tied, the two approaches can produce related patterns of iterative computation across depth (Kapl et al., 2026a; Kapl et al., 2026b).

This reuse of computation may also favor in-context learning (ICL), as suggested by initial evidence in both grown and looped models (Kapl et al., 2026b). ICL is the ability to use information supplied in a prompt or sequence without updating the model’s parameters (Brown et al., 2020). A model that repeatedly refines its representations might also be better equipped to extract and apply patterns from context. Yet, improved reasoning performance alone does not establish this ability. Predictions can rely on associations stored in the weights, on information inferred from the current sequence, or on both. Moreover, a model’s improvement in predicting later tokens and its ability to learn a task from demonstrations are related but distinct measurements, with potentially different underlying mechanisms (Olsson et al., 2022; Yin and Steinhardt, 2025).

Looped Transformers can learn synthetic regression and other data-fitting tasks with substantially fewer parameters than standard Transformers (Yang et al., 2024; Von Oswald et al., 2023). • Grown and looped language models benefit more from context. In the main 3B language-model comparison, both achieve larger early-to-late token-loss reductions than the dense baseline, with the grown model also attaining lower absolute late-token loss. Both models also achieve higher GSM8K accuracy across all demonstration counts. On RegBench, grown and looped models predict unseen formal languages more accurately, with their advantage emerging within the first string (Figures 1 and 2). • Growing and looping favor earlier acquisition and stronger retention of ICL. papers.title: Predictable performance is suboptimal, and what it means for model routing
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) differ in capabilities and costs, motivating routing methods that adaptively choose a model for each query. These methods rely on performance prediction: given a query, estimate whether a model will answer it correctly. Most routing methods train separate predictors of candidate models' performance to guide model selection. Our work shows that performance prediction only beats a simple baseline when the candidate model is suboptimal on the task or the performance predictor adds significant capacity relative to the candidate model. Specifically, we take a model's self-confidence, the probability it assigns to its chosen answer, as a baseline and study how much a performance predictor can improve on it. First, we show that any performance predictor that outperforms a model's self-confidence can be used to improve the model's loss: the predictor's advantage transfers exactly in log loss through recalibration. Second, accounting for the predictor's additional parameters, we bound its advantage by the model's suboptimality plus the gain from those parameters. Third, we extend our theoretical results to two-model cascades, which route queries to a more capable model when the first model is predicted to fail. Experiments with 16 language models on four benchmarks show that predictors gain a larger advantage over self-confidence on more suboptimal models. This advantage shrinks as models improve through finetuning. Cascading exhibits the same two patterns: predictor-based routing offers larger gains over confidence-based routing for more suboptimal models, and these gains diminish after finetuning.

Performance prediction estimates whether a model answers a query correctly (Kadavath et al., 2022; Shnitzer et al., 2024). These predictions can help routing systems decide when to trust an answer and when to call a stronger model (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Chen et al., 2024). By catching a weak model’s errors accurately, routing can achieve better performance at the same cost. But what makes a model’s errors predictable, and what does that reveal about the model?

In this paper, we study the predictability of a model’s performance relative to a simple baseline: the model’s self-confidence, the probability it assigns to its chosen answer. Our key observation is that any predictor that beats self-confidence can improve the model by the same amount. This means that a predictor’s advantage over self-confidence is limited by the model’s room for improvement. We formalize and test this connection, and extend the analysis to routing.

Suboptimality bounds excess predictability. We connect performance prediction and model improvement through recalibration: replacing the model’s confidence in its chosen answer with the predictor’s estimate, and normalising the rest. We call the predictor’s reduction in correctness log loss relative to self-confidence excess predictability. Recalibration reduces the model’s answer log loss by exactly the same amount (Proposition 1). We assume a scaling floor: the lowest answer loss achievable on a fixed task at each parameter budget (Assumption 1). The recalibrated model cannot beat the floor at the combined parameter budget of the model and predictor. This gives the bound (Theorem 1) excess predictability≤suboptimality+capacity gain.\boxed{\;\text{excess predictability}\;\leq\;\text{suboptimality}\;+\;\text{capacity gain}\;}. Here, suboptimality is the model’s gap to the floor at its own budget. The capacity gain is the decrease in the floor from adding the predictor’s parameters.

Greater excess predictability comes with greater suboptimality. Our upper bound does not imply that more suboptimal models are necessarily easier to predict beyond self-confidence. Empirically, however, we observe a positive association between the two. We conduct experiments on WinoGrande, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, and MMLU-Pro, using 16 language models from eight families, ranging from 7 to 12B parameters. Using the gap to the best observed answer loss on each task as a proxy for suboptimality, we find a positive association with excess predictability on all four tasks, with Pearson correlations of 0.98, 0.98, 0.93, and 0.65, respectively (Figure 1). We also finetune the models, retaining the 59 model-task pairs whose development accuracy improves. Answer loss falls in all 59 retained pairs and excess predictability falls in 55 (Figure 2), despite training separate 4B predictors for the released and finetuned models.

papers.title: DIAL: Steerable Language Models with Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels
papers.abstract: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are deployed across users and applications with different requirements for instruction-following [1]. Meeting these requirements involves choosing which instructions an LLM should follow and the appropriate level of adherence for each instruction. Without fine-grained control over adherence levels, users may need to revise an instruction and regenerate responses repeatedly to achieve the desired level of adherence. As an illustrative example, Figure 1(a) shows a user asking for a shorter answer, but the LLM’s response is too short for the user. Further prompting is then needed to obtain the desired response length, creating a frustrating user experience. Ideally, users could view responses generated at different adherence levels and select one with the desired length. More generally, fine-grained adherence control for different instructions would support a range of applications (Figure 1(b)). For personalization, a user could select the adherence level for writing-style or persona instructions according to their preferences [2, 3]. For parental control, parents could set the adherence level for child-safety instructions to help safeguard children [4]. A company could configure the adherence level for product-policy instructions to reflect its specifications [5, 6]. Motivated by these applications, we study “steerable language models” [7, 8] that provide fine-grained numerical control over adherence levels for general text instructions.

Ideally, users could view responses generated at different adherence levels and select one with the desired length. More generally, fine-grained adherence control for different instructions would support a range of applications (Figure 1(b)). For personalization, a user could select the adherence level for writing-style or persona instructions according to their preferences [2, 3]. For parental control, parents could set the adherence level for child-safety instructions to help safeguard children [4]. A company could configure the adherence level for product-policy instructions to reflect its specifications [5, 6]. Motivated by these applications, we study “steerable language models” [7, 8] that provide fine-grained numerical control over adherence levels for general text instructions.

Existing approaches for controlling adherence levels in LLMs are not jointly fine-grained, efficient, and scalable across general instructions. The most straightforward approach is prompting, but it does not reliably provide fine-grained control over the adherence level [9, 10]. In contrast, classifier-free guidance (CFG) [11] enables fine-grained control by computing two next-token distributions: one conditioned on the instruction and one unconditioned. It then combines their log probabilities to achieve the desired adherence level [12, 13]. However, this requires two forward passes per generated token, increasing inference cost. Activation steering provides a more efficient approach by editing the hidden states of a frozen LLM within a single inference pass [14, 15, 16, 17]. Adjustable steering strength offers a promising way to adapt an LLM at inference time [18]. However, conventional steering methods are not fine-grained because they are fitted to labeled examples that indicate whether an instruction is followed, without supervision at intermediate adherence levels. Increasing steering strength therefore does not reliably increase adherence and can reduce fluency and coherence [19]. Moreover, these methods require fitting for each instruction, limiting scalability. Text-conditioned steering methods learn to steer an LLM from instruction text and support instructions unseen during training [20, 21, 22]. However, they are trained on labeled responses without supervision at intermediate adherence levels, and flow-based variants add per-token inference overhead.

Importantly, DIAL provides fine-grained control over concept expression, with the concept score increasing monotonically across the range of adherence levels. papers.title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
papers.abstract: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.

papers.intro:
Mirrors are ubiquitous optical components used in a wide range of research and applications. They underpin fundamental studies of light-matter interactions. When light interacts with mechanical motion in an optomechanical system [1], a mirror needs to be simultaneously engineered for its optical and mechanical properties. The mirror should couple efficiently to the light field and support a low-loss mechanical mode. These properties determine, among others, the suitability of optomechanical systems for sensing of weak forces [2, 3, 4] or accelerations [5], for quantum technologies [6], for exploring the interplay of quantum mechanics with gravity [7, 8], or for probing of dark matter [9].

Fulfilling these requirements simultaneously is challenging. Highly reflective and mechanically compliant mirrors have been realized with suspended distributed Bragg reflectors [10, 11], high-contrast grating slabs [12, 13, 14], and two-dimensional photonic crystal slabs [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. These approaches, however, compromise between high reflectivity and low mechanical loss, which have conflicting requirements on the thickness of the mirror. The membrane-in-the-middle system [22] was developed as it seemed impossible to alleviate this compromise. In these systems, the mechanical device is separated from the optical component by inserting an ultracoherent membrane into a high-Finesse optical cavity [23, 24, 25]. However, these systems have stringent requirements on alignment accuracy to minimize optical scatter loss and to maximize optomechanical coupling.

papers.title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
papers.abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

The growing integration of wearable and digital health technologies into everyday life has created an expanding stream of longitudinal physiological data (spanning menstrual cycle phases, heart rate variability (HRV), skin temperature, and sleep quality) that is increasingly interpreted by patients themselves rather than by clinicians. Communicating these observations in accessible lay language is therefore a task with direct implications for patient safety and health literacy.

Large Language Models (LLMs) present a compelling mechanism for this translation. Recent work demonstrates that adapted LLMs can match or exceed medical expert performance on standard clinical summarization benchmarks Van Veen et al. (2024), and the field has seen rapid advances in factuality verification, constrained generation, and longitudinal narrative synthesis. Semantic drift, defined as the accumulation of semantic change as medical concepts move from clinical to public discourse, has been shown to be greatest at precisely this transition point Karakkaparambil James et al. (2026). Our work operationalizes this broader phenomenon in the context of automated summarization, introducing a five-category clinical alignment taxonomy and a constrained generation framework to systematically measure and mitigate misalignment across these dimensions.

Our setting is fundamentally different, generating patient-facing narratives directly from structured physiological observations, where faithfulness must be verified against raw evidence rather than a reference text. This gap is particularly consequential in menstrual health monitoring, where cyclical signals, intrinsic uncertainty, and the documented consequences of urgency miscalibration make evidence-grounded generation especially critical.

This paper makes the following contributions: • We formalize the structured-to-narrative summarization task for longitudinal physiological records and introduce an evaluation concept using a taxonomy of five semantic drift conditions: Faithfulness Violation, Epistemic Misalignment, Diagnostic Inference Overreach, Omission Drift, and Urgency Misalignment. • We design and implement a framework for the semi-synthetic generation of medically grounded menstrual health data. • We propose an LLM-based generation pipeline combining explicit evidence-grounding constraints, targeting each alignment category in the taxonomy, with RAG that supports simplification through retrieved lay-term definitions. • We systematically evaluate the clinical alignment of generated patient narratives along the defined taxonomy and derive preliminary insights on favorable configurations of such a setup in menstrual health monitoring. papers.title: PYTHIA, a transferable machine learning framework for simultaneous defect and adsorption site optimization
papers.abstract: Machine learning has permeated material optimization, providing high value. Nevertheless, its re- liance on a high number of samples limits its applicability to relatively explored material families. In this paper we extend the applicability of machine learning to novel and understudied materials through the PYTHIA (Probabilistic Yet Transferable Hierarchical Interaction Architecture) framework. Pythia utilizes two of the most powerful machine learning concepts, foundational models and transfer learning. The resulting model is used as a surrogate for a Bayesian Optimization scheme. papers.intro:
Adsorption plays an important role in the interaction of nanostructured materials with molecules and ions. These interactions depend on the types of atoms present and their local arrangement. Identifying stable adsorption structures also helps explain electrochemical reactions at metal surfaces [40]. For materials with different compositions or defects, this search becomes more difficult. Changes in the local atomic environment can affect both the preferred adsorption position and the strength of binding. To investigate this, Density functional theory (DFT) is widely used. Mapping the potential energy surface (PES) requires calculations for many molecular positions and orientations [47], a search that can be automated by various tools which help generate, screen, and relax these structures [30, 35]. Other methods examine different parts of the energy landscape. Minima hopping and evolutionary algorithms search for structures with low energies [14, 39]. The nudged elastic band (NEB) method finds minimum energy paths between two energy states [19], while metadynamics explores free energy landscapes [3, 52]. These methods provide useful information, but their computational cost can remain high when each energy evaluation requires a DFT calculation. The cost increases further when several substrate compositions and defect structures are studied.

These methods provide useful information, but their computational cost can remain high when each energy evaluation requires a DFT calculation. The cost increases further when several substrate compositions and defect structures are studied.

Machine learning can reduce the number of expensive calculations. It has been applied to many problems in materials research [32, 27, 24]. In atomistic simulations, machine learning models can describe surface reaction PESs [29] and predict adsorption energies on nanoclusters [15]. Graph neural networks have also been used to predict molecular adsorption energies on metals [34], and learned interatomic potentials can speed up adsorption searches [28]. However, these models need suitable training data. For a new adsorption system, generating enough DFT data can account for much of the total computational cost, often times providing a full system investigation before the model is even trained.

Active learning (AL) and Bayesian optimization (BO) help address this problem by using the available data to choose new calculations. Bayesian models can learn atomic interactions during simulations [17, 50], and uncertainty estimation is also an active area of research for molecular models [49]. Related approaches have been used for crystal structure prediction [51], the optimization of nanoporous materials [11], materials discovery with graph models [54], and catalyst screening through adsorption calculations [45]. Machine learning can also accelerate searches for saddle points and reaction paths [36, 22], as well as stable adsorbate geometries [20].

The choice of structural representation affects how well these methods work. BO has been used to search for molecular conformers by varying torsion angles [9]. The Bayesian Optimization Structure Search (BOSS) framework uses structural coordinates to explore energy landscapes [44]. Its applications include molecular adsorption on surfaces [16] and the search for molecular conformations on metal clusters [12]. These coordinates are useful when the main degrees of freedom can be identified in advance. However, a representation designed for one system may need to be changed when the molecular composition, substrate, or defects change. Learning a representation directly from atomic structures offers a way to handle these differences.

In our previous work, we developed AUGUR to identify adsorption sites by combining a graph neural network, Gaussian process (GP) regression, and BO [25]. AUGUR learns a structural representation through a graph neural network (GNN) and uses it to predict energies and estimate uncertainty via a GP, without requiring manually designed molecular descriptors. A very relevant question however is, how this approach can benefit from knowledge learned on other atomic systems. Such knowledge could reduce the amount of data needed for a new adsorption problem. This is particularly useful when the search includes several compositions or defect types, each with only a limited number of reference calculations.

Pretrained atomic models provide a starting point for this transfer. The MACE architecture [5] has been used to develop foundation models trained on many different structures [4]. The atomic features learned by these models can then be used in new applications. However, pretraining does not guarantee accurate adsorption energies for every system, especially when its chemical environments or reference calculations differ from those used in training. Previous work has shown that adapting a pretrained potential while keeping some parameters fixed can reduce the amount of training data required [38] and even extrapolate to new properties [26]. For adsorption searches, we also need a model that adapts to the available data and estimates uncertainty to guide the choice of new calculations.

For adsorption searches, we also need a model that adapts to the available data and estimates uncertainty to guide the choice of new calculations.

To address the above concerns we introduce PYTHIA, which combines a pretrained MACE model, a Transformer, GP regression, and BO. The pretrained MACE provides atomic features that contain relevant descriptors for an adjacent system and property. A Transformer [46] processes these features and produces a representation that has translated the features to the current system. This vector is then used as input for the GP that predicts the adsorption energy and its corresponding uncertainty. During training, the MACE parameters remain fixed, while the Transformer and GP are trained on data from the systems being studied. This allows the model to reuse features learned during pretraining and adapt them to the target energy prediction problem. BO then uses these predictions to select candidate defects and adsorption positions for further electronic structure calculations. This pipeline provides all the benefits of large and complex models, without the usual necessity of large datasets.

papers.title: A Robust Estimator for the Lyman-$α$ Forest 1D Power Spectrum at High Redshift
papers.abstract: The Lyman-$α$ (Ly$α$) forest flux power spectrum $P(k)$ is sensitive to a range of astrophysical and cosmological effects, including the thermal state of and large-scale fluctuations in the intergalactic medium and the nature of dark matter. Measuring $P(k)$ becomes increasingly challenging at high redshift, where fewer quasar spectra are available and higher Ly$α$ optical depths result in lower transmitted flux. In addition, observational effects and missing data complicate standard Fourier-transform estimators. Here, we validate a likelihood-based estimator for $P(k)$. The method constructs the pixel-level covariance matrix of the transmitted flux field using precomputed $k$-space integrals that account for instrumental resolution and pixelization, enabling direct maximum-likelihood inference of $P(k)$. We test the estimator using mock Ly$α$ forest spectra at $z \geq 5$, including analytic Gaussian realizations generated from known power spectra and forward-modeled simulation spectra incorporating observational effects relevant to high-redshift quasar surveys, such as finite spectral resolution, pixel sampling, noise, and missing data. We compare the recovered power spectra with both the input spectra and standard Fourier-transform estimates. We find that the likelihood-based estimator recovers the input power spectrum across the tested scales well within expected error and remains robust to the observational effects considered. This work establishes a framework for measuring Ly$α$ forest clustering with a robust, nearly optimal power spectrum estimator, with particular focus on quantifying large-scale fluctuations that may arise from ultraviolet background fluctuations or the late stages of reionization.

At z≳5z\gtrsim 5, measurements of the Lyα\alpha forest reveal strong sightline-to-sightline variations in transmission and rapid evolution in the effective optical depth, suggesting a late and highly inhomogeneous end to reionization that may extend to z∼5.3z\sim 5.3 (Becker et al., 2015; Becker et al., 2018; Eilers et al., 2018; Bosman et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; Kashino et al., 2020; Bosman et al., 2022). Additional constraints from dark pixel statistics (Fan et al., 2006; McGreer et al., 2011; McGreer et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2026) and stacked spectra around Lyα\alpha and Lyβ\beta dark gaps (Zhu et al., 2024; Spina et al., 2024) further support this picture. The enhanced scatter in the Lyα\alpha forest opacity at z>5.5z>5.5 cannot be explained by density fluctuations alone (Bosman et al., 2022), motivating models that invoke spatial fluctuations in the ultraviolet background (UVB) (Davies and Furlanetto, 2016; Gnedin et al., 2017; D’Aloisio et al., 2018) and the IGM temperature (D’Aloisio et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2018a; Wu et al., 2019). These fluctuations can arise naturally during a late, extended, and inhomogeneous reionization process, as ionization fronts heat different regions of the IGM at different times and ionizing photons are absorbed after traveling finite distances. Although alternative reionization histories can also explain the observed opacity fluctuations (Asthana et al., 2024, see, e.g.,), these mechanisms motivate investigating large-scale fluctuations in the Lyα\alpha forest as a probe of the ionization and thermal structure of the IGM.

The one-dimensional Lyα\alpha forest flux power spectrum, P⁡(k)P(k), quantifies the amplitude of transmitted flux fluctuations on different spatial scales. Measurements of P⁡(k)P(k) have been used to constrain a range of physical processes and cosmological parameters, including the thermal state of the IGM, the timing of reionization, the nature of dark matter, and the properties of dark energy (Boera et al., 2019; Villasenor et al., 2023; Iršič et al., 2024; González-Hernández et al., 2025; Garcia-Gallego et al., 2025; Garza et al., 2026, e.g.). The impact of large-scale fluctuations on Lyα\alpha forest statistics has also been investigated using both the power spectrum and the real-space autocorrelation function, its Fourier-space counterpart (Zuo, 1992a; Zuo, 1992b; Croft, 2004; Meiksin and White, 2004; McDonald et al., 2005; Gontcho A Gontcho et al., 2014; Pontzen, 2014; Pontzen et al., 2014; D’Aloisio et al., 2018; Meiksin and McQuinn, 2019; Oñorbe et al., 2019; Wolfson et al., 2023c; Gaikwad et al., 2023; Wolfson et al., 2023a; Wolfson et al., 2023b; Maity et al., 2026a; Maity et al., 2026b; Spina et al., 2026). Robustly measuring P⁡(k)P(k) across a range of scales is therefore important for extracting the physical information encoded in the Lyα\alpha forest.

Accurately measuring P⁡(k)P(k) requires a robust method for estimating the power spectrum from observed flux fluctuations. The standard approach uses Fourier transforms of the transmitted flux field, while likelihood-based methods estimate P⁡(k)P(k) by maximizing the likelihood of the observed flux fluctuations given a model for their covariance. These methods originate from power spectrum estimation techniques developed for CMB analyses (Tegmark, 1997; Bond et al., 1998) and were first applied to the Lyα\alpha forest by McDonald et al. (2006). Subsequent work developed and applied related likelihood-based approaches to Lyα\alpha forest power spectrum measurements (Palanque-Delabrouille et al., 2013; Karaçaylı et al., 2022; Karaçaylı et al., 2025, see e.g.,). Although these methods provide an alternative to direct Fourier-transform estimates, their performance depends on the likelihood assumptions, optimization procedure, and treatment of the data. Validating these choices is particularly important when measuring power across a broad range of scales and at high redshift, where the Lyα\alpha forest opacity is high and the transmitted flux field is more strongly non-Gaussian.

Recent analyses by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) collaboration have also demonstrated the use of multiple methods to measure the power spectrum from a large survey at z<5z<5 (Karaçaylı et al., 2025; Ravoux et al., 2025). Previous measurements by Viel et al. (2013) reported power spectra at z=5.0z=5.0 and z=5.4z=5.4, while Boera et al. (2019) measured the power spectrum at z=5.0z=5.0. More recent observations, including the XQR-30 sample (D’Odorico et al., 2023) and the ongoing GHOSTLy observing program (Bosman et al., 2026), offer opportunities to extend power spectrum measurements to higher redshifts and improve their precision. Robust estimation methods are needed to fully exploit these data, particularly in the presence of observational challenges such as missing data, which can complicate measurements on large scales where spatial fluctuations in the IGM may leave a measurable imprint on the power spectrum.

papers.title: Nonvanishing of 2-primary Kolyvagin classes via simultaneous quadratic twists
papers.abstract: Let $E/\mathbf{Q}$ be an elliptic curve, let $K=\mathbf{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ satisfy the Heegner hypothesis with $D<-4$, and fix a modular parametrization $\varphi$ with $\varphi(\infty)=O$. Under surjectivity modulo $2^L$, with $L\ge 2$, and a cohomological exclusion condition at level $4$, we construct a finite set of primes $T$ such that, writing $d_T=\prod_{q\in T}(-q)$ and $n_T=\prod_{q\in T}q$, the $2$-Selmer dimensions of $E^{d_T}$ and $E^{d_TD}$ are $0$ and $1$. The support size is bounded in terms of the initial Selmer dimensions, independently of $L$. Inspired by the work of Tian and Tian--Yuan--Zhang on congruent numbers, we construct a point $Q_T$ on the terminal twist and identify its Kummer class with the standard mod-$2$ Kolyvagin class. Using the low-corank $2$-converse and the $2$-primary Birch--Swinnerton-Dyer formula, we prove that its index $m_T$ in the full Mordell--Weil lattice satisfies $v_2(m_T)=v_2(c_\varphi)+\mathfrak{i}(E,K)$. The optimal Manin constant theorem supplies a $2$-indivisible parametrization $\varphi_0$, for which $κ^{\mathrm{std}}_{n_T,1}(\varphi_0)\ne 0$ if and only if $\mathfrak{i}(E,K)=0$. When the intrinsic index vanishes, the minimum terminal support size is $R=\min\{d_2(E),d_2(E^D)\}$, and the normalized standard classes have order $2^M$ for $1\le M\le L$. Full $2$-adic Galois image then gives strong nonvanishing.

papers.title: HideOut - User Protection Against Localization with Throughput Guarantees in Mobile Networks
papers.abstract: Channel state information (CSI) in cellular networks is primarily used to maintain quality of service (QoS), yet it leaks privacy-sensitive information, in particular the user equipment's (UE) location. CSI is reported in plaintext on a publicly available schedule; thus, capturing it on the air and using a well trained AI model to localize the UE is straightforward. This simplicity in the attack execution makes it a serious privacy vulnerability. Using conventional privacy enhancing techniques, such as additive perturbation from differential privacy, to protect location data can potentially degrade the downlink communication quality. We present HideOut, a client-side defense mechanism that preserves the user's location from neural-based localization methods, while maintaining their downlink Spectral Efficiency (SE). Unlike generic adversarial attacks, HideOut treats downlink SE as a strict constraint in an optimization setting. Under maximum ratio transmission (MRT) beamforming, we show that a user-selected SE loss budget can be converted into an angular rate-feasible constraint on the reported channel vector. HideOut then performs gradient-based localization obfuscation while projecting each update onto this rate-feasible set. We evaluate HideOut against four CSI-based localization architectures under both white-box and black-box assumptions. Across models, HideOut increases localization ambiguity (error) from approximately $1--2$ m to $72--85$ m while keeping downlink SE loss within a $1\%$ budget. These results show that CSI-based localization can be substantially degraded at negligible communication quality loss when adversarial perturbations are made aware of the wireless link.

Cellular networks are becoming sensing systems as well as communication systems. In 5G-Advanced and emerging 6G deployments, the same radio measurements that support beamforming and link adaptation can also be used to infer a User Equipment’s (UE’s) location. The 3GPP architecture already includes a Location Management Function (LMF) that collects positioning-related measurements from UEs (3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), 2024). Recent learning-based positioning systems further strengthen this capability. Neural networks can map channel state information (CSI) directly to UE coordinates, exploiting multipath, blockage, and other propagation effects that are highly location-dependent (Colpaert et al., 2023; Vuckovic et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025). Thus, CSI is no longer only a communication primitive, but also a high-resolution location signal.

This dual use creates a privacy risk. A UE must report CSI to receive efficient downlink service, but that same report may allow a network-side localization service to infer the UE’s precise position. Such location information can reveal sensitive attributes such as home and workplace, mobility routines, social relationships, and visits to sensitive places (Wang et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2025). Protecting only the location record after LMF is therefore insufficient: if the localization service can infer location directly from CSI, then privacy must be enforced before or during CSI reporting.

Coordinate-level defenses such as kk-anonymity, geo-indistinguishability, and local differential privacy perturb or generalize a location after it has already been estimated (Andrés et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022). This leads to the central challenge of this paper (Fig. 1): a UE cannot simply randomize or suppress its CSI to hide its location. The privacy mechanism must therefore satisfy two requirements simultaneously: it should increase the localization error of the network-side model, while guaranteeing that the protected CSI remains useful for downlink precoding. This privacy–service coupling is specific to cellular CSI feedback and is not captured by generic adversarial attacks or by prior WiFi-oriented signal-level privacy mechanisms.

papers.title: On the Adversarial Vulnerability of Neural Receivers with Unrolled LDPC Decoders
papers.abstract: Neural receivers for 5G New Radio (NR) match classical model-based receivers in link-level performance, but their robustness to adversarial perturbations at the receiver input remains underexplored. We show that standard gradient-based attacks applied end-to-end through an unrolled low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder fail to significantly outperform a matched-power Gaussian perturbation. We identify the failure as gradient masking caused by tanh saturation in the boxplus operation of the belief-propagation (BP) check-node update, with a per-iteration gradient norm decay of more than four orders of magnitude across ten unrolled BP iterations. Based on this finding, we propose two structurally independent loss functions that restore attack efficacy. L_BP routes the gradient through the unsaturated early iterations via per-iteration supervision, while L_LLR is a margin loss on pre-decoder log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) whose gradient bypasses the LDPC decoder entirely. Both loss functions increase the block-error rate (BLER) by one to four orders of magnitude at matched perturbation power, with the results reproduced on both the Sionna NeuralReceiver and DeepRx. At low PSR, L_LLR-optimized perturbations achieve up to three orders of magnitude higher BLER on unseen channel realizations than LBP-optimized perturbations.

papers.intro:
Neural-network-based receivers (NNRs) have emerged as strong candidates for physical-layer signal processing in 5G New Radio (NR) due to their ability to jointly learn channel estimation, equalization and demapping. Architectures such as DeepRx [1] and the Sionna NeuralReceiver [2] achieve link-level performance comparable to classical model-based receivers. As NNRs advance toward deployment, their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations of the received signal emerges as an operational concern. An attacker injecting a small perturbation at the receiver antennas can exploit the non-linear structure of the learned receiver to cause significant decoding errors.

Adversarial vulnerability of deep-learning (DL)-based wireless receiver components has been studied in modulation classification [3], semantic communications [4], deep neural network (DNN)-based channel estimation for orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) [5], and short-block neural decoders [6, 7]. Shen and Li [6] applied interval analysis to verify the robustness of neural decoders on the AWGN channel with BCH codes, while Lei et al. [7] have studied the fragility of transformer-based neural channel decoders under small AWGN channel perturbations. These works address standalone decoders over simplified wireless channel models, excluding NNRs integrated with unrolled LDPC belief propagation (BP) decoders.

The common assumption that computer-vision adversarial attacks transfer directly to wireless receivers fails for NNRs incorporating unrolled LDPC decoders in the back-propagation path. A standard end-to-end application of ℓ2\ell_{2}-FGM or PGD (PGD-E2E) against an NNR with an unrolled 5G NR LDPC BP decoder yields negligible degradation in the BLER; moreover, a matched-power Gaussian jammer achieves similar performance to such gradient-based attacks at low or moderate PSR. We identify this as gradient masking [10], not genuine robustness of the NNR.

PyJama [11] employs a Nachmani-style [12] multi-iteration loss function within Sionna for differentiable jammer power-allocation optimization. Our work differs in purpose, formulation, and target system. PyJama optimizes a 14-dimensional OFDM power allocation via gradient descent to train a learnable jammer against classical MIMO receivers. We design a 3584-dimensional complex ℓ2\ell_{2}-bounded perturbation against NNRs combined with unrolled LDPC decoders. The multi-iteration loss function in PyJama is deployed empirically as a tool, not as a countermeasure for gradient-masking. papers.title: JWST observations of the planetary nebula NGC 6302 IV: PAH spectral characteristics, formation and evolution
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and carbonaceous dust have been observed in Oxygen-rich planetary nebulae (PNe), yet their formation and evolution in these environments is an open question. We aim to study the formation and evolution of the PAHs in the O-rich PN NGC 6302, by characterizing the PAH emission throughout this object. We obtained JWST MIRI IFU spectroscopic observations of NGC 6302 pointed at its central source. From these, we extract four template spectra that are representative of the variation in PAH emission throughout NGC 6302. We detect the major PAH features at 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.2, and 12.7 $μ$m, and several minor PAH features. The template spectra vary in terms of their PAH feature widths, peak wavelengths, and relative intensities. The 11.2 $μ$m PAH feature is class B, typical for PNe. The 6-9 $μ$m PAH features are class A, which is less common for PNe. We estimate the PAH charge to be 75% cations on average, based on the 7.7/11.2 PAH feature ratio. The relative strengths of the 11-15 $μ$m PAH features indicate a range of PAH edge structures. To ensure consistency in our observations and explain variable PAH feature widths, we propose a variation in the size of the PAHs throughout NGC 6302, and suggest variation in the shielding of these PAHs. The PAHs range from large and non-compact, to small and compact. We find that NGC 6302 formed PAHs in-situ in the current PN phase, likely from small hydrocarbons formed by the photodissociation of CO.

papers.intro:
Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) are large, planar, carbonaceous molecules that pervade the cosmos (Allamandola et al., 1989; Tielens, 2008). This, combined with their stability granted by their large size and aromatic bonding, makes PAHs a key component of many astrophysical and astronomical processes. For example, PAHs are strong UV photon absorbers, enabling them to control the temperature of their surroundings in the neutral interstellar medium (ISM) via the photo-electric effect (Bakes and Tielens, 1994). PAHs also dominate the charge balance of their environments (Lepp and Dalgarno, 1988; Tielens et al., 2004). These properties make PAHs key players in star and planet formation, and in the evolution of galaxies.

PAHs also dominate the charge balance of their environments (Lepp and Dalgarno, 1988; Tielens et al., 2004). These properties make PAHs key players in star and planet formation, and in the evolution of galaxies.

PAHs are formed on Earth in sooting reactions, in which small hydrocarbons are converted into much larger species when exposed to high temperatures (Wang and Frenklach, 1997). It is therefore reasonable to assume that analogous astronomical environments would be a source of PAHs throughout the galaxy, namely in the outflows of carbon-rich Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars (“carbon stars”), where the abundance of free C makes them ideal for carbonaceous chemistry (Allamandola et al., 1989; Frenklach and Feigelson, 1989; Latter, 1991; Cherchneff et al., 1992; Cherchneff, 2012). Before entering the ISM, the ejected material is part of a Planetary Nebulae (PNe), which form from AGB and post-AGB stars. In a PNe, the now-exposed core of the star heats and processes the surrounding gas and dust. Subsequently, the material is dispersed into the ISM to form the next generation of star systems. The illumination from the central star and abundant gas and dust makes PNe chemical factories, and they serve as an important test bed for chemical modelling in astronomical environments (Tielens, 2008).

The above picture works well when the post-AGB star and subsequent PNe are C-rich (C/O ≥\geq 1). However, PAHs are also observed in O-rich stars and PNe (Sylvester et al., 1994; Gutenkunst et al., 2008; Guzman-Ramirez et al., 2014, C/O << 1: e.g.). In O-rich environments, available C is primarily locked up in CO, which should inhibit the formation of carbonaceous species, including PAHs. Thus the detection of PAHs in O-rich PNe challenge our assumptions of the conditions needed for PAH formation. As PAHs continue to be observed in environments that are unfavourable for sooting reactions, it is increasingly clear that new formation mechanisms are needed to fully capture the abundance of PAHs throughout the cosmos (Sandstrom et al., 2010; Matsuura et al., 2013, e.g.). With the advent of JWST, we can use its high spectral and spatial resolution to study the variation of PAH emission throughout astronomical objects in unprecedented detail. This enables us to further our understanding of PAH evolution and formation and to elucidate what these formation mechanisms might be.

papers.title: Searching for substellar companion candidates with Gaia. V. M dwarfs within 15 pc studied with absolute astrometry, radial velocities, and direct imaging
papers.abstract: In this work, we survey M-type stars within 15 pc observed by Gaia based on their colour, magnitude, and quality of astrometric data. We aim to detect new substellar companions using primarily Gaia astrometry and, when available, proper-motion anomaly (PMa) along with radial velocity (RV) and direct imaging (DI) data. We used the GaiaPMEX tool to search for bound companions around 582 M dwarfs. We identified all previously known stellar and planetary companions that were consistent with the Gaia excess signal. Then for all newly identified companions, we computed detection limits in the (mass, semi-major axis) parameter space using archival RV and DI data, to possibly rule out the presence of a stellar companion. The joint analysis of the parameter space allowed by astrometry and constrained by RV and DI provides tight constraints on the nature of the companion. We found 156 M dwarfs to have a bound companion within the Gaia sensitivity domain. The astrometric signals of 37 and seven of them are due to known stellar and substellar companions, respectively. We report 35 new substellar companions among which at least ten giant planets orbiting between 0.2 au and 2 au, with masses close to 1 M_Jup. We also report 77 substellar candidates, and provide detection limits using astrometry+RV+DI for 50 stars with known exoplanets and no significant Gaia excess noise. This work reveals a significant population of new substellar companions to M-type stars, challenging core accretion models. These results will be crucial inputs for estimating occurrence rates and studying the architecture of planetary systems around M dwarfs. Some new companions presented here, located beyond the water ice line, are prime targets for DI or coronagraphy observations with JWST or ELT.

papers.intro:
In the past three decades, thousands of exoplanets have been discovered, revealing a surprising diversity in orbits, masses, densities, and atmospheres, many of which differ significantly from those in our solar system. This diversity challenges existing theories of planetary formation and evolution, as well as the potential for life beyond Earth. Most discoveries come from transit photometry, notably with Kepler (Borucki et al., 2010) and TESS (Ricker et al., 2015), which primarily identify planets within an astronomical unit (au) from their stars due to operational constraints. However most exoplanets discovered around nearby stars were detected using the radial velocity (RV) method, with ground-based instruments such as SOPHIE on the 1.93 m telescope at Observatoire de Haute-Provence (Perruchot et al., 2008), or HARPS on the ESO 3.6 m telescope at La Silla Observatory (Mayor et al., 2003). Ground-based RV facilities also include Hamilton and HIRES, on the Lick and Keck telescopes (Vogt, 1987; Vogt et al., 1994), and CORALIE on the 1.20-m Swiss telescope at la Silla (Queloz et al., 1999), where the first planet around an M dwarf was jointly discovered (Marcy et al., 1998; Delfosse et al., 1998).

M-type stars, the most common in the Galaxy (Reylé et al., 2021; Henry and Jao, 2024), are a major focus for surveys because they are well-suited for detecting low-mass planets in their habitable zone (HZ). Most planets found around M stars are low-mass and orbit within 1 au, making them prime candidates for future atmospheric studies and biosignature detection (Meadows et al., 2023). However, a complete understanding of planet formation requires insights into the whole planetary system, including giant planets beyond a few au. Giant planets might indeed be a key factor in shaping the formation and evolution of planetary systems (Childs et al., 2019), particularly in the presence or absence of rocky planets in their HZ (Levison and Agnor, 2003). The radial distribution of giant planets can also provide valuable constraints on planet formation processes and early evolution when compared with predictions from population synthesis models (Schlecker et al., 2021). Moreover, their position relative to the water and CO snow lines is expected to play a key role in shaping the planetary systems and chemical contents (Öberg et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2013; Gonzalez and Michoulier, 2026). Companions forming inside or beyond the CO snow line may accrete different fractions of icy solids and gas, potentially leading to significant differences in their bulk and atmospheric composition.

Despite their importance, little is known about giant planets in M star systems. A dozen have been identified through transits within the 0.1−-1 au range (Delamer et al., 2024) or via RV (Morales et al., 2019), challenging classical core accretion models that do not predict efficient giant planet formation around low-mass stars (Laughlin et al., 2004; Kennedy and Kenyon, 2008) or alternative mechanisms like gravitational instability (Boss, 2006; Boss and Kanodia, 2023; Mercer and Stamatellos, 2020). Detecting giant planets on wider orbits is difficult with transit methods and challenging with RV due to the faintness and relatively high activity level of M stars. Additionally, studies like Lagrange et al. (2023) suggest that RV searches beyond 5−-8 au often result in biased estimates due to insufficient orbital coverage. This significant limitation can be effectively addressed by combining RV with Hipparcos-Gaia absolute astrometry (which also provides planetary masses), as shown by Philipot et al. (2023b).
