This work is part of a series of papers that make use of Gaia data to detect and characterise companions. The first paper of the series presented the GaiaPMEX tool (Kiefer et al. 2025a, Paper I), Papers II to IV report detections of companions to FGK stars (Kiefer et al. 2025b, Paper II), young stars (Lagrange et al. 2025, Paper III) and stars with debris disks (Lagrange et al. in rev., Paper IV). The aim of the present study is to detect substellar companions around nearby M stars. GaiaPMEX uses astrometric data from Gaia’s third data release (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2021a, hereafter GDR3) and Hipparcos data when available to build a two-dimension confidence map to constrain the mass and the semi-major axis (aa) of the companion. When combining these maps with RV and direct imaging (DI) detection limits, we can strongly constrain the orbit and characterise the companion.

papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.

papers.intro:
Reasoning large language models (LLMs) often overthink: they keep reasoning after the answer has stopped improving (Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Yet deciding when to stop requires more than knowing how likely the current answer is to be correct. A model may be uncertain about its current answer yet close to finding a better one. The same uncertainty may also occur when further reasoning is unlikely to help (Muennighoff et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2026b). Even a correct answer can be overturned by continued reasoning (Wang et al., 2026a). These situations call for different stopping decisions. Stopping is therefore a metareasoning problem. The model must assess what further computation is likely to achieve and whether that improvement is worth its cost (Russell and Wefald, 1991; De Sabbata et al., 2025).

The same uncertainty may also occur when further reasoning is unlikely to help (Muennighoff et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2026b). Even a correct answer can be overturned by continued reasoning (Wang et al., 2026a). These situations call for different stopping decisions. Stopping is therefore a metareasoning problem. The model must assess what further computation is likely to achieve and whether that improvement is worth its cost (Russell and Wefald, 1991; De Sabbata et al., 2025).

We separate outcome prediction from decision-making: first predict the outcomes of answering now or continuing, then learn when to act on those predictions. The decision depends on the trade-off between accuracy and computation (Wang et al., 2024). For a frozen reasoner with a fixed decoding rule, changing the token price changes how outcomes are valued, but not the outcome prediction targets at a given reasoning prefix. The predictive representation can therefore be reused across prices instead of being learned anew for each stopping objective.

We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which trains a compact probe (the BELT probe) (Shelmanov et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2026a) on a frozen LLM’s hidden states. papers.title: Discrete time liquids
papers.abstract: Discrete time crystals exhibit robust subharmonic oscillations, spontaneously breaking the discrete time-translation symmetry of a periodic drive. Since their emergence, the question of whether other types of temporal many-body order can exist has attracted considerable attention. Here we identify discrete time liquids -- a new form of spatiotemporal order characterized by short-range temporal coherence as a result of time-solitons. We study a two-dimensional spin system coupled to a finite-temperature cavity, whose fluctuations provide a noisy, approximately periodic drive with only finite temporal coherence. Remarkably, the spins nevertheless form a metastable state with robust period-doubled dynamics over an extended parameter regime. Unlike a time crystal, this state has only finite temporal coherence: individual trajectories stochastically switch between the two symmetry-related temporal configurations of the period-doubled response. We identify these switches as time-solitons: topological defects in temporal order that preserve local period doubling while destroying long-range temporal coherence, thereby producing the time liquid state. We propose a minimal model which reproduces the distribution of temporal correlations of the many-body system, suggesting a general description of the time liquid as a time crystal with a finite density of time-solitons. Because these solitons can occur at arbitrary times, ensemble averaging restores continuous time-translation symmetry, raising the intriguing possibility that discrete time liquids can exist in thermal equilibrium.

papers.intro:
Fluctuations are usually regarded as an enemy of order. In spatially ordered phases, they blur static patterns and can forbid long-range order in low dimensions [1, 2]; in dynamical systems, they dephase coherent motion and broaden sharp spectral features [3, 4]. Nevertheless, fluctuations can also play a constructive role. In order by disorder, fluctuations select ordered states that are not preferred at the mean-field level [5, 6]. In stochastic and coherence resonances, fluctuations optimize the response of nonlinear dynamical systems [7, 8, 9]. Both of these cases show that fluctuations can also create regularity rather than merely destroy it. This idea has recently expanded into the field of cavity-matter hybrids [10, 11, 12, 13]. There, the goal is to generate new phases of matter by amplifying electromagnetic fluctuations around a two-dimensional heterostructure through nanopatterning of the electromagnetic environment. In this article, we find that fluctuations not only generate new spatially coherent phases of matter, but can also give rise to many-body temporal order, producing what we term discrete time liquids.

papers.title: The PAU Survey: Active galactic nucleus galaxies in galaxy pairs
papers.abstract: Aims. Leveraging the high-precision photometric redshifts of the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS), we aim to investigate the connection between active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and galaxy pairs up to redshifts of $\sim1.0$. Methods. We identified 16,824 galaxy pairs with projected separations of $r_p < 100$ kpc and radial-velocity differences of $ΔV < 3500$ km s$^{-1}$. AGNs were selected by cross-matching PAUS galaxies with multi-wavelength AGN catalogues, yielding 270 AGNs in pairs out of a parent sample of 8,880 AGNs in PAUS. We constructed control samples of isolated AGNs; non-AGNs in pairs; and isolated non-AGNs matched in redshift, absolute magnitude, and environment. Results. Active galactic nuclei in pairs show progressively redder rest-frame colours with increasing redshift, particularly at redshifts of $z\gtrsim 0.5$, whereas isolated AGNs and non-AGNs in pairs show no significant colour evolution and remain at $\mathrm{M_g-M_r}\sim0.65$. Pairs hosting AGNs are also preferentially morphologically disturbed interacting systems found at smaller projected separations and velocity offsets, consistent with more dynamically advanced interactions. Conclusions. These results provide evidence of a redshift-dependent link between galaxy interactions and AGN activity, suggesting that interactions play an increasingly important role in triggering nuclear activity at intermediate redshifts. This study highlights the unique capability of PAUS to probe AGN-galaxy interaction connections beyond the local Universe with unprecedented statistical power.

Galaxy interactions have long been proposed as effective triggers for AGN activity, as tidal forces during close encounters can drive gas inflows towards central regions, potentially feeding SMBHs (Di Matteo et al., 2005; Hopkins et al., 2008, e.g.). Understanding when and how these interactions trigger nuclear activity across cosmic time is essential for constraining galaxy-evolution models (Alexander and Hickox, 2012; Harrison and Ramos Almeida, 2024).

In the local Universe, several studies point to a connection between galaxy interactions and AGN triggering. Observational studies of galaxy pairs show enhanced AGN fractions compared to isolated galaxies (Alonso et al., 2007; Koss et al., 2011; Ellison et al., 2013; Silverman et al., 2011). This enhancement becomes more pronounced as pair separation decreases and extends through the merger sequence, with peak AGN activity often observed in post-merger systems (Ellison et al., 2013; Goulding et al., 2018). Multi-wavelength studies further strengthen this evidence; for example, Li et al. (2023) identified AGNs using multi-wavelength diagnostics (X-ray, infrared, radio, and optical), finding a 36% excess of AGNs in post-mergers compared to non-interacting control samples.

These results support the scenario in which gravitational interactions and mergers can trigger gas inflows towards the central regions, feeding the SMBHs and enhancing the activity of AGNs, particularly in galaxies displaying clear morphological signatures of interaction.

The role of obscuration also appears to be relevant in the identification of AGNs, with mid-infrared (MIR) selected AGNs becoming increasingly prevalent, compared to optical AGNs, as pair separation decreases (Satyapal et al., 2014). For instance, merging systems are 5–17 times more likely to host dust-obscured AGNs than non-interacting galaxies (Weston et al., 2017; Secrest et al., 2020). These findings suggest that interactions may preferentially trigger dust-obscured nuclear activity, potentially contributing to discrepancies between AGN-selection methods.

Environmental factors introduce additional complexity. The local galaxy density affects the activity of AGNs independently of pair interactions (Kauffmann et al., 2003; Sabater et al., 2013; Coldwell et al., 2017, e.g.), with evidence suggesting that AGN fractions peak in small-scale associations rather than in larger groups (Duplancic et al., 2021). In addition, large-scale environments can influence the activity of AGNs, with studies showing different perspectives. Koulouridis et al. (2024) report fewer active galaxies in cluster centres compared to their outskirts, implying environment-dependent triggering mechanisms. In contrast, Rembold et al. (2024) find minimal differences in group mass and density between AGNs and control galaxies, suggesting limited environmental impact relative to galaxy interactions. Meanwhile, Ceccarelli et al. (2022) highlighted voids as favourable for AGN activity, proposing that secular galaxy evolution and gas inflows from the void interior can fuel central black holes, thus supporting AGN activity. Observations of AGNs in dwarf galaxies further indicate that while mergers can trigger nuclear activity, secular processes are often the dominant mechanism in these low-mass hosts (Eróstegui et al., 2025). However, this well-established paradigm faces significant challenges when extended beyond the local Universe. Recent studies using deeper surveys (0.3<z<2.50.3<z<2.5) have failed to detect a statistically significant excess of AGNs in pairs and post-merger systems or dense environments (Shah et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2021; Siudek et al., 2023; Dougherty et al., 2024).

Addressing these questions requires the precise identification of galaxy pairs across a wide redshift range, a task that has proven challenging with conventional techniques. Spectroscopic surveys provide accurate redshifts but suffer from limited area coverage and fibre collision constraints that systematically exclude close pairs. Traditional broad-band (BB) photometric surveys cover larger areas but lack the redshift precision necessary to reliably distinguish physical pairs from chance projections, particularly at intermediate redshifts.

papers.title: Resource-Aware Scheduling for Distributed Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) is a promising near-term approach for executing circuits that exceed the capacity of a single quantum processing unit (QPU). Prior work has made significant progress on circuit partitioning and reconstruction, but practical DQC requires more than cutting a circuit into smaller pieces. A runtime system must determine whether to execute the circuit intact, cut it for sequential execution on one QPU, or distribute it across multiple QPUs, while accounting for queueing, communication, reconstruction, and hardware constraints. We present a resource-aware scheduler for DQC that compares these execution alternatives at runtime using explicit models of QPU execution, communication, and host-side reconstruction, together with hardware-informed timing derived from simulated IBM QPUs. By treating communication and reconstruction as first-class scheduling costs, the scheduler selects execution plans using a more realistic view of end-to-end overhead than cutting-only approaches. Across our experiments, reconstruction accounts for over 83% of cutting overhead, distributed execution reduces P90 latency by up to 39% relative to uncut single-QPU execution, and scheduling overhead itself remains negligible, never exceeding 0.038% of end-to-end job latency. Together, these results show that DQC must be treated as a runtime scheduling problem over both quantum and classical resources, not just circuit partitioning.

papers.title: Homogenization of the Stokes equations with slender bodies
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the convergence of solutions of the Stokes equations in a domain perforated by slender bodies placed on a fixed periodic grid of size $2ε$ as the size of the bodies goes to zero and the number of bodies goes to infinity. We assume that the width $b_ε$ of the bodies vanishes faster than the length $a_ε$ of the particles. We identify the critical scaling regimes for $a_ε$ and $b_ε$ and prove that in this case the system is effectively described by the Brinkman equations.

papers.title: Couplings with prescribed maxima: A short proof of the quasi-copula characterization
papers.abstract: We provide a short probabilistic proof of the classical characterization of multivariate quasi-copulas, addressing the call for a simpler and more transparent proof expressed by Sempi (2017). Our approach is based on a coupling construction for random variables with fixed marginal distributions and a prescribed distribution of their maximum. In our main result, we show that such a coupling exists if and only if the maximum is stochastically no smaller than each component and the distribution of the maximum is dominated by the sum of the marginal measures. The construction applies to arbitrary distributions and relies only on a decomposition of the maximum law and monotone quantile couplings. A direct consequence of our main result is the existence of copulas with prescribed values along an increasing track.

papers.intro:
Quasi-copulas were introduced by Alsina et al. (1993) in the bivariate case and extended to arbitrary dimensions by Nelsen et al. (1996). They generalize copulas by retaining their boundary conditions, coordinatewise monotonicity, and Lipschitz continuity, without requiring dd-increasingness. Quasi-copulas arise naturally as pointwise infima and suprema of families of copulas, which need not be copulas themselves; see Nelsen et al. (2004). Consequently, they play an important role in dependence modeling, for instance, in deriving bounds for certain functional under partial dependence information. Examples include bounds for copulas with prescribed measures of association, such as Kendall’s tau or Spearman’s rho (Nelsen et al., 2001), as well as model-independent price bounds for multi-asset derivatives (Lux and Papapantoleon, 2017; Ansari et al., 2024). Applications to fuzzy aggregation are discussed in Arias-García et al. (2020).

Originally, quasi-copulas were defined as functions that agree along any increasing track connecting 𝟎\mathbf{0} and 𝟏\mathbf{1} in [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} with a copula, which may depend on the track. Theorem 4 below is the classical result of Genest et al. (1999) for d=2d=2 and Cuculescu and Theodorescu (2001) for arbitrary dd. It shows that the original definition is equivalent to a simple analytic characterization in terms of uniform marginals, coordinatewise monotonicity, and an ℓ1\ell^{1}-Lipschitz condition. This characterization is now commonly used as the definition of quasi-copulas.

Although the analytic conditions are elementary, the converse implication is considerably more involved: one must show that, for every increasing track, a function satisfying these conditions agrees with some copula along this track. The multivariate proof of Cuculescu and Theodorescu (2001) relies on finite interpolation problems, constructions involving partial measures, and a compactness argument. In his survey, Sempi (2017, Section 3) explicitly expressed the hope that this proof would eventually be replaced by a simpler and more transparent one.

papers.title: Query-Time Calibration of CLIP Features for Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
papers.abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. papers.title: Tracking the Emergence and Persistence of Abnormal Grain Growth in an Aluminum Alloy using Diffraction-Contrast Tomography
papers.abstract: Abnormal grain growth is inherently three-dimensional, making 3D tracking of grain evolution essential for understanding its underlying mechanisms. This study combines synchrotron-based diffraction-contrast tomography and phase-contrast tomography to characterize the three-dimensional grain structure and quantify the size and spatial distribution of second-phase particles in the aluminum alloy AA5252. Using an interrupted annealing protocol, we tracked the persistent growth of abnormal grains and the emergence of abnormal growth in a grain initially belonging to the matrix. Although second-phase particles effectively suppressed grain growth in the matrix, variations in local particle density showed no apparent correlation with either the emergence or subsequent rapid growth of abnormal grains. Instead, crystallographic misorientation and, more notably, neighboring grain size were identified as stronger predictors of abnormal growth rate. Matrix grains were consumed more rapidly when they were relatively small and shared high-angle grain boundaries with the growing abnormal grain. The same trends were observed for the grain that underwent a transition from normal to abnormal growth. Remarkably, even before the onset of abnormal growth, this grain was surrounded by smaller matrix grains with exclusively high-angle grain boundaries, while the local particle density was slightly higher than average. These findings suggest that the same microstructural characteristics facilitate both the emergence and persistence of abnormal grain growth, although the mechanism triggering the transition to rapid growth remains unresolved.

papers.intro:
Heating a polycrystalline material almost inevitably leads to coarsening of its underlying microstructure. In single-phase materials, the mechanism of coarsening is referred to as grain growth, and when this process proceeds in a more-or-less uniform manner, it is called normal grain growth. Under certain experimental conditions, normal grain growth can be suppressed such that only a subset of grains in the polycrystal is able to grow. These grains rapidly consume their slower-growing or completely stagnant neighbors (the grains making up the “matrix”), and the resulting growth mode is known as abnormal grain growth (AGG).

Heating a polycrystalline material almost inevitably leads to coarsening of its underlying microstructure. In single-phase materials, the mechanism of coarsening is referred to as grain growth, and when this process proceeds in a more-or-less uniform manner, it is called normal grain growth. Under certain experimental conditions, normal grain growth can be suppressed such that only a subset of grains in the polycrystal is able to grow. These grains rapidly consume their slower-growing or completely stagnant neighbors (the grains making up the “matrix”), and the resulting growth mode is known as abnormal grain growth (AGG).

AGG is associated with a transition from a unimodal to a bimodal grain size distribution (GSD) [1, 2]. Such bimodality can significantly alter the properties of crystalline materials, i.e., most metals and ceramics. Depending on the application, AGG may be desired, but usually it is not. For example, in grain-oriented silicon steels [3], AGG helps to develop a magnetically preferred orientation, which reduces core losses in electrical transformers. On the other hand, AGG is generally undesirable in steels, as it leads to a heterogeneous microstructure characterized by a small number of excessively large grains [4]. Such microstructural heterogeneity can compromise mechanical performance, as demonstrated in friction-stir-welded low-carbon steel, where AGG has been associated with reduced hardness and tensile strength [5]. Similar detrimental effects have been reported in other engineering alloys. In the nickel-based superalloy Inconel 718, which is widely used in aerospace applications due to its high strength and excellent fatigue resistance, AGG has been shown to significantly reduce fatigue life [6]. Beyond its effects on bulk mechanical properties, AGG can also impair surface quality. In 6xxx-series aluminum alloys used for lightweight automotive body panels, the formation of a few abnormally large grains within a finer-grained matrix can promote surface defects such as roping [7].

Any proposed mechanism for AGG, therefore, must be able to explain an abnormal grain’s emergence—the moment it begins outgrowing its neighbors—as well as its persistence in growing faster. (Here, we prefer to use emergence rather than nucleation to avoid confusion with phenomena such as recrystallization or phase transformations, for which nucleation is associated with an energy barrier.)

(Here, we prefer to use emergence rather than nucleation to avoid confusion with phenomena such as recrystallization or phase transformations, for which nucleation is associated with an energy barrier.)

Of the many mechanisms for AGG mentioned in the literature [8], the two most commonly cited are related to the presence of texture [9, 10, 2] and pinning particles [11, 12]. In textured materials, AGG can occur when a few grains deviate from the main component of crystallographic orientation in the specimen [2]. Because high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) typically have higher energies [13] and mobilities [14] than low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs), any above-average-sized misaligned grain that forms HAGBs with matrix grains belonging to the main component of crystallographic orientation can outgrow the surrounding matrix, whose grains are predominantly separated by LAGBs owing to the crystallographic texture. Similarly, AGG can also be observed in materials containing small, second-phase particles that retard or even completely prevent the migration of grain boundaries through Zener pinning [15, 16, 17]. According to Humphreys’ model for AGG [18], the largest grains in a pinned microstructure may continue to grow as long as they exceed their neighbors in size by a sufficiently large ratio, whereby the exact value of this threshold depends on the size and volume fraction of the pinning particles. In this scenario, persistence follows from the driving force for grain growth being able to overcome the particle pinning pressure whenever a sufficiently large grain comes into contact with a smaller matrix grain [18]. The growth advantage is maintained in this mechanism by the fact that, as a large grain grows, its size ratio relative to the matrix steadily increases, provided the matrix grains remain (nearly) pinned.

While AGG has long been studied in two-dimensional (2D) images of microstructures, only a handful of time-resolved three-dimensional (3D) measurements have appeared to date in the literature [19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. This scarcity persists despite the growing availability of nondestructive 3D imaging techniques [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30]. Because AGG is an inherently 3D phenomenon, such measurements are essential to capture the emergence of abnormal grains and to gain deeper insight into the mechanisms driving their persistent growth during prolonged annealing.

The proper characterization of these dynamics, however, is complicated by certain aspects of AGG itself. Even after conditions promoting AGG have been established, abnormal grains may fail to form within a given region under investigation, or their growth may proceed too quickly between annealing steps to reveal the trajectory taken by the abnormal grain through the matrix, obscuring the mechanisms involved. Moreover, technical difficulties in reconstructing polycrystalline volumes with bimodal grain size distributions often lead to an inaccurate determination of grain boundary (GB) locations precisely where the latter are most relevant to AGG: namely, at the interfaces between abnormal and matrix grains. The aforementioned challenges are even more pronounced in materials exhibiting extreme forms of AGG, during which abnormal grains grow to sizes at least an order of magnitude larger than the mean size of the matrix grains [8]. Conversely, it is precisely these materials that enable us to focus on the clearest cases of AGG, where one might expect the underlying mechanism(s) to be easiest to detect.

papers.title: Spark-Audio 1.0 Technical Report
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Spark-Audio 1.0, a speech foundation model trained on domestically produced computing infrastructure. The model accepts text and speech inputs and generates text outputs. It supports multilingual (99 languages) and multi-dialect (202 dialects) speech recognition, speech translation, audio perception and understanding, and both text- and speech-based dialogue, marking a shift from merely ``hearing clearly'' to genuinely ``understanding'' speech. Architecturally, Spark-Audio 1.0 couples a 0.65B-parameter dense audio encoder with a 30B-A3B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language model (LLM). The audio encoder is pretrained with representation-enhanced BEST-RQ and then refined through multi-task supervised training. The audio--LLM is trained through staged pretraining, followed by post-training that combines supervised fine-tuning with on-policy distillation. In total, the model is trained on 13 million hours of audio data together with large-scale text data. We evaluate Spark-Audio 1.0 on mainstream audio and text benchmarks, as well as on in-house test sets drawn from real-world application scenarios. Despite using substantially less audio training data than Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash, Spark-Audio 1.0 achieves comparable performance on most audio and text tasks, outperforms it in multilingual speech recognition, spoken dialogue, and real-world application scenarios, and approaches the performance of larger closed-source models. Nevertheless, there remains room for improvement in instruction following and complex audio reasoning. Finally, the successful training of Spark-Audio 1.0 on domestic hardware, including Huawei Ascend 910B and Hygon BW1000 chips, demonstrates the feasibility of a domestic technical pathway for building speech foundation models.

papers.intro:
Speech is one of the most natural and information-rich channels of human communication, yet conventional automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have long been optimized for a single objective: converting acoustic signals into verbatim text. Such systems excel at “hearing clearly” but discard much of what makes speech meaningful: paralinguistic cues such as emotion, speaker identity, age and gender, and prosodic information that carries intent across languages and dialects, as well as ambient sound events. As intelligent speech technology permeates daily work and life through input methods, translation devices, meeting transcription, customer service, and smart cockpits, the demand has shifted from transcription accuracy alone toward holistic speech understanding. Meeting this demand requires a foundation model that unifies acoustic perception with linguistic reasoning, rather than a collection of narrowly specialized ASR modules.

Such systems excel at “hearing clearly” but discard much of what makes speech meaningful: paralinguistic cues such as emotion, speaker identity, age and gender, and prosodic information that carries intent across languages and dialects, as well as ambient sound events. Meeting this demand requires a foundation model that unifies acoustic perception with linguistic reasoning, rather than a collection of narrowly specialized ASR modules.

Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) (Liu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026b; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) has made the speech foundation model paradigm (Chu et al., 2023; Chu et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Dinkel et al., 2025) increasingly attractive: by projecting continuous audio representations into the token space of a powerful LLM, a single model can be trained to perform recognition, translation, audio understanding, and dialogue within one unified framework. Representative multimodal systems such as the Qwen-Omni series (Xu et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026a) have demonstrated that a single model can maintain strong performance across text, image, audio, and video modalities, achieving state-of-the-art results on a large proportion of audio benchmarks. However, the practical deployment of such models faces significant challenges, particularly in the Chinese ecosystem. State-of-the-art speech foundation models are predominantly trained on foreign computing stacks, creating a hard dependency on restricted hardware and software ecosystems. The feasibility of training a competitive speech foundation model end-to-end on purely domestic infrastructure therefore remains an open and strategically important question. At the same time, competitive performance is commonly assumed to require ever-larger training data and model size, which makes training prohibitively expensive and raises doubts about whether models trained on less data can serve real-world applications.

The model accepts text and audio as input and produces text output, and is designed as a general-purpose base rather than a single-task system. Architecturally, it pairs a 0.65B-parameter dense audio encoder with a 30B-A3B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM, and is trained on 13 million hours of audio together with large-scale text corpora. Three design decisions distinguish our approach.

First, a semantically grounded, general-purpose audio encoder. The encoder is pretrained in three progressively expanding stages. In the first, self-supervised stage, we revise the BERT-based Speech pre-Training with Random-projection Quantizer (BEST-RQ) (Chiu et al., 2022) framework into a representation-enhanced variant by replacing the input of the quantizer with frozen deep semantic representations from a pretrained multilingual ASR encoder based on the Whisper large-v3 architecture. This injects semantic priors into the prediction targets without introducing an additional trainable tokenizer, and is designed to yield more compact discrete targets and a more discriminative prediction task that strengthens the modeling of fine-grained temporal structure. In this stage, we progressively expand the pretraining corpus from approximately 1.5 million hours to 2.6 million hours and ultimately to 13 million hours. In the second stage, we use large-scale multilingual speech recognition data for supervised training to reinforce the learning of multilingual semantic information. In the third stage, training is extended to multiple perception tasks—namely speech recognition, emotion, gender, age, and sound event recognition—so that the encoder acquires task-agnostic, general-purpose speech representations suitable for the audio-LLM.

Second, a staged training recipe that preserves linguistic competence. Audio–LLM pretraining proceeds in three stages: adapter-only alignment; full-parameter joint optimization of the encoder, adapter, and LLM on large-scale speech, audio, and text data; and long-context extension to 32K tokens with long-form speech and audio tasks. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with on-policy distillation (OPD), in which a frozen text-only teacher supervises the responses that the model generates from both audio and text inputs. This recipe is designed to avoid the “cognitive degradation” on text-centric tasks that commonly afflicts speech-augmented LLMs.

We evaluate Spark-Audio 1.0 on both public benchmarks and in-house test sets drawn from real-world application scenarios. The public evaluation covers audio benchmarks (including ASR, speech translation, audio understanding and spoken dialogue task) and text benchmarks (including general knowledge, instruction following, math and code task). The in-house test sets cover almost the same types of audio tasks as the public benchmarks, together with Chinese ASR under challenging acoustic conditions. Despite using only one-tenth of the training data of the comparably sized Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash, it achieves comparable and, in some cases, superior results on audio tasks, with clear advantages on realistic, application-oriented tasks, and approaches the performance of larger closed-source speech foundation models. papers.title: System-Level Evaluation of Uplink Access Schemes for Ambient IoT
papers.abstract: Ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT) devices operate under stringent energy constraints, relying on harvested power in the $μ$W-to-mW range and limited energy storage. The A-IoT air interface for active devices is still under development; we therefore use Narrowband Internet of Things (NB-IoT) as an implementable reference for evaluating autonomous Uplink (UL) access under harvested energy. Under these conditions, the standard NB-IoT contention-based Random Access (RA) procedure incurs substantial per-packet overhead, making UL access in dense A-IoT networks increasingly energy-expensive. Context-retaining UL access schemes reduce this overhead, but their energy-latency trade-offs are insufficiently studied in literature under realistic harvesting and protocol constraints. To address this gap, we extend the LENA-NB ns-3 module with solar energy harvesting, supercapacitor storage, and a hysteretic brown-out mechanism, and propose Hybrid Scheduling Request (HSR), a hybrid UL access scheme combining reserved request occasions with opportunistic contention. We compare RA, Scheduling Request (SR), HSR and an Idealized Fast Uplink Grant (FUG) serving as a performance bound. Results show that HSR reduces mean packet delay by up to 69% and SR reduces energy per delivered bit by up to 24%, both relative to RA.

The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)is standardizing Ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT)as a new class of cellular Internet of Things (IoT)devices targeting battery-less operation through ambient energy harvesting [4]. Release 19 specifies an air interface for passive devices that backscatter a carrier provided by the network [6, 5]. Release 20 extends the framework to active devices, including types 2b and C, which generate their own transmissions and therefore do not require an externally supplied carrier. The air interface for these active device types remains unspecified in the current Release 20 work item [7]. We therefore use Narrowband Internet of Things (NB-IoT), an already deployed low-power cellular IoTtechnology, as an implementable reference. Unlike conventional battery-powered NB-IoTUser Equipments (UEs), A-IoTdevices operate under extremely constrained energy budgets of microwatts to milliwatts. The harvested energy is commonly buffered in supercapacitors, which have lower energy density and higher self-discharge than batteries, making device operation dependent on instantaneous energy availability. Furthermore, their traffic is inherently sparse, consisting of short and infrequent Uplink (UL)reports rather than sustained data flows. Under these conditions, control-plane signaling can dominate the overall energy consumption, while insufficient harvested energy may trigger brown-out events that interrupt both communication and application execution [11].

papers.title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
papers.abstract: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.

Frontier models like Opus (Anthropic, 2026), Gemini (Google DeepMind, 2026), ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2026) have made a substantial leap in artificial intelligence by demonstrating reasoning capabilities that approach human performance in a variety of domains (Luo et al., 2024; Bermejo et al., 2025; Alohali et al., 2025; Street et al., 2026). In the current era of Agentic AI, we see a shift towards systems that are able to plan, act, use tools, and apply feedback loops for enhanced performance (Abou Ali et al., 2025; Pati, 2025; Xi et al., 2025). However, strong single-agent reasoning does not remove the need for collaboration. More complex tasks often require decomposing the problem, checking partial information, and integrating the conclusions generated by different reasoning parts. This motivates goal-oriented multi-agent behavior that goes beyond single-agent responses toward agent collaboration supported by memory (Zhang et al., 2025), reasoning (Subramaniam et al., 2025), or environmental interaction (Lan et al., 2024).

Recent multi-agent research has been applied to scientific experimentation (Ghareeb et al., 2026), embodied agents (Huang et al., 2023), or societal simulation (Gao et al., 2023). Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that multi-agent systems do not automatically outperform strong single-agent or repeated-sampling baselines (Xia et al., 2024; Kapoor et al., 2025), because critical information is lost during inter-agent coordination and verification processes fail (Cemri et al., 2025). In particular, a key limitation is that many multi-agent systems communicate after an agent has produced a complete output, leaving partial critical findings unavailable to peer agents while simultaneously overwhelming them with verbose, task-irrelevant reasoning traces that increase context overhead (Liu et al., 2024; Ning et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024). This motivates our core question, whether agents can collaborate more effectively by asynchronously sharing the intermediate findings, and allowing other agents to retrieve and reuse information during inference without exposing full reasoning traces.

We propose an asynchronous system based on shared memory buffer inference, referred to as Muffin, that enables exchange of agents’ novel insights. The general workflow is visualized in Figure 1. In the first step, an Orchestrator routes a user query based on the expected reasoning demands, i.e., whether a query can be solved directly or a multi-step reasoning is required. For more demanding queries, multiple agents are instantiated by assigning each of them a specialized role, and a subtask, both provided by the orchestrator. For an efficient exchange of relevant insights, a shared memory provides a controlled and selective exchange of intermediate findings. An agent only pushes relevant information into the buffer which is expected to help in making progress in a collaborative problem solving manner. We keep an agent’s own reasoning local. After a finite reasoning horizon, a Summarizer is fed the final messages from each agent along the agents’ meta information and the initial user query, to produce the final response.

papers.title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials
papers.abstract: Finite element model updating is among the most general approaches to discover constitutive models from structural experiments: since the displacement field is computed rather than measured, it accommodates arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy data. However, every loss evaluation requires a nonlinear finite element solve per load step, and training neural materials requires many such evaluations. Intrusive model order reduction lowers this cost while retaining boundary conditions and variational structure. How can a reduced model remain accurate while the network weights change at every training step? We combine proper orthogonal decomposition and energy-conserving sampling and weighting with adjoint sensitivities of the reduced model, and adapt both the trial space and the sampled elements along the optimization path. The constitutive law is a polyconvex neural network: a logarithmic normalization term, together with a zero-anchored input convex architecture and a growth term, renders the energy polyconvex, coercive, and non-negative by construction, independent of the trained weights. We demonstrate the approach on two experimental datasets and one synthetic three-dimensional example. For a two-phase specimen, training time decreases from nine hours to 41 minutes compared with a full-order identification, without loss of accuracy. In the three-dimensional example, six modes replace 48 672 degrees of freedom, 116 of 15 625 elements suffice to evaluate the internal forces, and training takes 13 minutes. In all cases, the identified material reproduces the measured reaction force and predicts the displacement field from the force alone. Hyperreduction makes the discovery of neural materials from structural data affordable while retaining the advantages of finite element model updating.

papers.intro:
A finite element simulation is only as predictive as its constitutive model. Neural materials, that is, constitutive models in which neural networks parameterize the energy and the dissipation potential [1], have changed how we obtain these models: constitutive artificial neural networks [2, 3], physics-augmented and input-convex architectures [4, 5], and their extensions to inelasticity [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] and multiphysics [11, 12, 13, 14] discover energies and dissipation potentials that satisfy thermodynamic principles by construction. The data to train them, however, are rarely pairs of stress and strain. What we measure in a structural experiment are displacement fields and reaction forces. This raises the question: How do we discover a neural material from measurements of a structure, and can we do so at a cost that is practical?

A finite element simulation is only as predictive as its constitutive model. Neural materials, that is, constitutive models in which neural networks parameterize the energy and the dissipation potential [1], have changed how we obtain these models: constitutive artificial neural networks [2, 3], physics-augmented and input-convex architectures [4, 5], and their extensions to inelasticity [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] and multiphysics [11, 12, 13, 14] discover energies and dissipation potentials that satisfy thermodynamic principles by construction. The data to train them, however, are rarely pairs of stress and strain. What we measure in a structural experiment are displacement fields and reaction forces. This raises the question: How do we discover a neural material from measurements of a structure, and can we do so at a cost that is practical?

Full-field measurements probe a rich set of deformation states within a single specimen, but stresses remain inaccessible, such that the material law has to be inferred from indirect observables [1, 15]. The available methods differ in whether they solve the forward problem [15, 16, 17, 18]. Methods that do not, such as the equilibrium gap [15, 19] and the virtual fields method [20, 21], evaluate balance of linear momentum directly on the measured displacement field. This idea underlies the unsupervised EUCLID framework [22], which has been extended to neural network models [23], constitutive artificial neural networks [24], experimental [25] and three-dimensional data [26], heterogeneous specimens [27, 28], sparse and noisy data [29], and optimized specimen design [30]. The equilibrium gap method has recently been used to calibrate physics-augmented neural networks for viscoelasticity [17] and finite-strain hyperelasticity [18], and the modified constitutive relation error offers a related route for thermodynamically consistent networks [31]. Material Fingerprinting [32, 33] and neural operators [34] go one step further and replace the optimization by a database lookup or by a single forward pass of a network trained on many specimens. These methods are fast, yet they rely on a dense displacement field, from which strains are computed, and on assumptions such as plane stress. It was shown that an under-resolved surface measurement and a non-negligible specimen thickness can affect the calibration [18], and that the coverage of deformation states governs how well the identified model generalizes. Simulation-based approaches instead compare measured and simulated responses in the spirit of finite element model updating [35]. Since the displacement field is the solution of a boundary value problem rather than an input, these approaches accommodate sparse and noisy data and, in principle, any specimen geometry, load path, and boundary condition that the finite element model resolves. They have been used to calibrate spline-based models [36, 37], physics-augmented neural networks [38, 39, 40], constitutive artificial neural networks [40], neural elastoplasticity [41, 42], and cohesive zone laws [43]. The same route extends to coupled problems, in which displacements, temperature, and reaction forces enter a single loss and the adjoint of the coupled residual provides the gradient [44]. Differentiable finite element solvers make this route practical, with sensitivities obtained by automatic differentiation or adjoints [45, 40, 42, 46], and beyond finite elements for image-based observations with particle methods [47]. In the terminology of [16], these are reduced approaches, in which the state is eliminated by solving the boundary value problem in every iteration.

The robustness of this route comes at a computational price. Each evaluation of the loss requires a nonlinear finite element solution for every load step, and each gradient additionally requires an adjoint solve with the tangent stiffness. For neural materials, whose parameters are weights and biases, this procedure is repeated over many optimization steps. Since the generalization of an identified model improves with the combination of specimens and load cases [18], the number of such solves per loss evaluation grows with the richness of the data. GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation reduce the cost of a single solve [45, 40], but not the number of degrees of freedom that enter it. This motivates us to ask: Can we reduce the cost of the forward model itself, while retaining the finite element model, its boundary conditions, and the physical structure of the constitutive network?

Projection-based model order reduction addresses this question in two steps [48]. First, a reduced basis, typically obtained by proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of solution snapshots, restricts the displacement field to a low-dimensional subspace. Second, because the nonlinear internal forces must still be assembled over all elements, hyperreduction approximates their evaluation on a small subset of the mesh. Hyperreduction follows two lines. Interpolation-based methods, such as the discrete empirical interpolation method [49] and the gappy-POD-based GNAT [50], approximate the nonlinear term by a few of its entries. Cubature-based methods select and weight a subset of elements. They start from the pioneering works of hyperreduction and cubature [51, 52], and lead to energy-conserving sampling and weighting (ECSW) [53] and the empirical cubature method (ECM) [54]. A recent variant does not select a subset of the integration points but places new ones in strain space, by clustering and subsequent empirical correction (E3C) [55]. In solid mechanics, POD with empirical interpolation was applied to hyperelasticity [56], and recent studies extend reduced models to finite-strain homogenization [57, 58, 59], nearly incompressible materials [60], viscoelasticity [61], and plasticity and damage [62, 63, 64]. Comparisons of hyperreduction schemes on nonlinear elasticity [65, 66] and component-wise reduced models coupled by mortar tying [67] address accuracy and reusability. In parallel, nonlinear manifolds replace the linear subspace [68, 69, 70], and non-intrusive surrogates learn the reduced model from data, with autoencoders [71] or physics-augmented neural networks [72]. The latter report a rapid divergence outside the training range, which shows that learned reduced models are reliable only within the range they were trained on.

papers.title: Signed Wasserstein distance for room impulse response comparison
papers.abstract: The nature of room impulse response signals is often adverse to a clear evaluation of similarity: they are sparse, rapidly varying, signed signals resulting from the complex interaction of room reflections and phase relationships. Therefore, conventional point-wise metrics may be sensitive to small temporal shifts and provide poor loss surfaces for optimization. In this paper, we propose an optimal transport-based distance for RIR similarity that explicitly accounts for the structure of impulse responses, inspired by the signed Wasserstein distance formulation. Optimal transport provides a natural framework for this problem, by comparing signals based on how their underlying distributions are displaced rather than requiring a one-to-one correspondence. We evaluate the proposed distance against commonly used audio baseline metrics through a series of room-parameter perturbation studies. The results demonstrate the advantage of using the signed Wasserstein metric for geometric evaluation tasks and show a promising performance for room parameter optimization within a differentiable Image-Source model.
papers.intro:
Evaluating the similarity of signals is a common but far from trivial problem in audio signal processing. For room impulse responses (RIRs), defining a meaningful similarity measure is an equally challenging task. Room impulse responses describe the sound propagation in an enclosed space and exhibit a highly structured temporal behaviour, through a combination of sparse early reflection peaks and a reverberant tail segment [17]. As a result, RIR characterization relies on these time-localized, signed signals, where even a small variation of room parameters can lead to a large deviation in identifying the corresponding target acoustic environment. This problem arises in a number of applications, ranging from room impulse response estimation and interpolation [7, 14], as well as optimization of parametric reverberation models like feedback delay networks [1, 6]. In these settings, the choice of similarity measure is critical to obtain a loss landscape favorable for optimization. Conventional point-wise objectives, such as LpL_{p}-losses can become poorly informative when corresponding reflections are misaligned in time, causing a large sample-wise error at the global scale [2, 9]. Spectral losses are also used to evaluate distances in terms of frequency content, but additionally suffer from their own limitations due to the choice of time-frequency resolution. [16, 12].

Evaluating the similarity of signals is a common but far from trivial problem in audio signal processing. For room impulse responses (RIRs), defining a meaningful similarity measure is an equally challenging task. Room impulse responses describe the sound propagation in an enclosed space and exhibit a highly structured temporal behaviour, through a combination of sparse early reflection peaks and a reverberant tail segment [17]. As a result, RIR characterization relies on these time-localized, signed signals, where even a small variation of room parameters can lead to a large deviation in identifying the corresponding target acoustic environment. This problem arises in a number of applications, ranging from room impulse response estimation and interpolation [7, 14], as well as optimization of parametric reverberation models like feedback delay networks [1, 6]. In these settings, the choice of similarity measure is critical to obtain a loss landscape favorable for optimization. Conventional point-wise objectives, such as LpL_{p}-losses can become poorly informative when corresponding reflections are misaligned in time, causing a large sample-wise error at the global scale [2, 9]. Spectral losses are also used to evaluate distances in terms of frequency content, but additionally suffer from their own limitations due to the choice of time-frequency resolution. [16, 12].

Optimal Transport (OT) provides a promising solution to this problem, thanks to its ability to compare distributions while accounting for the geometric displacement of the signals. The use of optimal transport was shown to be beneficial for audio comparison tasks, as well as effective loss function in deep learning frameworks [2, 15, 3]. Interestingly, we can identify a similar connection in a common representation in room acoustics. Under appropriate normalization, the L1L_{1} distance between Energy Decay Curves (EDCs) admits an exact interpretation as Wasserstein-1 distance of their temporal energy distributions. To our knowledge this equivalence has not been made explicit before, and it shows that OT is already closely related to well established energy-based distances for RIRs. However, the EDC representation discards the information tied to the signed structure of the raw RIRs, limiting the available signal characteristics employed in the similarity evaluation.

papers.title: MBABench-2.0: Evaluating AI Agents on Constructing Financial Spreadsheets Beyond Simple Verifiability
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets are the lingua franca of modern finance, driving valuation, forecast, audit, and many other core workflows of the industry. As LLM agents advance to automate knowledge work, spreadsheet construction is a natural and pertinent testbed. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate agents on fill-in-the-blank style tasks, where an agent performs minor edits in otherwise complete spreadsheets. This protocol fails to capture the most central and time-consuming part of the spreadsheet workflow: the modeling decisions, format design, and sheet layout regular knowledge workers need to toil through to build a workbook from scratch. We introduce MBABench-2.0, a benchmark of 101 original spreadsheet construction tasks, the hardest of which is estimated to take 33 hours for a modeler with 3+ years of experience. Unlike coding or math, where a unit test or a final answer can verify an agent's output, the quality of a financial spreadsheet that concerns readability, maintainability, or auditability, is not so simply verifiable. To holistically evaluate spreadsheet construction, we introduce 129 criteria spanning 12 categories that operationalize quality beyond the accuracy of the spreadsheet. Evaluating over 20 agents across 8 models and 4 harness types, we find that frontier agents rarely construct spreadsheets that are both accurate and meet our quality criteria: the top agent achieves a pass rate of only 16% on the benchmark. The benchmark demonstrates a substantial gap in spreadsheet building capability of current agents.

Evaluating this financial spreadsheet construction poses two main challenges. The first concerns data availability. Finance is broad, encompassing investment banking, private equity, corporate finance, wealth management, and more, making it costly to assemble a sufficiently large and diverse set of tasks. Exacerbating the issue, real financial data is often sensitive and proprietary, which precludes public release. Reflecting these constraints, BankerToolBench [13] focuses exclusively on investment banking, whereas MBABench-1.0 [28] covers finance broadly but releases only 3838 of its 202202 tasks, citing intellectual-property restrictions. The second challenge concerns evaluation. In practice, spreadsheets serve not just as calculation devices but also as collaborative communication tools, and miscommunication can be costly. During Barclays’ 20082008 acquisition of Lehman Brothers assets, a junior associate accidentally led the bank to purchase 179179 additional assets due to lack of clarity in the spreadsheet [7]. This communicative role of spreadsheets naturally demands additional quality criteria such as readability and auditability, beyond mere accuracy. To capture these broader quality criteria, GDPval [19] employs experts to manually annotate pairwise preferences, but this approach is costly to scale and hard to reproduce. The community thus needs a public benchmark that offers both breadth and scale in its tasks, and evaluates quality criteria beyond accuracy in a transparent, scalable manner.

This paper presents MBABench-2.0, a fully public benchmark comprising 101101 spreadsheet construction tasks that cover key financial fields including investment banking, corporate financial planning and analysis (FP&A), commercial banking, and wealth management. While the spreadsheet quality beyond calculation accuracy may seem nebulous, the industry in fact largely agrees on principles that one should follow in a high-quality spreadsheet [9] (e.g., stating units, or consolidating key assumptions in one place). Where these conventions leave room for interpretation, firms typically codify their own house standards for employees to follow. We therefore propose a taxonomy of 129129 criteria across 1212 categories, with the conventions left open fixed in house standards that every agent receives. For instance, No hardcoded numbers in formulas requires all calculations to use one coherent set of assumptions, and Numbers right-aligned requires numerical values to be right-aligned. Similar to Lau et al. [13] and Yen et al. [28], MBABench-2.0 employs a validated agentic judge to evaluate these quality criteria at scale. Following the difficulty taxonomy of Yen et al. For example, their models are hard to modify because timelines are fixed to a specific horizon, and they often contain deeply nested formulas that are hard to audit. These results suggest that current spreadsheet agents are still far from delivering professional spreadsheets.

papers.title: When Code Gets Cheap, Evaluation Gets Scarce: An Experience Report on AI-Assisted Agile Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Coding assistants are widely reported to speed up code production; most accounts stop there. We report the end-to-end construction and deployment of a compliance-critical, human-in-the-loop exam-grading system, built by a single developer who wrote no code by hand, protected by a gated process from stakeholder persona to audited behavior. The initial system was built in three working days and could grade a real cohort. We draw one claim from this experience: AI changes software engineering less by making programming faster than by changing what is scarce. Writing code becomes abundant. Reliable evaluation-knowing whether a result is correct and meets the actual need-remains necessary at every iteration and becomes the binding constraint. Engineering judgment remains a second scarcity. Several defects passed the test suite: they sat at the boundaries the tests had mocked, the browser and the language-model API, or appeared only in real use. Deployment exposed assumptions that local tests had missed. Moreover, an AI assistant acting across many steps bypassed process checkpoints until we made them enforceable gates. All of this was observed in a triple union: the developer was also the end user and domain expert, making expert judgment immediately available and evaluation as cheap as it can be. This favors the iteration gains, which may shrink where evaluation requires additional people or expertise, but makes the case a hard test for evaluation scarcity: evaluation still constrained progress. We draw five lessons: run a gated, traceable construction process; specify what is knowable and discover the rest against a running prototype; validate in the real environment; gate the assistant, not only the work; record decisions with their assumptions and the process state the assistant forgets. A second project showed similar patterns; an independent single-expert case corroborates the shift.

Software engineering has traditionally treated implementation as a substantial cost. Specifications, design reviews, and the division of labor help manage that cost. Large language model (LLM) coding assistants are now credited with large productivity gains [1]. But faster implementation raises a different question: what becomes costly when producing code is no longer the main constraint?

Software engineering has traditionally treated implementation as a substantial cost. Specifications, design reviews, and the division of labor help manage that cost. Large language model (LLM) coding assistants are now credited with large productivity gains [1]. But faster implementation raises a different question: what becomes costly when producing code is no longer the main constraint?

Most accounts of assistants look at a narrow slice of the lifecycle, the generation and correctness of code [2]. They say little about requirements, testing, deployment, operation, or the changing role of the human. The shift toward judgment and evaluation as potential bottlenecks has been anticipated [3], but rarely documented across the development lifecycle. We examine it by reporting on the construction and deployment of a real-world system, including its failures: a human-in-the-loop exam-grading application that graded a real cohort under data-protection constraints. An LLM proposes a score and a rationale for each student answer against a rubric; the instructor reviews, accepts, or overrides every score, and every decision is recorded. The first author, who has a software-engineering background, built the application with an LLM coding assistant without writing any source code by hand; the paper refers to her as the developer. The grading application has since gone into institutional use in a university pilot, and the same process built a second application, also in use; the lessons held on both.

papers.title: The Asymptotic Number of Anticodes in Hamming Spaces
papers.abstract: In the Hamming space $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, a $d$-anticode is a subset in which every pair of points has Hamming distance at most $d$, or equivalently, a set of diameter at most $d$. Let $m_q(n,d)$ denote the maximum size of a $d$-anticode and let $\mathcal{A}_q(n,d)$ be the family of all $d$-anticodes. We show that for fixed $q$, as $n\to\infty$, the total number of $d$-anticodes satisfies \[ |\mathcal{A}_q(n,d)|=2^{(1+o(1))m_q(n,d)} \] for $4\le d\le n-1$, except when $q=2$ and $d=n-1$. We also count linear $d$-anticodes, that is, subspaces of $\mathbb F_q^n$ with diameter at most $d$. For fixed $q$ and $d$, their number is polynomial in $n$. For growing $d$, we determine the exponential order as $q^{Θ_q(d^2+d\log_q(n/d))}$ in the sublinear regime and $q^{Θ(n^2)}$ when $d/n\toα\in(0,1)$. In the near-full regime $n-d=o(n)$, we obtain the sharper count $q^{(1/4+o(1))n^2}$. A random-generator construction further improves the binary lower bound for every fixed linear diameter.

papers.intro:
Anticodes are fundamental objects in coding theory and extremal combinatorics. Whereas error-correcting codes are designed to keep codewords sufficiently far apart, anticodes consist of sets of words whose pairwise distances are bounded from above. This simple definition gives rise to a rich class of combinatorial structures whose properties depend on the underlying metric and the imposed diameter constraint.

Anticodes are fundamental objects in coding theory and extremal combinatorics. Whereas error-correcting codes are designed to keep codewords sufficiently far apart, anticodes consist of sets of words whose pairwise distances are bounded from above. This simple definition gives rise to a rich class of combinatorial structures whose properties depend on the underlying metric and the imposed diameter constraint.

The study of anticodes has a long history, particularly in connection with classical extremal problems. A central question has been to determine the maximum cardinality of an anticode of prescribed diameter. In Hamming spaces, classical diametric theorems determine the maximum size of such families and describe the geometry of extremal configurations in a wide range of parameter regimes [14, 1, 2].

Beyond their intrinsic combinatorial interest, anticodes play an important role in coding theory. In particular, the code–anticode bound relates the minimum distance of a code to the diameter and cardinality of an anticode, generalizing the sphere-packing bound in suitable metric spaces [3].

Alongside these extremal questions, related enumeration questions have been studied for error-correcting codes in various metrics and algebraic settings (see, e.g., [5, 7, 10, 16] and references therein). Such results illustrate the value of enumeration in understanding large families of combinatorial objects. However, codes and anticodes satisfy fundamentally different distance constraints, so enumeration results for codes do not directly determine the number of anticodes.

papers.title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon's Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton-Schulz
papers.abstract: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW, yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD, the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon, on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton-Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon, about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Muon (Jordan et al., 2024b) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. It has matched or outperformed AdamW in language-model pretraining, from speedrun benchmarks (Jordan et al., 2024a) to large-scale training (Liu et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2025), and standard optimizers more broadly in vision (Jordan et al., 2024b; Pethick et al., 2025), diffusion (Schaipp, 2025), and tabular models (Gorishniy et al., 2026). For two-dimensional parameter blocks, Muon approximately orthogonalizes the momentum matrix with a few Newton--Schulz iterations, that is, it steps along an approximation of the polar factor polar⁡(G)=U​V⊤\mathrm{polar}(G)=UV^{\top} of G=U​ΣG​V⊤G=U\Sigma_{G}V^{\top}. The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent (Carlson et al., 2015a; Carlson et al., 2016; Carlson et al., 2015b) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024). It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods (Pethick et al., 2025), and Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off (Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024). Our main contributions are as follows. • One-step geometry (Section 3). We give closed-form line-search decreases for GD, SignGD, and PolarGD. Each method reaches the minimizer in one step under its own condition (Theorem 1): GD from every starting point only when the Hessian is a multiple of the identity, SignGD when the error has entries of equal magnitude and the Hessian preserves their signs (e.g., a diagonal Hessian), and PolarGD, for any positive-definite Hessian, when the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms. This explains why orthogonal initialization is special for PolarGD and diagonal structure for SignGD. In the worst case over iterates, however, the one-step comparison is pessimistic for PolarGD: its guaranteed decrease is smaller than GD’s (Theorem 3), although PolarGD is often faster over whole trajectories (Figure 1). • Rotation equivariance (Section 3.3). PolarGD is equivariant under orthogonal changes of basis, while SignGD is not (Theorem 2): rotating the problem rotates the PolarGD iterates but changes the SignGD trajectory. Accordingly, PolarGD keeps its performance when an ill-conditioned diagonal problem, such as a Zipf-type regression model of language data, is rotated, whereas SignGD degrades. • Implicit preconditioning (Section 4). papers.title: Role of Chalcogen-p States in the Optical Response of Bulk PtSe2 and PtTe2
papers.abstract: The type-II Dirac semimetals PtSe$_2$ and PtTe$_2$ are isostructural and isovalent layered compounds but exhibit distinct electronic properties. We measure the in-plane infrared reflectivity of bulk crystals between 10 and 300 K and compare the interband contribution to the optical conductivity with band-resolved density-functional calculations. At low temperature, the Drude spectral weight of PtTe$_2$ is an order of magnitude larger than that of PtSe$_2$. PtTe$_2$ also shows a broad mid-infrared absorption continuum, whereas the absorption of PtSe$_2$ remains weak. The calculations attribute this continuum to transitions from a predominantly chalcogen-$p$ band into a Pt-$d$ band. In PtTe$_2$, the chalcogen-$p$ band lies higher in energy, which lowers the onset of these transitions and increases the semimetallic band overlap, in line with the larger Drude spectral weight. The type-II Dirac points lie far below the Fermi level, so that transitions between the bands forming the Dirac cones do not contribute appreciably to the interband conductivity.

In addition, PtSe2 and PtTe2 host type-II Dirac fermions, which were predicted by first-principles calculations [18] and subsequently observed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) [47, 43, 30].

In addition, PtSe2 and PtTe2 host type-II Dirac fermions, which were predicted by first-principles calculations [18] and subsequently observed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) [47, 43, 30].

Bulk PtSe2 and PtTe2 show metallic resistivity, which is substantially lower in PtTe2 than in PtSe2 [47]. Quantum-oscillation and magnetotransport studies revealed a multiband electronic structure with several electron and hole pockets near the Fermi level EFE_{\mathrm{F}} [44, 48, 29]. Beyond these bulk properties, PtSe2 and PtTe2 exhibit a strong thickness dependence of their electronic structure [38, 21]. In thin layers, quantum confinement and weaker interlayer coupling open a band gap [27, 20, 8, 2], and semiconducting behavior has been reported for monolayer and bilayer PtSe2 and for monolayer PtTe2 [23]. Thin films of PtSe2 and PtTe2 have been explored for infrared photodetection [45, 46] and terahertz detection and emission [42, 7, 6].

Optical studies of PtSe2 have focused on thin films and exfoliated flakes. Ellipsometry and absorption measurements on films and flakes a few nanometers thick characterized the interband response from the near-infrared to the ultraviolet range [40, 13] and attributed the observed transitions to states derived from Pt-dd and Se-pp orbitals [36]. Terahertz spectroscopy and ellipsometry followed the thickness-driven semiconductor-to-semimetal transition [19, 26], while infrared absorbance and mid-infrared photocurrent measurements were performed on polycrystalline films [28, 11]. For PtTe2, electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) on bulk crystals revealed a plasmon near 0.5 eV, which was interpreted as a three-dimensional Dirac plasmon on the basis of an effective Dirac-cone model [32, 12]. Plasmon polaritons in PtTe2 films and nanoribbons were further studied by infrared spectroscopy and nanoimaging and were also interpreted in terms of Dirac fermions [24, 17]. Despite these studies, a comparison of the optical conductivity of bulk PtSe2 and PtTe2 is still lacking.

In this work, we present a temperature-dependent infrared study of bulk PtSe2 and PtTe2 single crystals. Using band-resolved density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we identify the bands and interband transitions responsible for the distinct optical responses of the two compounds. Because they are isostructural and isovalent, comparing them shows how the energy of the chalcogen-pp states relative to the Pt-dd states affects the free-carrier and interband responses. We also examine the contribution of transitions between the two bands forming the type-II Dirac cones.

papers.title: PiHand: Latent Hand-Object Interaction Priors for Physics-Based Policy Learning
papers.abstract: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.
