papers.title: Beyond Best-of-$k$: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.

Inverse problems arise across science and engineering whenever an unknown signal must be recovered from indirect measurements, including image restoration (Bertero et al., 2021), medical imaging (Song et al., 2022), and astronomical imaging (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 2019). Given an observed measurement yy generated through a known but potentially noisy measurement process, the goal of the inverse problem is to recover the original signal xx. The goal of posterior sampling is thus to generate candidate reconstructions that are simultaneously consistent with the measurement and the prior.

In Fourier phase retrieval, for example, multiple images can produce identical Fourier magnitude measurements (Fienup, 1982). These measurement-equivalent solutions therefore have the same likelihood, but can have very different posterior probabilities depending on their consistency with the image prior. In particular, we observe that existing phase-retrieval solvers applied to face images sometimes return a rotated or color-inverted face that is consistent with the measurement but implausible under a natural-image prior concentrated on upright faces. The challenge is therefore not simply to find measurement-consistent reconstructions, but to sample the measurement-consistent solutions supported by the prior.

Diffusion models provide strong image priors for posterior sampling (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). At each noise level, a diffusion model implicitly defines a denoiser that maps a noisy sample xtx_{t} to an estimate of the corresponding clean image; this diffusion denoiser can be used to incorporate the prior p⁡(x)p(x) during posterior sampling. Diffusion-based inverse solvers apply this prior information along a sampling trajectory, i.e., the sequence of intermediate states that evolves from a noisy sample toward a reconstruction. Existing methods primarily either tilt the unconditional reverse diffusion process using an approximate likelihood gradient (Zhang et al., 2025; Chung et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Boys et al., 2024) or alternate prior and measurement updates across noise levels (Wu et al., 2024; Xu and Chi, 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Ahmed and Makin, 2026). In these methods, the prior information available at each noise level is represented through a local denoising approximation centered on a single clean-image estimate, rather than explicitly maintaining multiple competing prior modes at intermediate timesteps.

When the measurement is ambiguous, as in the case of phase retrieval and other underdetermined inverse problems, following a sampling trajectory can lead to premature mode selection. At high noise levels, multiple prior modes may remain plausible, but the trajectory can only move towards one of them. Once a trajectory selects a particular prior mode, subsequent refinement primarily improves measurement consistency in the local neighborhood of that mode rather than considering more distant alternatives. This becomes problematic when (i) the selected prior mode is not consistent with the measurement, and (ii) its nearest measurement-consistent mode is not supported by the prior. Trajectory-based samplers can prematurely commit to this pair of modes, ultimately resulting in hallucinatory sampled reconstructions that are not supported by the true posterior or even the true prior. Best-of-kk evaluation partially masks this issue by generating multiple independent reconstructions and selecting the one closest to the ground truth (Chung et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). However, this selection uses information unavailable at test time and does not ensure that the produced samples are prior-consistent. Particle-based approaches maintain multiple candidates at intermediate timesteps (Cardoso et al., 2024; Dou and Song, 2024; Wu et al., 2023), but have primarily focused on linear inverse problems and particle diversity rather than prior-consistent sampling.

papers.title: A neural-network model to find correlations in astrochemical space
papers.abstract: The detection of new interstellar molecules is central to astrochemistry, and arguably the most transformative development in the field in past decade has been the increase in both number and diversity of detected species. Using natural language processing models, we develop a machine-learning pipeline, similar to other approaches reported in the literature, to connect molecular structures, encoded as chemical strings, and molecular column densities in TMC-1. The workflow generates astrochemically informed embeddings that can be employed in subsequent supervised learning tasks. These representations are used within a neural-network framework to perform column-density regression on both the original molecular inventory and out-of-distribution species. The resulting model achieves mean squared error values of 0.17/0.58 and mean absolute error values of 0.29/0.59, and coefficients of determination of 0.88/0.51 for the train+validation and validation datasets. The latent vectors learned by the model are rich mathematical objects that capture the underlying chemical relations and also the potential interstellar detectability of the molecule. Using these vectors in molecules obtained from systematic permutations of the TMC-1 inventory, we identify several promising candidates for future detection in this cloud, together with a large number of apolar species. By training the model on datasets reflecting different historical epochs of molecular detections in TMC-1, we show that recent molecular detections have substantially reshaped our understanding of interstellar chemistry, in a transformative, rather than incremental, way. Beyond accurate prediction of column-density trends for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution molecules, the latent-space representations produced by the model provide a stepping stone for developing new forms of data-driven astrochemical intuition and exploration.

papers.intro:
One of the main challenges in astrochemistry is to understand the chemical composition of the interstellar medium (ISM) in general, and in some regions that are considered as prototype of a specific chemistry. The chemical inventory of the ISM is continuously expanding, with a particularly strong boost in the last years. Taking as reference the number of molecules reported in the 2018 census of interstellar molecules (McGuire, 2018) of 204 molecules, the number of molecules detected in the ISM has increased in more than 70% (346 at the time of writing). This is a staggering figure considering the evolution of the discipline since the detection of the first molecule, CH (Swings and Rosenfeld, 1937). The detection of new interstellar molecules is undoubtedly not incremental, but has had a transformative impact on our understanding of the chemistry of the ISM. For example, the detections in recent years have shown a molecular panorama full of complex organics (Rivilla et al., 2020; Rivilla et al., 2021; Jiménez-Serra et al., 2022; Rivilla et al., 2023), exotic cumulenic species (Cernicharo et al., 2021a; Cernicharo et al., 2021c; Cernicharo et al., 2023b; Remijan et al., 2023; Cabezas et al., 2022; Esplugues et al., 2026), new metal-bearing compounds (Cernicharo et al., 2023a; Gupta et al., 2024; Tasa-Chaveli et al., 2025; Rey-Montejo et al., 2024), sulfur bearing molecules (Cernicharo et al., 2021g; Cernicharo et al., 2021f; Cernicharo et al., 2024a; Cernicharo et al., 2024b; Remijan et al., 2025; Sanz-Novo et al., 2025b; Araki et al., 2026), high-energy isomers (Cernicharo et al., 2022b; Molpeceres et al., 2025; San Andrés et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025; Sanz-Novo et al., 2025a) and cyclic species and PAHs (Cernicharo et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2018; Cernicharo et al., 2021d; McGuire et al., 2021; Cernicharo et al., 2021e; Cernicharo et al., 2022a; Cernicharo et al., 2021b; Sita et al., 2022; Loru et al., 2023; Cernicharo et al., 2024c; Wenzel et al., 2024a; Wenzel et al., 2024b; Fuentetaja et al., 2026; Cabezas et al., 2025; Wenzel et al., 2025). The list above presents a non-exhaustive, yet representative sample of recent detections highlighting the diversity of chemical families.

As a cold, dense region TMC-1 is known to be one of the test beds for astrochemical models (Agúndez and Cernicharo, 2026) and the prototypical source for the detection of new molecules, with detections in this source serving as stepping stones to the search in other sources (Burkhardt et al., 2021; Agúndez et al., 2023). The rapid expansion of molecular inventories has highlighted important challenges in our understanding of interstellar chemistry. While the continuous detection of new molecules stimulates experimental and theoretical efforts to understand their formation and destruction pathways, these studies struggle to keep pace with the number of detections. Consequently, many recently discovered species still lack well-established formation pathways or have not yet been incorporated into chemical networks. At the same time, identifying new molecular candidates is becoming increasingly challenging, as their selection relies heavily on chemical intuition and the availability of laboratory spectroscopic data. This is particularly relevant for unstable or highly reactive species, whose laboratory characterization can be difficult, summed to the high spectroscopic accuracy required for astronomical identification (Silva et al., 2023; Fuentetaja et al., 2024, e.g.,). Astrochemical models provide the fundamental framework for interpreting molecular observations, understanding the chemistry of the ISM, and suggest new candidates for detection. Yet, their predictive capabilities remain constrained by incomplete chemical networks, uncertainties in kinetic parameters, and observational limitations. Consequently, our picture of interstellar chemistry remains strongly influenced by the molecules we can detect, characterize, and model.

Since its publication, this methodology has been applied in several studies (Scolati et al., 2023; Fried et al., 2023; Remijan et al., 2023; Toru Shay et al., 2025a; Toru Shay et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026). The general strategy consists of compiling a molecular inventory for a given source, encoding molecular structures into numerical representations using unsupervised machine-learning techniques such as mol2vec (Jaeger et al., 2018), vicgae (Lee, 2021; Scolati et al., 2023), or Morgan fingerprints (Rogers and Hahn, 2010), and subsequently training a supervised model to relate these representations to observed molecular abundances. The resulting model can then be used to explore large chemical databases, such as Zinc (Irwin et al., 2020), to identify promising candidates for future detections or for astrochemical modelling. Despite its success, including its contribution to the detection of new interstellar molecules (Fried et al., 2024, like CH3​OCH2​CH2​OH\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{OCH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{OH}), candidate selection is typically based on proximity in the original embedding space and therefore primarily reflects structural molecular similarity rather than astrochemical relevance. Although chemical structure may, and in many cases certainly does, correlate with astrochemical relevance, this relationship does not hold uniformly across chemical space, as demonstrated later in this work.

papers.title: A Transparent 3-DoF Assistive Device for Upper-Limb Tremor and Ataxia Compensation: Design and Experimental Validation
papers.abstract: Assistive devices for patients with neurodegenerative movement disorders must combine high mechanical transparency with the ability to generate corrective interaction forces. Achieving both properties simultaneously remains challenging. This paper presents the completed iAssistADL platform, a 3-DoF assistive device for future tremor and ataxia compensation during activities of daily living. The system employs a transparency-oriented mechanical architecture with all actuators located at the base, resulting in low moving mass, decoupled kinematics, and high mechanical transparency. To compensate for friction-induced transparency limitations along the vertical axis, a hybrid control strategy is proposed that combines open-loop force rendering in the horizontal plane with closed-loop force control in the vertical direction. The platform is experimentally evaluated through transparency measurements and static and dynamic force-rendering experiments at representative configurations. Results demonstrate resistive torques below 0.1 Nm in the horizontal plane, end-effector forces of up to approximately 10 N throughout the workspace, and accurate horizontal force rendering up to 4 Hz. While the vertical axis remains limited by friction-induced dynamics at higher frequencies, the proposed system successfully combines high transparency with controlled force generation, establishing a promising hardware platform for future tremor and ataxia compensation.

Existing assistive devices often face a trade-off between transparency and force capability, as force-capable systems often introduce friction, inertia, and resistance that interfere with voluntary user motion. papers.title: MQAScore: Fine-Grained Text-Music Alignment Evaluation via Large Audio Language Model
papers.abstract: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.
papers.intro:
The field of music generation has evolved rapidly, with state-of-the-art text-to-music (TTM) systems now capable of generating high-fidelity and vocalized music. Alongside these advancements, text remains the primary conditioning modality, with prompts becoming more intricate to improve controllability. To evaluate text-audio alignment, existing studies predominantly rely on similarity-based metrics [28, 31] computing a global similarity score between text and audio embeddings. However, as shown in Fig. 1, a global similarity score summarizes all attributes in the prompt and audio into a single value, obscuring fine-grained semantic information and making the evaluation difficult to interpret. As text-to-music generation moves toward detailed, multi-attribute prompts, alignment evaluation should move beyond global similarity and focus on evaluating individual semantic concepts.

Moving toward such fine-grained concept-level evaluation raises two challenges. The first is to define the evaluation space, as musical captions span attributes ranging from descriptive (e.g., genre, instrument) to musicological (e.g., key, chord, tempo) ones. To address this challenge, we ground our taxonomy in two tagging schemes. CAL500 [22], which spans six dimensions: emotion, genre, instrument, vocal, usage, and acoustic qualities; MTG-Jamendo [3] instead groups affective and evocative tags into a single mood/theme category. We retain the first five CAL500 dimensions and follow the latter in naming the first one mood/theme, since listener-facing tags rarely separate how a clip feels from what it evokes; we reserve usage for the listening situation a clip is intended for. Their concepts are categorical, so the presence or absence of each concept in a clip is well defined, although detection difficulty varies across dimensions [16]. We exclude acoustic qualities, which reflect audio fidelity rather than semantic alignment. Moreover, we also exclude musicological concepts such as those defined by the Pandora’s Music Genome Project [19] (e.g., harmony, rhythm), which remain difficult to detect by LALMs [13, 26].

papers.title: CoWriter: Guiding Methodological and Synergetic Human-LLM Co-Authoring
papers.abstract: While LLMs have transformed text generation, standard chat-and-canvas interfaces often reduce human authoring to quite passive supervision, causing review fatigue, over-reliance on AI, and the sidelining of the human role in long-form, source-grounded writing. Prior systems typically address isolated writing phases, leaving comprehensive end-to-end human-LLM collaboration largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce CoWriter, a proactive agentic scheme that adapts expert human (co-)authoring methodologies from cognitive science to flexibly steer the entire writing workflow while actively encouraging the user to engage. In an exploratory user study, compared to a standard LLM baseline, authors using CoWriter better expressed their perspectives and maintained a higher sense of document ownership, supported quantitatively by $2.2\times$ more successful agent engagements. Furthermore, external reader judges rated the resulting texts higher in "human touch" qualities like storytelling and integrating unique personal experiences. Overall, our results demonstrate that proactively engaging users through established human practices is beneficial for effective LLM-supported co-authoring, providing useful methodologies, techniques and insights for future research on collaborative agents.

Writing has been a fundamental human activity for millennia. Recently, though, Large Language Models (LLMs) have reshaped how we create texts, making LLM-assisted writing one of the most widespread uses of these models (Chatterji et al., 2025). Nowadays, authors increasingly rely on LLMs, through standard chat or interactive canvas interfaces, to alleviate demanding authoring tasks like synthesizing sources and drafting large blocks of content (Mysore et al., 2025). LLMs now significantly lower the writing barrier with fast, fluent text generation, empowering a diverse range of users to compose complex, multi-page documents.

LLMs now significantly lower the writing barrier with fast, fluent text generation, empowering a diverse range of users to compose complex, multi-page documents.

Yet, such LLM-boosted text generation often comes at the expense of sidelining the human role and effectiveness in the authoring process. This comes with over-reliance on LLM outputs along with challenges like verifying text faithfulness and review fatigue (Buçinca et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2025). Indeed, few recent works explored improving human-LLM co-authoring processes, addressing concrete aspects such as pre-writing brainstorming Jiang et al. (2024), outlining Zhang et al. (2026) and turn-based initiative-taking Shao et al. (2026). However, an agentic scheme that actively engages the human throughout the entire co-authoring process, from brainstorming to reviewing, remains under-explored.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach towards bridging these gaps in the complex setting of long-form, source-grounded authoring. Our research hypothesis is that effective synergetic human-LLM co-authoring may be achieved by properly adapting established expert methodologies for human-human co-authoring. To explore it, we present CoWriter, an agentic scheme following the seminal cognitive-science work of Flower and Hayes (1981) and its prominent extension to writing teams by Lowry et al. (2004). These works formalize distinct writing activities (such as brainstorming, outlining, drafting, and reviewing) and, for teams, collaborator roles (e.g., leaders, writers, and reviewers). Our adaptation steers the writing process flexibly through these activities, while keeping the human author fully engaged and influential all along.

papers.title: A Sharp Distributional Lower Bound for Planar Discrepancy
papers.abstract: We prove that the unnormalized discrepancy function of every $n$-point set in the unit square has absolute value at least $c\sqrt{1+\log n}$ on a set of measure at least $η$, with absolute constants $c,η>0$. Consequently, its $L_p$-quasinorm is bounded below by $c\,η^{1/p} \sqrt{1+\log n}$ for every $p>0$.

papers.title: Arithmetic Conditions for the Invertibility of Circulant Matrices over Finite Fields
papers.abstract: This paper investigates arithmetic conditions, over finite fields, for the invertibility of circulant matrices whose first row is $(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$, in terms of linear constraints on the entries $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$. The coefficients of such linear constraints are determined by field traces arising from Frobenius orbits of roots of unity, and under additional assumptions they are given by Ramanujan sums reduced modulo the characteristic of the given field. These results provide finite-field analogues of the corresponding criteria over $\mathbb{Q}$, where the relevant Ramanujan-sum linear constraints can be formulated without such additional assumptions, while also showing some differences caused by reduction modulo the characteristic. The constraints can often determine invertibility using aggregate information about the entries of a row, rather than the particular pattern of the entries. We also discuss the polynomial gcd criterion, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for invertibility and yields further consequences for special families of circulant matrices.

papers.title: Nature of the bosonic edge phase in a double quantum spin Hall insulator
papers.abstract: Field-theoretic analysis has predicted that the edge of a double quantum spin Hall insulator (DQSHI) can undergo an interaction-driven transition from a phase with fermionic edge modes into one with only bosonic modes. All single-fermion edge excitations are gapped in this bosonic edge phase, but fermion pairs remain gapless, leading to distinct experimental signatures. We numerically simulate the interacting DQSHI edge and verify the existence of the bosonic edge phase. This calculation requires an explicit bulk embedding of the DQSHI edge, due to its mixed anomaly between charge and $S^z$ conservation. We hence employ segment DMRG on an infinite two-dimensional cylinder, where the DQSHI bulk is modeled in terms of two copies of the spin-up lowest Landau level, combined with their time-reversed counterparts. We find that interactions can open a single-fermion gap at the DQSHI edge while fermion pairs remain gapless, matching the predictions for the bosonic edge phase. We find the scaling of the single-fermion gap with interaction strength to be consistent with field-theoretic calculations, and discuss the relevance of the bosonic edge phase to twisted homobilayers of WSe$_2$ and MoTe$_2$. We elaborate on the methodological extension of the segment geometry used here to other topological phases with edge anomalies.

Topological phases of matter characteristically display a bulk-boundary correspondence, where the gapped topological bulk is accompanied by gapless edge modes [34, 63, 57, 24, 66]. However, this is not a one-to-one relationship. The same bulk can realize multiple different edges, and the same edge can be realized by different bulk phases [8]. While there are canonical instances of such ambiguity, as it is always possible to attach a lower-dimensional subsystem to a given edge [9, 86, 1], there are also systems that host multiple edges with fundamentally distinct physical properties emanating from the same topological bulk theory [31, 62, 3, 48].

Topological phases of matter characteristically display a bulk-boundary correspondence, where the gapped topological bulk is accompanied by gapless edge modes [34, 63, 57, 24, 66]. However, this is not a one-to-one relationship. The same bulk can realize multiple different edges, and the same edge can be realized by different bulk phases [8]. While there are canonical instances of such ambiguity, as it is always possible to attach a lower-dimensional subsystem to a given edge [9, 86, 1], there are also systems that host multiple edges with fundamentally distinct physical properties emanating from the same topological bulk theory [31, 62, 3, 48].

One of the paradigmatic systems where this occurs is the double quantum spin Hall insulator (DQSHI) [26, 2, 49, 85, 38, 87]. The DQSHI is a topological phase protected by charge conservation and SzS^{z}-spin conservation, with spin Chern number Cs=2C_{s}=2 [71]. Since the DQSHI bulk is adiabatically equivalent to two decoupled (single) quantum spin Hall insulators (QSHIs) [40, 41, 5, 4, 46, 51], one would expect the DQSHI edge to host two pairs of helical fermionic modes, i.e., two chiral spin-up fermions and two anti-chiral spin-down fermions. However, continuum field theory analysis has shown that this is not always the case. Under consideration of electronic interactions, the DQSHI edge can undergo a transition to a new bosonic edge phase with the very same symmetries yet only one pair of non-chiral bosonic edge modes [6, 53]. All single-fermion excitations are gapped in this phase while fermion pairs, which can be recast as bosons, are gapless. Importantly, the fermion-to-boson edge transition can occur without gap closing in the DQSHI bulk [76].

In the bosonic edge phase, however, the single-fermion gap only allows for backscattering in units of 2​e2e, producing a doubled Fano factor of F=2F=2 [92, 76]. While the bosonic edge phase of the DQSHI is well established within the framework of continuum field theory, it has yet to be confirmed that this phase can be realized in an explicit microscopic model. This requires a numerical approach. One may expect that the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) would be well suited for this task, as it is an exceptionally powerful tool for studying strongly correlated 1D systems [83, 82, 69, 35, 70]. Still, the edge modes of the DQSHI are anomalous [12, 67, 80, 45, 23]: specifically, they carry a mixed anomaly between spin- and charge-conservation, which is canceled out by the topological bulk of the DQSHI [7, 78, 52, 13]. This anomaly is an obstruction to realizing the DQSHI edge modes in a symmetric and local 1D lattice model. Simulating the DQSHI edge in DMRG in a strictly 1D geometry would therefore require either breaking a relevant symmetry of the edge or working in a momentum-space basis. The former is inappropriate for studying a symmetry-protected topological phase. The latter leads to volume-law entanglement entropy and to an anti-sparse, i.e., all-to-all, Hamiltonian upon inclusion of interactions, rendering it impossible to scale up the calculations to larger system sizes.

papers.title: $π$-Flux Tuning of Quantum Paramagnetism in the Triangular-Lattice Hubbard Model
papers.abstract: We compare two time-reversal-symmetric triangular-lattice Hubbard models at half filling: the zero-flux model and a staggered $π$-flux model with zero and $π$ flux through oppositely oriented triangles. Although both reduce to the same Heisenberg model at leading order in the strong-coupling limit, their distinct charge fluctuation profiles yield different quantum paramagnetic regimes. Combining a strong-coupling expansion with infinite density matrix renormalization group (iDMRG) calculations, we find that the positive ring-exchange of the zero-flux model promotes spontaneous chirality, consistent with its notion of a chiral spin liquid at intermediate coupling. In the staggered-$π$-flux model, whose noninteracting limit is a Dirac semimetal, the ring exchange changes sign and disfavors chiral order and we find no resolvable scalar chirality. This renders flux-tuned ring-exchange an efficient discriminator between chiral and non-chiral quantum paramagnets at finite coupling.

papers.title: Extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity in the hole-doped Hubbard model
papers.abstract: The two-dimensional Hubbard model was originally proposed as the minimal model of uniform $d$-wave superconductivity in the cuprate high-temperature superconductors, but recent calculations with relevant parameters in a realistic doping regime have often found other ground states. Further, uncertainty remains over such results due to the intrinsic bias of different computational methods. Here we address this uncertainty through state-of-the-art neural tensor network and neural backflow state simulations, enabled by large-scale GPU computation, that together reach an unprecedented variational accuracy on lattices with up to 1024 sites. At $1/8$ doping in the pure Hubbard model, as well as with next-nearest-neighbor hopping relevant to the hole-doped cuprates, we reveal a near degeneracy among a low-energy uniform $d$-wave state, superconducting stripes, and non-superconducting stripe states on the milli-$t$ energy scale. Our work rebalances the narrative that the Hubbard model supports a single dominant order in relevant parameter regimes towards a picture of extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity.

papers.intro:
The Hubbard model is a paradigmatic model of strongly correlated electrons [4, 69]. Despite its simple form, the two-dimensional (2D) Hubbard model is believed to capture the essential physics of high-temperature superconductivity (SC) [10, 52], and can be realized directly by ultracold fermionic atoms in optical lattices [26, 82, 58, 40]. In the cuprate materials that the Hubbard model aims to describe, uniform dd-wave superconductivity is found at optimal doping, while in certain cuprates other low-temperature orders can also be observed [47, 29]. For example, there is evidence for various unidirectional orders such as spin-density waves (SDW), charge-density waves (CDW), stripes (with intertwined spin and charge modulations), and even more exotic orders such as pair-density waves in several materials at low doping [47, 29], and these have been argued to either coexist with, be intertwined with, or compete with superconductivity.

With a next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′≈−0.2t^{\prime}\approx-0.2 relevant to the hole-doped cuprates [3, 66], the conclusions are more varied. Again at 1/81/8 doping, robust superconductivity coexisting with partially filled stripes has been reported in a DMRG/CP-AFQMC study [91] and a neural Pfaffian study [73], whereas other simulations using infinite PEPS [67] and other NNBF states [36, 35] have found non-superconducting stripes, while a DMRG study found only a CDW with short-range pairing [46].

While it is possible to make progress through the consensus of different techniques which individually have uncertainties larger than the energy scale of competing orders—for example, the study of stripes in Ref. [95] involved an energy spread across methods of roughly 0.010.01 tt, larger than the energy difference between competing stripe wavelengths—the only way to eliminate this uncertainty is to improve the absolute accuracy of the simulations. To this end, we employ variational wavefunctions that can in principle be improved to arbitrary accuracy and that in practice we push to the precision of a few milli-tt on lattices with up to 1024 sites. We employ two variants of NNBF [57], which have recently demonstrated high accuracy in Hubbard model studies [36, 17, 73, 56, 35, 72], as well as a newly introduced neural tensor network state [23], namely the neural-network fermionic PEPS (NN-fPEPS). The rationale for using multiple variational forms is that each relies on an underlying fermionic ansatz that may impose a bias in the calculation. The Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) [7] and Pfaffian NNBF states have been argued to favor paired states [88], while the fermionic PEPS (fPEPS) [20, 50, 62, 30] underlying the NN-fPEPS wavefunction favors low entanglement, a very different starting point. In each case, through intensive optimization of the underlying computational infrastructure, as well as through deploying large-scale graphics processing unit (GPU) computation, we push each variational form to the practical limits of accuracy. As we shall detail below, this leads to new findings and insights regarding the ground-state order in the hole-doped Hubbard model.

papers.title: Spin polarization in a chiral ladder: elastic and inelastic environments
papers.abstract: We study how the transport window and environmental reinjection determine the spin polarization transmitted through a minimal two-leg chiral ladder. The model contains time-reversal-invariant helical spin--orbit coupling, spin-independent interchain hopping, and nonmagnetic contacts with two orbital modes per lead. Sublattice symmetry makes the coherent spin-transmission kernel exactly odd in energy. A window centered on the symmetry point therefore gives zero integrated spin current, whereas a displaced window selects an uncanceled spectral interval. The resulting polarization reverses between enantiomers and vanishes in the decoupled-chain, zero-spin--orbit, and equivalent-strand limits of this model. We compare uniform absorption, energy-resolved elastic probes, and thermalized voltage probes at the same finite bias, including reinjection whenever probes are present. Charge conservation alone does not prohibit enhancement of the integrated spin signal: the elastic-probe response can increase at finite bias even where its linear-response counterpart decreases. Thermalized probes can also lift the centered-window zero that elastic probes preserve. Absorption and reinjection also change the transmitted charge, so enhancement of spin current and enhancement of normalized polarization must be distinguished. Static onsite disorder produces sample-dependent fluctuations; its signed ensemble mean is reported with uncertainty and is not forced to vanish in a displaced window. These results identify the energy interval and reservoir prescription that must be controlled when interpreting dephasing trends in minimal models relevant to chirality-induced spin selectivity.

papers.intro:
Spin-selective electron transport through chiral molecular conductors raises a specific question about the environment: does a change in the measured spin signal reflect loss of coherence, removal of particles, redistribution in energy, or a change in the charge used to normalize the signal? The present work separates these effects in a minimal chiral ladder. Its central result is a controlled comparison at equal finite bias: a charge-conserving elastic reservoir prescription can enhance the integrated spin signal even when the same prescription suppresses the linear-response signal. At the symmetry-centered window, elastic reinjection preserves an exact zero while thermalized reinjection can produce a finite signal. The energy window and the reinjection rule are essential parts of a statement about environment-assisted spin filtering.

papers.title: LieGROG: A Lie algebra approach for calibrating GRAPPA operators
papers.abstract: Purpose: In multi-coil acquisitions based on non-Cartesian k-space sampling, image reconstruction using GRAPPA Operator based gridding (GROG) can provide advantages with respect to the non-uniform FFT (NUFFT): It waives both the need for calculating a density compensation function, and for transferring back and forth between Cartesian and non-Cartesian points in iterative algorithms. Non-trivial noise propagation and self-calibration limited to specific trajectories, however, have contributed to GROG being rather sparsely applied so far. Theory and Methods: The group structure of the GRAPPA Operator allows estimating its generator as a single joint fit for all k-space dimensions within the associated Lie algebra. Assuming a linear regime, the generator can be fitted using subsequent pairs of sampling points from nearly any arbitrary non-Cartesian read-out. This approach called LieGROG was evaluated against classical GROG calibration and NUFFT/Toeplitz, using simulations with an analytic ground truth and various 2D and 3D MR-scans employing typical non-Cartesian trajectories. Results: Throughout all applications, LieGROG proved to provide fast, robust and straightforward calibration of the GRAPPA Operator. It clearly outperformed the classical GROG calibration approaches in terms of noise amplification. LieGROG matched the results of the NUFFT/Toeplitz-based reference MR reconstructions closely, while being 6 to 189 times faster and reducing peak VRAM by 20 to 45% in the 3D experiments. Conclusion: LieGROG transforms GROG into a more versatile and stable tool, ultimately aligning non-Cartesian imaging with the standard, FFT-based reconstruction pipelines established for Cartesian scans.
papers.intro:
Compared to standard Cartesian scanning, non-Cartesian k-space trajectories have several advantages, such as increased robustness against motion, improved scan-efficiency and a general higher flexibility. However, it also renders image reconstruction more complex, as data have to be transferred to a regular grid prior to the application of the fast Fourier Transform (FFT). The standard solution is convolution gridding and the associated non-uniform FFT (NUFFT [1, 2]), which in brief grids onto the Cartesian lattice by convolving with a (Kaiser-Bessel) kernel, corrects sampling density by an estimated function (density compensation function, DCF), applies an oversampled inverse FFT and finally an apodization correction.

papers.title: Multichoice Modeling: Exploring Decision Configuration Space under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Decision support has become sophisticated at exploring uncertainty, but much less so at representing the architecture of the decision itself. As a result, the decision space is often narrowed before uncertainty is analyzed, leaving interactions among choices and the effects of alternatives they imply largely invisible. This paper introduces multichoice modeling, a framework for making large decision configuration spaces explicit and computationally explorable under uncertainty. Drawing on the logic of rugged landscapes, we conceptualize such problems as contingent performance landscapes, where interdependent choices generate configuration-specific outcomes whose value changes across uncertain futures. The computational framework combines multidimensional decision and uncertainty spaces in a single simulation. Further, variance-based sensitivity analysis is used for identifying influential choices, and conditional distribution analysis for comparing configuration-specific performance profiles. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies: a manufacturing process upgrade, M&A strategy, and mortgage design. By contrasting conventional uncertainty-only analysis with multichoice modeling, the cases show how opening the decision configuration space can reveal unexpected complementarities, near-best configurations with different risk profiles, and strategies that were not apparent as alternatives at the outset.

papers.intro:
In investment appraisal, cost-benefit analysis, operations, finance, and risk management, actions must be evaluated under uncertain future conditions. Therefore, the treatment of uncertainty has become a central aspect of decision support (Saltelli et al. 2020, Scoones 2024). Yet a form of residual determinism remains in the specification of the decision architecture itself. Exploratory modeling often examines how a single system or policy behaves under uncertainty (Bankes 1993, Kwakkel et al. 2013). Robust decision-making evaluates a limited set of candidate strategies across many plausible futures (Lempert et al. 2006, Marchau et al. 2019). Real options analysis frequently focuses on valuing or optimizing either a single or a limited set of generic flexibilities (Dixit and Pindyck 1994, Trigeorgis 1996, Kozlova 2017). Consequently, decision support often remains confined to narrowly defined decision situations, in which only a small subset of the available strategic degrees of freedom is examined.

There is an emerging call for opening up the decision space itself (Hämäläinen et al. 2024, Stepanov et al. 2024, Colorni and Tsoukiàs 2020). Unlike the decision analysis field, strategy research has long recognized that a strategy is not a single decision, but a configuration of multiple interdependent choices (Levinthal 1997, Rivkin 2000). Drawing on the concept of rugged landscapes, this literature shows that when choices interact, the performance contribution of any choice depends on the broader configuration in which it is embedded. Yet the rugged-landscape perspective is primarily used as a behavioral and evolutionary lens in explaining how firms search and adapt, whereas strategy evaluation raises a qualitatively different decision-support problem.

Yet the rugged-landscape perspective is primarily used as a behavioral and evolutionary lens in explaining how firms search and adapt, whereas strategy evaluation raises a qualitatively different decision-support problem.

Consider an example of a battery supply strategy for an electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer. The firm faces multiple interdependent choices, including whether to make or buy batteries, whether to own upstream mining assets, which chemistries to support, which suppliers and regions to rely on, which transportation routes to choose, how much inventory buffer to arrange, and whether to use long-term contracts or spot purchasing. These choices are interdependent and interact with each other: battery chemistry determines suppliers and production assets; vertical integration alters the value of diversification and contracting decisions; transportation, inventory, and sourcing choices jointly determine supply-chain resilience and cost. External uncertainties, such as EV demand, raw-material prices, regulation, geopolitical disruptions, and transport bottlenecks, further complicate the decision landscape by altering which configurations prove robust, fragile, or unexpectedly valuable. There could be thousands of possible combinations of choices that form distinct strategies, most of which are never evaluated or even formulated. The relevant question is therefore no longer how a given strategy performs under uncertainty, but which combinations of choices give rise to attractive strategies across multiple uncertain futures.

We further propose multichoice modeling as a methodological framework for making such decision-uncertainty spaces explicit and computationally explorable. The approach represents a decision problem as a set of admissible choice configurations. Choices may be independent or conditional, mutually exclusive or multiple-selection, and may include option-like alternatives. The choice configurations are simulated jointly with uncertainty realizations, producing a dataset that links choices, uncertainties, and performance outcomes. Efficient variance-based sensitivity analysis and conditional projections are then used to identify influential choices and compare the performance profiles induced by their combinations. Rather than framing the problem as the fixed set of alternatives that existing methods can handle (Quade 1980), strategies can emerge as combinations of interdependent choices under uncertainty.

papers.title: Set-theoretic inevitability
papers.abstract: After defining the concept of inevitability for statements with the modal logic of forcing, we raise the question of which statements are inevitable under $\mathsf{ZFC}$ and under large cardinal hypotheses. We show that $\mathsf{SOA}$ (defined as $\mathsf{ZFC}^-$ + $\mathsf V=\mathsf{HC}$) plus the $\boldsymbolΣ^1_2$-perfect set property is $\mathsf{ZFC}$-inevitable, and that Projective Determinacy is inevitable in the theory of $\mathsf{ZFC}$ with a proper class of Woodin cardinals. We then discuss the possible conceptual significance of these results for the foundations of set theory.

papers.title: Sequential Monte Carlo Sampling of Feasible Regions Represented by R-Functions
papers.abstract: Feasible-region sampling and volume estimation become increasingly inefficient when constraints define only a small fraction of a convenient bounding domain. We combine R-functions, which encode compound feasibility as a continuous signed field, with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers. The proposed construction exploits not only the sign of the R-function, which determines exact feasibility, but also its continuous negative values outside the feasible set, which provide graded information on constraint violation. Logistic intermediate distributions use this information to guide particles progressively towards feasibility, while the final target distribution remains uniform on the feasible region. Experiments on intersections and unions, including disconnected cases of hyperballs, show substantial variance reductions relative to direct rejection sampling, with the statistical advantage generally increasing as the feasible fraction decreases. For sufficiently small feasible regions, these advantages persist even after accounting for computational cost. To isolate the benefit of continuous R-function information, we also compare the proposed method with an SMC sampler with a region-only (RO) construction that uses the same sequential particle machinery but retains only binary feasible/infeasible information. We demonstrate that the R-function-informed SMC method concentrates particles in the feasible region earlier and produces lower-variance volume estimates than RO.

papers.intro:
Sampling from constrained regions and estimating their volumes are fundamental tasks in uncertainty analysis, reliability analysis, and process systems engineering (Au and Beck, 2001; Kucherenko et al., 2025; Boukouvala and Ierapetritou, 2012). A simple approach is direct rejection sampling: points are generated uniformly from a convenient bounding domain and retained when they satisfy all constraints. Although straightforward and exact, rejection sampling uses only binary membership information, and its efficiency deteriorates in direct proportion to the feasible fraction of the bounding domain. When this fraction becomes small, very large numbers of samples may therefore be required to obtain an adequate representation of the feasible region or an accurate estimate of its volume.

Sampling from constrained regions and estimating their volumes are fundamental tasks in uncertainty analysis, reliability analysis, and process systems engineering (Au and Beck, 2001; Kucherenko et al., 2025; Boukouvala and Ierapetritou, 2012). A simple approach is direct rejection sampling: points are generated uniformly from a convenient bounding domain and retained when they satisfy all constraints. Although straightforward and exact, rejection sampling uses only binary membership information, and its efficiency deteriorates in direct proportion to the feasible fraction of the bounding domain. When this fraction becomes small, very large numbers of samples may therefore be required to obtain an adequate representation of the feasible region or an accurate estimate of its volume.

R-functions (Rvachev, 1978; Rvachev, 1982; Shapiro, 1992) provide an alternative representation of constrained regions by combining multiple inequalities into a single continuous signed function whose sign determines feasibility and whose zero level set represents the boundary (Kucherenko et al., 2025). Importantly, the R-function contains more information than a binary feasible/infeasible indicator: its continuous negative values outside the feasible region provide graded information about constraint violation. In this work, we exploit this additional information within a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampling framework (Del Moral et al., 2006), which has been arguably underused in statistics despite its advantages (Dai et al., 2022). In this framework, a sequence of logistic intermediate targets uses the continuous R-function to guide particles progressively towards feasibility, while the final hard target remains uniform on the feasible region. The associated SMC estimate of the normalising-constant ratio also provides an estimate of the feasible volume.

The design choice studied here is a bridge that preserves equal target density throughout the feasible region while using signed constraint values outside it. papers.title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

AI agents are moving from isolated tools to interacting populations [1, 2]. Multi-agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) already operate in finance [3, 4], defence [5], social media [6], and personal assistance [7]. The centrality of conventions has motivated experimental work on their emergence in AI multi-agent systems, often based on minimal models that capture the core coordination mechanisms. One such model is the naming game, in which pairs of agents try to coordinate on a name [16]. Theoretical studies [17, 18, 19] and laboratory experiments with humans [20, 21, 22, 23] have shown that, in the naming game, conventions can emerge spontaneously from repeated local interactions.

Recent simulations with populations of LLM-based agents have revealed similar patterns. AI agents playing the naming game can reach global conventions through local interactions, although these interactions can produce collective biases absent in individual agents [24]. The strength and form of these biases vary with population size in nonlinear, model-dependent ways [25]. Established conventions can also be overturned. A committed minority, a group of agents that always promote an alternative, can tip the whole population once it exceeds a critical fraction [26, 21]. This critical mass is key to the stability of these systems because it measures a social attack surface: the number of adversarial agents needed to overturn a convention a population has already settled on [27]. Critical mass has been measured at 25%25\% in experiments with human groups [21], ranges from 10%10\% to 40%40\% in theoretical models depending on their assumptions [26, 28], and spans 2%2\% to 67%67\% in AI populations depending on the underlying LLM [24].

Here, we study how network topology shapes the formation of conventions in LLM populations and their robustness to committed minorities. We use the policies extracted from four LLMs by Flint et al. [25], which allow simulations of up to 10510^{5} agents. We place them on four topologies: a fully connected network, equivalent to the well-mixed setting; two uncorrelated networks with power-law degree distributions [35], one heterogeneous and one nearly homogeneous; and a random regular network. We find that networks change how fast consensus is reached and, for some word pairs, which convention wins and whether it is reached at all. For three of the four models, the fully connected network is the fastest and the random regular network the slowest. In two cases, the networks with the lowest mean degree also reverse which convention wins. Networks homogeneous and low average degree restore restore consensus for one of the two word pairs that fail to converge when well-mixed, requiring the presence of dynamical correlations between neighbouring agents. Hubs reach a given level of coordination earlier than low-degree nodes, spreading the consensus to the rest of the network. Yet they are the cheapest place from which to overturn a convention. In every condition we tested, the critical fraction is lowest when the committed agents occupy the hubs and highest when they occupy the low-degree nodes. Overall, our work extends the study of LLM populations from well-mixed to networked settings, and identifies the structure of interactions as a key factor in how the collective behaviour of multi-agent AI systems emerges and how it can be exposed to adversarial attack.

papers.title: CrisiLangs: A Multilingual Resource for Crisis Warning Generation
papers.abstract: Communicating with the public during an emergency entails issuing warning messages promptly. In Europe, it often requires producing them in more than one language. Recent work has shown that language models can be trained to generate warning messages as a crisis unfolds, but the available data covers only English. To fill this gap, we present CrisiLangs, a multilingual extension of CrisiText (an English dataset of crisis events paired with warning messages written according to expert communication guidelines) to Italian, Bulgarian, German, and Greek. Expert native speakers translated the warning messages of 1,000 events drawn from 411 scenarios, for a total of 5,000 event-message pairs across five languages. We test the resource to fine-tune a multilingual model on all five languages jointly, with and without the emergency guidelines in the prompt, and compare it with a zero-shot baseline. The fine-tuned models outperform the baseline on ROUGE-L, BLEU and BERTScore in every language and configuration. In a human preference study, low decoding temperatures receive the most preferences in all five languages and in both configurations, while the effect of the guidelines varies by language.

papers.intro:
Timely and effective communication is a critical aspect of crisis management: during an emergency, authorities must inform the population about what is happening and about what to do, and they must do it repeatedly as the situation evolves. This has to be done under time pressure and the volume of information handled during an event is a recognized source of stress for emergency operators Misra et al. (2020). The issue is even worse in Europe, where nations are linguistically diverse (and many have multiple official languages) and there is a high cross-border mobility. Therefore, warnings issued in a single language can fail to reach part of the population they are meant to protect. Issuing the same alert in several languages, at the speed an emergency requires, complicates the work of operators. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence, and in particular Large Language Models (LLMs), which can interpret and produce text, offer a way to support this task Foubert et al. (2026).

One way to avoid sending automatically translated content to civilians would be to generate messages directly in the target language. papers.title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
papers.abstract: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

papers.title: Optimal cosmological cross-correlation analysis with U-Net-based processing
papers.abstract: Cosmological cross-correlation analyses are commonly based on two-point statistics, which are optimal for Gaussian random fields but do not capture all relevant information in the presence of non-Gaussianity, which is ubiquitous in late-time cosmic fields. This motivates investigations of higher order statistics, and one method is to use machine learning to construct a correlation-optimized tracer field that can utilize cross-correlation information beyond two-point statistics. Using a tracer field as input and a paired target field as part of the cost function, we test whether a U-Net can learn a transformed tracer field that maximally correlates with the target field. We train a 1D U-Net on paired simulated fields and study controlled cases based on Gaussian and log-normal random fields. We train and quantify performance using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the target field and compare the network output with the analytic linear solution known in the Gaussian limit. For Gaussian fields, the U-Net reproduces the expected linear solution closely and behaves as an effective matched filter in frequency space. For log-normal fields, the network departs from the linear estimator and achieves an improved correlation with the target field, increasing the mean Pearson correlation from 0.857 for the linear estimator to 0.953 for the U-Net output. This indicates that the network is sensitive to information beyond the power spectrum. These controlled 1D experiments show that U-Net-based tracer transformation can effectively extract correlation-relevant information beyond the power spectrum, providing a promising framework for enhancing cosmological cross-correlation analyses.

papers.intro:
Modern cosmology increasingly relies on statistical inference from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS), and a key challenge is to extract maximal information from these complex fields. In recent years, machine learning methods, and in particular Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 2015), have been applied to a wide range of cosmological inference tasks. These include parameter estimation and model discrimination from galaxy density and weak gravitational lensing fields (Gupta et al., 2018; Fluri et al., 2018; Kacprzak & Fluri, 2022; Lu et al., 2023; Gong et al., 2024; Jeffrey et al., 2025, e.g.), 21-cm tomography during cosmic dawn and reionization (Gillet et al., 2019, e.g.), strong gravitational lens modeling (Perreault Levasseur et al., 2017, e.g.), analysis of the 1D Lyman-α\alpha forest (Nayak et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025, e.g.). CNN-based analyses have also been used for multifield cosmological inference from hydrodynamical simulations (Villaescusa-Navarro et al., 2021). Among these architectures, the U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) is especially well suited to map-to-map regression problems. Its encoder-decoder structure, together with skip connections, enables the network to combine local information with multi-scale contextual features while preserving spatial resolution in the output. U-Nets have therefore been successfully applied in various cosmological analyses, including weak-lensing map reconstruction (Jeffrey et al., 2020), mitigation of polarization leakage in neutral hydrogen mapping (Gao et al., 2023), and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) foreground cleaning (Petroff et al., 2020).

This motivates a U-Net-based approach to learning a correlation-optimized tracer field from two fields, that is, a transformation of the input field where the transformation parameters depending on the local environment of the input field are learned by CNNs, so that the transformed field is optimized to correlate with the target field. The U-Net architecture is well suited to this map-to-map learning task because it captures multi-scale features without imposing an explicit functional form. The goal of this paper is therefore to test whether a U-Net can learn a correlation-optimized tracer field that captures information beyond standard 2-point statistics and thereby improves the signal-to-noise ratio of downstream cross-correlation analyses. This can be subsequently applied to various cosmological cross-correlation scenarios, such as the late-time Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect, which relies on cross-correlating the primary CMB anisotropies with large-scale structure (LSS) tracers (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2022, e.g.), or CMB lensing tomography, which cross-correlates the reconstructed CMB lensing convergence with galaxy overdensity fields to constrain the amplitude and growth of structure (Krolewski et al., 2021; Farren et al., 2024, e.g.).

In machine learning applications, it is often difficult to determine whether an acceptable, a superior, or an optimal solution has been achieved. Here, however, we can study controlled scenarios that allow to evaluate whether the U-Net based 2-point approach can indeed extract the full cross-correlation information. The Gaussian case provides a useful benchmark, since the expected behaviour is analytically tractable, while the log-normal case introduces a more realistic form of non-Gaussianity commonly encountered in LSS applications.

papers.title: The Inverse Mapper Problem for Two-Dimensional Data
papers.abstract: The Mapper algorithm is a popular graphical tool for data visualization and exploration in topological data analysis (TDA). It takes as input a data set $X$ and returns a graph that aims to capture the underlying topological features of these data. The Mapper algorithm has several parameters that need to be specified by the user: a $\textit{filter function}$ $f:X\to Y$ where $X$ is often a point cloud data set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $Y$ is the $\textit{reference space}$ that is often a lower dimensional Euclidean space, a $\textit{cover}$ of $f(X)$, and a $\textit{clustering algorithm}$ that is applied to the pre-image of each element in the cover. In this paper, we consider the following question: What graphs can occur as the output of the Mapper algorithm? It is known that when $Y=\mathbb{R}^3$, any graph can be a Mapper graph. In this work, we focus on a more practical case where the filter function is $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$. We consider two different scenarios. In the first scenario, we fix the parameters of the Mapper algorithm, but vary the data. This way we characterize exactly the graphs that can occur for several choices of parameters. In the second scenario, we fix the data set but vary the parameters. This can be seen as a way to understand how much the output can differ depending on the choices of parameters.In both settings, we find close connections to classical topics in graph drawing.

While it has successfully been applied in many applications [3, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 21, 22], the underlying theory, in particular the interplay of all the parameters, is not yet fully understood [1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 20]. From this point of view, the inverse problem is a natural question as it characterizes the graphs that can occur as the output of the Mapper algorithm. papers.title: Quantum Phases and Structural Transitions of Bosons in Bubble-Shaped Confinements
papers.abstract: We investigate the structural properties and superfluid behavior of soft-core bosons confined in a spherical bubble trap at large particle numbers ($N \le 1800$). Using Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations with worm algorithm sampling in continuous space, we show that increasing $N$ drives a sequence of layering transitions: beyond the established bilayer supersolid, a third concentric layer of clusters emerges at $N \approx 1800$. By analyzing the distribution of permutation cycles distribution, we demonstrate that a finite superfluid fraction ($f_s \approx 10\%$) persists even in this multi-layer regime. These findings clarify the role of particle number in driving layer formation on curved manifolds, offering a concrete guide for future experiments with bubble-trapped bosons.

papers.intro:
Supersolidity, the simultaneous appearance of crystalline order and superfluidity in the same many-body state [1], has long been sought in solid 4He [2] and ultracold bosonic gases [3]. Bosons interacting through a soft-core potential, which is zero beyond a certain range and remains finite at zero separation, provide one of the cleanest theoretical routes to capture the main features of the supersolid phase [4, 5, 6]. Above a critical density, the ground state spontaneously breaks translational symmetry to form a cluster crystal, with each site occupied by a mesoscopic, delocalized boson cluster, while the exchange of particles between clusters sustains a finite global superfluid fraction [1, 7].

In the last few years, extensive theoretical studies have explored the behavior of weakly interacting bosons on a sphere. Bereta et al. obtained the semiclassical critical temperature for Bose–Einstein condensation in spherical box and shell traps [28]. Tononi and Salasnich showed that, on a zero-thickness two-dimensional sphere, curvature restores a finite condensation temperature that would be forbidden in flat two-dimensional space (corresponding to the limit of infinite radius) [29]. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations have shown that, in a finite-thickness shell, superfluidity survives at the mesoscopic scale, up to a thousand particles [30]; a subsequent review placed these results in the broader context of shell-shaped atomic gases, emphasizing that condensation and superfluidity are, in principle, distinct transitions whose separation is itself controlled by curvature [31]. These studies, however, are restricted to the weakly interacting, dilute regime. The natural question is what happens when interactions are strong enough to drive the system toward crystallization — the regime addressed by the present work. Using Path Integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations, we have characterized the bubble-trapped system in a sequence of three studies. In the first work [33], we tuned the strength of quantum fluctuations (i.e., the boson mass) to drive a direct crystal-to-superfluid melting of a single layer of clusters, in good quantitative agreement with the corresponding two-dimensional flat-space result [6]. This picture was also discussed in Ref. [34], further including Earth’s gravity effects in a small system. Extending the particle number to a few hundred, and simultaneously weakening the trapping potential, revealed a richer phase sequence: a cluster crystal state with polyhedral symmetry, for small quantum fluctuations; a bilayer supersolid, in which a second layer of clusters emerges while crystalline order persists, for intermediate fluctuations; and a uniform, structureless superfluid shell, at larger fluctuations. The present paper extends this picture pushing the PIMC simulations to a previously unexplored large-NN regime, where an additional, third layer appears.

papers.title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.
papers.intro:
Ion channels are critically important therapeutic targets for channelopathies, playing foundational roles in the pathophysiology of epilepsy, cancer, and pain management. Consequently, identifying which proteins or peptides target specific ion channels is a central objective in drug discovery. Venomous organisms have independently evolved ion channel-targeting compounds across at least a dozen phyla over hundreds of millions of years (Casewell et al. 2013; King 2011). This convergent evolution produces a striking biological paradox: calcium, potassium, and sodium channel compounds from cone snails, spiders, scorpions, sea anemones, and snakes accomplish related functional disruptions through wildly divergent primary sequences and 3D folds (Olivera and Teichert 2007; Klint et al. 2012). For AI-driven drug discovery, capturing this structural and sequential flexibility requires robust representation learning paradigms. Specifically, these paradigms must learn to bypass surface-level sequence homology to identify the invariant topological features that actually dictate target binding. Previous computational efforts to map protein-ion channel interactions have utilized Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) (Sevgen et al. 2025), physicochemical property mapping (Chou 2001), sequence-based Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM) (Lin et al. 2023) + Random Forest architectures (Achimba et al. 2026), and family-specific tools like ICTCPred (Zhang et al. 2016). However, these deep learning models share a critical vulnerability: an inability to generalize to unseen proteins. Because they are typically evaluated under random train/test splits, classifiers tend to learn phylogenetic features rather than functional ones. We define the phylogenetic trap as the phenomenon where models achieve artificially inflated accuracy by memorizing evolutionary lineage leaked across random train/test splits, rather than learning generalized functional features. In practice (such as screening newly sequenced venom transcriptomes from uncharacterized species), a method that achieves 85% accuracy under a random split but 6% on an unseen taxon provides no scientific value.

papers.title: Can AI Co-Design Structures? An AI Agent for Early-Stage Structural Design
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models and agentic workflows offer a new paradigm to early-stage structural design translating design intent into structural models. Although text-to-3D approaches have demonstrated that natural language can be used to produce visual, mesh-based geometric models, structural design requires domain-specific geometric arrangements and semantically rich data types. This paper introduces a proof-of-concept workflow for prompt-to-structure generation using an AI agent connected to a COMPAS-based structural modelling API through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Through controlled modelling operations, the agent creates and modifies a graph-based structural data model composed of explicit building elements. The resulting artifacts can be inspected, modified, serialised, and further connected to downstream AEC workflows. The approach is demonstrated through selected prompt-to-structure examples and by progressive and editable design sequences that resemble typical iterative structural design workflows. The results are preliminary, but demonstrate the possibility of combining natural language, agentic workflows, and domain-specific structural data structures as a first step toward AI-assisted structural co-design.
papers.intro:
Structural design is not only a process of satisfying performance constraints but also a creative discipline in which form, force, materials, and construction logic are negotiated together. Torroja emphasized the role of intuition and imagination in the conception of structural form [26], while Billington described structural art as the integration of efficiency, economy, and elegance [4]. From this perspective, early-stage structural design cannot be reduced to the automatic generation of final solutions, but rather is an iterative process in which designers progressively develop their final result.

Previous work on computational structural design and engineering education has focused on making this exploration more creative and interactive by introducing geometry-based approaches to structural understanding [25, 1, 27, 17], developing computational tools to explore families of structural forms [21, 12, 24] and performing topology exploration rather than just looking for a single optimal design [19, 22, 6]. Further developing this line of work, text-enhanced structural design systems have introduced language as an interface for form-finding and conceptual exploration [9], including graph- and transformer-based algorithms [5]. In this context, recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows offer a new paradigm to early-stage structural design where AI systems can better understand design intent, create and edit 3D artifacts towards a co-design process.

papers.title: Moving Regions, Not Moving Objects: Segmenting What Actually Moves under Camera Motion
papers.abstract: Moving object segmentation is conventionally formulated at the sequence and object level, marking an entire instance as moving once it moves anywhere in a video. Recent instantaneous formulations distinguish moving from stationary intervals, but still generate masks at the object level through frozen segmentation foundation models. Because the mask is derived from an instance-level proposal, motion is typically attributed to the entire instance rather than localized to the regions that actually move. Moreover, such instance-level predictions can produce masks even when no part of the instance is actually moving, revealing a more fundamental issue: motion is not an intrinsic property of an instance; it can only be determined by comparing at least two frames. Building on this premise, we introduce MoRSe, which jointly interprets two frames to predict a moving-region mask, distinguishing actual scene motion from apparent motion induced by the camera. A single RGB encoder replaces multi-stage foundation stacks, so no optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask generator is needed at inference. We release MoRSe-5K, a benchmark of 42 sequences with Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic settings designed to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish and localize moving and stationary regions under different camera and scene motion conditions. MoRSe outperforms both specialized moving object segmentation methods and dense 4D reconstruction methods with motion-thresholded predictions, while producing the fewest false positives on sequences where nothing moves.

It prevents dynamic correspondences from corrupting structure from motion and SLAM, and provides physically grounded signals for 4D reconstruction. Whether a region is moving cannot be determined from its appearance alone: the same object may be stationary for one frame pair and moving for another, while a static wall may appear to move when the camera moves.

Existing methods usually follow one of two pipelines. Some estimate motion with optical flow or point tracks and then use a segmentation model to complete the mask. Geometry explains camera motion, while the segmentation stage recovers object extent (Xie et al., 2024b; Xie et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025; Goli et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). Errors can accumulate across correspondence, prompting, and mask propagation. Other methods reconstruct dense 4D motion and obtain a mask by thresholding the predicted displacement.
