papers.title: Local Discrimination of Binary Classifiers via Localized AUC Functional
papers.abstract: Risk prediction models are frequently evaluated with AUC, which means that during evaluation we are blind to performance heterogeneity, which could lead to bad decision-making in clinics. In this work, we aim to change that by identifying patient cohorts for whom the risk prediction model might not be an accurate predictor. To separate these cohorts, we use a version of the weighted AUC, which we call Localized AUC or LAUC. Using this metric, we build a method that we coin LOCATOR. This method is able to identify cohorts of patients for whom the risk prediction model is inaccurate. We test this method both in real-world data and in simulations. We also build a statistical background for the use of Localized AUC for our purposes.

papers.intro:
Binary classification models are some of the most widely used models. Their applications range from detection/diagnosis to prospective risk stratification. Therefore, an accurate and nuanced assessment of their quality of performance is of paramount importance. Yet, the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristics Curve [7] (AUROC, also known as AUC, c-index, concordance index, Harrell or Uno c-index), a widely used measure of model performance, rarely exceeds 0.80 across guidelines-recommended models (Khan et al., Circulation 2024 [8]). It is well below its theoretical maximum of 1.0 and has room to grow. However, current methods cannot identify, without loss of power, where this room is. The focus of this paper is to develop reproducible methods that identify, without loss of power, where the deployed classifier performs well or not so well, and separate genuine heterogeneity from cohort artifacts to guide model improvement in low-competence regions.

Several treatment guidelines rely on official binary classifiers that inform risk stratification for millions of people. Systematic COronary Risk Evaluation 2 (SCORE2) [19] and Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs (PREVENT) [12] models are embedded in European and US prevention guidelines, respectively, and supply the risk estimates that decide lipid- and blood-pressure-lowering therapy for hundreds of millions of adults [12]. Before release, these models are validated in external cohorts by reporting discrimination, calibration, and reclassification statistics. AUROC, a measure of a model’s ability to separate events from non-events, is a ubiquitous measure of model discrimination. It is often reported as one number per external cohort. However, a single per-cohort number cannot rule out the possibility that the model may separate events from non-events well in one region of covariate space and no better than chance in another. Patients in the weak regions receive systematically less accurate risk estimates and, therefore, less appropriate treatment. Indeed, accumulating evidence suggests that the performance of risk prediction models, including PREVENT, is not uniform across all patient subgroups [20]. Traditional approaches to investigating these performance variations typically rely on predefined, dichotomous subgroup classifications (e.g., smokers vs. non-smokers) [15]. While informative, such methods rely on subsetting the data and may fail to capture more complex, multidimensional patterns of phenotypic heterogeneity due to quick loss of power. There is no established estimand for local discrimination without subsetting the data, so heterogeneity is difficult to locate, quantify, or test without quickly loosing power.

There is no established estimand for local discrimination without subsetting the data, so heterogeneity is difficult to locate, quantify, or test without quickly loosing power.

In parallel, the concept of phenomapping has recently emerged [13]. Developed to assess heterogeneity of treatment effect in randomized controlled trials, it leverages the full breadth of data. By quantifying inter-individual similarity based on multiple clinical features (e.g., using Gower distance [6]), phenomapping allows for the discovery of contiguous, data-driven patient subgroups with heterogeneous treatment effect. This approach has been successfully applied to identify heterogeneity of treatment effects in clinical trials [13]. It relies on estimating the average per-person hazard, and therefore cannot be directly translated to AUROC. In this paper, we introduce a localized AUC functional LAUC, that, for a reference risk prediction model, estimates AUC for an index participant i using all participants weighted by similarity to i. By using the localized AUC functional, our LOCATOR algorithm avoids subsetting data altogether.

papers.title: Sparse power spectrum for passive scalars under Pierrehumbert flow
papers.abstract: We study the long-time Fourier distribution of driven passive scalars transported by an incompressible alternating shear flow (the Pierrehumbert flow) subjected to IID random phase shifts, in the regime of strong shear-strength. With a novel and self-contained proof, we establish (i) a quantitative version of the cumulative Batchelor's law; (ii) quantitative negative regularity mixing estimates; and (iii) a strong form of `sparsity' -- unevenness in the distribution of Fourier mass in radial sectors in frequency space. Our method uses the strong shear-strength assumption to handle a purely deterministic scalar driving term.

papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of Search Space Complexity and Efficiency for Time-Synchronous End-to-End ASR Models
papers.abstract: Search is a central component of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems and has been deeply investigated for classical ASR modeling based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). However, in work on current sequence-to-sequence ASR architectures it is often simplified to a small fixed-size beam search without external Language Model (LM). In this work, we present a comparative analysis of search space complexity and efficiency for Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and neural transducer models under different pruning strategies and LM configurations. We show that these end-to-end (E2E) models work with a small search space most of the time but exhibit large temporary peaks in hypothesis count during periods of uncertainty. Score-based pruning dynamically adapts the search to model uncertainty, leading to a significantly lower Real-Time Factor (RTF). Our results highlight the limitations of search with low fixed-size beam pruning and provide practical guidelines for efficient search in E2E ASR.

papers.title: Typed Template Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Fuzzing software with complex inputs has been a longstanding challenge. Traditionally, fuzzers either programmatically encode language constraints, requiring significant engineering effort, or rely on users to declare grammars and constraints. Recent LLM-based fuzzers address these drawbacks but introduce new issues. Some use LLMs for test generation, sacrificing throughput and producing invalid inputs when the LLM makes mistakes. Others rely on language-specific parsers, static analysis, and AST manipulation libraries. We introduce Typed Template Fuzzing (TTF), a lightweight LLM-based fuzzing methodology. The key idea is to use LLMs in a preprocessing step to transform seeds into typed templates. The typed templates then enable semantically aware, mutation-based fuzzing without language-specific parsers, type checkers, or further LLM queries during fuzzing. By exploiting the correspondence between seeds and templates, TTF can moreover repair LLM mistakes. We have implemented TTF in our tool Typos, which we evaluate across 21 input languages, including C, C++, Go, Rust, SystemVerilog, Scala, and Java, as well as libraries such as PyTorch and Qiskit. In a six-month fuzzing campaign, we reported 135 bugs, 128 of which were previously unknown. Perhaps most notably, on average 96% of Typos's mutants are valid, coming close to the validity rates of domain-specific fuzzers. Our evaluation further shows Typos's benefits over the state of the art.

Fuzzing is an automated testing technique for generating high input volumes to trigger unexpected behavior. Compilers, interpreters, constraint solvers, and libraries feature complex input languages, making it challenging to generate semantically valid input to exercise deep program behavior.

Fuzzing is an automated testing technique for generating high input volumes to trigger unexpected behavior. Compilers, interpreters, constraint solvers, and libraries feature complex input languages, making it challenging to generate semantically valid input to exercise deep program behavior.

Traditionally, two families of fuzzers address this challenge. Domain-specific fuzzers (Yang et al., 2011; Livinskii et al., 2020) programmatically encode input language constraints. While often producing valid input at a near-perfect rate, they require significant engineering effort to build and cannot be easily adapted to evolving languages. Domain-agnostic fuzzers include AFL-based (Zalewski, 2016; Fioraldi et al., 2020), grammar-based (Purdom, 1972; Hodován et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019), and language-based fuzzers (Steinhöfel and Zeller, 2022). These approaches either achieve low validity rates or require users to declare grammars and language constraints.

Domain-agnostic fuzzers include AFL-based (Zalewski, 2016; Fioraldi et al., 2020), grammar-based (Purdom, 1972; Hodován et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019), and language-based fuzzers (Steinhöfel and Zeller, 2022). These approaches either achieve low validity rates or require users to declare grammars and language constraints.

Recently, researchers have been using LLMs to address the shortcomings of the two fuzzing families (see Table 1 for a taxonomy). One way is to use LLMs for test generation in the fuzzing loop (Xia et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). While such an approach incurs low user effort, the drawback is that almost every mutant relies on a new LLM query, making fuzzing slow and costly. Moreover, LLM mistakes cannot be corrected, resulting in a high proportion of invalid mutants. LegoFuzz (Ni and Li, 2025) uses LLMs to produce a corpus of self-contained functions for mutating C programs. While LegoFuzz frees the fuzzing loop from LLM calls, it needs C-specific AST manipulation tooling and cannot repair LLM mistakes. MetaMut and Once4All (Ou et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026) use LLMs to generate code. Both feature repair mechanisms but remain domain-specific as the LLM-generated code relies on language-specific tooling (e.g., AST manipulation, parsing). Most recently, GenToo (Vikram and Padhye, 2026), an agentic approach for writing fuzzers for Java libraries, was proposed. While GenToo has an LLM-free fuzzing loop and repair for LLM mistakes, it is domain-specific, i.e., it relies on Java-specific static analysis.

We propose Typed Template Fuzzing (TTF), a lightweight LLM-based fuzzing approach. Its key idea is to use an LLM to create typed templates from a set of initial program seeds once, upfront, in a preprocessing step. The resulting typed templates contain annotations with type and scope information but are otherwise identical to the original seed programs. This correspondence allows us to repair LLM mistakes using a simple repair procedure. Given the typed templates, TTF chooses an expression at random and replaces it with a newly generated one of the same type. TTF has several distinctive advantages. First, TTF does not require domain-specific tooling such as a parser or type checker. Second, it does not need repeated LLM calls in the fuzzing loop or LLM-based iterative refinement. We realize Typed Template Fuzzing in a practical tool Typos, which we have extensively evaluated across 21 input languages. Our results reveal that Typos’s mutated test inputs are valid in 96% of cases on average, nearly matching purpose-built domain-specific fuzzers and outperforming or matching the previous state of the art in LLM-based fuzzing. We further conducted a bug-hunting campaign of 6 months on 27 targets across 21 languages, including GCC, G++, Clang, Clang++, rustc, Go, gccgo, javac, scalac, JerryScript, cvc5, Z3, slang, solc, Roslyn (csc), erlc, kotlinc, Lua, Perl, PHP, CPython, DuckDB, SQLite, scriptc, tsc, PyTorch and Qiskit. papers.title: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics
papers.abstract: Collective ordering in correlated electron systems emerges from microscopic dynamics, yet the evolution of observable textures need not admit a closed, memoryless description. We introduce a graph-recurrent neural network (GRNN) framework that learns such emergent dynamics directly from trajectories without specifying microscopic equations of motion. The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.

papers.title: A Hörmander spectral multiplier theorem for fractional Hardy operators
papers.abstract: We consider the fractional Laplacian with added critical or subcritical Hardy potential, called Hardy operator. We prove a Hörmander spectral multiplier theorem, i.e., the boundedness of sufficiently smooth multipliers of these Hardy operators on Lebesgue spaces. The range of admissible Lebesgue exponents is optimal, but the smoothness assumption is probably not. The proof combines the Helffer--Sjöstrand formula with a quantitative Jaffard lemma for operator-valued matrices.

papers.title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Online Policy Distillation (OPD) often outperforms offline methods such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) by training on trajectories sampled directly from the student. However, standard OPD trains the student to follow the teacher at every state of the trajectory, assuming that teacher guidance is always beneficial. We instead distinguish between what the teacher prefers and what actually helps the current student succeed. We introduce Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation (AOPD), which weights teacher actions by their counterfactual advantage under the student. Teacher actions that improve the student's expected outcome are reinforced, while those that do not are downweighted. Directly computing these advantages requires trying alternative teacher actions at each step and running new rollouts from each. Instead, we show that the AOPD objective can be estimated using only standard student rollouts and their terminal rewards. Our estimator uses teacher importance weights on the student-sampled actions to provide unbiased advantage-weighted supervision, without any additional rollouts or reward evaluations. This allows AOPD to focus teacher supervision on actions that help the current student while preserving the rollout efficiency of standard OPD. Experiments on math, coding, and Medqa show gains over distillation and RL baselines in both external-teacher and self-distillation settings.

papers.intro:
Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a stronger teacher to a smaller student model by training the student to imitate the teacher’s outputs. Offline distillation is a common approach that uses fixed teacher-generated trajectories. But this approach can lead to a mismatch between the training trajectories and the states the student generates itself. Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a stronger teacher to a smaller student model by training the student to imitate the teacher’s outputs. But this approach can lead to a mismatch between the training trajectories and the states the student generates itself. Although the trajectories now come from the student, the objective remains to match the teacher, without distinguishing which teacher actions improve the student’s chance of success (Liu et al., 2026).

This limitation also applies to on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which replaces the external teacher with a privileged version of the student itself, such as conditioned on ground-truth solutions (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). Whether external or privileged, the teacher may choose an action from which it can solve the problem, while the student cannot complete the remaining steps correctly. Conversely, distillation discourages a valid student solution when it differs from the teacher’s preferred approach. Thus the question is whether the teacher action at every state increases the student’s chance of success. An action should be credited according to its impact on the student’s task success, not simply the teacher’s preference (Chen et al., 2026; Saadi and Wang, 2026).

papers.title: Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts
papers.abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body-environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.

papers.intro:
Deploying humanoid robots in human-centric environments requires capabilities well beyond stable bipedal walking. Traversing cluttered and geometrically constrained environments often demands stepping across sparse footholds, climbing onto obstacles, crawling through confined spaces, or leveraging the upper body for support. These multi-contact behaviors fundamentally diverge from conventional locomotion. Instead of adhering to a prescribed pattern of foot contacts, the robot must continuously determine the spatial, temporal, and anatomical distribution of its environmental interactions. Achieving this capability while remaining robust to disturbances and generalizing to previously unseen terrain remains a central challenge for humanoid mobility.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for teaching quadrupedal and bipedal robots to swiftly navigate rough [20, 53, 18, 38, 29, 1, 7], sparse [42, 15, 12, 55], and even parkour [63, 14, 6, 26, 37, 17, 16, 58] terrains without reference motions. Similar principles have increasingly been applied to humanoids, enabling robust behaviors that adapt well to terrain variations [35, 10, 64, 59, 25, 44, 50, 41, 12, 58, 62, 60, 21, 8]. However, extending this paradigm to whole-body motion control introduces a massive combinatorial space. The robot must simultaneously determine which anatomical parts establish contact, the precise spatial and temporal distribution of those contacts, and the coordinated kinematics of the remaining degrees of freedom. Encoding these complex interactions indirectly through task objectives requires extensive reward shaping, where minor adjustments can yield drastically different contact strategies [48]. Consequently, while pure RL provides a powerful mechanism for robustness, reward signals alone offer insufficient structure for efficiently discovering complex whole-body behaviors.

Consequently, while pure RL provides a powerful mechanism for robustness, reward signals alone offer insufficient structure for efficiently discovering complex whole-body behaviors.

An alternative is to provide this structure directly through reference motions. Motion-imitation methods such as DeepMimic [34] reframe behavior discovery as a constrained tracking problem, enabling highly dynamic and coordinated whole-body motions. More recent systems extend this idea to humanoids using large motion datasets, retargeting, and learned motion priors [9, 13, 51, 57, 22, 2, 23, 54, 40, 27]. Such approaches naturally produce coordinated and human-like behaviors because the reference specifies not only the desired task outcome but also how the entire body should achieve it. Yet a tracking controller can only execute a suitable motion if an appropriate reference can first be generated for the current environment. During deployment in previously unseen environments, this shifts the central problem from control to reference generation.

During deployment in previously unseen environments, this shifts the central problem from control to reference generation.

One solution is therefore to generate these references online. Model-based approaches can use trajectory planners to provide dynamically feasible motions that are subsequently tracked by a learned controller [15, 19], given a user-specified velocity or goal command. This decomposition combines explicit reasoning about environmental geometry with the robustness of learned control. Yet it also makes deployment dependent on a whole-body planner, which can be computationally expensive and inherits the modeling assumptions and failure modes of the planning system. For highly dynamic locomotion with intermittent multi-contact interactions, generating accurate full-body trajectories in real time remains particularly challenging.

For highly dynamic locomotion with intermittent multi-contact interactions, generating accurate full-body trajectories in real time remains particularly challenging.

Recent work has consequently begun replacing model-based reference generation with learned motion generators or planners [52, 61, 47]. These methods provide a promising route toward more expressive whole-body behaviors by learning the distribution of feasible motions from data. Nevertheless, generating complete motion trajectories remains a high-dimensional prediction problem. Generalization to environment configurations not represented in the motion data often requires substantial data augmentation, and small trajectory errors can become consequential when steppable or contactable regions are sparse. In such environments, producing a motion that is kinematically plausible is insufficient: the predicted interaction with the environment must also be physically accurate.

A related line of work attempts to close the gap between reference-based training and autonomous deployment by composing, augmenting, or distilling reference motions into perceptive policies [49, 43, 45, 46, 3]. Wu et al. [49], for example, use motion matching to compose retargeted human skills into obstacle-adaptive reference trajectories, train tracking experts, and subsequently distill these behaviors into a vision-based policy. Wang et al. [43] introduce a generalist humanoid locomotion framework that trains multiple specialist policies for diverse skills and distills their expertise into a single vision-based policy through case-adaptive specialist selection, enabling unified locomotion control without reference motions at deployment. Wang et al. [45, 46] propose a hybrid imitation learning framework that combines reference motion tracking with adversarial imitation learning, enabling a unified controller to preserve the naturalness of motion data while improving skill composition and adaptation to procedurally generated environments. Chen et al. [3] introduce a single perceptive whole-body policy that autonomously transitions between conventional locomotion and parkour skills without reference motions or skill labels at deployment, using terrain-conditioned reference augmentation during training to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors from a small set of motion seeds. These approaches demonstrate that motion data can provide valuable priors for highly dynamic humanoid behaviors. However, they require machinery for adapting and composing full-body motions across environmental variations. As the diversity and required geometric precision of the terrain increase, constructing references that cover the relevant combinations of obstacle geometry, contact location, and skill transition becomes increasingly difficult. This raises a fundamental question: how much of a reference motion does a robot actually need in order to learn generalizable whole-body locomotion?

papers.title: Non-uniqueness for the forced one-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson equation
papers.abstract: We prove non-uniqueness for the forced one-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson equation on the whole space. More precisely, for every finite $p$, we construct a nonnegative ion density, smooth for positive times, and a source $S\in C([0,1];L^1(\R^2))$ with $S(0)=0$, for which there exist two distinct nonnegative distributional solutions $f_\pm\in C([0,1];L^1(\R^2))$ with the same zero initial datum and with spatial densities bounded in $L^p(\R)$ uniformly in time. The result is sharp in terms of the integrability of the spatial densities: our solutions have Lipschitz electric fields, and we show that in this class uniqueness holds as soon as the spatial density is bounded.

papers.title: Lenses make many points: Pure point spectrum disproves Simon's $L^2$ conjecture
papers.abstract: For every $d\ge2$ and $0\leσ<1/3$, we construct with LLM-assistance a smooth bounded nonnegative lens-type potential $V$ with arbitrarily small $\|V\|_\infty+\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|x|^{1-d+σ}|V(x)|^2 dx$, such that $-Δ+V$ has only pure point spectrum in $(0,\infty)$. Thus, we show that Barry Simon's $L^2$ conjecture, Problem 8 in "Schrödinger operators in the twenty-first century", is false.

papers.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where user trust is crucial (Chen et al., 2024). Here, non-experts frequently rely on LLM-generated rationales, treating them as transparent windows into the model’s decision-making (Barez et al., 2025). However, this trust is often misplaced. While techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and Chain of Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2023) produce highly plausible text, they optimize for human preference rather than mechanistic transparency. Consequently, these explanations are frequently unfaithful to the model’s internal logic (Mayne et al., 2026; Matton et al., 2025; Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023). Alarmingly, even researchers sometimes misuse these persuasive post-hoc rationalizations with true explanations (Barez et al., 2025).

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where user trust is crucial (Chen et al., 2024). Here, non-experts frequently rely on LLM-generated rationales, treating them as transparent windows into the model’s decision-making (Barez et al., 2025). However, this trust is often misplaced. While techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and Chain of Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2023) produce highly plausible text, they optimize for human preference rather than mechanistic transparency. Consequently, these explanations are frequently unfaithful to the model’s internal logic (Mayne et al., 2026; Matton et al., 2025; Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023). Alarmingly, even researchers sometimes misuse these persuasive post-hoc rationalizations with true explanations (Barez et al., 2025).

This fundamental disconnect is a critical barrier to safe deployment. Specifically, standard CoT prompting suffers from severe causal opacity driven by attention leakage, the phenomenon where dense, global attention mechanisms allow a model to implicitly bleed information across its entire context window rather than strictly depending on preceding logical steps. Because of this leakage, generated reasoning may appear perfectly logical while remaining entirely disconnected from the final prediction. For instance, Turpin et al. (2023) demonstrate that when provided with subtle context biases or unstated hints, models will heavily exploit these heuristics to derive an answer, yet completely omit them from their generated explanations, fabricating a step-by-step rationale that was never utilized. Furthermore, Lanham et al. (2023) reveal that actively modifying, degrading, or intervening on early CoT steps often yields surprisingly little impact on the downstream output. Together, these phenomena prove that standard autoregressive reasoning frequently acts as a superficial justification, rather than a sequence of causally relevant steps that drive the model’s behavior. Although recent frameworks have attempted to resolve this opacity via alignment training (Paul et al., 2024) or question decomposition (Radhakrishnan et al., 2023), they still evaluate steps within shared contexts, inevitably suffering from continued attention leakage.

papers.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
papers.abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.

papers.intro:
The physical systems and infrastructure that modern society runs on (hospitals, schools and university campuses, office and laboratory buildings, power distribution, water and transportation networks) are designed by professional physical engineers. Demand for this engineering work is rising rapidly: the American Society of Civil Engineers estimates a $3.7 trillion gap over 2024–2033 between what U.S. physical infrastructure needs to reach a state of good repair and forecasted investment (American Society of Civil Engineers, 2025), and worldwide infrastructure investment needs are forecast to reach $94 trillion by 2040 (Global Infrastructure Hub and Oxford Economics, 2017). Delivering even a single campus building, such as a new university laboratory, takes electrical, mechanical, structural and civil engineers to size its power distribution and feeders, its heating, cooling and ventilation plant, its frame and foundations, and its site grading and stormwater systems. They work to legally binding codes and physical laws (fig. 1), and their designs are signed off by licensed professionals, because errors in the design are costly and potentially catastrophic. Engineering design services represent hundreds of billions of dollars in annual economic activity (U.S. engineering-services firms alone report over $300 billion in yearly revenue (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024)), making professional physical engineering a high-value frontier for AI agents.

As fig. 1 illustrates across the four domains of PLE, a real-world physical engineering job requires far more than answering a textbook prompt: (A) Structural Engineering (Roof deck design) requires sizing steel roof decking, open-web joists and lateral diaphragm framing under gravity, snow-drift and shear loads so member demand stays within code capacity; (B) Civil Engineering (Site design) requires laying out a phased campus, access roads and utility corridors around delineated wetland buffers as a 3D IFC model; (C) Electrical Engineering (LV cable sizing) requires sizing low-voltage switchboards, overhead cable trays and 32 feeder and branch circuits under ampacity and voltage-drop limits; and (D) Mechanical Engineering (Cooling-tower LCC) requires selecting heat-rejection equipment, pumps and piping to meet thermal load within hydraulic flow limits while minimising 25-year life-cycle cost. Each task is long-horizon, spread across many documents in native formats, and combines retrieval, spatial and physical modelling, code compliance and cost optimisation, yet it is unusually measurable. Its deliverables are real engineering work products that can be checked against the governing documents and physics, so both the eligibility and the economic quality of a design can be scored objectively.

No existing benchmark measures this economically valuable work comprehensively, and the benchmarks that come closest are already too easy for leading agents. Existing engineering benchmarks for language models are mostly question answering over textbook problems or rule documents (Zhou et al., 2025; Doris et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024), or self-contained toy design and optimisation problems whose full specification fits in the prompt (Guo et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2026). Others target an isolated tool or modality, such as finite-element software (Mudur et al., 2025), CAD generation (Khan et al., 2024; Doris et al., 2026), circuit design (Lai et al., 2024; Bhandari et al., 2024) or drawing revision (Li et al., 2025). Solving those benchmarks does not get real engineering design work done, i.e., none requires an agent to navigate a realistic, messy, multi-format project corpus and issue a complete, billable engineering deliverable. The general professional-work benchmarks GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2025) and APEX-Agents (Vidgen et al., 2026) are closest in spirit. They grade with expert pairwise preferences or expert rubrics. However, in physical engineering, a rubric of binary checks alone cannot tell a merely code-compliant design from an economically competitive one, e.g. two wire schedules can both satisfy every code check while one costs over 20% more to install.

We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 expert-grade professional physical engineering tasks for AI agents, spanning electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering. Unlike prior academic or single-tool benchmarks, PLE is built for realism and direct economic value: solving a task in PLE means completing a real-world engineering assignment. Each task places an agent in a sandboxed environment that holds a realistic project file system of PDFs, spreadsheets, CAD/BIM drawings (DXF/DWG/IFC), correspondence and logs. The agent has tool access for documents, spreadsheets and code execution, and must produce cited, production-format deliverable files such as engineering memos, calculation workbooks, equipment schedules or 2D/3D drawings. We build the benchmark through two complementary routes: • Expert-Authored tasks. Practising engineers from the expert pool of our data vendor (Mercor) create tasks end to end inside realistic project “environments”, written as the real engineering requests a colleague or client would send on an active job. Each task is graded by a weighted rubric of binary, evidence-bound criteria (Vidgen et al., 2026) (section 3.1). • Co-Authored tasks. Practising engineers write the task briefs, and an adversarial Creator–Solver agent pipeline builds each task’s environment and grader from real, licensed engineering documents (Xu et al., 2026). Every task is iteratively redesigned until a frontier solver agent no longer saturates it, and passes an independent ground-truth audit. Mercor’s experts then validate or intensify the difficulty of every task (section 3.2). These tasks are scored by both rubric-style constraints and an economic or performance objective, which complements the rubric-only scoring of the expert-authored tasks. We evaluate 14 frontier models under seven publicly available agent harnesses (fig. 2). The best configuration, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, which demonstrates the difficulty of real-world physical engineering work.

papers.title: Comparing local and global optimization reveals untapped hybrid potentials for machine learning-based inverse planning
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models for normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) can be embedded directly into inverse treatment planning, but the resulting optimization problems are generally nonconvex, and the choice between global and local optimization involves a trade-off between optimality guarantees and computational cost. Two open-source frameworks for ML-based inverse planning were compared: OptiCL (global mixed-integer optimization via constraint learning) and pyanno4rt (local nonlinear optimization via end-to-end differentiation). Logistic regression, linear support vector machine, and feed-forward neural network NTCP models for grade 2+ xerostomia and grade 2+ radiation pneumonitis were embedded. Plan optimization was performed for eight head-and-neck (HN) photon cases and seven lung proton cases. The plans were compared by target coverage, OAR dose metrics, spatial dose agreement, post-hoc predicted NTCP, and runtime. A projection-based gradient approximation was introduced to embed decision trees. In addition to that, warm-starting, constraint strengthening, and pruning were investigated as hybrid strategies for combining local and global optimization. Comparing OptiCL and pyanno4rt across the HN and lung treatment plans revealed broadly consistent dose distributions. Mean differences (OptiCL}$-$pyanno4rt [95% CI]) were small: for HN cases, -0.16 Gy [-0.37, 0.06] (parotid) and -0.00 Gy [-0.01, 0.00] (PTV); for lung cases, -0.52 Gy [-1.10, 0.06] (total lung) and -0.04 Gy [-0.07, -0.01] (PTV). Mean NTCP differences amounted to -0.08 p.p. [-0.49, 0.33] (HN) and -1.73 p.p. [-2.68, -0.77] (lung). OptiCL tended toward lower OAR doses and predicted NTCP, but required higher wall-clock runtime. Hybridization of the decision tree-based HN plan eliminated 80% of binary decision variables without compromising plan quality.

papers.intro:
Inverse planning has traditionally relied on physical dose constraints and dose-volume histograms (DVHs) as surrogate measures for biological outcomes. This detaches the optimization process from the underlying clinical balance between tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP), formulating it as a dosimetric trade-off: “How can I maximize the physical dose to the tumor while minimizing it for organs-at-risk (OARs)?”. Consequently, optimization mostly relies on dose surrogate objectives—such as quadratic deviations from empirical dose prescriptions—in which dose-volume objectives and population-based tolerance doses stand in for individual complication risk, rather than directly minimizing the predicted toxicity for the individual patient. As a result, plans that satisfy all dose-volume criteria may still be suboptimal with respect to individual complication risk, while personal risk factors and their interplay with dose remain unaccounted for during optimization.

Recent advancements in machine learning (ML) for TCP and NTCP modeling, e.g. [1, 27, 31, 20, 10] for specific modeling approaches and [19, 4] for systematic reviews, have catalyzed a definitive shift toward outcome-driven inverse planning [32, 24, 2] which asks the more pertinent question: “How can I maximize tumor control while minimizing the occurrence of post-treatment complications?”. ML architectures have already selectively demonstrated superiority over classical radiotherapy treatment outcome models [41, 42, 37, 15, 27], not only for reasons of outperforming them in terms of predictive quality, but also thanks to their capacity to synthesize high-dimensional and heterogeneous inputs [23]. Such inputs range from dosiomics [35], radiomics [41, 42], demographics and clinical variables to potentially complex and large-scale multi-omics data [22]. By inferring the complex, nonlinear relationships between patient features and treatment outcomes, these models facilitate “high-fidelity” personalized planning tailored to a specific patient’s risk profile.

By inferring the complex, nonlinear relationships between patient features and treatment outcomes, these models facilitate “high-fidelity” personalized planning tailored to a specific patient’s risk profile.

Moving from physical surrogates to NTCP-driven objectives, however, also requires a new perspective on optimization. Conventional optimizers and treatment planning systems (TPS) can accommodate individualized planning as long as the NTCP model is additive in its dosimetric and non-dosimetric inputs and relies on a single dominant dose metric; in this case, the contribution of the patient-specific covariates can be factorized out and translated into a personalized dose constraint. This approach reaches its limits, however, when the model is not linearly separable or when several dosimetric predictors enter simultaneously, so that the trade-off between them is defined by the model rather than by a single tolerance value.

To fully leverage ML-based NTCP models in inverse planning, the prediction function should therefore be embedded directly within the optimization model. In this setting, the optimizer evaluates the NTCP prediction for every candidate dose distribution, with the patient-specific covariates (e.g., demographics or radiomic shape descriptors) held fixed at the values of the individual patient. Importantly, this does not require any assumption about how dosimetric and non-dosimetric inputs interact within the model, allowing the full prediction model to be incorporated without having to derive patient-specific dose constraints for each model structure. Depending on the model and its dose-dependent features, the resulting optimization problem may be nonconvex in the fluence, motivating different strategies for solving the embedded prediction problem.

[28] propose a framework inspired by optimization by constraint learning (OCL), which reformulates ML models as linear or mixed-integer constraints. This enables rigorous global optimality guarantees via solvers such as branch-and-bound, but at the cost of poor scalability and restricted model complexity. Conversely, the end-to-end differentiation framework introduced by [34] prioritizes computational efficiency, leveraging gradient-based methods to handle even highly expressive, nonlinear models. While this approach performs well on large-scale problems, it does not generally provide global optimality guarantees, as local nonlinear optimization may terminate at stationary points that are not globally optimal. In the context of radiotherapy, this distinction has direct implications for plan quality: a local optimizer may converge to a suboptimal stationary point of a nonconvex NTCP objective, yielding a plan whose predicted complication risk exceeds that of the globally optimal solution to the same problem, without providing the planner with any indication that a better solution exists. Conversely, the computational cost of global optimization determines whether NTCP-based planning is compatible with time-sensitive clinical workflows, including interactive planning, replanning, and multi-criteria exploration. Whether, and to what extent, local and global solutions differ for realistic NTCP models is therefore an empirical question that this study seeks to address.

To this end, we investigate the trade-off between global optimality and computational efficiency in ML-based inverse planning by comparing two optimization frameworks: OptiCL [30], which implements OCL, and pyanno4rt [33], which utilizes end-to-end differentiation. Analyzing treatment plans generated across eight head-and-neck (HN) and seven lung cancer cases (120 plans total), we quantify dosimetric and NTCP-based differences between these platforms. Here, predictions for normal-tissue toxicities are incorporated into model-based optimization functions, utilizing NTCP models for grade 2+ xerostomia and radiopneumonitis. Although technically feasible, TCP models and outcome-based optimization in a broader sense are outside the scope of this study, leaving tumor control evaluated purely dosimetrically. To explore the feasibility of hybridization, i.e., the transfer of information from the local nonlinear solution (optimized fluence and predicted NTCP) to the global mixed-integer solver, we leverage the nonlinear programming (NLP) solution of a decision tree-based HN plan to inform warm-start, strengthening, and pruning techniques. This approach allows to presolve the mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulation within OptiCL and reduce the computational complexity.

papers.title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. papers.title: Search for Ultra-Relativistic Magnetic Monopoles with LHAASO-KM2A
papers.abstract: Ultra-relativistic magnetic monopoles traversing the atmosphere are expected to initiate extensive air showers characterized by a muon deficit and a compact lateral profile. Using 1438.81 live days of data from the LHAASO-KM2A array, we present a search for these cosmic particles within the Lorentz factor range of $10^5$ to $10^7$. A machine-learning classifier utilizing lateral shower shape observables from the electromagnetic detectors is deployed to separate the signal from the hadronic background. No statistical excess above the background expectation is observed, and upper limits at the 90\% confidence level are established on the isotropic monopole flux. The resulting upper limit is $2.6 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ at $γ= 10^5$ and reaches $8.8 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ at $γ= 10^7$, which improves upon the astrophysical Parker bound by over three orders of magnitude. This work establishes constraints on the monopole flux within a previously unconstrained velocity window.

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of 3D-Printed Freeform Waveguides with a Transformation Optics-Based Beam Propagation Method
papers.abstract: An efficient numerical method is introduced for simulating wave propagation in 3D-printed freeform waveguides, referred to as photonic wire bonds (PWBs). This approach integrates transformation optics (TO) with curvilinear meshing to map the original 3D freeform PWB structure onto a straight waveguide, which possesses anisotropic material characteristics. The resulting waveguide is then analyzed using an anisotropic full-vectorial beam propagation method (BPM). To validate the performance and effectiveness of the proposed TO-BPM algorithm, a comparison is made with the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) technique. Our approach reduces the simulation time by more than two orders of magnitude, depending on the degree of trajectory bending, in combination with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 3.9% in power transmission simulation relative to the FDTD.

papers.intro:
Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) have emerged as essential building blocks for a broad spectrum of applications, enabling advancements across various technological domains. These include high-speed communication systems [4], cutting-edge artificial intelligence frameworks [17], ultra-fast signal processing techniques [5], precision optical metrology [20], as well as innovative solutions in life sciences and biophotonics [10]. The ability to integrate multiple photonic functions on a single chip has revolutionized these fields, providing unparalleled performance, miniaturization, and energy efficiency. From a technological perspective, photonic integrated circuits (PICs) primarily utilize planar designs, which are fabricated through well-established microfabrication techniques, including layer deposition and two-dimensional patterning via high-resolution electron-beam or deep-UV lithography [8]. In recent years, these traditional fabrication approaches have been complemented by two-photon lithography, which allows for the in-situ creation of three-dimensional freeform structures, thereby significantly improving the capabilities of planar PICs [25, 15, 26]. An especially intriguing method involves the use of 3D-printed freeform waveguides, referred to as photonic wire bonds (PWBs) [11]. These waveguides facilitate the interconnection of optical chips, such as those found in high-performance photonic multi-chip modules [25, 15]. A crucial feature of the PWB concept is its capability to address inherent alignment errors in the optical chips. This is achieved by adjusting the trajectory and geometry of the PWB to match the precise locations of the coupling facets. These positions are determined solely during the fabrication process and must be converted into a low-loss PWB design within seconds before printing. Currently, this is achieved using computationally efficient heuristic algorithms for PWB design, which select a smooth path to link the relevant optical interfaces [11, 14, 16]. Although this method is quick and produces satisfactory outcomes, it is unable to predict the PWB loss. In contrast, solvers based on first-principle Maxwell’s equations, such as those using the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method, have been investigated for PWB modeling [16]. However, even when adapted to the specific case of moderately bent planar waveguides through the use of transformation optics (TO), these solvers remain too slow [16]. The beam-propagation method (BPM) has been used for the efficient simulation of wave propagation in both isotropic and anisotropic media. However, due to its assumption of paraxial propagation, the technique encounters challenges when dealing with freeform bent structures [6]. Various BPM algorithms have been investigated to enhance the speed of electromagnetic simulations for integrated optical waveguides. Xu et al. [24] introduced suitable for planar waveguides with anisotropic materials. Lu et al. [13] proposed a method using a scalar BPM combined with a curvilinear coordinate system to model bent slab waveguides. Kawamura et al. [9] applied a full-vectorial BPM along with coordinate transformation to model tapered planar waveguides. An efficient Maxwell-based 3D freeform waveguide modeling and design tool is hence still lacking.

papers.title: SARIA: Persistence-Aware KV Caching with Coordinated DRAM--SSD Reload for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM agents usually reuse long context prefixes, making key value (KV) caching crucial for reducing prefill latency. SSDs provide a low-cost extension to limited DRAM capacity but introduce two key challenges. Eagerly persisting all KV cache blocks incurs substantial write traffic and rapidly consumes finite SSD endurance. Meanwhile, the small number of SSDs provisioned in typical GPU servers limits aggregate reload bandwidth, making SSD-resident KV cache much slower to retrieve than that in DRAM and inflating prefill latency. We present \textsc{Saria} (Selective Admission and Reload for Inference Acceleration), a KV caching system that jointly manages DRAM and SSD by exploiting the session-level temporal locality of LLM agents to reduce SSD writes and accelerate cache reload. On the write path, \textsc{Saria} uses eviction and reuse history to selectively persist KV cache blocks that exhibit reuse opportunities beyond their DRAM residency, avoiding unnecessary writes for KV cache already hosted in DRAM. On the read path, \textsc{Saria} promotes selected SSD-hit KV cache blocks from GPU memory into DRAM after prefill, allowing subsequent reuse within the same session to reduce SSD read traffic while limiting DRAM contention. A transfer coordinator paces DRAM reads while SSD transfers are active, allowing both paths to make progress and efficiently share GPU ingress bandwidth. We implement \textsc{Saria} on LMCache MP and evaluate it using workloads from TraceLab and WEKA, covering both full-attention and hybrid-attention models. The results show that \textsc{Saria} reduces SSD writes by 57.1--58.9\% compared with popular full duplicate caching and the mean time to first token (TTFT) by 42.3--79.7\% over DRAM-only caching.

To account for finite SSD endurance, Saria uses repeated DRAM evictions as evidence that a block needs SSD persistence. This is because requests within the same session often reuse KV cache blocks while they remain in DRAM, but contention from other active sessions or long inter-request intervals can evict these blocks before they are reused. Therefore, repeatedly evicted KV cache blocks have high potential for reuse after DRAM eviction. We also persist exceptionally popular KV cache blocks (based on their reuse counts) before they are evicted. To fully utilize GPU ingress bandwidth, Saria also uses the residual GPU ingress bandwidth to serve DRAM reloads for other requests (§4.5).

papers.title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
papers.abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.

papers.title: Can We Trust Evaluations of AI Weather Forecasts for Extremes? How Evaluation Protocols Shape Model Rankings
papers.abstract: AI weather models perform competitively with traditional physics-based models at a fraction of the computational cost, and they are thus already used operationally. However, studies reach conflicting conclusions about their ability to forecast extreme weather events, and comparisons across studies are complicated by differing evaluation protocols. We discuss the challenges that arise when comparing AI and physics-based weather forecasts for extreme events. Within a common experimental design, we find that model rankings are highly sensitive to the choice of evaluation metrics: the considered physics-based model tends to perform best when evaluation is restricted to observed extreme events, whereas AI models generally perform better when evaluated using weighted scoring functions. A contingency table analysis shows that AI models underpredict the frequency of extremes, so that their scores are generally dominated by misses, while the physics-based model forecasts extremes more frequently and its scores are dominated by false alarms. Different evaluation metrics penalise these errors differently. Further score decompositions confirm that the score differences arise primarily from miscalibration rather than discrimination ability. This sheds light on the contrasting results in the literature, and highlights the importance of the evaluation metrics used to evaluate AI models.

The value of weather forecasts lies in their ability to aid decision making. Since extreme weather events typically lead to the largest socio-economic impacts, accurate and reliable forecasts for these events are particularly valuable. These contrasting results may partly reflect differences in how the models are evaluated. Generally, AI model performance is not characterized by a single intrinsic quantity, but depends on the data, task, evaluation metric, and comparison protocol. Consequently, benchmark design can affect both reported performance and model rankings (Flach, 2019; Liao et al., 2021). Similar design choices arise when evaluating AI weather prediction models, which are often compared using different datasets, forecast models, definitions of extreme events, and evaluation metrics. While existing benchmark datasets (Rasp et al., 2024, e.g., WeatherBench 2,) facilitate standardized comparisons, important choices remain regarding how model performance should be assessed, with additional theoretical challenges arising for extreme events (Lerch et al., 2017; Brehmer and Strokorb, 2019).

Within a common experimental design, we compare deterministic (i.e. point-valued) forecasts from three state-of-the-art AI weather models to a physics-based model employed operationally at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF). The models are compared when predicting record-breaking heat, cold, and wind events. Predictive performance is assessed using multiple evaluation metrics. papers.title: On the Calibration of Isotonic Distributional Regression
papers.abstract: Isotonic distributional regression (IDR) has recently been proposed as a non-parametric technique for probabilistic forecasting via the estimation of conditional distributions under order restrictions, based on continuous outcomes from deterministic model outputs. IDR has been widely used and multiple studies report promising performance and well-calibrated forecasts across application domains. We document a peculiar out-of-sample artifact of IDR, where probability integral transform (PIT) values are rational fractions with empirical frequencies resembling Thomae's function, an effect which thus far seems to have been overlooked. This phenomenon is demonstrated empirically using meteorological data and a simulation study. We further provide a theoretical explanation linking the spiking behavior to the discrete structure of the isotonic fits, and discuss how this artifact can be mitigated via smoothing approaches.

papers.title: Conservative Finite Element Methods for Kirchhoff-Type Equations
papers.abstract: We construct and analyse a fully discrete scheme for a Kirchhoff-type nonlinear integro-differential equation in two spatial dimensions with time-dependent coefficients. The scheme combines a symmetric three-layer time discretization of Crank--Nicolson type with a conforming finite element method of arbitrary polynomial degree $p$ and a Picard iteration for the nonlinearity. We prove that the Picard iteration is well defined and, that the iterates converge to the Ritz projection of the exact solution measured in fractional-power norms of the discrete Laplacian. Running the same energy argument in the unshifted norms, and under the same hypotheses, we then obtain the optimal order $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p+1} + τ^2 )$ in $L^2$ and $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p} + τ^2 )$ in $H^1$ for the full error. For the homogeneous problem with constant coefficients, the exact solution of the scheme moreover preserves a discrete energy identically. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions reproduce the predicted second order in time and the full spatial order $h^{p+1}$ in the $L^2$-norm.
papers.intro:
Kirchhoff-type equations constitute an important class of nonlocal partial differential equations arising from the classical model proposed by Kirchhoff as an extension of the linear theory of vibrating strings; see [17]. In this model the tension varies according to the total stretching induced by the displacement, so that the principal part of the equation depends on a global quantity involving the solution itself, typically its Dirichlet energy. In two spatial dimensions, the equation models the transverse vibrations of an elastic membrane whose effective tension depends on its total deformation energy, a setting that arises in contemporary work on nanomechanical oscillators [35]; allowing the material parameters to depend on time reflects the variation of those properties during vibration, for instance under thermal fluctuation or strong external driving [29, 32].

Numerical methods for Kirchhoff-type equations have a long history. Christie and Sanz-Serna [8] combined a finite element discretization in space with a Crank–Nicolson scheme in time for the one-dimensional problem with constant coefficients. In [24], Peradze proposed and analyzed a numerical scheme combining a sine-based Galerkin spatial discretization with a Crank–Nicolson-type time-stepping method for the nonlinear one-dimensional homogeneous Kirchhoff string problem with constant coefficients. Gudi [15] investigated a finite-element approximation of a second-order nonlinear elliptic boundary value problem that arises as the stationary counterpart of the generalized Kirchhoff equation. More recently, Mallik [22] developed and analyzed a hybrid high-order finite element method for a nonlocal nonlinear elliptic boundary value problem of Kirchhoff type, establishing optimal-order convergence in the discrete energy norm. Rogava and Tsiklauri [26, 27] analysed symmetric three-layer semi-discrete schemes in an abstract setting and established local convergence; the one-dimensional problem with time-dependent coefficients was treated in [28], and related schemes appear in [25, 34, 33]. papers.title: A Universal Constitutive Relation for Static Droplet Retention
papers.abstract: Under applied forcing, static droplet retention is accompanied by contact angle asymmetry, with unequal apparent contact angles on opposite sides. Yet, the relation between the asymmetry and forcing lacks a common constitutive basis. Here, we show that the asymmetry emerges from minimizing the forcing-dependent free energy. The response of the asymmetry to forcing defines a susceptibility whose zero-forcing value yields a universal constitutive relation between the asymmetry and forcing. The constitutive relation is quantitatively validated across liquids, volumes, and forcing levels.

Droplet retention on solid substrates is widespread in nature, as seen in raindrops clinging to leaves and windows, and is important in technologies including coating [8], printing [7], and liquid manipulation [6]. A basic manifestation of such retention under forcing is static contact angle asymmetry, in which a stationary droplet exhibits different apparent contact angles on its fore and aft sides [9, 16]. How this asymmetry relates to the applied forcing is therefore central to understanding droplet retention.

Droplet retention on solid substrates is widespread in nature, as seen in raindrops clinging to leaves and windows, and is important in technologies including coating [8], printing [7], and liquid manipulation [6]. A basic manifestation of such retention under forcing is static contact angle asymmetry, in which a stationary droplet exhibits different apparent contact angles on its fore and aft sides [9, 16]. How this asymmetry relates to the applied forcing is therefore central to understanding droplet retention.

For decades, the forcing–asymmetry relation has been formulated from different physical viewpoints. Three representative formulations are summarized as follows: (i) The Kawasaki–Furmidge model [12, 10] starts from the capillary traction acting along the contact line; integrating its component along the forcing direction yields a force proportional to contact angle asymmetry, with the contact line geometry entering through a empirical factor. (ii)The McHale model [14, 15] recasts droplet retention as an Amontons-like friction law, in which the normal load is replaced by a capillary normal force. The applied forcing is then related to this load through an effective friction coefficient determined by contact angle asymmetry. (iii) The Tadmor model [20, 19] attributes the forcing–asymmetry coupling to interfacial deformation induced by the uncompensated normal component of surface tension. The strength of this coupling is governed by an interfacial modulus. Despite these distinct formulations, whether the forcing–asymmetry relation admits a common constitutive basis remains unresolved.

The applied forcing is then related to this load through an effective friction coefficient determined by contact angle asymmetry. The strength of this coupling is governed by an interfacial modulus. Despite these distinct formulations, whether the forcing–asymmetry relation admits a common constitutive basis remains unresolved.

In this Letter, we resolve this long-standing ambiguity by demonstrating that the forcing–asymmetry relation emerges as a macroscopic equilibrium response governed by the free energy landscape. We incorporate the pressure field generated by the applied forcing consistently into both the interfacial and bulk contributions to the droplet free energy. Minimization over the resulting free energy landscape selects the equilibrium state, from which both apparent contact angles and their asymmetry follow. As the forcing varies, these selected states trace a branch, with the local variation of the asymmetry quantified by a susceptibility. Near the unforced state, we obtain a constitutive relation linking the forcing to the contact angle asymmetry, with the zero-forcing susceptibility as the response coefficient.

papers.title: The deepest X-ray view of a kiloparsec scale jet at z=6.1
papers.abstract: The mechanism responsible for the high-energy emission observed in kiloparsec-scale jets across cosmic time remains poorly understood. The relativistic jet associated with the z=6.1 AGN PSO J030947.49+271757.31 is the highest-redshift large-scale jet currently resolved in X-rays, providing a unique opportunity to study these structures. We present new Chandra observations, combined with archival data, for a total exposure of 360 ks. The increased exposure allowed us to resolve the extended X-ray emission into two distinct, slightly resolved components and perform spatially resolved spectral analyses. The extended emission has a photon index of Gamma = 2.25 (+0.45, -0.44), steeper than that of the core (Gamma = 1.86 +/- 0.09), and an extended-to-core luminosity ratio of 18%. Simulations using the Chandra image as input show that an AXIS-like mission could increase the detected photon statistics by a factor of approximately 17. We resolve the kiloparsec-scale jet into two main components and constrain its spectral properties. This is the most distant and one of the most X-ray-luminous large-scale jets currently known. Future X-ray missions with arcsecond-scale angular resolution could enable more detailed studies of such systems and reveal a population of fainter high-redshift jets beyond Chandra's reach.

papers.intro:
Relativistic jets, generated by accreting supermassive black holes (SMBHs), are an essential part of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) evolution and feedback. They can transport a large amount of energy and release it onto the host galaxy and surrounding intergalactic medium (Fabian, 2012; Blandford et al., 2019, see). Observations with the Chandra X-ray Observatory showed that most of the extended radio jets from AGN have high-energy counterparts detectable up to hundreds of kpc away from the central SMBH (e.g., Schwartz et al. 2000; Sambruna et al. 2004; Connor et al. 2021). However, despite the detection of hundreds of such systems (Harris & Krawczynski, 2006, e.g.), these data have not yielded a homogeneous consensus in their interpretation but rather has given rise to a controversy with profound implications for relativistic jet composition and physics (e.g., Georganopoulos et al. 2006; Tavecchio 2021; Meyer et al. 2023).

Based on one of the first and most popular scenarios, high-energy radiation observed in kpc-scale jets is produced through the Inverse Compton interaction of the electrons within the jet with the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) photons (IC/CMB), which are up-scattered into the X-ray and γ\gamma-ray band (Tavecchio et al. 2000; Celotti et al. 2001). papers.title: Matrix-Free Local Multigrid for $C^1$ Hermite Discretizations on GPUs
papers.abstract: I present a matrix-free local multigrid method for $C^1$ tensor-product Hermite discretizations on adaptively refined Cartesian meshes, using the clamped biharmonic problem as the model problem. Extending a cell-wise primal-dual formulation to Hermite elements, I enforce continuity through a constraint operator that is never formed. At refinement edges, geometric prolongation supplies both the trace and its normal derivative, so the local V-cycle needs no edge operator and no hanging-node machinery. For the cubic element, an even-odd decomposition based on the signed reflection symmetry of the Hermite basis, applied along two axes, splits the element matrix into four dense $16\times16$ blocks and reaches 85% of peak memory bandwidth. Chebyshev-Jacobi and vertex-patch smoothers both preserve conformity by construction. In three dimensions on one NVIDIA A100 in double precision, conjugate gradients preconditioned by the Chebyshev-Jacobi V-cycle need five or six iterations on uniform meshes and solve at up to 4.23 million cells per second. On locally refined meshes the count rises to at most sixteen, ordered by the fraction of cells on a refinement edge and nearly equal for both smoothers.

Their efficiency on tensor-product elements rests on sum factorization and fast quadrature, developed in the spectral and h​php finite element literature [34, 32]. Efficient solves require smoothing and inter-grid transfer to preserve the operator’s advantages in data movement, local arithmetic, and parallelism.

papers.title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
papers.abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

papers.intro:
To date, transmission spectroscopy has proven to be one of the most powerful techniques available for the characterization of exoplanetary atmospheres. With the operational success of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the exoplanet community has increasingly focused on the “small star opportunity.” This approach leverages the favorable planet-to-star size ratio inherent to M-dwarf and late K-dwarf systems to probe the atmospheres of sub-Neptune and Earth-sized planets [8, 16]. However, these lower-mass host stars are generally more active than Sun-like stars. The presence of surface inhomogeneities, such as starspots and their bright counterparts, faculae, presents a major challenge for exoplanet transmission spectroscopy [9, 10]. When an exoplanet transits a spotted star, the unocculted stellar surface spectrum can differ significantly from the transit chord. This causes stellar spectral features to be imprinted onto the planetary transmission spectrum. Ultimately, this stellar contamination can mimic or suppress true atmospheric features in the intrinsic planetary spectrum.

The Pandora SmallSat, selected under the NASA Astrophysics Pioneers Program, is designed to directly address this challenge by disentangling stellar and planetary signals. Successfully launched on January 11, 2026, into a Sun-synchronous low Earth polar orbit, Pandora employs a dual-channel observational approach. The observatory simultaneously captures visible photometry (∼\sim0.4–0.7 μ\mum) to measure time-varying stellar brightness and near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy (∼\sim0.8–1.6 μ\mum) to probe planetary atmospheric composition along with stellar spectral variations. By combining these datasets, the mission aims to provide the robust data necessary to accurately identify water- or hydrogen-dominated atmospheres.

However, the transition from ground-testing to in-orbit operations presented unique environmental and operational complexities. Consequently, Pandora has undergone an extended commissioning phase. This additional time was necessary to fully characterize the flight performance of the detector assemblies and refine the spacecraft’s observational parameters.

This provides valuable insight into Pandora’s in-flight capabilities for delivering the precision multi-wavelength observations required to reliably characterize exoplanet atmospheres.
