papers.title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. II. The Multi-component Age-Metallicity Structure of the High-$α$ Disk
papers.abstract: Whether the high-$α$ disk experienced a continuous or episodic star-formation history remains an open question. Here we investigate the age--metallicity distribution of the high-$α$ disk using approximately 145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants with $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]>-1$, 6.5~kpc $\lesssim R\lesssim9.5$~kpc, and $|Z|\lesssim1.5$~kpc. We adopt a forward-modelling framework that accounts for individual age and metallicity uncertainties and corrects for sample selection effects. The reconstructed distribution reveals two components: a broad, dominant population peaking at $\sim10.6$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.38$, and an older, more metal-poor population peaking at $\sim12.4$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.79$. These features suggest an episodic history of star formation and chemical enrichment in the high-$α$ disk, qualitatively consistent with cosmological simulations in which recurrent gas accretion drives variations in the star formation rate. The age of the older component is close to the $\sim12.3$~Gyr epoch inferred for the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles accretion event, suggesting a possible connection between this early interaction and enhanced disk star formation. There is tentative evidence that the dominant population is possibly composed of two sub-components with age distributions peaking at $\sim11.1$ Gyr and $\sim10.0$ Gyr, respectively. Together, these results favour a picture in which the high-$α$ disk was built through recurrent episodes of enhanced star formation rather than a single temporally smooth phase, even for the regime of ${\rm [Fe/H]}>-1$.

papers.intro:
The age–metallicity relation (AMR) is a fundamental diagnostic of Galactic chemical evolution, encoding the coupled histories of star formation, gas accretion, chemical enrichment, and dynamical assembly in the Milky Way. The observed morphology of the AMR, however, depends critically on the precision of stellar age estimates. Large age uncertainties can blur intrinsically coherent structures in the age–[Fe/H] plane and thereby obscure the underlying evolutionary sequences. This limitation is particularly important for the Galactic disk, where the metallicity evolution is not simply monotonic with time (age) [4, 8, 36, 13, 24, 28, 34, 1, e.g.,].

Observations reveal two prominent disk populations in the age–[Fe/H] plane: an old, high-α\alpha population associated with (but not identical to) the thick disk and a younger, low-α\alpha population associated with the thin disk. The latter itself also comprises at least two components: an outer-disk component characterized by a clear negative AMR, and a more metal-rich inner-disk component whose AMR exhibits clumps and blobs [14, 13, 20, 28, 34]. These discontinuous features in the AMR appear broadly consistent with predictions from cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, which suggest that galaxy mergers and episodic gas infall can trigger bursty star formation and imprint distinct sequences or stellar groups in the age–[Fe/H][\mathrm{Fe/H}] plane [26, 33, e.g.,]. More specifically, using FIRE-2 cosmological simulations, S. Yu et al. [39] find that thick-disk stars formed predominantly during an early phase of bursty star formation.

papers.title: Invisibilization as a Source of Probability Bias in Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models are aligned to avoid using protected attributes such as race, ethnicity, and gender to inform their responses. Therefore, they increasingly refuse or hedge when such attributes appear in a prompt. However, if a system must decide how much to learn from what people tell it, it is costly to refuse valuable information because of its source. In this article, we measure the cost of declining information in a two-urn game with an exact Bayesian answer. We present leading LLM models from two developers (OpenAI and Anthropic) with a prompt that requires them to decide how far to trust an unverifiable report from a participant whose description we randomize across ten configurations (6,600 sessions). We show that leading models often decline to assess the reporter, treating information as worthless at rates set by the description rather than by the evidence. At its widest, models decline a Black-described reporter 46% of the time and a white-described reporter 9%; yet, when they do assess the information, the Black-described reporter receives slightly more trust. The bias is invisible to audits that compare average trust or look only at assessed cases. It grows with reasoning effort, follows words rather than categories (models invoke race for "Black" but not for its Spanish translation negro, and never for "Indigenous"), and worsens under warning instructions a practitioner would try first. We also present a scoring option that reduces the refusal rate bias. When a model's trust is scored against revealed truth over repeated rounds, it credits identical records equally. In four of five configurations from Anthropic and OpenAI, the racial gap in trust falls below 0.02 by the last rounds.

papers.title: The ALMA-QUARKS survey: A Keplerian Circumbinary Disk Candidate in the High-mass Star-forming Region IRAS 08303-4303
papers.abstract: We present the ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations of IRAS 08303-4303, a high-mass star-forming region, with an angular resolution of $\sim 0.3''$ ($\sim 700$ au at the distance of 2.35 kpc). Six dense condensations are identified in the 1.3 mm continuum, and at least four of them are associated with molecular outflows. The estimated outflow parameters, particularly mass outflow rates $\geq 10^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, suggest that the driving sources are high-mass young stellar objects. Two of the condensations are forming a wide protobinary system with a separation of $\sim 900$ au. They reside within a single rotating structure, identified as a circumbinary disk which has a mass of about 2 $M_{\odot}$. This structure is traced by multiple molecular lines and exhibits a Keplerian rotation pattern. Based on the Keplerian rotation assumption, the enclosed mass is derived to be between 32 and 61 $M_{\odot}$: 22-43 $M_{\odot}$ for the primary and 10-18 $M_{\odot}$ for the secondary. The circumbinary disk is on the whole gravitationally stable, yet some parts with Toomre $Q < 2$ indicate potential fragmentation. Various molecular lines reveal a streamer-like structure connecting to the circumbinary disk, suggesting transfer of material from the envelope to the protobinary system through it. Despite the observational rarity of such circumbinary disks around high-mass YSOs, the high binary fraction among massive stars underscores their significance. This source, therefore, serves as a key laboratory for understanding the formation of high-mass binary systems.

papers.intro:
High-mass stars (M≥8​M☉M\geq 8~M_{\sun}) typically form within dense regions of molecular clouds, known as hubs, where filaments converge [28, 58, 119]. These potential high-mass star-forming regions may exist as prestellar cores for <104<10^{4} years [30, 100, 77]. During the early stages of high-mass star formation, stellar embryos with masses less than 8​M☉8~M_{\sun} are IR-quiet protostars [11, 76, 77, 88]. Protostars become IR-bright when the stellar embryos reach M≥8​M☉M\geq 8~M_{\sun}, entering the high-mass protostellar object (HMPO) stage [76, 77, 88]. The HMPO stage can be further divided based on chemical characteristics into two categories: chemically poorer (earlier) HMPOs [36] and later, hot molecular cores (HMCs) that exhibit molecular-rich chemistry [36, 63, 87]. HMCs are characterized by rich spectra of complex organic molecules (COMs), high temperatures (≳100\gtrsim 100 K), and compact source sizes (≲0.1\lesssim 0.1 pc) [23]. Eventually, when the ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the embedded high-mass (proto)star ionizes the surrounding gas, a hyper-compact Hii (HCHii) or ultra-compact Hii (UCHii) region is formed. Due to the short evolutionary timescales, multiple stages can overlap; for instance, line-rich HMC chemistry and emission from ionized gas may coexist within the same core [63]. Additionally, because high-mass stars typically form in clusters, individual cores at varying evolutionary stages are frequently observed in close proximity to one another [65].

Protostars become IR-bright when the stellar embryos reach M≥8​M☉M\geq 8~M_{\sun}, entering the high-mass protostellar object (HMPO) stage [76, 77, 88]. The HMPO stage can be further divided based on chemical characteristics into two categories: chemically poorer (earlier) HMPOs [36] and later, hot molecular cores (HMCs) that exhibit molecular-rich chemistry [36, 63, 87]. HMCs are characterized by rich spectra of complex organic molecules (COMs), high temperatures (≳100\gtrsim 100 K), and compact source sizes (≲0.1\lesssim 0.1 pc) [23]. Eventually, when the ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the embedded high-mass (proto)star ionizes the surrounding gas, a hyper-compact Hii (HCHii) or ultra-compact Hii (UCHii) region is formed. Due to the short evolutionary timescales, multiple stages can overlap; for instance, line-rich HMC chemistry and emission from ionized gas may coexist within the same core [63]. Additionally, because high-mass stars typically form in clusters, individual cores at varying evolutionary stages are frequently observed in close proximity to one another [65].

Around an accreting protostar, the centrifugal force of rotating material typically balances gravity, leading to the formation of a rotationally supported structure. While this often results in a Keplerian disk (v∝r−0.5v\propto r^{-0.5}, 118), actual disks frequently exhibit deviations from a strict Keplerian profile due to additional physical factors, such as self-gravity, internal gas pressure in hot disks, and magnetic braking effects. Some of the infalling material is ejected as a bipolar outflow, a process driven by complex magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) that helps carry away excess angular momentum [102]. This disk-outflow system is crucial for massive young stellar objects (MYSOs), as it protects the accretion process from the intense radiation (L≥103​L☉L\geq 10^{3}~L_{\sun}) pressure exerted by the central protostars [57]. Recently, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) has identified Keplerian disk candidates around several MYSOs [10, 47, 46, 45, 37, 73, 75, 69, 109], some of which extend up to a few hundred au. These disks are often associated with COMs such as acetonitrile (CH3​CN\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{CN}, e.g., 47, 46) and methanol (CH3​OH\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{OH}, e.g., 46, 109). In certain cases, refractory molecules like sodium chloride (NaCl, e.g., 39, 38, 97) or hydrogen recombination lines from ionized gas (e.g., 74) can be used to trace the presence of these disks. In contrast, bipolar molecular outflows are usually traced using carbon monoxide (CO, e.g., 114). Silicon monoxide (SiO) line emissions frequently indicate central jet-like features along the axes of broader CO outflows (e.g., 68).

High-mass stars are often found in binary or multiple star systems. Multiple surveys, mainly in the optical and near-infrared regimes, have shown that the multiplicity fraction—defined as the proportion of primaries having at least one companion—among main-sequence high-mass stars exceeds 90% [81]. Despite this high percentage, the early formation phases of such massive binary systems remain largely unexplored. In low-mass binary systems, we can observe large rotating structures that surround both protostars and their accretion disks, commonly referred to as “circumbinary disks”, e.g., L1551 NE [95, 96], L1551 IRS 5 [25], [BHB 2007] 11 [3]. However, circumbinary disks have only been observed around a very limited number of massive proto-binary systems. One example is the massive protobinary system IRAS 16547–4247 in which a circumbinary disk was detected using the well-known disk tracer CH3​CN\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{CN} [97], along with other COMs, such as methyl formate (CH3​OCHO\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{OCHO}, 116).

MYSOs are rare and are predominantly found at distances exceeding 2 kpc. This distance poses significant challenges for observational studies due to limitations in spatial resolution. However, the deployment of the ALMA has made it possible to resolve the small structures surrounding these distant objects. One notable statistical survey focused on high-mass star-forming regions in the galactic plane is the “ALMA Three-millimeter Observations of Massive Star-forming regions (ATOMS)” project [65]. The ATOMS project observed 146 massive protoclusters at a wavelength of 3 mm with resolutions ranging from 1″ to 2″. Additionally, 139 of these protoclusters were further observed at a wavelength of 1.3 mm by the “Querying Underlying mechanisms of massive star formation with ALMA-Resolved gas Kinematics and Structures (QUARKS)” project [67]. The QUARKS project achieved high resolutions of ∼\sim0.′′\farcs3, while also covering large-scale flux up to 27″ through Atacama Compact 7-m Array (ACA) observations [112]. The QUARKS frequency band captures numerous molecular tracers of disks and outflows (as detailed in Table 2 of 67), making it particularly well-suited for investigating various aspects of disk-outflow systems surrounding MYSOs.

papers.title: EP J062132.0+623837: A Multi-wavelength Study of a Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Discovered by Einstein Probe
papers.abstract: EP J062132.0+623837 is a new X-ray source identified in 14-day binned survey data from the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe (EP). Subsequent X-ray observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board EP localized the source to the central region of the galaxy 2MASX J06213207+6238390 at $z=0.084$. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the multi-wavelength data for this object. During the FXT and Swift/XRT follow-up, the source remained X-ray active, with observed luminosities of $(3-9)\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and its X-ray spectra were well described by power-law models with photon indices of $Γ\sim1.5$. The optical spectrum of the host galaxy clearly reveals a broad-line active galactic nucleus (AGN) exhibiting significantly enhanced broad Balmer emission lines compared to an archival spectrum obtained four years earlier, thereby marking a changing-look transition from Type 1.8 to Type 1.5. Furthermore, long-term optical and mid-infrared light curves indicate that the nucleus underwent dramatic brightening around 2010 and has since shown substantial variability. Given the spatial coincidence and multi-wavelength behavior, we identify EP J062132.0+623837 as a changing-look AGN, initially detected by EP and subsequently confirmed to exhibit large-amplitude variability across multiple bands. This case study demonstrates the great potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys for discovering changing-look AGNs, paving a new avenue for their systematic identification as a powerful complement to ongoing optical surveys.

papers.intro:
Changing-look active galactic nuclei (CLAGNs) are a remarkable class of accreting supermassive black holes that undergo dramatic spectral-state changes on humanly accessible timescales. Their defining observational signature is the appearance, disappearance, or strong change of the broad emission-line component, often accompanied by substantial continuum variability across multiple wavebands [37, 43, e.g.,]. CLAGNs provide a valuable probe of the inner accretion flow, the ionizing radiation field, and the response of the broad-line region (BLR) and circumnuclear dust, and have therefore become an important topic in time-domain studies of black hole accretion [59]. Large optical time-domain surveys have further shown that CLAGNs are not isolated curiosities, but part of a broader population of strongly variable AGNs uncovered in recent years [24, 74, e.g.,].

Their defining observational signature is the appearance, disappearance, or strong change of the broad emission-line component, often accompanied by substantial continuum variability across multiple wavebands [37, 43, e.g.,]. CLAGNs provide a valuable probe of the inner accretion flow, the ionizing radiation field, and the response of the broad-line region (BLR) and circumnuclear dust, and have therefore become an important topic in time-domain studies of black hole accretion [59]. Large optical time-domain surveys have further shown that CLAGNs are not isolated curiosities, but part of a broader population of strongly variable AGNs uncovered in recent years [24, 74, e.g.,].

The changing-look phenomenon encompasses a wide range of spectroscopic behaviors. In the most dramatic cases, an AGN transitions from a Type 1 spectrum, characterized by prominent broad Balmer emission lines, to a Type 2 spectrum dominated by narrow emission lines [37, 61, e.g.,], or vice versa [22, 72, e.g.,]. In low-redshift AGNs, changing-look behavior can also include transitions among intermediate Seyfert subclasses, such as Types 1.2, 1.5, 1.8, and 1.9. These classifications are traditionally based on the visibility and relative strength of the broad Balmer components [52, 53, 54, e.g.,], and can in some cases be quantified using empirical flux ratios involving Hβ\beta, Hα\alpha, and [O iii] [12, 70, e.g.,]. Recent studies have increasingly recognized such intermediate-type transitions as part of the broader changing-look AGN (CLAGN) phenomenon [13, 38, 26, 59, e.g.,]. In this sense, CLAGNs are best understood as manifestations of dramatic AGN state changes, rather than as a narrowly defined class of events [59].

Most CLAGNs have so far been discovered through optical routes. One major path has been the identification of large-amplitude optical variability in wide-field surveys, followed by spectroscopic confirmation of the changing-look nature of the source [43, 24, e.g.,]. Another has been the direct comparison of repeated optical spectra, which remains one of the most straightforward ways to establish changes in the broad-line appearance [37, 73, e.g.,]. Systematic multi-epoch spectroscopic searches have further expanded the CLAGN census, including recent DESI-based work that has substantially increased the known sample and explicitly incorporated intermediate-type transitions into the broader CLAGN search framework [26]. These optical approaches have produced the majority of currently known CLAGN samples and have established the phenomenological diversity of the class [74, 59, e.g.,].

Mid-infrared (MIR) variability provides a complementary and increasingly important discovery route. Because the hot-dust emission traces reprocessed radiation from the central engine and is less sensitive to dust extinction than the optical continuum, MIR light curves can help distinguish intrinsic accretion-state changes from simple obscuration scenarios [62, 41, e.g.,]. In addition, systematic searches based on large-amplitude MIR variability and MIR color evolution have proved effective in selecting CLAGN candidates, opening a selection channel that is especially valuable for host-dominated or dust-affected systems [63, 33].

In principle, the X-ray band should be one of the most sensitive tracers of changes in black-hole accretion activity, since it directly probes the innermost accretion flow and corona [59]. Wide-area X-ray surveys such as eROSITA have dramatically improved the census of X-ray sources and variable AGNs [48]. Indeed, eROSITA has already been used to discover a new changing-look Seyfert galaxy [45]. However, the systematic discovery of CLAGNs from X-ray data has remained comparatively limited, because existing survey strategies are generally better suited to all-sky coverage and long-term variability studies than to the frequent, low-latency identification and immediate follow-up of changing-look behavior across the sky. Yuan et al. 76), with repeated soft X-ray monitoring by the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) and rapid follow-up by the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT), opens a new opportunity for identifying changing-look AGNs from the X-ray band.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning for JWST Galaxy Images and Low Resolution Spectra
papers.abstract: A self-supervised multimodal model recovers galaxy stellar masses from sparse JWST data that lack the multi-band coverage required by traditional SED fitting. We train on single-band F150W imaging paired with observed-frame 1-2 $μ$m PRISM spectra and obtain a joint image-spectrum representation that recovers stellar mass at $1<z\le3$ with $R^2 \sim 0.9$ and $σ_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.24$ dex; cross-modal CLIP alignment further raises single-modality performance by $ΔR^2 = +0.04$ (imaging) and $+0.09$ (spectroscopy), narrowing the gap to joint-modality inference. The code and documentation are available at \href{https://github.com/2003cy/neurips2026_ssl_jwst}{GitHub}.

Extragalactic parameter inference relies on translating observations into physical properties. Spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting [26, 54, 40, 32, 28] achieves this through broad-band wavelength coverage that breaks degeneracies between stellar age, dust, and metallicity [9, 10, 33]. Space-based surveys such as JWST and the upcoming Roman Space Telescope now reach wider fields, but individual sources increasingly lack the multi-band observations needed to break these degeneracies [52, 45, 61, 35].

papers.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
papers.abstract: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception. In this report, we present WeVisOne-VL (WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes. Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special <OBJ> token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL. Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries. By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.

papers.intro:
Perceiving and understanding the visual world has long been a central pursuit of computer vision [46, 25, 70, 32, 5, 45, 1, 94]. An intelligent visual system must be able to recognize what is present in an image, identify which object a user is referring to, and determine where these objects exist. Such capabilities establish the foundation for a wide range of real-world applications, such as content creation [65], industrial inspection [37], autonomous driving, and embodied intelligence [18].

An intelligent visual system must be able to recognize what is present in an image, identify which object a user is referring to, and determine where these objects exist. Such capabilities establish the foundation for a wide range of real-world applications, such as content creation [65], industrial inspection [37], autonomous driving, and embodied intelligence [18].

Over the past decade, computer vision has made remarkable progress toward this goal. From conventional detection and segmentation models (e.g., YOLO [86] and DETR [5]), to open-world perception models (e.g., Grounding-DINO [67] and SAM [45]), and more recently to large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [1], this field is being driven toward more unified, general, and powerful visual systems. This evolution has substantially broadened the concepts that a model can recognize and the instructions that it can follow. However, when both performance and efficiency are considered, current models are still far from satisfactory for real-world deployment. They often hallucinate non-existent objects, misinterpret user intent when encountering unfamiliar object descriptions, or overlook non-salient instances, leading to incomplete recall.

Data Engine. We develop a unified data engine that connects semantic discovery with instance-aligned supervision for object detection, referring localization, segmentation, and matting. To guide targeted acquisition and task-specific annotation, the engine organizes category concepts and compositional referring expressions in a shared knowledge graph. It then combines complementary localization experts to generate spatial candidates and consolidates their predictions through visual-language verification of query–instance correspondence. Building on these verified localizations, the engine generates binary masks to extend supervision to the pixel level while preserving target identity across tasks, with manual spot checks for additional quality control. For matting, it further leverages expert predictions and curated data to support a dedicated annotator that provides continuous alpha supervision. Finally, the engine uses reviewed model errors to guide subsequent acquisition, annotation correction, and hard-example sampling, enabling iterative refinement of the training data.

Model Design. WeVisOne-VL consists of a VLM backbone and a lightweight pixel decoder. Built on Qwen3-VL [1], WeVisOne-VL casts a broad range of vision tasks as structured next-token prediction, generating object labels and spatial coordinates autoregressively. For compact and efficient output, we introduce a group of dedicated tokens (from <0> to <1000>) to encode normalized coordinates [40]. For dense prediction tasks, the model generates a special <OBJ> token after each predicted bounding box, whose hidden state serves as a latent representation of the corresponding instance. The pixel decoder combines this instance representation with multi-level features from the shared ViT to produce predictions over the full image canvas. In this way, WeVisOne-VL supports both discrete and dense predictions without relying on a separate large segmentation model [48, 122, 68, 61].

Training Pipeline. We train WeVisOne-VL in a curriculum pipeline consisting of three-stage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by mixed-task Reinforcement Learning (RL). Stage 1 establishes task alignment, teaching the model to follow task instructions and produce well-formed structured outputs. Stage 2 introduces high-resolution and dense perception data to improve the recall of small and crowded objects. Stage 3 further incorporates pixel-level tasks, extending the model from discrete localization to dense prediction. For RL, we first select samples on which the SFT model is most uncertain, then apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over the mixture of tasks. This on-policy optimization effectively improves the localization accuracy, while suppressing repeated or hallucinated predictions.

papers.title: Mixed-Precision Coalesced Matrix-Free Multigrid with Vertex-Patch Smoothing
papers.abstract: I present a geometric multigrid solver for the Poisson equation with continuous cubic elements in three dimensions, smoothed by a multiplicative vertex-patch Schwarz method with exact local solves. All fields are kept in persistent cell-wise storage, where every cell holds its own copy of each shared degree of freedom. The patch smoother yields a continuous solution without any exchange between cells. On the GPU, the patch update is computed in registers, one cell per thread, and the cells of a patch exchange data by warp shuffles, so shared memory is avoided almost entirely. Despite the low occupancy that this design implies, the arithmetic of the patch update runs close to the FP32 peak. Fast diagonalization, merged transforms, and a reflection symmetry of the patch then reduce the arithmetic until a sweep moves its data at $87\%$ of the bandwidth of a plain device copy. The hierarchy therefore runs in single precision inside a double-precision outer iteration. Rounding the unassembled residual destroys the cancellation between opposite-sign copies of shared degrees of freedom; exchanging the copies between cells in double precision performs this cancellation before rounding, without changing the dual vector they represent. With this \emph{rebalancing}, the cycle converges as in double precision and independently of the mesh size, the error converges at the optimal rate down to the precision of the solve, and the solver reaches over $400$ million degrees of freedom per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Geometric multigrid with matrix-free, sum-factorized operator evaluation is an established solver for high-order finite element discretizations of elliptic problems on GPUs [12, 13]. The arithmetic throughput of GPUs has grown faster than their memory bandwidth [33], so the operator evaluations, transfers, and smoothers of a V-cycle run at the rate at which they move their data. Single precision halves the bytes per value and doubles the arithmetic peak, and since a preconditioner needs no full accuracy, the hierarchy can run in FP32 inside an FP64 outer iteration without limiting the accuracy of the solution [11, 13, 6].

Matrix-free GPU kernels stage their intermediates in shared memory between the stages of sum factorization [14, 13], and its bandwidth can become their limit, as for the GPU patch smoother of [6]. The register file is both larger and faster than shared memory [18], and registers are the direct operands of the arithmetic instructions. The price is occupancy: the more registers a thread holds, the fewer warps are resident to hide latency by switching between them. A kernel with low occupancy has to hide latency by independent instructions within each thread instead, and can then still reach the peak arithmetic rate [26].

papers.title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism underpins modern large language models, yet their dynamics remain only partially understood. Recent perspectives interpret attention blocks as interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limits correspond to gradient flows of energy functionals on spaces of probability densities on $\mathbb R^d$ equipped with Wasserstein-type metrics. We extend this viewpoint by deriving accelerated attention blocks from inertial, Nesterov-type damped Hamiltonian dynamics on these density spaces, developing the geometry and differential calculus needed to make the construction rigorous. In particular, we introduce a local-mobility geometry for the Otto-Wasserstein and softmax-Wasserstein settings, and a quotient Stein geometry that resolves the degeneracy of the linear-attention kernel to yield a well-defined metric and differential calculus. We provide rigorous foundations when softmax attention admits a gradient-flow formulation and when its inertial counterpart admits a damped Hamiltonian on explicitly characterized domains. For linear attention, we obtain a finite-dimensional solution theory with sharp conditions for global existence versus finite-time second-moment blow-up. We further prove a quantitative link between continuous moment blow-up and the discrete-layer depth at which token norms cross a prescribed threshold. Finally, motivated by the finite-token geometry, we propose geometric corrections to token and momentum updates. In decoder-only, nanoGPT-style experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText, these corrections lower validation negative log-likelihood on next-token prediction relative to momentum-only controls.

papers.title: Quantum K-structure constants and cylindric Grothendieck polynomials for Grassmannians
papers.abstract: We use the partition functions of a five-vertex exactly solvable lattice model from statistical mechanics to give new combinatorial formulae for the Schubert structure constants of torus-equivariant quantum K-theory rings of Grassmannians. The proofs build on our earlier results where we identified the transfer matrices of these lattice models geometrically as multiplications by the Hirzebruch $λ_y$ classes of the tautological subbundle and the (dual) quotient bundle. The structure constants are solutions of a system of linear equations with coefficients given by the partition function. This system may be solved explicitly by specializing the Hirzebruch parameter $y$ to an equivariant parameter, leading to explicit formulae using Cramer's rule. Furthermore, we give an alternative combinatorial construction of the partition functions in terms of sums over cylindric set-valued tableaux, which we call cylindric Grothendieck polynomials. The latter generalise McNamara's factorial skew Grothendieck and Yeliussizov's modified Grothendieck polynomials and can be thought of as an equivariant K-theoretic version of Postnikov's toric Schur function. We also provide new polynomial representatives for equivariant K-theory classes of Richardson varieties and their variants.

papers.title: Formal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
papers.abstract: Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's \texttt{mathlib} provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in \texttt{mathlib} by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment

papers.intro:
Formal mathematics uses proof assistants like Lean (Lean Community, 2024) to express definitions, theorems, and proofs in a precise, computer-verifiable language, ensuring correctness through explicit verification of every logical step. The possibility of automated proof checking in formalized mathematics can improve mathematical workflows in a number of ways: peer-reviewing of proofs can be partially foregone (and has been, for certain exceptionally long proofs (Gonthier, 2008)), immediate feedback can help train students and AI and the argumentative structure of a proof becomes clearer (Tao, 2025). However, writing formal mathematics remains difficult and time-consuming, since even simple mathematical arguments often require substantial low-level detail and a steep learning curve for proof assistants (Kaliszyk and Rabe, 2020). To make formalization accessible, community-driven libraries such as mathlib for Lean have expanded the accessibility of formal mathematics by providing reusable collections of formalized definitions and proofs (The mathlib Community, 2020; Lean Community, 2024). Usage of these libraries is essential for driving down the detail needed in writing formal proofs. However, the sheer volume of statements along with their technical content makes it difficult to get an overview on the available content. To mitigate these issues, it would be important to integrate formal libraries within informal bases of mathematical knowledge, which novice users are more proficient in interpreting. In particular, systems that can map informal mathematical statements to their corresponding formalized versions would significantly reduce the effort required to navigate and reuse existing formal libraries. On the other hand, machine-readability of formal libraries also makes them a highly practical resource for knowledge graphs, such as the mathematics-specific MaRDI (MaRDI Consortium, 2023) knowledge graph, as relationships between theorems are explicit and traceable. In contrast, links between informal research output can be difficult to interpret or require use of hallucination-prone language models in their creation (Satpute et al., 2026).

papers.title: TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
papers.abstract: Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}

To answer this question, we present TrustedCode, a framework within the confines of a closed-loop system to translate Python program into WhyML specification language, noted for its strengths as a formal verification framework and support for back-end provers. This will incorporate an LLM, the Why3 software as well as an iterative repair sequence using LangGraph to produce a provably correct program. To correct LLM errors, we integrate a method to identify and classify capability gaps. This method moves beyond the current binary pass-fail metric to a concrete and structured classification methodology to specifically isolate the LLMs gaps in its understanding of types, theory, syntax, and semantics. Finally, we provide a practical analysis on the performance of the framework, including evaluating the capacity gaps of the LLM and the way they were fixed. This provided a holistic overview of the current state and limitations of LLM models for this application.

papers.title: Where Did the Light Come From? Diagnosing Cast-Shadow Reasoning in VLMs and Borrowing the Missing Shadow Prior from Image Generation Models
papers.abstract: Shadows are observable consequences of latent physical causes, arising from the interaction between illumination, object geometry, and scene structure. A model that understands shadows should be able not only to read a shadow's direction, but also to infer where a shadow should fall when it is absent, and to judge whether a shadow is physically consistent with the scene. We introduce ShadowBench, built from real photographs, which poses these three questions to vision-language models (VLMs). From each scene, we build a correct-shadow, a shadow-removed, and a human-annotated wrong-direction state. Evaluating 19 open VLMs (2B to 78B) and frontier proprietary models, we find that VLMs read a visible shadow's direction well above chance and improve with scale, yet infer the absent direction only weakly and fall to chance at judging physical consistency even under a bias-free two-alternative test that removes the yes-bias of single-image naturalness questions. Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, and even then only modestly and far below humans. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) does not help. The missing ingredient is not reasoning but knowledge that image generation models (IGMs) already hold. Routing a VLM through an IGM lifts its inference well above its direct attempt and helps it flag the wrong-direction shadows it otherwise accepts. Cast-shadow direction is a single facet of illumination understanding, but the sharp gap it reveals between VLMs and IGMs suggests image-generation or reconstruction objectives as a route toward illumination-aware VLMs.

papers.title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
papers.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

papers.intro:
Mechanistic models of neural activity, from single-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley neurons to neural mass models of cortical columns, offer parameters that are biologically interpretable in a way purely statistical decoders do not provide. The Jansen–Rit model [1] is a canonical case: a six-state neural mass model of a cortical column that reproduces electroencephalography (EEG) rhythms from a small number of physiologically grounded parameters. Fitting such models to data remains hard [2, 3, 4]. Their dynamics are nonlinear, and the likelihood of the observed data given the model’s parameters p⁡(x∣θ)p(x\mid\theta) has no closed form, since it would require marginalizing over the full space of stochastic input trajectories consistent with the observed output [5]. Classical approaches, including grid search, moment matching, and approximate Bayesian computation, scale poorly as the number of free parameters grows [6].

Simulation-based inference (SBI) completely sidesteps evaluating intractable likelihoods by training a neural density estimator directly on simulation outputs, learning an amortized mapping from data features to a posterior over parameters [6, 7, 8]. Gonçalves et al. [9] established this approach for mechanistic neuroscience models, applying neural posterior estimation to single-neuron and small-circuit models, and showed that hand-designed summary-statistic embeddings are often sufficient for accurate, well-calibrated inference.

[9] established this approach for mechanistic neuroscience models, applying neural posterior estimation to single-neuron and small-circuit models, and showed that hand-designed summary-statistic embeddings are often sufficient for accurate, well-calibrated inference.

In scientific applications of SBI, it becomes crucial to understand how each feature of the data contributes to parameter inference. Normally, a feature’s contribution is established only after training; the gold standard in SBI is retrain-based ablation, in which the model is retrained with one feature excluded and the change in the inferred posterior is quantified, a causal measure by construction. This is the procedure the current practice guide points to for assessing which features constrain parameters [10], and the criterion against which Beck et al. [11] validated a faster analytic alternative, Feature Selection through Likelihood Marginalization. Both measure the effect that excluding a feature actually has on the posterior: one by performing the exclusion directly, the other by approximating it analytically. An appealing, cheaper alternative is to learn the weighting itself by incorporating a small differentiable gate, trained end-to-end with the rest of the network. The gate multiplies each feature by a weight in (0,1)(0,1), and after training it can be read as importance at no extra cost. Indeed, gates of exactly this form are reported in various settings: as electrode importance in EEG deep learning [12, 13]; and, in tabular learning and forecasting, the reading is built into the methods themselves, through learned input masks [14], attention-based feature selection [15], and variable-selection layers [16]. In SBI, however, the idea appears not to have been taken up (although it has been suggested [17]), and we believe it could be attractive in principle, since the standard ablation test costs one full retraining per feature.

Evidence regarding the interpretability of learnable gates in deep-learning pipelines is still mixed, however. On the one hand, architectures built for feature selection do sometimes recover known relevant variables on synthetic data. For example, TabNet’s sparse masks identified ground-truth features [14]; importantly, however, their weights are not generally guaranteed to represent importance. More negative evidence comes from the UCI Adult dataset, where learned mask and attention scores showed little agreement with KernelSHAP, a method that estimates each feature’s contribution to a prediction [18]. Results from natural language processing (NLP) are similarly cautionary: attention weights sometimes tracked input effects, but too inconsistently to provide reliable importance measures [19]. In EEG, explanation quality also depends on the method: saliency failed a model-randomization check, whereas DeepLIFT did not [20, 21]. More fundamentally, jointly trained selectors can encode predictions in their masks [22], while unconstrained multiplicative scales may be non-identifiable under downstream rescaling [23]. Taken together, these findings suggest that learned weights can be informative without necessarily providing reliable importance estimates. That uncertainty extends to SBI, where the relationship between learned weights and retrain-based ablation remains largely unexplored.

We compare the gating and ablation measures of importance directly in a Jansen–Rit EEG model (Figure 1). Neural posterior estimators (NPEs) are trained over four mechanistic parameters: connectivity strength, input drive, the joint excitatory/inhibitory timescale-scaling factor, and inhibitory synaptic gain. These parameters are inferred from simulated EEG, using seven statistical-summary features computed at five electrodes. Two gated variants, independent (sigmoid) and competing (softmax) per-feature weighting, are compared against an ungated baseline in terms of model performance, and against the gold-standard measure of feature importance, obtained by retraining the full pipeline from scratch with each feature excluded in turn and measuring the resulting drop in posterior accuracy. We only use simulated EEG data in order to have a clean ground truth to evaluate the feasibility of the gating method. papers.title: The exponent $1/4$ in three complexity bounds: integer bases, continued fractions, and the $(3/2)^n$ steering word
papers.abstract: Let $ξ$ be a real algebraic irrational number and $p(n,ξ,b)$ the number of distinct blocks of length $n$ in its base-$b$ expansion. Bugeaud and Evertse proved in 2008 that $p(n,ξ,b)/(n(\log n)^η)$ is unbounded for every $η<1/11$. We prove this for every $η<1/4$. We also prove the analogous bound for the continued fraction expansion of an algebraic number of degree at least three, with every exponent $δ<1/4$. Bugeaud announced this statement in 2013 with an unspecified $δ>0$. Finally, the subword complexity of the steering word of $(3/2)^n$ exceeds $C\,k(\log k)^η$ infinitely often for every $η<1/4$ and every $C$. The three proofs share one count: $\varepsilon^{-1}$ classes times $\varepsilon^{-3}$ subspaces from the quantitative Subspace Theorem of Evertse and Ferretti. The subspaces are then disposed of at the cost of a logarithm, with no further power of $\varepsilon^{-1}$. All three results, and the quantitative Subspace Theorem they rest on, are machine-verified in Lean~4.

papers.title: Safety-constrained position tracking of a flexible transmission system
papers.abstract: We consider safety-constrained position tracking for a flexible transmission system consisting of a torsional shaft driven by a motor and connected to a gravitationally loaded inertia. The coupled PDE-ODE dynamics admit a semilinear formulation in which the linear input-output system is impedance passive and the gravitational torque enters as a bounded, globally Lipschitz perturbation. We establish an energy dissipation inequality for the nonlinear model and show that a position-funnel controller with supervised damping admits a unique global closed-loop trajectory. In particular, the motor-angle tracking error remains strictly inside a prescribed time-varying funnel, which can be chosen to enforce safety bounds on the motor angle.

papers.title: FiLM-CAM: Keyed Feature Modulation for Conditional-Access Watermarking
papers.abstract: We propose FiLM-CAM; a conditional-access image watermarking approach that enforces authorized encoding, decoding, and removal through keyed feature modulation. A secret key conditions a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) mechanism that transforms the internal representation of the watermark signal before embedding, thereby coupling the payload to the key at the feature, rather than pixel level. The same key must be presented to condition the decoder to correctly recover the payload embedded in an image. To enforce conditional access, we train the system to maximize the performance gap between authorized and unauthorized use, ensuring reliable extraction under the correct key while inducing failure under incorrect keys. In addition, we design our encoder to estimate the watermark residual invariant to the presence of pre-existing watermarks. This design enables conditional watermark removal via simple re-encoding and subtraction of the residual using iterative refinement, contingent on knowledge of the secret key. We evaluate FiLM-CAM across multiple watermarking encoder-decoder backbones, demonstrating that keyed feature modulation serves as an effective, architecture-agnostic conditional access module (CAM) for image watermarking.

papers.intro:
Generative AI raises societal concerns over media integrity, given the speed and scale at which synthetic or misleading imagery can be produced and disseminated. Invisible watermarking has emerged as a practical mitigation, embedding imperceptible signals into image content that either flag the presence of AI-generated content (AIGC) [23, 20] or enable content re-identification to establish provenance for media authenticity [11, 16], rights [7, 6] and licensing [15].

It is not always desirable for such watermarking to be openly accessible. Organizations may wish to control (or ‘condition’) access to the encoding and/or decoding of watermarks to protect against spoofing, unauthorized removal, or monitoring. This has led to a proliferation of private watermarking encoder–decoder models, each trained independently for an individual organization, imposing a deployment burden on implementers who must distribute and maintain multiple private decoders. It would be more efficient to train a watermarking framework in which access control is intrinsic to the model’s operation i.e., where encoding, decoding, and removal are functionally contingent on possession of an authorized key, without requiring separate models for each private deployment.

papers.title: Attention-guided classification and tumor localization of combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinomas (cHCC-CCA) are a type of cancer that share components of two other primary liver cancers: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA). Accurate diagnosis of cHCC-CCA, of which the behavior may resemble that of either HCC or CCA, remains a challenge due to strong intratumoral heterogeneity. Since the prognoses differ between liver cancer types, it is necessary to improve their morphological characterization and recognition in order to accurately identify cHCC-CCA. In this work, we use whole slide images (WSIs) of the two main types of liver cancer (HCC and CCA) and cHCC-CCA, stained with Hematoxylin-Eosin-Safran (HES), to train a classification model that can distinguish between these subtypes and provides a potential solution for localizing different types of tumors in the combined liver cancer images.

papers.intro:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) are the major primary liver carcinomas, whereas combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA) exhibits both hepatocytic and cholangiocytic differentiation [2]. This morphological heterogeneity motivates computational approaches for both whole-slide image (WSI) classification and component localization. Calderaro et al. [3] used a classifier trained on pure HCC and intrahepatic CCA (iCCA) to characterize HCC-like and iCCA-like morphology in cHCC-CCA. Beaufrère et al. papers.title: On the Hodge conjecture for hyper-Kähler varieties of generalized Kummer type of dimension divisible by four
papers.abstract: We prove the Hodge conjecture for all hyper-Kähler varieties of generalized Kummer type of dimension $2n$ with $n+1$ a prime number, and all powers of these varieties. For any variety $X$ of generalized Kummer type of dimension divisible by 4, we show that the Lefschetz standard conjecture for $X$ implies the Hodge conjecture for $X$ and all its powers.

papers.title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
papers.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.

papers.intro:
In-context learning (ICL) enables models to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations without parameter updates [9, 14]. While this capability is well established in Large Language Models (LLMs), extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains more challenging [64, 22]. The challenge is not simply that demonstrations contain images. Effective multimodal ICL requires binding visual evidence to textual outputs in demonstrations and transferring this visual–linguistic association to the query. However, recent MLLMs often fail to fully leverage visual information in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and simply mimicking the text demonstrations [12].

Prior work has largely improved multimodal ICL by selecting useful demonstrations or adapting models to ICL-formatted data. Retrieval- and ordering-based methods [6, 38, 13] retrieve and rank ICL demonstrations based on their similarity to the query. Despite their effectiveness for ICL in LLMs, they are highly sensitive to prompt design and sample order in multimodal ICL, often underperforming even random selection [63]. In contrast, ICL training-based methods tune MLLMs on ICL datasets [15, 12, 26, 22], while task vector-based methods [39, 54] use ICL data to extract task vectors that steer hidden states, replicating the effect of demonstrations. Despite their effectiveness, we observe that their reliance on ICL datasets limits their generalization (Fig. 2): they perform well on the same ICL benchmark used for training or task vector extraction, but drastically degrades on other ICL benchmarks. Moreover, training on ICL datasets can cause catastrophic forgetting on previously well-solved tasks (e.g., simple VQA) (Fig. 5). More fundamentally, since ICL in LLMs is widely considered an emergent capability from pre-training rather than explicit supervision on ICL-formatted datasets [36, 40], this raises a key question: do ICL data-dependent methods address the root cause of poor multimodal ICL, or merely improve performance on their training benchmarks?

In this work, rather than relying on ICL benchmarks, we investigate a more fundamental limitation that hinders multimodal ICL by asking why multimodal ICL fails and what prevents MLLMs from effectively using demonstrations. Prior work has shown that visual hallucination [56, 30, 17], where outputs include nonexistent objects or inconsistent visual details, is a key factor behind poor multimodal ICL [51]. With further analysis, we find that poor visual grounding, a phenomenon attending to irrelevant regions instead of task-relevant visual evidence, significantly contributes to these hallucinations during multimodal ICL. Specifically, we reveal that this issue is particularly pronounced for personalized identifiers unseen during pre-training: while MLLMs can ground correctly on generic identifiers common in training data (Fig. 1-(a)), they struggle with personalized identifiers (Fig. 1-(b)). This limitation is critical, as real-world multimodal ICL often involves personalized references, where demonstration captions include identifiers such as a dog named “John” rather than generic concepts like “dog” [46, 47]. Since such concepts cannot be reliably inferred from pre-trained priors alone, correct predictions rely more directly on accurate visual grounding.

Motivated by this, we propose ProCoRe (Proposition-level Contrastive Reward), which improves multimodal ICL by enhancing visual grounding. Instead of relying on ICL datasets, ProCoRe trains MLLMs to distinguish visually contrastive samples (e.g., Fig. 9), drawing inspiration from contrastive learning that fine-grained discrimination improves visual representation [11]. Specifically, it generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions (i.e., distinct propositions for each caption and common propositions), and applies contrastive reinforcement learning to align each proposition with its corresponding image while discouraging alignment with mismatched images. By operating at the proposition-level rather than on sentence-level, ProCoRe enables MLLMs to capture both distinctive and shared visual features. papers.title: QICOM: Open-Source Software for Reproducible Image Quality Evaluation, Blinded Assessment, and Radiomic Comparison
papers.abstract: QICOM (Quality Image COMparator) is open-source software for quantitative image comparison, paired radiomics, and blinded assessment. It saves processing settings, image identities, measurements, and response mappings so a comparison can be reopened and recalculated. We evaluate reference agreement, responses to controlled perturbations, and recovery of saved analyses. Synthetic experiments cover 37 quantitative descriptors using independentnumerical references and separate upstream integration comparisons. The QICOM/MIRP backend meets the reference tolerances for all 482 numeric IBSI 1 digital-phantom entries and all 1,622 entries across configurations A-E of the public CT reference case; these comprise 1,804 feature/aggregation comparisons and 300 preprocessing diagnostics. Restricting masked SSIM and HFEN to complete kernel support removes the observed dependence on excluded pixels. In a synthetic filtering example, stronger smoothing increases SSIM while worsening MSE and HFEN relative to milder smoothing and changing GLCM contrast more strongly. Reopened radiomics projects reproduce all 43 feature pairs per comparison, and two blinded deliveries return four correctly mapped scripted responses. These experiments document the calculations and data transfers linking the three workflows.

papers.intro:
The evaluation of medical imaging technologies, image-processing methods, and acquisition protocols often combines quantitative analyses with qualitative assessments. Quantitative approaches characterize image properties such as intensity differences, noise, tissue contrast, and structural similarity. Region-of-interest (ROI) measurements include signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), whose interpretation requires appropriate noise estimation, particularly when reconstruction or post-processing changes noise characteristics. Reference-based metrics provide complementary measures of image fidelity. For example, the ErisNet CT-denoising study combined mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), visual information fidelity (VIF), and edge preservation measures with ROI measurements of attenuation and noise [1]. Azour et al. [2] similarly combined SSIM and Fréchet Inception Distance with radiologist assessments of image quality and lesion conspicuity.

Structured visual assessment examines anatomical visibility, perceived noise, artifacts, and confidence in image interpretation. Reader scores can be evaluated using visual grading analysis (VGA) and visual grading characteristics (VGC), alongside statistics that quantify agreement between observers [3]. These methods have been applied to compare optimized X-ray protocols [4] and AI-reconstructed knee MRI with standard imaging [5], and to evaluate MRI protocols for total hip arthroplasty planning [6]. When the objective concerns pathology detection, diagnostic accuracy studies compare reader decisions against a predefined reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis characterize detection performance, while free-response ROC (FROC) methods additionally incorporate lesion localization. Analyses involving multiple readers and cases must account for both sources of variability and the dependence between observations [7, 8]. These task-specific evaluations address whether changes in image appearance affect diagnostic performance.

Combining these evaluations requires numerical measurements, radiomic features, and reader responses to remain linked to the same images and processing conditions. However, the necessary methods are often distributed across separate applications and custom scripts. Researchers may need to learn different interfaces, adapt images and masks to tool-specific requirements, and reconcile exported results. A reproducible workflow must therefore preserve image identifiers, masks, analysis settings, and blinded response mappings. Relevant settings include slice or volume selection, intensity scaling, discretization, and the spatial support of ROI calculations. Recording these choices supports repeated calculation and examination of the relationship between numerical and observer-based outcomes.

This study presents QICOM and evaluates three questions: whether its measurements agree with analytical and external references; how they respond to controlled perturbations and spatial restrictions; and whether saved inputs, settings, and outputs support re-execution of a complete comparison. Numerical phantom experiments assess reference agreement and metric behavior. IBSI digital-phantom and CT comparisons evaluate radiomic extraction, including five preprocessing configurations applied to the same acquired CT case. A synthetic filtering example follows the same images through all three workbenches, including export, reopening, and repeated calculation, while scripted responses test blinded delivery and recovery of source conditions. These experiments assess computational agreement and workflow reproducibility; human perceptual validity and diagnostic performance require subsequent evaluation.

papers.title: Transfer Meta-Learning for State Space Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Nonlinear system identification often requires costly experimental campaigns and separate model fitting for each different instance (target system) of a given system family. To reduce this burden, meta-learning approaches reuse information acquired across related systems. In particular, in-context meta-learning enables zero-shot prediction from a brief target system context (i.e., a short input-output trajectory), but generally yields large black-box sequence predictors without exposing an explicit state space model. Conversely, compact structured state space models are suitable for simulation, estimation, and control, but are usually fitted or adapted separately for each target system. To bridge this gap, we introduce a transfer meta-learning extension of state space autoencoders. The method reuses a pretrained encoder, whose weights remain fixed, to extract a compact representation of the target system from its context. An affine parameterization maps this representation to the parameters of a compact neural state space model without target-specific adaptation; the resulting model contains orders of magnitude fewer parameters than the reference in-context predictors from the literature. We evaluate zero-shot prediction and simulation performance on held-out system instances from Buck-Boost converter and Bouc-Wen oscillator system families, comparing performance against individually fitted baseline models.

papers.intro:
In conventional system identification workflows, a dedicated model is estimated from data collected on the system under consideration, with limited to no reuse of data acquired from related systems (Chakrabarty et al., 2023). This approach becomes especially impractical when commissioning large populations of similar devices, as conducting informative excitation experiments on every single unit is costly, time-consuming, and potentially intrusive. A promising solution to this hurdle is offered by few-shot learning techniques, where knowledge acquired across related system instances is leveraged to initialize a model, which is subsequently adapted using only limited data collected from the unseen target system. Within this paradigm, two primary strategies exist: transfer learning, which repurposes features or weights pretrained on possibly different source domains to accelerate target modeling, and meta-learning, which explicitly optimizes a shared model structure alongside a dedicated mechanism for rapid target adaptation (Finn et al., 2017; Kirchmeyer et al., 2022; Blanke and Lelarge, 2024). In neural network-based state space modeling, meta-learning has been demonstrated to significantly outperform conventional model-level transfer learning (i.e., fine-tuning the weights of a model pretrained on a single related system) in scarce data regimes (Chakrabarty et al., 2023).

Most established meta-learning algorithms rely on optimization-based adaptation, such as model-agnostic meta-learning and its variants (Finn et al., 2017; Chakrabarty et al., 2023). Although effective, these methods still require a target-specific training phase at deployment time. More recently, several in-context meta-learning approaches have emerged as an appealing training-free alternative, where a sequence model directly processes a short input–output record, i.e., the so-called context, and predicts the target dynamics in a purely feedforward manner (Forgione et al., 2023; Rufolo et al., 2025). Since these methods infer target dynamics from context through feedforward evaluation without target-specific adaptation, we refer to these in-context approaches as zero-shot.

Most established meta-learning algorithms rely on optimization-based adaptation, such as model-agnostic meta-learning and its variants (Finn et al., 2017; Chakrabarty et al., 2023). Although effective, these methods still require a target-specific training phase at deployment time. More recently, several in-context meta-learning approaches have emerged as an appealing training-free alternative, where a sequence model directly processes a short input–output record, i.e., the so-called context, and predicts the target dynamics in a purely feedforward manner (Forgione et al., 2023; Rufolo et al., 2025). Since these methods infer target dynamics from context through feedforward evaluation without target-specific adaptation, we refer to these in-context approaches as zero-shot.

Despite their flexibility, current in-context system identification approaches leave open an important gap between rapid zero-shot prediction and usability of the learned models within classical model-based engineering tools. Indeed, many of them rely on large sequence models, such as Transformers or deep state space sequence models, whose large parameter count and memory footprint complicate embedded deployment or real-time execution on resource-constrained platforms (Forgione et al., 2023; Rufolo et al., 2025). Second, these sequence models predict the input–output behavior of an unseen system without necessarily exposing useful state dynamics or a compact state space representation suitable for downstream estimation and control (Forgione et al., 2023; Rufolo et al., 2025). Furthermore, in-context meta-models are inherently tied to the specific system class observed during their initial training. When faced with fundamentally different system classes, existing approaches require computationally demanding retraining from scratch or tuning of the entire architecture (Piga et al., 2024). Transferring representations learned by a pretrained meta-model across distinct system classes without updating its parameters therefore remains largely unexplored in system identification.

We address both questions by introducing Transfer-Meta State Space AutoEncoders (Transfer-Meta SSAEs). Specifically, we extend the SSAE identification framework of Masti and Bemporad (2021) to a transfer meta-learning setting by generating its model parameters from a brief measured input–output trajectory. We reuse a pretrained encoder from Rufolo et al. (2025), keeping its weights fixed, and learning to aggregate its representations into a compact characterization of the target system. Inspired by the meta-learning approach of Forgione et al. (2025), an affine mapping directly computes the SSAE model parameters from this representation. Our approach is therefore zero-shot: we obtain the target-model parameters through feedforward evaluation, without target-specific adaptation or optimization. For each family, the model is evaluated on held-out parameterizations and compared with individually fitted SSAEs and a nonlinear input–output baseline in prediction and simulation.

papers.title: Concentration inequalities for vector-valued martingales
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish several deviation inequalities for the norms of vector-valued martingales, achieving bounds of the same quality as those available in the classical one-dimensional setting. Our results extend and refine previous work by Pinelis (1994) and Hayes (2005) in this area.

papers.title: Astrometric detection of rocky exoplanets from inexpensive space platforms
papers.abstract: The detection of orbiting exoplanets by way of astrometric monitoring of the host star to reveal gravitationally induced reflex motion requires extreme precision and measurement stability when targeting Earth-mass objects. Despite this, astrometry is widely regarded as the most promising avenue for the most desired of all targets: true Earth analogue systems in the solar neighbourhood. Formerly thought to require flagship class investment, recently several smaller concepts such as the TOLIMAN and SHERA missions have shown that detections are possible, at least in principle, from more modest space platforms. A key enabling feature is that these missions exploit narrow-angle astrometry. Observing only multiple star systems where the target provides its own astrometric reference greatly alleviates the challenges confronted by traditional astrometry with its reliance on distant, faint field stars. This principle underlies the TOLIMAN mission, for which progress and status is reported. However, only a tiny handful of nearby star systems are suited to such a TOLIMAN-like architecture. This paper discusses speculative optical concepts featuring ultra-stable telescopes of modest (<0.5m) aperture designed for astrometric monitoring of isolated single stars at the micro-arcsecond scales required for the discovery of Earth mass objects orbiting sun-like stars in temperate orbits. In simulation, highly sought-after neighbourhood systems such as Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti can be exhaustively searched for rocky planets with dedicated observing campaigns spanning several years, all from relatively inexpensive orbital platforms.

papers.title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
papers.abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.
