Autonomous navigation in off-road environments depends on an accurate representation of terrain traversability [1, 2]. Unlike structured roads, off-road terrain exhibits substantial geometric variation, where slope, roughness, and step height directly affect robot stability and mobility. We focus on LiDAR, which is widely used for terrain perception due to its ability to provide accurate distance measurements. However, in practical environments, LiDAR observations are inherently sparse, irregularly distributed, and affected by measurement noise and occlusion. Therefore, uncertainty is an intrinsic property of terrain perception.

Autonomous navigation in off-road environments depends on an accurate representation of terrain traversability [1, 2]. Unlike structured roads, off-road terrain exhibits substantial geometric variation, where slope, roughness, and step height directly affect robot stability and mobility. We focus on LiDAR, which is widely used for terrain perception due to its ability to provide accurate distance measurements. However, in practical environments, LiDAR observations are inherently sparse, irregularly distributed, and affected by measurement noise and occlusion. Therefore, uncertainty is an intrinsic property of terrain perception.

Recent work has begun incorporating probabilistic terrain models into traversability analysis and path planning to account for this perceptual uncertainty [3]. In most such approaches, however, geometric features are computed from a single deterministic elevation estimate, typically the posterior mean of a probabilistic terrain elevation model [4]. Approaches that explicitly enumerate elevation uncertainty commonly use it only as a mask or inject it into the cost through heuristic inflation, rather than propagating it through subsequent feature extraction [5]. Such mean-first strategy introduces a fundamental limitation for traversability estimation because geometric features are usually nonlinear mappings of elevation. By Jensen’s inequality, the expected feature generally cannot be recovered by evaluating a nonlinear mapping at the expected elevation. This issue can arise, for example, near a partially observed negative obstacle as shown in Fig. 1. There, mean elevation field may smooth the underlying discontinuity and underestimate its risk. More generally, extracting features directly from the expected elevation can suppress terrain variations that are critical for identifying steep slopes, steps, and partially observed regions. Furthermore, treating elevation uncertainty independently at individual cells neglects the spatial correlations of continuous terrain. Since geometric features are inherently neighborhood operators instead of one location, their uncertainty depends on the joint uncertainty of the underlying elevation patch. Ignoring these spatial dependencies can therefore further prevent faithful characterization of traversability [6].

We address these limitations by formulating terrain traversability estimation as a probabilistic terrain representation problem. The terrain surface is modeled as a continuous stochastic function using a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP). We draw function-space realizations from the SVGP posterior, obtaining spatially correlated elevation fields. For each realization, slope, roughness, and step height are computed and combined into a traversability cost, from which an empirical distribution of traversability costs is obtained across the realizations. The mean and standard deviation of this distribution characterize the expected traversability cost and its associated uncertainty, respectively. Based on these moments, a risk term is constructed using an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into the cost function of a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller, forming a risk-aware navigation framework. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. • Terrain traversability estimation is formulated as a probabilistic terrain representation problem, explicitly propagating perception and elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. • A function-space sampling strategy based on the posterior used to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and characterize uncertainty in nonlinear geometric and traversability mapping. • A risk-aware MPPI navigation framework integrating ProTrav with UCB-based risk, validated across diverse terrains in both simulation and real-world experiments. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on terrain traversability estimation. Section III introduces preliminary methods and concepts. Section IV presents the proposed probabilistic terrain traversability representation and risk-aware navigation framework. Section V describes the simulation and real-world experiments. Section VI concludes the paper.

papers.title: Initial-boundary value problems for linear lattice differential equations
papers.abstract: We study initial-boundary value problems for linear lattice differential equations on the half-line. We first give a systematic account of fundamental solutions for equations with general finite-range interactions. We then develop complementary approaches based on reflection, the Laplace transform, and the unified transform method, obtaining contour integral and Bessel-function representations of solutions. For the semidiscrete diffusion equation, we justify these representations for continuous boundary data and initial data of polynomial growth, establish uniqueness in the corresponding growth class, and derive spatial estimates and long-time properties, including asymptotic periodicity. We also treat nonhomogeneous equations, Robin boundary conditions, nonsymmetric coefficients, and a class of time-dependent coefficients. Finally, higher-order examples illustrate how the unified transform approach extends beyond second-order equations.

papers.intro:
Lattice differential equations describe systems whose spatial variable is discrete while time remains continuous. They arise both as models of interacting discrete systems and as spatial discretizations of partial differential equations. On the whole lattice, translation invariance makes fundamental solutions and convolution formulas natural tools for studying initial-value problems. On a half-line, the presence of a boundary introduces additional questions: how to incorporate prescribed boundary values into an explicit solution formula, how to justify that formula under weak assumptions on the data, and how the boundary influences the long-time behavior of the solution.

papers.abstract:
For positive powers of the discrete Dirichlet Laplacian $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$, non-trivial Hardy weights exist if and only if $0<σ<3/2$. For $0<σ\leq 1$, an explicit optimal Hardy weight for $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$ was obtained by Das and de la Fuente-Fernández. Their ground state argument does not apply when $1<σ<3/2$, because the off-diagonal matrix entries of $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$ are no longer all non-positive. Nevertheless, we show that their result is true for the entire subcriticality range $0<σ<3/2$. For $1<σ<3/2$, our argument combines the factorisation $$(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ=
abla_{\mathrm{D}}^{*}(-Δ_{\mathrm{N}})^{σ-1}
abla_{\mathrm{D}},$$ where $
abla_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $-Δ_{\mathrm{N}}$ are the discrete Dirichlet gradient and the discrete Neumann Laplacian, respectively, with a suitable two-term ground state representation. In addition, we use these arguments to derive another explicit family of optimal Hardy weights for any $σ\in(0,3/2)$.

papers.title: Mn-deficient Ni-Mn-Ga alloys: phase transitions, magnetic properties, and disappearance of martensitic transformation
papers.abstract: Composition gradients formed during directional solidification are generally considered undesirable in Ni-Mn-Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys. However, these gradients offer a highly effective platform for systematically investigating composition-property relationships under identical growth and heat-treatment conditions. To exploit this approach, one Mn-deficient and two near-stoichiometric Ni-Mn-Ga oligocrystals were grown by optical zone remelting and characterized by X-ray fluorescence mapping, optical microscopy, X-ray diffraction, low-field magnetic measurements, and vibrating-sample magnetometry. The ingots contained elongated grains and axial compositional gradients, primarily associated with the redistribution of Mn and Ga, whereas Ni remained relatively uniformly distributed. The martensitic and premartensitic transformation temperatures generally increased with increasing Mn content. Neither transformation was detected between 10 and 400 K in specimens containing 20.5-22.0 at.% Mn, all of which had $e/a < 7.40$. In contrast, both transformations were observed in the investigated specimens containing at least 22.1 at.% ($e/a \geq 7.46$). This abrupt change may indicate a possible electron-concentration threshold for the occurrence of these transformations. Saturation magnetization increased with Mn content up to 25.8 at.%, reaching 96.9 A m$^2$/kg at 10 K and 71.2 A m$^2$/kg at 300 K. Post-growth annealing increased the transition temperatures and changed the low-field magnetic response. The results indicate that composition-gradient oligocrystals serve as an effective platform for investigating the relationships between composition, structure, and magnetic properties in Ni-Mn-Ga alloys with the same processing history.

papers.title: Generalized Infinite Hidden Markov Models
papers.abstract: We introduce a flexible Bayesian nonparametric hidden Markov model for longitudinal data based on the hidden hierarchical Dirichlet process. Unlike the classical infinite hidden Markov model, the proposed model allows transition probabilities to change over time. In particular, this model provides a framework that operates between homogeneous and heterogeneous Markov model formulations, allowing the rows of the transition probability matrix to be clustered ac- cording to their temporal evolution. Inference is performed through a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which enables the joint estimation of model parameters, latent variables, and number of states, within a unified framework. Simulation studies under both homogeneous and heterogeneous transition regimes show that the proposed model tends to recover the true latent structure, whereas the infinite hidden Markov model tends to overestimate the number of states when transitions vary over time. Two applications illustrate the ability of the model to detect changes in the transition dynamics.

In the analysis of longitudinal data, accounting for unobserved heterogeneity in a flexible and interpretable way is crucial. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) achieve this by assuming that the observed process is driven by a discrete latent process following a Markov chain, with transition probabilities that fully encode the temporal dependence structure; see Bartolucci et al. (2012) and Zucchini and MacDonald (2009) for comprehensive reviews. When the number of latent states of an HMM is unknown, a Bayesian nonparametric approach based on the hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP, Teh et al., 2006) provides a natural infinite-state extension, known as the HDP-HMM or infinite HMM (Beal et al., 2002; Fox et al., 2008). In this model, each row of the infinite transition matrix is a random measure distributed as a Dirichlet process (DP), and the rows are tied together through a shared DP-distributed base measure. This hierarchical construction guarantees that the same set of destination states can be revisited across different departure states, while imposing time-homogeneity.

It is worth noting that many longitudinal and time-series applications call for time-heterogeneous transition mechanisms, which can change with time while still borrowing strength across time points and across states (Hughes et al., 1999; Bartolucci and Pennoni, 2007). Accommodating such a heterogeneity requires grouping the transition distributions themselves across time points; a natural nonparametric prior for clustering distributions, in addition to the observations they generate, is the nested Dirichlet process (NDP, Rodríguez et al., 2008). In fact, as soon as two samples share a single observation, their underlying random distributions are forced to coincide almost surely. In the longitudinal setting, this means that the transition kernels at two different time points collapse to the very same distribution as soon as a single common destination state is observed, which is clearly undesirable.

Building on the HHDP, we propose the generalized infinite hidden Markov model (GIHMM). In this construction the transition kernel associated with departure state is allowed to be time-varying. More in detail, the proposed GIHMM provides a flexible framework that lies between the homogeneous and heterogeneous HMM formulations. In particular, the model allows the rows of the transition probability matrix to be clustered in a suitable way.

Our proposal offers several advantages. First, it jointly accounts for heterogeneity at two levels. At the state level, units are clustered into latent states at each time point. At the distributional level, the transition distributions of each departure state are clustered across time, so that changes in the transition dynamics can be detected. Both levels are jointly accommodated within a single framework. Second, the model offers a compromise between flexibility and parsimony. Homogeneous HMMs assume a single transition matrix for the whole process, which may be too restrictive in the presence of change points. Fully heterogeneous HMMs, on the other hand, specify a different transition matrix at each time point, thus limiting the borrowing of information across time points even when the data suggest a homogeneous transition dynamic. The proposed model bridges these two extremes and includes both as special cases: each row of the transition matrix may change over time, but the same transition distribution can be shared across several time points. The temporal structure of the transition dynamics is informed by the data rather than a priori imposed. Third, all model components can be jointly estimated within a single Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, avoiding the comparison of a potentially prohibitive number of parametric specifications. In particular, we consider a Metropolis-within-Gibbs algorithm, which is based on the finite approximation of the DP (Muliere and Tardella, 1998; Ishwaran and James, 2001). However, instead of truncating the stick-breaking representation of the DP, we use the finite Dirichlet approximation of Ishwaran and Zarepour (2002).

papers.title: CoHelix: Event-Based Multi-Propeller Rotation-Rate Tracking with Shared Projective Geometry
papers.abstract: Estimating propeller rates from a moving event camera requires separating blade rotation from the changing image geometry. Background activity mixes with blade events, while repeated blade appearances admit half- and double-rate ambiguities. We propose CoHelix, a recursive filter that estimates one shared homography and separate rotation states for four rigidly mounted, coplanar propellers. Each admitted event updates its assigned rotation state, and its accepted geometry measurements correct the shared homography used to interpret later events from every propeller. We report lock, the fraction of evaluated time for which an estimate remains within 2% of synchronized ground truth, because mean error alone does not show how long a tracker follows the true rate. With fixed-rate initialization, leave-one-recording-out evaluation on moving-camera data gives CoHelix 62.9% lock, compared with 39.8% for HelixTrack and 22.2% for EventPro. With other settings fixed, allowing four geometry contributors instead of one raises lock from 3.4% to 62.9%. On a private target-follower dataset with a different target quadcopter, CoHelix retains the measurement settings selected on moving-camera data and uses a fixed initial rate. It reaches 95.9% lock, compared with 56.2% for HelixTrack and 61.1% for EventPro.

papers.title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA.

Since the standard CLIP text encoder is restricted to a 77-token context window (Radford et al., 2021), contemporary methods have primarily addressed this bottleneck by extending context lengths (Zhang et al., 2024), enhancing local spatial alignment (Choi et al., 2025), or incorporating structural priors via auxiliary objectives (Ruan et al., 2026).

Departing from existing literature, we revisit long-text alignment through a human-centric lens: humans do not process complex visual scenes uniformly, but naturally attend to specific, salient regions (Borji et al., 2013; Kumain et al., 2025). Our preliminary analysis of text-to-image retrieval on long-text benchmarks (Onoe et al., 2024; Truong et al., 2025), as shown in Fig. 1(b1), reveals that state-of-the-art alignment methods (Zhang et al., 2024; Choi et al., 2025; Ruan et al., 2026) rely disproportionately on scattered text describing visual prominence, i.e. salient text, while overlooking the surrounding non-salient context, i.e. contextual text, despite its semantic value for retrieval (details in Sec. 3). When we progressively reduce the ratio of salient text (α\alpha) within a query, the retrieval performance (R@1) of existing models degrades significantly faster than when an equivalent amount of text is removed at random. We term this failure mode as saliency collapse: Information-dense salient evidence provides an attractive retrieval shortcut. Overreliance on this shortcut can prevent models from effectively using the remaining contextual evidence when salient cues are weakened. This exposes a critical limitation for downstream tasks such as text-to-image retrieval, as humans can subjectively prioritize different aspects of a scene (Rahman and Bruce, 2015; Liang et al., 2018; Zangrossi et al., 2021). As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), when asked to describe the same image, user A might focus on more prominent foreground objects than user B.

A truly robust vision-language aligned model must go beyond simple token extension to represent both salient visual prominence and the complementary, non-salient context. To address saliency collapse in long-text alignment, we propose Robust Saliency-aware Alignment (RoSA), a novel finetuning framework that exploits auxiliary learning to explicitly reinforce both salient and contextual content alignment in long text. RoSA decomposes the original image-text pairs into two complementary views: a salient view of image-text pair featuring visually prominent regions, and a contextual view of image-text pair featuring the remaining non-salient context. These decomposed views then serve for auxiliary alignment objectives, together with the primary image-text alignment objective. Specifically, the auxiliary alignment objectives contain i) saliency-focused contrastive alignment that operates among the salient views, ii) context-preserving contrastive alignment that operates among the contextual views, and iii) visual anchoring that prevents severe visual representation drift. Importantly, the saliency-guided decomposition is a fine-tuning phase only, introducing no additional inference cost.

papers.title: AI Enhanced Cerenkov Luminescence Microscopy
papers.abstract: Cerenkov Luminescence Microscopy (CLM) enables the visualization of radiotracer uptake in three-dimensional (3D) tumor spheroids but is limited by low photon statistics and spatial blurring caused by positron transport. Here, we present a Monte Carlo (MC)-guided deep learning framework for CLM image restoration. Using TOPAS/Geant4, we developed a physical model of heterogeneous 3D tumor spheroids to simulate positron transport, Cerenkov photon generation and optical propagation. A dataset of 15,360 paired degraded and idealized ground-truth (GT) images was generated from 80 simulated spheroid geometries and used to train a supervised Content-Aware Image Restoration (CARE) network. Compared with the self-supervised Noise2Void (N2V) denoising method, CARE achieved substantially lower reconstruction errors on synthetic validation data, reducing the mean squared error from 0.0492 to 0.0051. Training stability and noise robustness analyses further demonstrated high reproducibility of the restored images. The trained CARE model was subsequently applied to experimental CLM images acquired from 27 U87 tumor spheroids following 18F-FDG uptake. The restored images exhibited more localized intensity distributions and higher local contrast and signal-to-noise ratios compared with raw and N2V-processed images. These findings, aligned with the 3Rs principles of animal experimentation, demonstrate the potential of physics-based supervised restoration to mitigate both noise and positron-induced spatial broadening in CLM.

papers.intro:
Ultra-low-light microscopy is used to study biological processes, tumor metabolism and radionuclide distribution at the cellular level. Rather than relying on external excitation like conventional fluorescence, these techniques detect the intrinsically weak optical signals typically produced by bioluminescence or radionuclide decay. In order to deal with such low photon emission yield, a light-tight environment and a highly sensitive, low-noise detector [40] are required. Common techniques include Bioluminescence Microscopy (BLM) [49, 33] and Radioluminescence Microscopy (RLM) [45, 24, 38, 25]. Recently, Cerenkov Luminescence Microscopy (CLM) [1] has been developed as a possible complementary approach to RLM for the imaging of different radionuclides. This technique is based on the detection of Cerenkov radiation emitted when charged particles, such as positrons (β+\beta^{+}) generated during radionuclide decay, travel through a dielectric medium at a velocity exceeding the local phase velocity of light. Above this Cerenkov kinetic energy threshold, the transient polarization induced by the passage of the charged particle results in electromagnetic fields that interfere constructively, producing optical photons [8, 7, 23]. Because the resulting optical signal is proportional to the radiotracer distribution without requiring any external excitation source, Cerenkov light emission has long been exploited in Cerenkov Luminescence Imaging (CLI) for macroscopic preclinical applications [41, 4] and human imaging [42]. Recently, Alborghetti et al. [1] extended the use of CLI to the microscopic scale, demonstrating the feasibility of detecting Cerenkov emission to image [18F]FDG uptake in three-dimensional (3D) glioblastoma (GBM) spheroids. The use of CLM opens new possibilities for studying radionuclide uptake heterogeneity, tumor metabolism and radiopharmaceutical distribution with an effective pixel size of a few microns. From a translational perspective, CLM could be used as an imaging tool for in vitro pharmacological and radiotherapy (RT) screening. More precisely, CLM performed in combination with a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical can then visualize, at microscopic resolution, any possible treatment effects. For example, it has been shown that CLM was able to detect differences of [18F]FDG uptake in GBM spheroids treated with RT [1]. One of the advantages of CLM lies in the use of 3D in vitro models rather than live animals. This approach is thus in line with current ethical guidelines promoting the Replacement, Reduction and Refinement (3Rs) of animal experimentation in scientific research [21]. Despite its potential, CLM is limited by two physical effects linked to the production of Cerenkov radiation within the sample. The light yield of Cerenkov emission is low and, thus, CLM requires exposure times on the order of minutes to collect an image [1]. The low photon emission of CLM necessitates the use of pixel binning, which might limit the image spatial resolution. Secondly, because Cerenkov photons are emitted along the travel path of the charged particle, the detected optical signal is a slightly blurred version of the true radiotracer spatial distribution [1]. In order to account for these physical effects, the use of computational image restoration algorithms, alongside hardware optimization, is needed. Classical filtering algorithms, such as Gaussian smoothing, wavelet thresholding or non-local means [48, 10, 30, 6, 14], tend to suppress high-frequency details along with noise and are fundamentally unsuited to recover physical blurring. In contrast, deep learning (DL) approaches have shown substantial capabilities for low-light microscopy [44, 27]. Modern architectures, including convolutional and residual networks [39, 51], generative adversarial networks [15], transformer-based models and diffusion probabilistic models [18, 35], have been increasingly applied to low-light and photon-limited imaging. More specifically, frameworks such as Content-Aware Image Restoration (CARE) [47] and networks tailored to volumetric bioluminescence [33] have successfully recovered high-resolution biological structure from acquisitions with a low Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR). In this work, we present a simulation-driven DL framework to overcome the fundamental limits of CLM mentioned above, as shown in Fig.1. Because the experimental ground-truth (GT) images without positron blur cannot be acquired, we utilize Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to explicitly model the physics of positron transport and Cerenkov photon generation, producing matched pairs of synthetic noisy and GT images. These paired data are then used to train a fully supervised probabilistic restoration network (CARE) capable of simultaneous denoising and spatial deconvolution. To show the impact of accurate simulated training data on CLM improvement, we evaluate this approach against Noise2Void (N2V) [26, 5], which is a self-supervised, denoising-only network.

papers.title: Kinetic-inductance Parametric Amplification in Superconducting Hybrid Magnonics
papers.abstract: Parametric amplification enables sensitive microwave detection and signal processing by amplifying weak signals with minimal added noise. Here, we demonstrate kinetic inductance mediated parametric amplification in a hybrid magnonic system comprising a nonlinear NbN nanowire resonator strongly coupled to a yttrium iron garnet sphere. The resonator exhibits four wave mixing and nonlinear frequency pulling, enabling parametric amplification both away from and within the magnon-photon strong coupling regime. In the magnon detuned regime, we observe 7 dB gain, while coupling to the YIG magnon shifts the parametric amplification response by ~20 MHz and yields 3.4 dB gain in the hybrid mode. Thus, magnon photon coupling provides a route to magnetically tune the spectral position of kinetic inductance parametric amplification. At higher pump powers, the system transitions to a self oscillatory regime featuring comb-like sidebands and probe activated nonlinear mode mixing. These results establish hybrid magnonics as a platform for tunable nonlinear microwave amplification and dynamics.

papers.title: Austerity, Gender, and Multidimensional Deprivation Among Older Europeans: Evidence from SHARE
papers.abstract: This paper studies whether fiscal consolidation is associated with deeper multidimensional deprivation among older women than among older men, and through which channel. Using six waves of SHARE across eleven European countries, it builds a multidimensional deprivation index spanning functional health, economic insecurity, and social exclusion, and relates it to the cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB) at the country-wave level in a two-way fixed-effects model. Consolidation raises deprivation on average with a null average gender gap, which is later found to conceal regional heterogeneity where the gender gap is positive and significant in Southern and Eastern Europe, and absent in Continental/Nordic Europe. This regional pattern holds under individual clustering but does not survive clustering at the country level. Further, the economic insecurity channel the literature would predict runs in the opposite direction, with men's measured insecurity rising more steeply than women's; this is the only dimension whose interaction survives country-level inference. Social exclusion exhibits a larger gender effect, concentrated in the Eastern and Southern Europe, but it is significant only under individual clustering. The gendered cost of austerity among older Europeans is therefore neither uniform across welfare regimes nor routed through income, though the evidence for its social channel is inconclusive.

papers.intro:
The 2010s wave of fiscal consolidation across Europe has been well studied. The literature have examined its effects on output, employment, and, more recently, income inequality (Fatás and Summers, 2018; Konstantinou, 2024). The body of work, however, has been slower to ask who within the household and across the life course absorbs the adjustment. Public expenditure cuts do not fall evenly on individuals, instead they are amplified by existing patterns of employment, care responsibility, and entitlement, which are themselves gendered. A growing number of studies on gender disparity argues that austerity is not gender-neutral (Rubery, 2015; Kushi and McManus, 2018; Perugini et al., 2019), although they focus overwhelmingly on working-age labour markets and household income. Little is known about how consolidation is experienced by older women and men. This is an important distinction to be taken into consideration, as their exposure runs through different and more concentrated channels. the first is pension entitlement which is accumulated (or not) over a working life, the second is reliance on public health and long-term care, and the third is unpaid care work, which is common at an age when people both give and receive care.

These channels matter because old age is where life-course disadvantage accumulates. For most women, their lifetime earnings and pension entitlements might reflect decades of interrupted participation, often caused by part-time or unpaid caregiving (Elson, 2016). This disadvantage is exposed when public pensions, healthcare, and long-term care are cut, as often happens during consolidation. Cash-based measures of hardship capture the income side of this exposure but they say little about functional health, service access, or social participation. These dimensions become salient once people leave the labour market and depend more on public provision. Therefore, a purely income-based reading of austerity’s welfare cost is likely to underestimate its gendered incidence among older cohorts.

papers.title: Collinear motions in constant curvature spaces, and coplanar motions in $\mathbb{R^4}$
papers.abstract: A collinear motion of an $n$-body problem is one in which the $n$-bodies always lie along some, possibly moving, geodesic during their evolution. We prove that every collinear motion of $n\geq 3$ bodies in a constant non-zero curvature space is necessarily contained in some fixed constant curvature space of dimension at most three. For natural systems admitting energy and angular momentum integrals, we further show that every such motion is necessarily a relative equilibrium: evolving under uniform rotation while maintaining constant mutual distances. These results extend certain classical results on collinear motions in Euclidean spaces, initiated by P. Pizzetti, to general spaces of constant curvature. The same methods also yield a partial answer to a question of A. Wintner. Namely, we show that any concave and always coplanar motion in the Euclidean 4-body problem, where the moving plane containing the bodies sweeps out an $\mathbb{R}^4$, must be self-similar: maintaining constant mutual distance ratios over the motion.

To fix the ideas, the first interesting case asks: what are those solutions of an n≥3n\geq 3-body problem such that, at each instant, the nn-bodies are contained in some line? There is of course a trivial answer to this question: we can let the nn-bodies evolve along any fixed line, by giving them any initial positions and velocities all aligned along said common line. Are there other examples? Where the bodies evolve along a moving line? Yes: the classic Euler-Moulton solutions to the nn-body problem [9], [25]. For these solutions the nn-bodies lie in a specific mass dependent configuration. During the motion, their directing line sweeps out some fixed 2-plane while their mutual distances maintain constant ratios (a self-similar motion, also sometimes called ‘homographic’). Anything else? As it turns out, no, there is nothing else to add. The complete description of collinear motions of a Euclidean nn-body problem consists in the motions along some line with fixed direction and the Euler-Moulton solutions (see figure 2). papers.title: Generalized MLS and LS-SVR for Allen-Cahn Equations on Spheres
papers.abstract: This work extends least-squares support vector regression (LS-SVR) based on the generalized moving least squares (GMLS) approximation to the numerical solution of partial differential equations on spheres. We show that the proposed approach constructs a kernel-based approximant in its dual form and establishes its connection with the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Furthermore, solving the PDE through the proposed LS-SVR framework is shown to be equivalent to solving a smoothing problem or a kernel ridge regression problem in the corresponding RKHS. As applications, the method is employed to solve the Allen-Cahn equation and its conservative counterpart on spheres. An implicit first-order operator-splitting scheme is used to separate each model into linear and nonlinear subproblems. The linear subproblem is discretized by the backward differentiation formula and approximated at each time step using LS-SVR derived from a GMLS-based collocation formulation, while the nonlinear part is treated analytically. The resulting scheme is shown to admit a unique numerical solution at every time step. For the conservative Allen-Cahn model, a correction procedure is incorporated to preserve mass. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Overall, the numerical techniques applied to the surface PDE problems fall into two groups, i.e., the intrinsic and embedded narrow band methods (cf. [10, 17, 18, 20, 22, 31, 33, 34, 39, 41, 44, 53, 61]). The first group of these methods attempts to find an approximation to the differential operator in the original dimension. Of course, this approach faces difficulty with the inherent coordinate distortions or singularities arising in the metric terms of the differential operators (cf. [20]). In the second group, the differential operators are extended to the extrinsic coordinates, which avoids all coordinate singularities. Accordingly, any standard numerical methods such as the finite difference (FD) schemes on 3​D3D regular nodes and the finite element method (FEM) on unstructured meshes can be implemented. Of course, these methods increase the computational costs because they solve the problem in a dimension at least one greater than the original dimension of the main equation. papers.title: A unified quantitative approach to Chiti and Kohler--Jobin inequalities
papers.abstract: We obtain two quantitative results related to classical rearrangement inequalities for the first Dirichlet eigenvalue. The first one is a quantitative version of Chiti's reverse Hölder inequality. More precisely, for every $1\le q<p<\infty$, we prove that the deficit controls, up to translations, the $L^q$ distance between a first eigenfunction of a bounded domain and the first eigenfunction of the ball having the same first eigenvalue. The second result concerns the Kohler--Jobin inequality and gives a quantitative estimate in terms of the $L^\infty\!\to L^2$ distance between the corresponding Dirichlet resolvents. In both cases, the main idea is to find a suitable superlevel set of the first eigenfunction which is almost optimal for the Faber-Krahn inequality.

papers.title: RankAlign: Vision-Language Representation Alignment via Rank Transformation
papers.abstract: While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that vision and language models converge toward compatible latent geometries, recovering class-level correspondences between unpaired modalities without cross-modal supervision remains challenging. Existing relational matching methods compare within-modality similarity kernels directly, although the same semantic structure may be represented through different numerical parameterizations across modalities. We propose RankAlign, a rank-based normalization strategy for class-level unpaired vision-language matching. RankAlign transforms each within-modality similarity kernel into an ordinal relational representation before permutation matching, while leaving the correspondence space and matching solver unchanged. The resulting representation is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations of similarity values while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching. We provide exact-recovery and stability guarantees that characterize correspondence recovery under both exact and partial ordinal agreement. Experiments across diverse frozen vision and language encoders and multiple datasets demonstrate improved and more stable class-level correspondence recovery, including under label corruption and domain shift.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in foundation models have fundamentally redefined representation learning across diverse modalities. While self-supervised vision encoders like DINO [1] and large-scale language models [3, 17] have matured within their respective domains, multimodal contrastive frameworks such as CLIP [15] and SigLIP2 [22] have further bridged the two modalities. These architectures induce sophisticated latent representations that capture intricate structural and semantic nuances. Yet, despite this progress, the geometric alignment between visual and language representation spaces remains poorly understood when encoders are trained independently on disparate datasets. This poses a significant challenge for class-level unpaired cross-modal matching, where category structure is available within each modality, while the correspondence between visual and textual categories remains unknown and must be recovered.

Representation similarity and the Platonic hypothesis. Independently trained visual and language models frequently exhibit a striking convergence toward compatible representational structures. This phenomenon is formalized by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, which posits that scaling and data diversity drive neural networks toward shared latent geometries that encode the statistical regularities of the world [6]. In vision-language settings, visual and textual encoders learn compatible relational structures despite disparate training objectives [10, 19]. Although methods such as CCA [5], SVCCA [16], and CKA [8] provide quantitative measures of representational similarity, they rely on direct numerical comparisons that are inherently sensitive to modality-specific scale distortions and biases.

Class-level unpaired vision-language matching. The emergence of a shared embedding space raises the fundamental question: can explicit correspondences between vision and language representations be recovered when independently trained encoders receive no paired supervision? Traditional alignment relies on image–caption pairs or manually verified correspondences to learn a cross-modal mapping. We instead study class-level unpaired vision-language matching with known within-modality groups and an unordered candidate set of textual concepts, where visual groups and a set of candidate textual concepts are available but their cross-modal correspondence is unknown. Supervision is confined to constructing class-level representations within each modality, with no paired image–text samples, cross-modal anchors, or verified correspondences provided to the matching procedure. When reliable cross-modal anchors are available, supervised alignment is often simpler and more practical. Our goal is to determine whether independently trained encoders contain sufficient relational structure to recover correspondence without such anchors. This zero-anchor setting can arise when visual groups and a candidate textual ontology are collected or maintained independently, so that both sides are available but their correspondence has not been verified. In this regime, correspondence recovery can reduce the need for manually established cross-modal anchors and also serves as a diagnostic of structural compatibility between independently trained representation spaces. More broadly, it tests whether cross-modal correspondence can emerge from relational structure alone, without shared training data or explicit cross-modal supervision. Recent work frames this problem as matching pairwise relationships between embeddings [19]. Such formulations arise naturally in kernel alignment [2], graph matching via quadratic assignment [23], and structural optimal transport, most notably the Gromov-Wasserstein (𝒢​𝒲\mathcal{GW}) distance [14, 24].

papers.title: The Critical 2D KPZ Process
papers.abstract: This work constructs a non-trivial solution to the ill-defined two-dimensional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation at criticality: a distribution-valued stochastic process on the plane, which we call the Critical 2D KPZ Process. It arises as the limit in law of centred log partition functions of two-dimensional Gaussian directed polymers at criticality, viewed as discretised KPZ solutions. It is also a measurable function of the Critical 2D Stochastic Heat Flow (SHF) via a renormalised Cole-Hopf transformation, obtained as the limit of the centred logarithm of the spatially mollified SHF as the smoothing is removed. The Critical 2D KPZ process is non-Gaussian and its covariance displays a log-log blow-up near the diagonal. Gaussian fluctuations emerge when averaging on shrinking spatial scales. The results presented here were obtained through extensive interactions with generative AI (ChatGPT 5.5, 5.6 and 6); see Appendix C for more details. The proof builds on key recent and older advances in our field, combined in novel ways with substantial AI input. We view this manuscript as a "community project" that represents more than a decade's collective effort. We have worked on making the presentation as accessible as possible, highlighting the main ideas and their relations to the literature.

papers.title: Eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems
papers.abstract: We have identified numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triple star systems from observations made with the space telescope TESS. For many of these systems we can potentially determine their dynamical and astrophysical parameters with high precision, in some cases even without the use of radial velocity data. In the present paper we report the comprehensive study of eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems, taken from this larger sample: TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, 385933895. Besides the photometric data from the TESS observations, we obtained supplementary ground-based photometric measurements, as well as radial velocity measurements for some of the systems. The eclipse timing variation curves extracted from the TESS data and from the ground-based follow up data, the photometric light curves, radial velocity data, and the spectral energy distribution are combined in a complex photodynamical analysis to yield the stellar and orbital parameters for all of the investigated systems. The outer periods are in the range of 63-294 days, including the currently sixth tightest known triple system, TI 385933895 with an outer to inner period ratio of 9.82. We find that all of the triples are nearly coplanar, with mutual inclination angles of <=2.5deg. Despite such flatness, we still detect eclipse depth variations in TIC 220456364 that are induced by orbital plane precession. Moreover, we find that TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple system. Finally we make some statistical assessments of a number of the orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances of these systems.

It was only 15 years ago, when the discoveries of the first two triply eclipsing triple star systems were reported (Carter et al., 2011; Derekas et al., 2011). These novel findings were based on investigations of the photometric data from the Kepler-spacecraft (Borucki et al., 2010). Later, further photometric observations with the Kepler space telescope led to the discovery of more than a dozen additional triply eclipsing systems. While a few subsequent discoveries of triply eclipsing triples were reported sporadically with the use of other space-borne and ground-based instruments (Borkovits, 2022, see the list of), the discovery of triply eclipsing triples became routine only with the advent of the TESS space telescope (Ricker et al., 2015). Due to its monitoring of the entire sky over the past eight years11 1 This monitoring covers some 5% of the sky for a month before the field of regard is moved. The higher the ecliptic latitude of a source, the longer it continues to be monitored., by now TESS has found more than a hundred triply eclipsing triple star candidates.

papers.title: GigaBench: Benchmarking Learnable Representations for Gigapixel Image Compression and Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Learnable Representations (LRs) can fit parametric families of functions to diverse kinds of signals. These emergent neural-native data formats are gathering interest in the scientific community due to their compactness, resolution-agnosticism and amenability to direct neural processing. On the other hand, gigapixel images are becoming increasingly widespread across a variety of scientific, cultural, and industrial domains. In this paper, we present GigaBench, the first benchmark and experimental evaluation focused on deploying LRs with gigapixel imagery. GigaBench includes images collected, acquired, and synthetically rendered across diverse domains, and addresses image compression and super-resolution. We adapt a representative set of LRs, spanning Implicit, Hybrid, and Explicit methods, so as to operate reliably at the gigapixel scale on consumer hardware. Through systematic evaluation across reconstruction quality, model size, compression and inference times, we identify consistent trends across methods and suggest actionable guidance for future investigation.

papers.intro:
The emergence of Learnable Representations (LRs) has opened up a different paradigm for image storage, reconstruction and processing. Rather than representing an image as a discrete grid of pixel values, LRs enable encoding it as a continuous function, defined by a set of optimizable parameters, that maps spatial coordinates to color values. Prominent variants of LRs include Implicit Representations [45, 30, 12], which encode an image in the weights of an MLP; Hybrid Representations [36, 48, 10], which additionally incorporate spatially localized learnable features; and Explicit Representations [55, 28], which represent images using Gaussian primitives. LRs have attracted significant attention for their compactness, resolution-agnosticism and amenability to direct neural processing. As a matter of fact, several recent works [15, 52, 20, 3] have shown how the learned parameters can be fed into specifically designed meta-networks to perform downstream tasks like classification and retrieval, without requiring reconstruction of the original discrete signal. Such property positions LRs as a pathway to a new generation of neural-native data formats.

On the other hand, digital imaging is undergoing a quiet resolution revolution, as gigapixel images are becoming increasingly common across a variety of scientific, cultural, and industrial domains, from whole-slide pathology imaging [7, 14] and satellite remote sensing [11] to high-fidelity museum digitisation and panoramic photography [24]. Yet, the paradigms and tools for handling images at this scale remain largely anchored to classical pipelines, designed in an era when such resolutions were inconceivable. Hence, we pose a timely research question concerning whether and how LRs can be effectively deployed for gigapixel-scale images, and which of their variants show the greatest promise for enabling adoption within this increasingly relevant regime. However, despite the favourable properties of LRs and the increasing adoption of gigapixel imagery, the current literature lacks a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of LR methods on gigapixel images. Indeed, the reported experimental findings primarily concern datasets with much lower and more conventional resolutions, typically ranging from less than one megapixel to a few megapixels, where the computational cost of fitting LRs remains easily tractable. The gigapixel regime, however, introduces fundamentally different challenges, as fitting a single image may require hours of training, naive partitioning strategies introduce boundary artifacts, and memory constraints force architectural compromises that do not arise at standard resolutions. Adapting existing LRs to this setting is therefore a non-trivial task.

In this paper, we introduce GigaBench, a benchmark specifically designed to address the aforementioned scientific questions and foster research into the design of LR approaches suitable for gigapixel imagery. We curate a collection of gigapixel images across diverse domains and evaluate LRs on compression and super-resolution under controlled settings. Our evaluation spans the three main families of approaches: Implicit, Hybrid and Explicit Gaussian-based Representations. Our analysis reveals several consistent trends across the three families. Hybrid representations achieve the highest reconstruction fidelity but are structurally limited to moderate compression ratios, as their grid-based components impose a memory floor that prevents compression at extreme rates. On the other hand, they neatly outperform other LR approaches when it comes to super-resolution, although a human evaluation suggests that the merits of LR at the gigapixel scales are somewhat uncertain compared to classical methodologies, such as bicubic interpolation. Implicit representations, by contrast, can provide high to extreme compression ratios, trading fidelity for compression. Explicit representations exhibit the most variable intra-family behaviours in both compression and super-resolution, with performance depending heavily on the chosen parametrisation. Across all families, no single approach dominates uniformly as the optimal choice depends on the target compression or super-resolution ratio, as well as on the quality-speed trade-off.

Across all families, no single approach dominates uniformly as the optimal choice depends on the target compression or super-resolution ratio, as well as on the quality-speed trade-off.

Our contributions can be summarised as follows: (i) we introduce a curated benchmark of gigapixel images spanning 10 scenes and different domains, released publicly to foster future research; (ii) we provide a systematic comparison of representative Implicit, Hybrid, and Explicit representations to gigapixel image compression and super-resolution; (iii) we characterise the practical trade-offs among the specific methods evaluated across fidelity, speed, and downstream usability, offering concrete guidance for researchers and practitioners working in this emerging regime.

papers.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
papers.abstract: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) store knowledge in their parameters, making information outside or newer than their pre-training data hard to access or update (Lewis et al., 2020). Such external knowledge may be organised as text-attributed graphs (He et al., 2024). We can incorporate this information into an LLM either by textualizing the graphs, i.e., constructing verbalized descriptions of nodes and edges, or through graph soft prompting, i.e., providing a learned representation generated by a graph neural network (GNN). Verbalisation has two limitations: its token cost grows with the amount of graph content included, and serialisation imposes a sequence order on facts that have no intrinsic order. Expressive Graph soft prompting aims to offer an alternative interface for conveying relational information without verbalising every node and edge. G-Retriever (He et al., 2024) supplies the same underlying graph via both channels. However, this design introduces an identifiability issue: because the graph content is already present in textual form, improvements in answer accuracy alone cannot distinguish whether the model relies on the graph token, the verbalized graph, or both. Furthermore, the training objective does not explicitly enforce that the graph-derived token encodes graph-specific information when the textual channel suffices. Consequently, a token computed from the graph may degenerate into a graph-invariant soft prompt.

This study evaluates the proposed mechanism by quantifying both the information encoded in graph-derived tokens and the information that the large language model (LLM) causally exploits during inference. In addition to answer accuracy, we assess gold-answer log-likelihood to capture subtler shifts in the model’s output distribution, and we employ decoding-based probes to measure the recoverability of question, answer, and graph attributes from internal representations. Graph-free control conditions preserve the projector architecture and the full training pipeline while ablating the graph input itself.

Applying this protocol to G-Retriever uncovers an unanticipated phenomenon that we call token collapse, which also recurs in subsequent graph-prompting methods. Specifically, across several graph encoders, benchmark datasets, LLM families, and fine-tuning regimes, the token representations generated by G-Retriever are nearly invariant with respect to the input graph (Figure 1). Moreover, substituting these input-dependent projected tokens with a fixed alternative yields no resolved answer-level effect under the default configuration; indeed, a learned constant token that never observes any graph matches or even surpasses the performance of the full model. These results indicate that the collapsed token operates primarily as a soft prompt rather than as a carrier of graph-specific information. Although likelihood-based analyses show that perturbing the token can modulate the output distribution, such sensitivity alone is insufficient to demonstrate input- or graph-conditioned utilization.

We associate collapse with two factors: a projector that suppresses variation in the encoder representations and an answer objective that does not require this variation to be preserved. Our ablations implicate both factors, although they do not isolate either as the sole cause. We address them with a two-stage pipeline that first aligns and freezes the graph encoder, then trains separate graph-token and prompt-token pathways. The resulting tokens no longer collapse, but non-collapse alone guarantees neither graph use nor improved accuracy. Depending on the benchmark and training configuration, they may encode the question, an answer prior, graph information made redundant by the text, or graph information that the LLM uses to answer. This distinction matters because task improvements may otherwise be attributed to graph–language alignment even when they arise from the verbalised graph or a graph-independent soft prompt. By separating token variation, graph content, and downstream use, our protocol makes alignment empirically testable and provides concrete criteria for developing graph–language models that preserve and use task-relevant graph information beyond what is already supplied by the textual channel.

papers.title: Grushin spherical harmonics in non-degenerate dimension one
papers.abstract: The Grushin Laplacian $Δ_α= Δ_x +|x|^{2α}Δ_y $ is a degenerate elliptic operator in $\mathbb{R}^{h+k}$ that degenerates on $\{0\} \times \mathbb{R}^k$. We explicitly compute the Grushin spherical harmonics on the gauge sphere $\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^{h+k} : |x|^{2(α+1)}+(α+1)^2|y|^2=1\}$ and the corresponding spectrum when the non-degenerate dimension $h=1$, a case not covered by the existing literature. The eigenfunctions consist of homogeneous Grushin-harmonic polynomials of degrees $n \equiv 0,1 \pmod{α+1}$, even and odd in the $x$-variable respectively, which can be described in terms of Jacobi polynomials.

papers.intro:
Riemannian symmetric spaces are among the most extensively studied objects in Riemannian geometry. In submanifold theory, an “extrinsically” symmetric submanifold is defined in analogy with Riemannian symmetric spaces, namely by requiring the existence of an extrinsic symmetry at each point of the submanifold; such a submanifold is simply called a symmetric submanifold. This notion was first introduced in [10], particularly for submanifolds in Euclidean space, and has since been the focus of considerable research; see, for example, [4, 9, 24, 27, 30]. Note that the definition of a (locally) symmetric submanifold clearly implies that the submanifold is “intrinsically” (locally) symmetric.

papers.title: Verus-Insight: Towards Explainable Artifact Detection in AI-Generated Videos
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.

papers.title: Fit-error corrected auxiliary master equation approach for low-temperature nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory
papers.abstract: The auxiliary master equation approach (AMEA) is a nonperturbative impurity solver for steady-state nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). It replaces the physical hybridization function by that of a small auxiliary open quantum system, whose parameters are fitted to reproduce it, and then solves the resulting many-body problem essentially exactly. AMEA's accuracy is thus limited by the quality of this fit: since the fastest-varying part of the hybridization is set by the distribution function, whose Fermi edges sharpen at low temperature, the fit tends to overestimate the temperature, especially for weak reservoir coupling. For the auxiliary hybridization itself, however, AMEA's self-energy is essentially exact. We correct for the fit error by estimating, via an approximate solver applicable to arbitrary hybridization functions, the ratio between the self-energies of the physical and auxiliary hybridizations, and using it to extend AMEA's self-energy from the auxiliary to the physical case. This fit-error correction becomes exact whenever either the fit or the approximate solver is exact. We benchmark the scheme using the nonequilibrium Kajueter-Kotliar iterated perturbation theory (IPT), generalized here to spin-polarized solutions, as the approximate solver; other approximate solvers, such as the noncrossing approximation, can be used as well. Applied to an Anderson impurity model with a spin-polarized bath, and within DMFT to a Hubbard layer weakly coupled to two metallic reservoirs, the correction largely removes the spurious heating from the AMEA fit and from insufficient thermalization by the reservoirs, while preserving the correct description of the Mott insulator, which IPT alone cannot fully recover.

papers.intro:
Correlated electron systems driven into a nonequilibrium steady state by a current or a bias display a wealth of phenomena, ranging from the dielectric breakdown and resistive switching of Mott insulators [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] to the current-induced manipulation of magnetic order. The latter is the operating principle of antiferromagnetic spintronics, in which the Néel vector of metallic antiferromagnets such as CuMnAs and Mn2Au is reoriented by current pulses [10, 11, 12], and it has received renewed interest with the discovery of altermagnets [13]. Correlated antiferromagnetic Mott insulators respond to a current as well: in Sr2IrO4 it lowers the Néel temperature [14], and in Ca2RuO4 it drives an insulator-to-metal transition whose current-carrying states can coexist with, or suppress, the antiferromagnetic order [15]. A question that accompanies all these experiments is whether the observed effect is an intrinsic nonequilibrium phenomenon or merely a consequence of Joule heating, and the answer is often far from obvious [16, 17, 18, 15, 19, 20].

A question that accompanies all these experiments is whether the observed effect is an intrinsic nonequilibrium phenomenon or merely a consequence of Joule heating, and the answer is often far from obvious [16, 17, 18, 15, 19, 20].

From the theoretical standpoint, a driven system reaches a stationary state only if the injected energy is removed by a dissipative environment [21, 22, 3]. The temperature of the electrons or, more generally, their nonequilibrium distribution function is then an outcome of the balance between injection and dissipation rather than an input parameter. Since broken-symmetry phases such as magnetic order exist only below a characteristic temperature, whether they survive a drive depends on how far this distribution departs from a cold Fermi function [23, 24, 25]. A theory that aims to separate intrinsic nonequilibrium effects from heating must therefore describe the distribution function accurately at temperatures well below the ordering scale, and it must not heat the electrons on its own.

papers.title: Diagnosing the Explicit-to-Applied Theory of Mind Gap in LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. To assess recovery, we compare structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and our proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters on answered support questions through action reconstruction. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-oss-20B, recovery depends on the model, task, and intervention. On SimpleToM, reminders combined with BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 percentage points; reminders account for most of the overall improvement, with BSTTT adding 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond reminders across models. Contextual examples often outperform weight updates, while BSTTT remains stronger in specific model-benchmark settings. Temporal belief tracking remains difficult despite partial recovery. These findings show that aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance. We recommend decomposed reporting of explicit and applied accuracy alongside intervention comparisons that establish which failures are recoverable and under what conditions.

papers.intro:
Theory of Mind (ToM) is the capacity to attribute beliefs, intentions, and emotions to other agents and to reason about how those states shape behavior (Premack and Woodruff, 1978; Baron-Cohen et al., 1985). This capacity encompasses two qualitatively different competencies. Explicit ToM is recognizing that another agent holds a particular mental state. Applied ToM is using that recognition to predict behavior, anticipate consequences, or evaluate actions. The two can dissociate (Apperly, 2012). Reporting a single accuracy that averages recognition and application questions obscures this distinction. Figure 1 illustrates the dissociation on SimpleToM: Llama-3.1-8B recognizes mental states at 99.4% yet predicts the resulting behavior at only 28.9%, a 70.5-point explicit-to-applied gap. Its overall accuracy of 51.5% hides both near-perfect recognition and weak application. This explicit-to-applied gap motivates two hypotheses. Under a capacity-limitation hypothesis (H1), models lack some of the reasoning capabilities required to translate recognized mental states into reliable behavioral predictions. papers.title: Granulation-driven spectral irradiance variability of Sun-like stars
papers.abstract: Granulation,caused by convection in low-mass stars like the Sun, introduces small amplitude variations in the stellar brightness on timescales of minutes to hours. Often referred to as flicker or microvariability this signal can impede detecting Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars via stellar transits. Stellar flicker can also introduce uncertainties in determining stellar fundamental parameters and cause errors of up to 10% in the radius determination of transiting exoplanets. Both sources of uncertainties will propagate into planetary transmission spectra and resulting atmospheric retrievals. We present a method for modelling stellar flicker that enables scaling the flicker of Sun-like stars between different wavelengths and passbands to facilitate better solar-stellar comparisons. We use the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic code MURaM to simulate the granulation pattern on a Sun-like star and employ the radiative transfer code MPS-ATLAS for the spectral synthesis of the MURaM output, producing lightcurves of the granulation signal in various wavelengths and at different disc positions. Using these synthetic lightcurves, we establish scaling relations in the time and frequency domain between different wavelengths and passbands routinely used in stellar observations, such as the Kepler and TESS space telescopes. We find that the variability caused by granulation is very well correlated across wavelengths from 300 to 6000 nm, enabling scalings from one wavelength regime to another. We present the scaling sensitivities in different passbands and wavelength regimes that can be used to facilitate solar-stellar comparisons and help estimate stellar flicker in observations using photometric passbands and low-resolution transmission spectra.

papers.intro:
Stellar variability is currently regarded as one of the main limiting factors of not only detection of Earth-sized exoplanets but also characterisation of the atmospheres of exoplanets via a technique called transmission spectroscopy (Seager and Sasselov, 2000). This stellar ‘noise’ comes in various forms: on cool stars like the Sun dark features (spots) and bright counterparts (faculae) are the dominant source of stellar brightness variations on timescales longer than the stellar rotation. Faculae and spots are both surface manifestations of magnetic fields generated in the interior regions of Sun-like stars. (Solanki et al., 2006; Shapiro et al., 2017). On shorter timescales, convection drives granulation, causing luminosity variations referred to as ‘microvariability’ or ‘stellar flicker’. Despite the amplitude of this latter signal being significantly smaller compared to the amplitude from the magnetic activity (Aigrain et al., 2004; Shapiro et al., 2017, i.e.,),(hereafter 1) the convective granulation signal introduces uncertainties in the determination of planetary radii. In photometry in particular, this planetary-radius uncertainty can be between 1% (Chiavassa et al., 2017) and 10% Sulis et al. (2020). These radius uncertainties also affect planetary transmission spectra, hence will influence any atmospheric retrievals, and therefore need to be accounted for in characterizations of exoplanet atmospheres (see Rackham et al., 2023, for review). Additionally, Bonifacio et al. (2018) reported that ignoring granulation effects can lead to underestimation of the stellar effective temperature by up to 200 K and overestimation of gravity by up to 0.5 dex if stellar colours (i.e., differential photometry) are used to determine stellar fundamental parameters, which again impact the characterisation of exoplanet atmospheres.

(1995)) to approximate the solar variability on various timescales via decomposing these different scales in the power spectrum. Later work by Van Kooten et al. (2021) (hereafter 33) showed the limitations in understanding of solar-stellar connections and our modelling efforts. However, the Kepler filter system is operating in different wavelength ranges than the three VIRGO/SPM filters, which introduces a bias (Basri et al., 2013).

When we speak about granular flicker, we mostly talk about signal that comes from regions that are free of large-scale or strong magnetic fields (i.e., outside of spot and faculae regions, which not only carry large magnetic fields but also inhibit convection). However, even in the quiet solar photosphere, we find small patches of polarities with (comparatively) weak magnetic fields. To advance modelling of solar and stellar granulation, it is therefore essential to include the effects of small-scale dynamo (SSD) action. Currently, only the MURaM code takes such effects into account (Vögler et al., 2005; Schüssler and Vögler, 2008; Rempel, 2014). In order to study the wavelength dependence of the granular flicker and establish a means to predict the flicker in different passbands, radiative transfer on the MURaM output is performed with the Merged Parallelised Simplified ATLAS code (Witzke et al., 2021, MPS-ATLAS). This work presents a proof-of-concept study of utilising 3D MHD calculations for stellar flicker and provides scaling relations to predict the flicker in stars similar to the Sun.

papers.title: Closing All-Exp Gaps in Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximum Constraint Assignment
papers.abstract: We prove the all-exp property for the Traveling Salesman Problem with the $2$-opt neighborhood, and for $(3,2,2)$- and $(2,3,2)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment with the flip neighborhood. The all-exp property states that infinitely many instances have an initial solution from which every sequence of improving moves to a local optimum, and hence every run of local search, has exponential length. For the Traveling Salesman Problem, the all-exp property was previously known for every $k$-opt neighborhood with $k \ge 3$, so our result for $2$-opt completes the picture for all $k$-kopt neighborhoods. In $(p,q,r)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment, each constraint involves at most $p$ variables, each variable occurs in at most $q$ constraints, and each domain has size $r$. Decreasing any of the parameters of $(3,2,2)$ or $(2,3,2)$ yields a problem in which every sequence of improving flips has polynomial length, so both Maximum Constraint Assignment results are tight. All three results settle long-standing open problems. Our proofs build on a common construction idea, which reveals a close connection between the local-search dynamics of the three problems.

papers.intro:
Local search is a fundamental algorithmic approach for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Starting from an initial solution, a local-search algorithm repeatedly replaces the current solution with a better solution from a well-defined neighborhood, until a local optimum is reached. Despite the simplicity of this approach and its excellent practical performance for many problems, the worst-case behavior of local search can be surprisingly complicated. Johnson, Papadimitriou, and Yannakakis introduced the complexity class PLS to capture the difficulty of finding locally optimal solutions [12]. Schäffer and Yannakakis later defined tight PLS-reductions and showed that problems proven PLS-complete via such reductions exhibit particularly strong forms of hardness [20].

Local search is a fundamental algorithmic approach for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Starting from an initial solution, a local-search algorithm repeatedly replaces the current solution with a better solution from a well-defined neighborhood, until a local optimum is reached. Despite the simplicity of this approach and its excellent practical performance for many problems, the worst-case behavior of local search can be surprisingly complicated. Johnson, Papadimitriou, and Yannakakis introduced the complexity class PLS to capture the difficulty of finding locally optimal solutions [12]. Schäffer and Yannakakis later defined tight PLS-reductions and showed that problems proven PLS-complete via such reductions exhibit particularly strong forms of hardness [20].

One such form of hardness concerns not the complexity of finding a local optimum but the number of iterations performed by local search. A first indication of such hardness is the is-exp property: there are infinitely many instances, each with an initial solution, from which at least one sequence of improving moves to a local optimum has exponential length. This alone, however, does not imply that local search necessarily takes exponentially many iterations. Whenever several improving neighbors are available, a pivot rule determines which one is chosen, and a suitable pivot rule may avoid the long sequence and reach a local optimum much faster. The strongest possible negative result is that a problem has the all-exp property: there are infinitely many instances, each with an initial solution, such that every sequence of improving moves from this initial solution to a local optimum has exponential length. Equivalently, even under an optimal pivot rule, local search started from these initial solutions requires exponentially many iterations. Every problem shown to be PLS-complete via a tight PLS-reduction has the all-exp property [20]. However, the all-exp property can also be established by direct constructions, which work even for problems not known to be PLS-complete.
