One of the most prominent local-search heuristics is kk-opt for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). The case k=2k=2, called 2-opt, was already studied by Croes in 1958 [3] and is the oldest and simplest local-search method for the TSP. In each iteration, 2-opt replaces two edges of the current tour with two other edges such that the resulting tour is shorter. The kk-opt heuristic generalizes 2-opt by replacing up to kk edges in each iteration. Both 2-opt and kk-opt for general kk have been studied extensively, theoretically as well as experimentally; see, for example, [1, 10, 2, 11, 9, 22].

This makes it more difficult to implement the desired state transitions independently.

papers.title: Energy-rate equidistribution for adaptive SSAV--BDF2 integration of gradient flows
papers.abstract: We develop an adaptive time-stepping strategy for scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) schemes combined with variable-step BDF2 discretization for gradient flows. The strategy selects step sizes based on the instantaneous energy dissipation rate and enforces monotonicity of a computable symmetric energy through a step rejection mechanism. We show that the step-size rules used in practice correspond to equidistributing a monitor function along the energy curve, connecting energy-adaptive time stepping to the classical theory of r-adaptive mesh methods. The monitor $g = |\dot{E}|$ is asymptotically optimal as it minimises the leading-order maximum symmetric-energy discrepancy for a given number of steps. A combined monitor that switches to $g = \sqrt{|\dot{E}|}$ near equilibrium caps step growth without degrading this error bound. The arclength parameter $β$ used in prior work is shown to be the ratio of the largest permitted step to the energy-error tolerance. The controller is paired with the SSAV--BDF2 discretization. Accepted steps satisfy monotonicity of the symmetric energy, from which we deduce a bound on the physical energy that is uniform in the number of steps, $\sup_n E(u^n) \le E(u^{0}) + τ_1 + O(Δt_{\max}^2)$, and the scheme achieves second-order global accuracy under standard step-ratio restrictions. Numerical experiments on Cahn--Hilliard, Ohta--Kawasaki, Phase--Field Crystal, and functionalized Cahn--Hilliard models confirm the theory and demonstrate the method's efficiency.

papers.title: Pos4CHD: A Positive-Free Mask-Guided Counterfactual Synthesis Framework for Fetal Congenital Heart Defect Analysis
papers.abstract: The scarcity of positive cases remains a major bottleneck in developing automated diagnostic systems for fetal Congenital Heart Defects~(CHDs), particularly for rare subtypes. Although normal cases are accessible with effort, positive cases are hard to collect due to low incidence rates and privacy concerns, causing severe class imbalance or absence of positive training samples. Existing works resort to synthesizing positives with conditional generative models, but they are task-specific and require positive training samples, hindering application for fetal CHDs. To this end, we propose a positive-free mask-guided counterfactual generation framework for fetal echocardiography, namely Pos4CHD, which enables realistic, high-quality synthesis of pseudo-positive samples from semantic masks, with only normal samples at hand. Technically, we first develop FE-Gen, a mask-guided generative model tailored for fetal heart ultrasound synthesis that mitigates histogram drift and enhances image-mask spatial alignment. Building on FE-Gen, Pos4CHD employs a mask-to-image generation paradigm for CHD synthesis. It first manipulates semantic masks to simulate fetal-heart structural anomalies and then renders anatomically consistent images. Extensive experiments on in-house datasets, together with expert evaluations, demonstrate the visual fidelity~($-12.97$ FID) and anatomical consistency~($+3.96\%$ DSC) of synthesized images. Further validations across diverse real-world CHD diagnosis tasks exhibit promising results and consistent increments, including zero-shot classification~(achieving $93.25\%$ ACC on EbA and $72.92\%$ ACC on TAPVC), lesion detection~($+6.95\%$ mAP50 on VSD), and anatomy segmentation~($+10.49\%$ DSC on fetal heart) compared with baselines. Codes and models are publicly available on \href{https://github.com/DREAMXFAR/Pos4CHD}{GitHub}.
papers.intro:
Fetal congenital heart defects (CHDs), characterized by heterogeneous structural anomalies, are one of the leading causes of infant mortality, which affects approximately 0.80.8∼\sim1.0%1.0\% of live births [1, 2]. Fetal echocardiography, i.e., fetal heart ultrasound, is the primary tool for prenatal examination due to its radiation-free, low-cost, and real-time nature. Clinicians typically examine fetal heart anatomical structures using standardized cardiac views [3] like the Four-Chamber (4CH) view, Three-Vessel and Trachea (3VT) view, etc., which provide essential and vital references for cardiac function analysis. This practice helps early detection and diagnosis of various CHD subtypes, including Ebstein’s Anomaly (EbA), Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC), Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), etc., contributing to improved worldwide pregnancy healthcare [4].

More importantly, given the wide range of CHD subtypes (≥\geq2727), although normal cases are accessible through clinical efforts, positive cases for rare CHDs are often out of reach owing to low incidence rates (<<1/10,0001/10,000) [2] and privacy constraints. This positive-sample scarcity hinders the training of downstream models, leading to severe class imbalance and potential generalization issues [6].

Recent advances in generative models, e.g., diffusion models, offer a promising solution to medical data scarcity via image synthesis. Existing studies focused on improving image fidelity [7, 8] and anatomical plausibility [9, 10] across different imaging modalities, and adapting generative foundation models for medical applications [11, 12, 13]. Conditional generative models, e.g., Stable Diffusion (SD) [14] and ControlNet [15], further enable task-specific conditional guidance to synthesize images with desired properties. Practices (see Fig. 1) include class labels or text prompts [16, 17] for anatomical description, layouts [18] for lesion position and size, segmentation masks [19, 20] for structure and shape, with optional reference images [21, 22] to provide extra context for local variations. Such methods can produce paired image-condition data for augmentation purposes and benefit various downstream tasks including classification, segmentation, and multi-center generalization [10, 23]. Despite these advances, directly applying such approaches to fetal CHD synthesis remains challenging. First, most works are designed for specific tasks and limited scenarios. We need to redesign a framework for fetal CHD synthesis, where the complicated cardiac anatomy and heterogeneous CHD subtypes raise the complexity. Second, current methods [24, 25, 26] require positive samples to learn lesion-specific textures and structures, implicitly assuming the availability of positive cases. But this assumption is violated because of the absence of fetal CHD samples, particularly for rare subtypes. Third, existing works lack fine-grained control over synthesized images. As shown in Fig. 1, given that CHDs are mostly structural anomalies, the class labels and text prompts offer limited spatial control, where the anatomical plausibility of synthesized positives depends on generative priors and is hardly guaranteed. Though bounding boxes offer locations and enable simulation of position and size variations, they still fall short in depicting morphology and fine-grained variations, thus insufficient to distinguish anatomical differences across CHD subtypes. Therefore, we raise the question: can we design a unified framework to synthesize realistic and anatomy-consistent samples of diverse CHD subtypes for downstream analysis, with only negative samples at hand?

Firstly, considering the absence of publicly available datasets, we collect ∼\sim8k fetal 4CH views and ∼\sim500500 expert-annotations covering 14 key anatomical structures (Sec. III-C1), and train FE-Gen (Sec. III-C2), a mask-conditioned generator for fetal echocardiography, which features: 1) learnable semantic queries that enhance the spatial alignment between synthesized images and conditioning masks, and 2) a regularization term that mitigates the histogram drift when adapting diffusion models for ultrasound with improved image fidelity. Building on FE-Gen, Pos4CHD (Sec. III-B) utilizes a mask-to-image generation strategy to synthesize fetal CHDs from normal samples. Specifically, it first manipulates cardiac masks to simulate structural anomalies with respect to clinical prior knowledge, realizing rule-based counterfactual mask generation for fetal CHDs. Then, FE-Gen renders corresponding echocardiographic images guided by masks, yielding spatially aligned pseudo-positive samples. IV-B2). Notably, models trained solely on synthesized data can generalize well to real samples.

papers.title: Universal Synthesis of Large-Area Hybrid Perovskite Monolayers Enabling Lithography-Free, Low-Static-Power Optoelectronics
papers.abstract: Solution-phase synthesis of monolayer hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites is constrained by rapid out-of-plane crystal growth, uncontrolled nucleation, and strong interlayer aggregation, yielding flakes of only a few μm. We introduce a steric-engineering ternary-solvent growth strategy to synthesize monolayer and few-layer A2MX4 hybrid perovskites with exceptionally large surface areas. By combining alcohol cosolvents with an amine additive, out-of-plane stacking is suppressed. Using (PEA)2CuCl4 as a model system, monolayers with lateral areas exceeding 1000 μm2 are achieved, representing a massive dimensional increase over conventional methods. Molecular dynamics and quantum-chemical calculations show that longer-chain alcohols reorganize precursor solvation, while solvent volatility prolongs edge-mediated precursor transport during annealing. This strategy demonstrates universal applicability across diverse organic spacer cations (PEA+, F-PEA+, PentA+), metal centers (Cu2+, Mn2+, Pb2+), and halides (Cl-, Br-, I-). The large lateral dimensions enable direct, solvent-free electrical contact fabrication via physical shadow masking, bypassing chemical degradation from solvents used in conventional lithography. Planar devices fabricated from isolated ultrathin (PEA)2PbI4 channels exhibit ultra-low dark currents down to the 10^-15 - 10^-13 A range, enabling femtowatt-to-picowatt static power consumption, ~ 0.2 pW at 5 V, a 250-fold reduction relative to drop-cast films, while maintaining a high light-to-dark current ratio of 4.3 x 102. This work establishes precise steric and solvation control as a paradigm for scalable, compositionally diverse, low-static-power monolayer 2D perovskite optoelectronics.

papers.title: GraphCAD: Geometry-Aware Diffusion on Edge-Adjacency Graphs for CAD Generation
papers.abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.

papers.intro:
The foundation of modern engineering and manufacturing depends critically on Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models for the rigorous specification of physical objects (Shivegowda et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026). Although automating the synthesis of such models is highly desirable for accelerating design workflows, the inherently hybrid structure of CAD data makes this problem particularly challenging (Patel et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c). In practice, CAD data is most commonly represented in the Boundary Representation (B-rep) format (Jayaraman et al., 2023), which defines 3D models through parameterized faces, edges, and vertices, jointly encoding the geometric and topological information necessary for a complete description of the shape (Jones et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025). As a result, directly synthesizing B-reps remains notoriously difficult, since it requires modeling continuous geometric parameters and discrete topological connectivity in a unified manner (Guo et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024a).

Although automating the synthesis of such models is highly desirable for accelerating design workflows, the inherently hybrid structure of CAD data makes this problem particularly challenging (Patel et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c). In practice, CAD data is most commonly represented in the Boundary Representation (B-rep) format (Jayaraman et al., 2023), which defines 3D models through parameterized faces, edges, and vertices, jointly encoding the geometric and topological information necessary for a complete description of the shape (Jones et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025). As a result, directly synthesizing B-reps remains notoriously difficult, since it requires modeling continuous geometric parameters and discrete topological connectivity in a unified manner (Guo et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024a).

Prevailing approaches typically model B-reps either as sequences of commands (Li et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2024a) or as Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) programs (Ren et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2023). While these paradigms are intuitive, they often struggle to preserve strict topological integrity (Xu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b). In sequence-based generation, for example, a small error in an early operation can propagate through the entire construction process, ultimately producing disjoint loops, non-manifold edges, or entirely invalid geometries. More recently, methods such as BrepGiff (Guo et al., 2025) and GraphBRep (Lai et al., 2025) have sought to mitigate these topological issues by abstracting B-reps into Face-Adjacency Graphs (Jayaraman et al., 2021). By leveraging the structural advantages of graph representations, these methods have shown promising results. However, because they typically rely on UV-domain sampling to approximate geometry and do not explicitly anchor generation to a 1D wireframe scaffold, they remain limited in enforcing the precise boundary constraints required for high-fidelity industrial CAD models.

More recently, methods such as BrepGiff (Guo et al., 2025) and GraphBRep (Lai et al., 2025) have sought to mitigate these topological issues by abstracting B-reps into Face-Adjacency Graphs (Jayaraman et al., 2021). By leveraging the structural advantages of graph representations, these methods have shown promising results. However, because they typically rely on UV-domain sampling to approximate geometry and do not explicitly anchor generation to a 1D wireframe scaffold, they remain limited in enforcing the precise boundary constraints required for high-fidelity industrial CAD models.

To address these limitations, we revisit prevailing graph formulations and introduce GraphCAD. In contrast to prior approaches based on Face-Adjacency Graphs, where nodes correspond to complex trimmed surfaces, our method adopts a new graph construction paradigm centered on 1D wireframe edges. Specifically, we propose the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), which redefines the fundamental graph unit from faces to edges. Under this formulation, each node represents a topological edge augmented with hybrid attributes, including curve types and spatial parameters.

papers.title: Archive coverage constrains abstaining retrieval for transient stability screening more than conditional accuracy
papers.abstract: Power-grid transient stability is assessed by simulating credible faults, but repeating simulations as operating conditions change is costly, motivating faster critical clearing time estimators. Within the AI-ASSIST project, we developed a retrieval-based estimator around three adopted requirements: estimates retain their supporting states, retrieval abstains without compatible support, and support statistics are tested against observed error. Abstention turns estimator uncertainty into a demand on the archive. Exact switching-configuration equality is used. The dense synthetic BUS39 archive covers 99.9996% of 1,044,797 records; the operational ELES archive covers 73.47% of 322,823 records. At query time, 59.37% of ELES states have an earlier same-topology candidate. Under causal availability, retrieval covers 56.34% of records; on records covered under both protocols, mean absolute error increases by 10.0%. No tested support diagnostic ranks first on both grids. Most tested supervised regressors have lower error than retrieval on BUS39, all higher on the matched retrieval-covered ELES population. On ELES, gradient boosting becomes more accurate than retrieval when temporally adjacent states are excluded, so the accuracy trade depends on the archive. Under the adopted compatibility key, archive availability constrains deployment more than conditional accuracy on ELES. Compatible coverage and chronological availability are auditable before an estimator is fitted.

papers.intro:
Transient stability describes whether a power grid’s generators remain in synchronism after a large disturbance, such as a short circuit. It is assessed by simulating the grid’s dynamic response to candidate faults and measuring the critical clearing time (CCT), the longest fault duration for which the system still returns to synchronous operation once the fault is cleared [1]. Time-domain simulation is the reference method, but a full contingency screen may take longer than an operating state remains current [2, 3].

The shift from synchronous generation toward converter-interfaced wind and solar generation can reduce synchronous inertia where it displaces synchronous machines and introduce new stability and control challenges [4]. Many data-driven methods use post-fault trajectories or phasor measurements [5, 6, 7, 8], as reviewed in [9]. These methods incorporate information about the developing transient but cannot assess the pre-fault window. Other methods predict directly from steady-state pre-fault conditions [10], which is the setting considered here. Both groups commonly return one class label or scalar CCT for an assumed fault location, although supervised models can predict predefined sets of fault scenarios [11]. Such predictions do not identify the historical states underlying an estimate, and abstention has been studied separately from stability assessment [12, 13, 14, 15].

A case-based alternative retrieves, for a new pre-fault state, historical or simulated states with similar conditions and aggregates their known outcomes [16]. Applied to transient stability, this follows earlier instance-based and clustering approaches [17], within a longer line of data-driven security assessment [18, 19, 20] and recent work on making stability predictions interpretable [21]. papers.title: Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering with Shuffler-Based Anonymization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel one-shot federated clustering approach based on evolving fuzzy clustering and shuffler-based anonymization. In federated clustering, each round reveals additional model information to the server and can increase the opportunity to infer properties of local datasets, even when raw samples are never shared. Consequently, fewer client-server exchanges and unlinkability are important, so transmitted information cannot be attributed to any single client. Data-stream clustering algorithms, which learn in a single pass over the data, align well with the one-shot federated learning paradigm, where a single communication round can be sufficient. The proposed Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering (eFDPC) method combines evolving fuzzy data-stream clustering and density peak clustering in a federated setting. Each client independently evolves micro-clusters from private data mini-batches through cluster addition and merging. To limit communication, density peak clustering is applied to the learned micro-clusters and only the selected peaks are transmitted, rather than the full local models. A shuffler-based layer is introduced between the clients and the server to anonymize contributions prior to reconstruction and global peak selection. We consider a peak-only variant, eFDPC-P, as well as eFDPC-G with server-side label propagation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets show that eFDPC outperforms recent federated clustering baselines in one-shot settings and scales to higher-dimensional, non-IID data.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Knowledge graph-to-text (KG-to-text) generation verbalizes a set of knowledge graph triples into fluent natural language. While fine-tuned encoder-decoder models have long been the standard approach, recent LLMs are becoming increasingly competitive. We benchmark recent LLMs against fine-tuned encoder-decoder models, using reference-based metrics and graph-grounded reference-free LLM-based evaluation validated against human annotations. We observed that recent LLMs substantially narrow, and in several settings close, the gap with fine-tuned models on reference-based metrics, while performing better on graph-grounded metrics. LLM-based evaluation scores show limited correlation with reference-based metrics, suggesting that the two approaches capture different aspects of generation quality. Graph-grounded evaluation reveals that prompted models produce fewer contradictions and triple omissions than fine-tuned models, and these errors increase more rapidly with graph size for fine-tuned models, highlighting differences between the two approaches that reference-based metrics may not fully capture.

papers.intro:
Knowledge Graphs store information in the form of structured triples as (subject, relation, object). The task of verbalising the knowledge graphs into natural language sentences is a significant and well-studied problem within the natural language generation domain. With the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), it is important to understand how effectively recent models perform this task. In this paper advances the evaluation of recent pre-trained models on graph-to-text benchmark datasets, We investigate the performance of five recent model families spanning diverse architectures: dense decoder-only (Gemma-4-E4B-it, Gemma-4-31B-it, Team et al. (2026), Granite-4.2 IBM Research (2026)), mixture-of-experts (Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Team et al. (2026), Nemotron-3 Blakeman et al. (2025)), encoder-decoder (T5-Gemma2 Zhang et al. (2025)), closed sourced GPT-5 Singh et al. (2025) on the following knowledge graph datasets: WebNLG17 Gardent et al. (2017), WebNLG20 Ferreira et al. (2020) (English subset), and DART Nan et al. (2021). For evaluating the performance of KG-to-Text generation systems, the most commonly used metrics are reference-based like BLEU, METEOR, ChrF++, and BLEURT. However, BLEU Papineni et al. (2002), METEOR Banerjee and Lavie (2005), and ChrF++ Popović (2017) judge the generated text based on surface similarity to the reference text and do not evaluate its semantic meaningfulness. BLEURT Sellam et al. (2020), on the other hand, is a learned metric designed to mimic human evaluation. Additionally, we have found that different researchers use different sets and implementations of metrics, which makes it difficult to compare the results with the published State-of-The-Art (SoTA) approaches. Therefore, we have used an elaborate set of metrics consisting of BLEU, METEOR, ChrF++, Rouge-L, BLEURT, BERTScore Zhang et al. (2019), BARTScore Yuan et al. (2021), and PARENT Dhingra et al. (2019) and have categorized them into three different categories based on the function of the metrics. Additionally, we have also studied LLMs as judge category of metrics as source- grounded or reference-free judges and explored how useful and reliable these metrics can be for evaluating LLM-generated text in terms of criteria that cannot be explicitly judged by the standard NLG metrics. We frame the following research questions on the benchmark datasets and try to find the answers: RQ1. Under one scoring pipeline with a multi-reference protocol, where do recent prompted LLMs (GPT-5 mini, Gemma-4-31B, Granite-4.2-30B, Nemotron-3-Ultra) and a LoRA-adapted Hu et al. (2021) encoder-decoder (T5-Gemma2) model stand against fully fine-tuned T5-large, per metric and per dataset? RQ2. Do the reference-based metric families agree with one another and with a source-grounded judge on these LLM generated outputs? RQ3. What does an LLM judge measure on KG-to-text outputs, when two different LLM judges are compared and validated against human annotation? RQ4. Do fine-tuned and prompted systems make the same kind of errors? Our contributions are: 1) a unified evaluation of five recent model families against fine-tuned T5-large on three benchmarks with eight reference-based metrics, showing that compared with earlier published zero-shot results the gap has narrowed from tens of BLEU points to a few, with parity on neural metrics and a remaining lead for fine-tuning on BLEU, BARTScore and PARENT scores (RQ1); 2) an analysis of metric agreement showing that the reference-based families agree among themselves and not very strongly with a source-grounded judge (RQ2); 3) a two-judge BinEval Cho et al. (2026) evaluation of all outputs, validated against 220 human-labelled outputs (two model outputs on the same 110 graphs) with adjudicated error types, establishing that the LLM judges reproduce human omission labels triple by triple and detect contradictions and entity corruptions, and that they do not detect unsupported elaboration (RQ3); 4) the finding that, by the human standard, the fine-tuned and the prompted systems have a faithfulness problem in a similar share of outputs but of different kinds: corruption and omission against elaboration(RQ4).

papers.title: Dynamics of random recurrent neural networks: colored noise and sublinear activations
papers.abstract: We study the dynamics of recurrent neural networks with random couplings, sublinear odd activation functions, and temporally correlated noise. Using large N methods, we determine stationary correlations and distinguish the loss of local linear stability from the onset of chaos, characterized by a positive largest Lyapunov exponent. These thresholds delimit an intermediate regime in which local instability coexists with asymptotic stability under a common noise history. Their separation depends on both the noise correlation time and the asymptotic growth of the activation function. We show that internal noise with any finite correlation time cuts off the divergence of the network's intrinsic correlation time tau_corr at the edge of chaos; it exhibits a critical scaling tau_{corr,max} propto 1/sqrt{D_0}, where D_0 is the integrated noise strength. Static random input instead produces coincident thresholds and a divergent correlation time. We also calculate the frequency-dependent participation dimension from a four-point correlation function. Its zero-frequency value is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold. Numerical simulations support the large-network predictions and reveal appreciable finite-size effects.

papers.intro:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) play a key role for various computational tasks in biological and artificial systems [16, 29]. An important goal is to understand their dynamics, given that the dynamical state of the system strongly influences its computational capabilities [19]. The seminal work of Sompolinsky, Crisanti and Sommers [24] established that large recurrent networks with random, asymmetric couplings and nonlinear activation can undergo a transition to chaos. Crucially, networks that operate near the transition to chaos are found to perform optimally [2, 26, 27]. The dynamical mean-field theory of [24] characterized the activity correlations and largest Lyapunov exponent. Subsequent path-integral work provided a systematic derivation of the mean-field description and its stability properties [4]. These results made random recurrent networks a tractable setting for studying how microscopic interactions generate complex temporal activity.

Subsequent path-integral work provided a systematic derivation of the mean-field description and its stability properties [4]. These results made random recurrent networks a tractable setting for studying how microscopic interactions generate complex temporal activity.

Fluctuating inputs add important modifications to this problem. Correlation theory for stochastic neural networks showed how network interactions shape temporal and cross-neuron correlations [10]. Additive noise was shown early to suppress chaos in random neural networks [18]. Deterministic periodic input can also suppress intrinsic chaos, with an effectiveness that depends nonmonotonically on the driving frequency [20]. For driven random networks, [22] found that time-dependent internal white noise can suppress chaos and shift its onset to stronger recurrent coupling. Their analysis also revealed the existence of an intermediate regime between the onset of local instability and the transition to chaos. Thus, the response to a small perturbation and the long-term growth of differences between trajectories describe distinct aspects of the dynamics. The intermediate regime is locally unstable but nonchaotic. These two transitions also provide a useful framework for interpreting changes in population covariance and effective recurrent coupling [23]. Related work on spiking circuits identified mechanisms for asynchronous chaotic rate fluctuations with distinct characteristic time scales [13].

In this work we study two aspects of RNNs that can qualitatively affect the dynamics: the temporal structure of disordered input and the activation function. First, prior works have mostly focused on the case of internal white noise, which corresponds to a vanishingly small correlation time. However, realistic internal fluctuations arising from neural and synaptic processes can persist over a finite interval. We will model this with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) input that introduces a tunable correlation time τn\tau_{n}. Varying τn\tau_{n} allows us to ask how internal colored noise affects network correlations, local instability and the onset of chaos. Second, the activation function affects the dynamics in key ways. In this work we study two aspects of RNNs that can qualitatively affect the dynamics: the temporal structure of disordered input and the activation function. We will model this with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) input that introduces a tunable correlation time τn\tau_{n}. Second, the activation function affects the dynamics in key ways. Many classical analyses use a bounded, saturating response, but other response shapes may be relevant over the range of activity sampled by the network. For example, type-I excitability is associated with a square-root dependence of firing rate on input near onset [7, 12, 15]. Our goal is to determine, both theoretically and via numerical simulations, the dynamics of RNNs. In particular, we seek to understand how the colored noise and the form of the activation function affect the unstable dynamics and the development of chaos. papers.title: Cosmological Inference with Gravitational-Wave Dark Sirens and 21-cm Intensity Mapping: Forecasts for LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA with MeerKAT and SKAO
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) and 21-cm intensity mapping (IM) are emerging as complementary cosmological probes: GWs provide direct luminosity-distance measurements, while neutral-hydrogen (HI) IM traces the matter distribution in redshift space. Their synergy offers a promising avenue for precise measurements of the Hubble constant. Within a standard-siren framework, we perform a joint cosmological and population analysis using $\mathcal{O}(150)$ mock GW detections with SNR > 12, as projected for one year of observations at LVK O5 sensitivity. We combine these with mock HI intensity maps from MeerKLASS and SKA-Mid, and study how observational limitations in both the GW and IM data affect the $H_0$ constraints. We find that uncertainty in GW parameter measurements is a dominant limitation on the cosmological constraints. Neglecting this uncertainty, the inclusion of HI information enables sub-percent constraints on $H_0$. We also find that observational effects in the HI surveys weaken the constraints, although they remain tighter than those obtained without HI information (spectral sirens). Despite accounting for HI IM observational limitations, including HI information reduces the $H_0$ uncertainty relative to the spectral-siren results by 61% for MeerKLASS and 53% for SKA-Mid. Because our results are based on a single realisation, they should be interpreted in light of possible realisation-to-realisation variability. Beam convolution most severely weakens the constraints. Instrumental noise can induce multimodality in the posterior, potentially biasing the inferred parameters. The results are sensitive to foreground under-cleaning and over-cleaning. Partial sky coverage has a relatively small impact. In the most realistic scenario, which accounts for both GW and HI IM limitations, we obtain $H_0$ precision estimates of 10% and 15% for MeerKLASS and SKA-Mid, respectively.

papers.intro:
Gravitational-wave (GW) detections from compact binary coalescences (CBCs) provide a direct measurement of the luminosity distance, enabling their use as standard sirens when associated with an independent redshift measurement (Schutz, 1986). Establishing a direct relationship between redshift and luminosity distance is key to resolving the Hubble tension (Planck Collaboration, 2020; Riess and others, 2022). GW cosmology offers a new, independent way to constrain the present-day expansion history of the universe. We distinguish between bright sirens when an electromagnetic counterpart is identified, and dark sirens otherwise. For instance, the gamma-ray counterpart to the binary neutron star GW170817 (The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration, 2017; The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration and others, 2017b) enabled a precise redshift estimation, leading to a tight constraint on H0H_{0} (The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration and others, 2017a). However, most events detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) network are binary black hole (BBH) mergers (The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, the Virgo Collaboration, and the KAGRA Collaboration, 2026) which motivates the development of alternative methods to infer redshift. A possible approach is to construct a redshift prior from the distribution of matter in the sky region of the GW event. This method, known as the galaxy-catalogue method, was first introduced using galaxy surveys (Schutz, 1986; Del Pozzo, 2012; Fishbach and others, 2019; Soares-Santos and others, 2019; Palmese and others, 2020; Gray and others, 2020; Gray et al., 2022), as compact objects are expected to form and merge in dense environments with a high star-formation rate (SFR) such as galaxies. This approach is used in combination with the spectral sirens method, leveraging features in the redshifted mass distribution of the GW population, to jointly infer cosmological and population parameters (Gray and others, 2023; Mastrogiovanni and others, 2023; The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration and the KAGRA Collaboration, 2026). The latest LVK results constrain H0H_{0} to approximately 20% using dark sirens alone, improving to approximately 12% when the bright siren GW170817 is included (The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration and the KAGRA Collaboration, 2026). This is, however, not yet sufficient to address the Hubble tension. The constraining power of the galaxy-catalogue method is limited by catalogue incompleteness across relevant redshifts and by the difficulty of accurately characterising completeness as a function of redshift and galaxy properties. Without precise galaxy redshift estimates and sufficient galaxy support in the GW events three-dimensional localisation volume, the efficiency of the galaxy-catalogue method is significantly reduced (Gray and others, 2020; The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration and the KAGRA Collaboration, 2026). Heterogeneous sky coverage across combined galaxy surveys further complicates the modelling of catalogue completeness. Finally, large GW distance and sky-localisation uncertainties result in broad three-dimensional localisation volumes containing many potential host galaxies, limiting the constraining power of the analysis.

This work considers neutral hydrogen (HI) intensity mapping (IM) (Bharadwaj and others, 2001; Battye et al., 2004; Wyithe et al., 2008; Chang and others, 2008; Kovetz and others, 2017; Liu and Shaw, 2020; Bernal and Kovetz, 2022) which allows for the rapid surveying of large cosmological volumes by charting emission from the 21-cm hyperfine transition line, observed at radio frequencies (ν0=1420.405​MHz\nu_{0}=1420.405~\rm{MHz}). The abundance of HI and its association with large-scale over-densities (Villaescusa-Navarro and others, 2018) make it an indirect indicator of the regions where CBCs are most likely to occur. It provides an alternative to optical electromagnetic tracers that can mitigate the limited completeness of current spectroscopic galaxy surveys at z≳0.5z\gtrsim 0.5, while offering much finer redshift resolution than is typically achievable with pre-stage IV optical surveys. Single-dish IM observations, such as those from the SKA Observatory (SKAO) (SKA Cosmology SWG, 2020) and MeerKAT’s Large Area Synoptic Survey (MeerKLASS) (Santos and others, 2017), have a poorer angular resolution, observationally limited by the radio telescope beam size. Both ongoing and near-future IM surveys are expected to reach ≳10,000\gtrsim 10{,}000\,deg2 of sky coverage, with e.g. MeerKLASS (Cunnington and others, 2026) making them a particularly promising resource for advancing GW cosmology.

The synergy between GW sources and HI IM has been previously discussed by Scelfo and others (2022) and Schulz and others (2026) to probe astrophysical and cosmological models with cross-correlation methods, and by Mukherjee and Dizgah (2022) to study CBC formation channels. Instead, we forecast how HI IM support enhances cosmological constraints from dark sirens by extending redshift support beyond the galaxy catalogue regime. An analogous approach, referred to as radio sirens, was investigated in Dupletsa and others (2026) which forecasts the constraints on H0H_{0} that can be achieved from the synergy between third-generation GW networks and the SKAO. Meanwhile, this paper provides a realistic evaluation of the LVK network capabilities with both MeerKAT and SKAO, accounting for observational and instrumental limitations. See Baker and others (2026) for a recent review of the various synergies between GW detections and SKAO.

This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the generation of mock data consistent with our forecasted data products. Section 3 outlines the construction of a redshift prior based on the HI distribution from intensity maps. Section 4 introduces the hierarchical Bayesian framework used for the analysis. We present our results in Section 5 and conclude in Section 6, discussing their implications along with possible extensions of this work.

papers.title: Asymptotical results on the automorphism groups of canonical double cover of graphs
papers.abstract: The canonical double cover $BX$ of a graph $X$ is the direct product $X\times K_2$. A graph $X$ is stable if every automorphism of $BX$ is induced by automorphisms of $X$ and $K_2$, and unstable otherwise. We prove several asymptotic results on stable and unstable graphs. In particular, we show that the automorphism group of the canonical double cover of almost every graph has order $2$, and consequently that almost all graphs are stable. We also prove that the dominant sources of instability are having twins and being disconnected, in that order, and that graphs arising from a known construction are the next step in this hierarchy.

Canonical double covers have proven to play an important role in algebraic graph theory and have been studied from a variety of perspectives. For example, their connections with symmetric {0,1}\{0,1\}-matrices were studied by Marušič, Scapellato and Salvi [11], their regular embeddings by Nedela and Škoviera [12], their isomorphisms by Pacco and Scapellato [13] and their symmetry properties in the context of 22-fold covers by Feng, Kutnar, Malnič and Marušič [2].

Wilson gave several sufficient conditions for a graph to be unstable, which he then used to formulate conjectures characterising instability in four families of graphs: circulants, Rose Window graphs, toroidal graphs and generalized Petersen graphs [16]. A lot of work has been done on the stability of circulant graphs. Wilson’s conjecture was shown to be false by Qin, Xia and Zhou, who also proved that there are no nontrivially unstable arc-transitive circulants [14]. It was proven by Fernandez and the second author that there are no nontrivially unstable circulants of odd order [3]. Morris extended this result by proving that there are no nontrivially unstable Cayley graphs on abelian groups of odd order [17]. In [8], several constructions of unstable circulants were presented, and unstable circulants of order twice a prime were classified, whereas in [9] unstable circulants with valency at most 77 were classified. The connection between stability of Cayley graphs and properties of Schur rings was studied in [7]. Nevertheless, the full classification of unstable circulants remains an open problem. In [19], Xia, Zhang and Zheng proved that almost all Cayley graphs on abelian groups are stable.

Moreover, we have already noted that, asymptotically speaking, graphs with twins and disconnected graphs are the dominant sources of instability. Being bipartite is much further down the list, see for example Lemma 3.2. It is also lower than graphs arising from Construction 1.5. For this reason, Theorem 1.6 and Theorem 1.7 immediately hold with “unstable twin-free connected” replaced by “nontrivially unstable”.

papers.title: OGLE-2012-BLG-0563: Relative Proper Motion Constraint from Keck Follow-up finds the correct Lens
papers.abstract: We present Keck/NIRC2 adaptive optics imaging results of planetary microlensing event OGLE-2012-BLG-0563. We find that the OGLE-2012-BLG-0563L planetary system consists of a 1.12 +/- 0.09 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a 0.81 +/- 0.04 solar-mass host star at a distance of 5.49 +/- 0.56 kpc from the Sun. This event has a lens-source separation of 23.28 +/- 0.48 mas, which is the smallest lens-source separation measured to date with Keck AO data. We find that the incorrect solution - which identifies the Northeast (NE) star as the source star - is favored if one only considers the discovery paper, the Fukui et al. (2015) solution, or an unconstrained model. However, by performing an image-constrained light curve model fit using the relative proper motion direction constraint from the Keck follow-up data, we demonstrate that the correct solution identifies the NE star as the lens star. The discrepancy in the unconstrained models is driven by systematics in the FTS and MOA B & C data, alongside the impact of the relative proper motion direction constraints. This outcome offers two important lessons for future Roman data analysis: (1) thoroughly verify systematics across all passbands and identify the precise origin of chi-squared differences, and (2) utilize image-constrained light curve modeling incorporating relative proper motion direction constraints to identify the correct lens.

papers.intro:
Gravitational microlensing is unique in its ability to detect low mass exoplanets [11] beyond the snow line [59], where the formation of giant planets is thought to be most efficient [100, 88]. The Roman Galactic Exoplanet Survey (RGES) was selected in the 2010 decadal survey [16, 107] to utilize this uniqueness and measure exoplanet demographics beyond the Kepler mission.’s reach. The aim of this survey is to detect low mass planets beyond the snowline of their hosts and measure the masses of the hosts and the planets. The high resolution capability of the Roman telescope will enable it to do mass measurement of both the hosts and the planets. Currently, as part of a precursor study for RGES, we are developing the mass measurement methods for the exoplanets that are detected from the ground.

OGLE-2012-BLG-0563Lb was first discovered by OGLE collaboration on May 1, 2012 using the 1.3 m Warsaw telescope. Later, on May 18, 2012, the MOA collaboration noticed this event as well using the 1.8 m MOA II telescope. On May 20, the μ\muFUN collaboration circulated an alert that the event was peaking at a high magnification, which means that the source star was approaching very close to the lens star on the sky plane. In such a case, there is a high probability that the light curve will show anomalous features around the peak if the lens star hosts a planet. Both μ\muFUN and ROBONET groups started to take frequent observations of this event with telescopes from Chile, New Zealand and Australia. On May 21, MOA reported the detection of an anomaly as a result of its high cadence observations. The event peaked at around May 21 with the maximum magnification of more than 600, around which the event was well covered by several telescopes in New Zealand and Australia. As a result, a quick look at the light curve clearly showed an anomalous asymmetric feature around the peak, meaning that the lens star hosted a companion. The discovery of this planet was led by Fukui et. al. [54].

The event was also observed with the 8.2m high resolution Subaru telescope with AO (Adaptive Optics) instrument Infrared Camera and Spectrograph (IRCS, Kobayashi et al. 2000) on July 28, 2012. Note that this was observed only 2 months after the peak of the event. Fukui et. al. [54] measured the excess flux on top of the source and published the mass of the host and the planet. Fukui et. al. [54] reported that it is a Saturn mass planet orbiting a 0.34 M⊙M_{\odot}star at 1.3 kpc distance. In the current paper, we observed the same event with Keck using NIRC2 AO instrument on July, 2018. We report a different mass measurement than the Fukui et. al. [54] paper. In our NIRC2 Keck observation, we find that the lens is partially separated from the source, which makes the PSF elongated. We fit two stars in elongated PSF to detect the lens and source separately - this method is known as image elongation method. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope ( hereafter, Roman telescope) [107] includes the RGES [99] , that will detect and measure the mass of hundreds of exoplanets in orbits extending from the habitable zone to infinity (i.e. unbound planets). The microlens exoplanets discovered by Roman will not require follow-up observations since the Roman observations will also have high enough angular resolution to detect the lens (and planetary host) stars [14]. The RGES will observe the galactic bulge in six to eight epochs across the 5 year time-span. Hence the maximum time separation between two epochs will be about ∼\sim 4.5 years. This is because, in spite of the prime mission being 5 years long, the time difference between the first and the last galactic bulge season will be about 4.5 years. For example, a planetary event detected in the first epoch, will be going through lens-source separation in the final epoch. For an average of 5 mas/yr relative lens-source proper motion, the separation between lens and source in 4.5 years would be around 23 mas. The lens separation measured in this paper is 23.28±0.4823.28\pm 0.48 mas . Roman will measure masses of a lot of events like this.

This event is observed as part of our NASA Keck Key Strategic Mission Support (KSMS) program whose main purpose is to refine the mass measurement method, and optimize the Roman exoplanet microlensing survey observing program. We are conducting a systematic exoplanet microlensing event high angular resolution follow-up program to detect and determine the masses of the exoplanet host stars with our NASA Keck KSMS program [23]. This is supplemented by HST observations [32] for host stars that are most likely to be detected [13]. This program has already revealed a number of microlens exoplanet host stars that are resolved from the source stars [126, 26, 37, 119], and others that are still blended with their source stars, but show a significant elongation due to a lens-source separation somewhat smaller than the size of the point spread function (PSF) [14, 21, 33]. This program has also recently provided mass upper limits of a Jovian planet orbiting a White Dwarf host. The event reported in this paper is also observed by HST (Hubble Space Telescope) which will be reported in companion paper Bennett et al. 2026. papers.title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
papers.abstract: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of real-world short queries paired with ground-truth Mathlib statements makes this ambiguity even more intractable. We argue that this is essentially a data problem. Through adversarial training, we scale up the generation of labeled short and ambiguous queries, and learn to disambiguate user queries at both model-level fine-tuning and input-level query rewriting. On the human-curated MathlibQR benchmark, our Lean Finder V2 sets a new state of the art, with at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib semantic search engines. On top of our state-of-the-art retriever, optimized query rewriting further improves MathlibQR retrieval. On unlabeled queries from human and coding-agent interactions, Lean Finder V2 is ranked as the strongest system. Integrated with Claude Code, Lean Finder V2 improves proof success on downstream theorem-proving task. Lean Finder V2 is available at: https://leanfinder.github.io/

Advances in the Lean proof assistant and its central library Mathlib are turning formal mathematics into a collaborative and verifiable workflow (De Moura et al., 2015; Moura & Ullrich, 2021). Spanning a broad range of mathematics, Mathlib now contains more than 400,000 theorems and definitions across roughly 10,000 files (Lean Prover Community, 2026). At this scale, effective theorem search is essential for both human and automated formalization, enabling users and systems to efficiently identify and reuse relevant results from Mathlib’s large and growing library, and its quality shapes end-to-end proof success (Lu et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Avigad & Massot, 2020). Alongside rapid progress in specialized Lean provers (Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025), agentic systems have achieved tremendous success from competition mathematics to frontier research. Many of these systems rely on Mathlib search engines to locate reusable results during proof construction (Liu et al., 2026; Varambally et al., 2026; Ju et al., 2026; Dressler, 2025).

In this paper, we introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that excels on ambiguous queries while retaining strong performance on context-rich queries. Lean Finder V2 addresses a data bottleneck caused by the scarcity of labeled ambiguous queries. We synthesize ambiguous query-declaration pairs as training data to improve the retriever through model-level adversarial training, and the same synthetic data is used in input-level prompt optimization for query rewriting. At the model level, a RL-trained attacker generates challenging and ambiguous queries for Mathlib declarations, with a difficulty reward that targets weaknesses of the retriever and an alignment reward that keeps each query faithful to its source declaration. These synthetic query-declaration pairs improve the retriever, whose feedback recalibrates query difficulty. papers.title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.

papers.intro:
Dexterous manipulation skills are critical components of surgical robotics tasks such as needle insertion, knot tying, and tissue retraction [1]. In recent years, significant progress has been made in applying deep reinforcement learning (RL) to accomplish such complex autonomous or semi-autonomous subtasks [2, 3]. This progress has been largely enabled by the development of high-fidelity surgical robot simulators [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. However, a key limitation of RL-based surgical robotics lies in its reliance on privileged state information, which typically assumes accurate and noise-free access to the physical states of surgical objects, with limited integration of visual perception [10]. This issue is particularly pronounced in fine manipulation tasks such as needle handling, where even minor deviations in object pose can lead to task failure [2].

In recent years, significant progress has been made in applying deep reinforcement learning (RL) to accomplish such complex autonomous or semi-autonomous subtasks [2, 3]. This progress has been largely enabled by the development of high-fidelity surgical robot simulators [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. However, a key limitation of RL-based surgical robotics lies in its reliance on privileged state information, which typically assumes accurate and noise-free access to the physical states of surgical objects, with limited integration of visual perception [10]. This issue is particularly pronounced in fine manipulation tasks such as needle handling, where even minor deviations in object pose can lead to task failure [2].

Recently, benchmarks have been proposed to provide a diverse set of learning-based tasks that capture varying levels of dexterity and precision required in the surgical context [8]. Benchmarks provide standardized platforms for evaluating autonomous policies. Nevertheless, surgical manipulation tasks still remain highly challenging due to their stringent requirements for precision, robustness, and safety in constrained operating environments.

Benchmarks provide standardized platforms for evaluating autonomous policies. Nevertheless, surgical manipulation tasks still remain highly challenging due to their stringent requirements for precision, robustness, and safety in constrained operating environments.

To reduce the reliance on privileged state information, vision-based policy learning provides an alternative by directly mapping visual observations to control actions [11, 12, 13]. Such policies can avoid state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines by leveraging visual information to learn task-relevant representations. However, learning effective control policies directly from visual observations via RL remains a major hurdle in surgical robotics. In the context of surgical manipulation tasks, the difficulty is further amplified by the severe visual sparsity of task-relevant objects. For instance, the needle and instruments of surgical robots often occupy only a few pixels in high-resolution RGB observations, making reliable perception and localization hard to achieve. Furthermore, the instability of RL exacerbates the training difficulty in such sparse and precision-critical settings [14]. Imitation learning (IL) defines a stable training objective, which transforms RL into supervised learning given a large number of expert demonstrations as data labels [15, 16]. However, compared with general robotic manipulation tasks, such as opening bottles or folding clothes, expert demonstrations for laparoscopic manipulation tasks are much more expensive and scarce.

In the context of surgical manipulation tasks, the difficulty is further amplified by the severe visual sparsity of task-relevant objects. For instance, the needle and instruments of surgical robots often occupy only a few pixels in high-resolution RGB observations, making reliable perception and localization hard to achieve. Furthermore, the instability of RL exacerbates the training difficulty in such sparse and precision-critical settings [14]. Imitation learning (IL) defines a stable training objective, which transforms RL into supervised learning given a large number of expert demonstrations as data labels [15, 16]. However, compared with general robotic manipulation tasks, such as opening bottles or folding clothes, expert demonstrations for laparoscopic manipulation tasks are much more expensive and scarce.

To facilitate vision-based policy learning under these limitations, policy distillation provides an effective approach for transferring knowledge from a state-based policy to an RGB-based policy [17, 18, 19]. The state-based policy has access to privileged robot and object state information and serves as the teacher, and the RGB-based policy then learns to reproduce the teacher’s behavior from visual observations and robot proprioceptive states. Such knowledge transfer provides guidance for learning visuomotor policies from high-dimensional visual inputs, enabling the vision-based policy to acquire effective manipulation behaviors without relying on privileged state information during execution. However, most studies on policy distillation consider discrete action settings, such as those in Atari games, and thus the potential of policy distillation for continuous-control surgical robotic manipulation remains unexplored.

In this work, we propose a policy distillation framework for continuous-control laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, we proposed a distribution-matching-based policy learning approach that overcomes the limitation of previous methods by Gaussian alignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through both theoretical analysis and empirical validation. We employ SurRoL [8] as the simulation environment, where a Patient Side Manipulator (PSM) executes the manipulation task while an Endoscopic Camera Manipulator (ECM) provides RGB observations. During training, the state-based policy has access to all privileged state information, including the coordinates and orientations of all objects, and serves as the teacher for the vision-based policy. In contrast, the vision-based policy only receives RGB observations and robot proprioceptive states, and is trained to distill the behavior of the state-based teacher without accessing privileged object states during execution. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we provide insights into various distribution matching objectives for policy distillation, which may serve as a useful reference for future research on vision-based policy learning in surgical robotics manipulation. papers.title: Anomalous polar chains in halide perovskites
papers.abstract: Local polar distortions, their collective ordering, and their field-driven reversal have been studied extensively in ferroelectric perovskites for decades. Here we identify an unusual behavior in the ferroelectric halide perovskite CsGeBr3 using large-scale molecular dynamics with first-principles-trained interatomic potentials. In its nominally cubic phase the Ge off-centering forms one-dimensional polar chains that extend over at least tens of nanometers and relax on nanosecond timescales, four orders of magnitude slower than in BaTiO3 and PbTiO3, with CsSnBr3 in between. The cubic CsGeBr3 phase is a dynamically disordered state in which oppositely polarized chains flip throughout the crystal, and a long-lived one-dimensional local polarization coexists with zero net polarization. A simple three-dimensional perovskite thus hosts long-ranged one-dimensional polar correlations with remarkably slow dynamics. In the ferroelectric phase the same chains set a one-dimensional switching mechanism, in which the polarization reverses chain by chain.

papers.intro:
Ferroelectrics possess a spontaneous polarization that can be switched between symmetry-equivalent states by an electric field [51, 37], underpinning applications in memory, sensing, and actuation [45, 43]. Oxide perovskites such as BaTiO3\text{BaTiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} and PbTiO3\text{PbTiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} are well-studied examples, yet their atomic-scale behavior, particularly that of BaTiO3\text{BaTiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, continues to invite discussion. A central question is how collective lattice vibrations, described by soft-mode theory [9, 10], and the ordering of local off-centered displacements, described by order–disorder models [11, 7], combine to produce the ferroelectric transition [4, 55, 46]. In cubic BaTiO3\text{BaTiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, anisotropic displacement correlations have been interpreted through both one-dimensional chains [11, 32, 46] and strongly anharmonic soft-mode dynamics [25, 40], a question revisited recently with large-scale simulations and real-space imaging [22, 58]. Calculations have also identified favorable parallel alignment along chains together with antipolar coupling between neighboring chains [57]. Connecting these local arrangements to their spatial extent and relaxation dynamics remains important for a coherent microscopic picture of ferroelectricity.

However, connecting these findings across the spatial and temporal scales of collective ordering remains challenging. In particular, the extent, dynamics, and role of correlated displacements in polarization reversal remain less well understood than in oxide prototypes.

papers.title: Bulk stability of bimolecular stochastic chemical reaction networks
papers.abstract: We establish criteria for stability in the bulk of planar stochastic chemical reaction networks with mass-action kinetics. Using Poincaré compactification, we characterize the asymptotic drift and show how stochastic fluctuations can prevent escape along transversally repulsive branches of the limiting deterministic flow. We construct a Lyapunov function by combining local estimates near these branches with dissipative estimates in the neighboring regions. The criteria cover a wide class of networks and in particular apply beyond weakly reversible and strongly endotactic networks. Together with compatible boundary estimates, these criteria imply positive recurrence.

papers.intro:
Stability is a fundamental requirement for the study of the long-time behavior of chemical reaction networks. For stochastic models, stability is often understood as (positive) recurrence, giving an invariant probability measure on each closed irreducible class and allowing one to study the system at stationarity. This is especially important in the multiscale setting, where the effective dynamics of slow variables are often obtained by averaging over the stationary distribution of a fast subsystem [10, 25]. Establishing such a reduction requires control of the fast dynamics, including their stability and the relevant moment bounds.

Chemical reaction networks admit two classical descriptions. The deterministic model follows concentrations through a system of mass-action ordinary differential equations. The stochastic model tracks molecular copy numbers through a continuous-time Markov chain, retaining the fluctuations that are particularly important at low copy numbers [21]. Under the natural volume scaling, the deterministic equations arise as a law of large numbers limit of the stochastic dynamics on finite time intervals [27, 28]. However, this connection does not, by itself, identify their long-time stability properties.

Stability in this context has been extensively studied in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Starting with the theory of complex balance [23, 18], the deterministic literature has developed structural conditions relating the reaction graph to persistence and permanence, notably weak reversibility and endotacticity [13, 14, 22]. Related conditions also play a central role in the stochastic theory. Complex balance yields product-form stationary distributions [8, 6], while the geometry of strongly endotactic networks underlies stochastic Lyapunov estimates and large-deviation results [1, 2, 5].

The two descriptions can nevertheless behave very differently near the boundary of the state space, where some species have low copy numbers. Extinction, trapping near the boundary and changes of recurrence class can occur in the stochastic model without a corresponding deterministic behavior [9, 7, 4, 5]. In the bulk, where all species have large copy numbers, the stochastic drift is instead well approximated by the deterministic vector field. Much of the stability analysis in this region has consequently treated the stochastic dynamics as a perturbation of the deterministic one, using deterministic inward drift to construct stochastic Lyapunov functions [2, 5]. This suggests a close correspondence between the two models in the bulk, but does not establish an equivalence of their stability conditions.

We constructed a network whose deterministic system contains a trajectory that diverges in finite time in the interior of the state space, while the stochastic model is positive recurrent. The divergent trajectory is repulsive in the transverse direction, and stochastic fluctuations push the process away towards regions where the dynamics dissipate. While an earlier example based on a special choice of rate constants appears in [6, Example 4], the system from [3] displays the stabilization by noise for generic choices of such constants. These examples show that deterministic bulk stability is not necessary for stochastic stability.

The goal is to give conditions on the deterministic vector field that guarantee sufficient stability (encoded through Lyapunov-type dissipation inequalities) in the bulk of the stochastic system. Building on the ideas of [3], we focus on its behavior at infinity: which curves lead to infinity, and whether they attract or repel neighboring trajectories. Our aim is to introduce new ideas and a new approach to studying stochastic dynamics in the bulk, without seeking a complete classification of bulk stability.

papers.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.
papers.intro:
The reconstruction of a hidden function from existing samples is a long-standing problem across science and engineering, especially when acquiring samples proves expensive and/or challenging, e.g., in computational fluid dynamics, wireless sensor networks-based data gathering, or robot-based exploration. Such a problem, referred to as “data-driven regression” or “interpolation”, is a well-investigated topic [15], addressing the need for fast, accurate, and reliable estimates.

Such a problem, referred to as “data-driven regression” or “interpolation”, is a well-investigated topic [15], addressing the need for fast, accurate, and reliable estimates.

There have been many previous works on data-driven regression, with classical methods relying on basis function fitting [7, 16], kernel functions [2, 11], training parametric surrogate models, e.g., neural networks [1]. However, there is need to choose/build a function library, kernel, and/or an architecture, which is consequential for the resulting accuracy and computational burden. Another class of methods rely on direct samples weighting [12, 6], which however do not account for quadratic and/or curvature-related trends, affecting prediction accuracy for reconstructing nonlinear functions from sparse samples. Other approaches do not assume nor fit an a priori known/designated function form, and choose their estimates from an admissible set. Examples include nonlinear set membership (NSM) methods [8, 9], Lipschitz-based interpolation [5], and kinky inference [3], whose heritage we take for our proposed method. Aside from point-value estimates, uncertainty quantification is investigated in different forms in [8, 3, 11, 7], among others, a relevant quantity for exploration-based sampling.

In many compelling applications like emergency response and robotic exploration, rapidly accumulated samples and evolving data sets must influence the next decisions, e.g., to take an action or select the next sampling points. For exploration in particular, the uncertainty measure is also a mission decision metric, rather than a post hoc reported quantity. Therefore, there is demand for approaches that balance accurate predictions, informative and tight uncertainty bounds, and computational efficiency: in particular, a low latency between a data set update and a prediction.

This paper proposes a new formulation to use local information to estimate the state at a prediction point (also referred to in this paper as ‘query point’). Without assuming a functional form nor parametrised model, we use regularity assumptions on the underlying functions and draw the Taylor relationships between the query point and neighbouring samples, computing the admissible set of state values and derivatives. Our method builds on NSM, kinky inference, and Lipschitz interpolation, but they only exploit a first-order regularity assumption, so their uncertainty bounds grow linearly with distance from the closest sample. Our method, on the other hand, uses a Lipschitz-continuous Hessian with latent gradients and Hessians; these account for the local curvature leading to uncertainty that shrinks with the cube of the sample neighbourhood radius in the noiseless case. Our method, on the other hand, uses a Lipschitz-continuous Hessian with latent gradients and Hessians; these account for the local curvature leading to uncertainty that shrinks with the cube of the sample neighbourhood radius in the noiseless case. Our contributions are the following:

1. We cast the regression problem as a joint set estimation of admissible values and derivatives, using only (zeroth-order) function value samples, and regularity assumptions. As a result, we arrive at a point estimate, and the uncertainty bounds on the state and its derivatives. 2. We derive the information radius—not just on the value estimate at the query point, but also its derivatives—for the function smoothness class we consider. Furthermore, in the noiseless case, we establish consistency on the value and derivatives as the samples set becomes dense. 3. We use our results to build a practical regression algorithm which, given a samples set and a query point, solves small linear programs to simultaneously estimate the state and derivatives, as well as their corresponding uncertainty bounds. Our new Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) needs no offline training: every prediction is a per-query, on-demand solve, and therefore does not require any retraining in face of evolving (appended, changed) data sets.

We tested Diona in a nonlinear regression benchmark involving six functions of three to eight dimensions against a Gaussian process (GP), a neural network (NN), nonlinear set membership (NSM), radial basis functions and inverse distance weighting. In the noiseless cases, Diona had lower errors than the GP especially with the densest data sets. It also gave tighter uncertainty bounds than NSM while covering the true value within those bounds at more than 95% of query points in four functions, similar to GP. In noisy cases, Diona’s accuracy advantages were swept away, although it remained competitive with the other methods. Furthermore, in the time that the GP needs to train, Diona produced around 10410^{4} predictions (10210^{2}–10310^{3} predictions within the training time of a GPU-trained NN). Diona’s timing advantage pays off in regimes where data sets change often and relatively few predictions are needed between updates.

papers.title: Paying for Information, Not for Clicks: A Block-Level Publisher Content Marketplace for AI Answers
papers.abstract: We propose a publisher content marketplace that allocates payments for information used in AI-generated answers. The unit of attribution is a ``lego block:'' a distinct fact or piece of commentary that may appear in articles from multiple publishers. A simple news-reading model connects three payment rules: equal sharing among all publishers reporting on a block, rewarding the publisher who reported a block first, and rewarding indispensable contributions. Each can be represented within a Shapley-value framework. We evaluate the framework using answers to 1,974 search-engine queries about a heavily covered news episode. When attribution considers only the articles retrieved for an individual query, most cited blocks appear unique, and the rules produce nearly identical allocations. A global index covering the full news corpus reveals overlap across publishers, making the choice of payment rule consequential. Premium publishers, defined as established outlets with substantial newsgathering operations, receive 42% of allocated value under equal sharing, compared with 46-50% under a first-publication rule, depending on the treatment of publication timestamps. These findings highlight the importance of a shared global index that records which publishers provide each block and when they published it. Attribution restricted to the sources retrieved for an individual answer lacks the information needed to distinguish these payment policies.

Saliency and scanpath models are developed almost exclusively on natural photographs, yet paintings are composed by artists to guide the viewer's eye and differ from photographs in texture, colour and abstraction. We introduce \avatt, a free-viewing eye-tracking dataset on

For every painting we release individual scanpaths with fixation timing and eye--screen distance, fixation maps, saliency maps smoothed at one degree of visual angle, temporal saliency videos and rich art metadata. We benchmark classic and deep saliency models against human agreement, revealing substantial headroom for art-aware models, and rank 44 scanpath-similarity measures, including a new language-free family of image-encoder metrics built on ten CNN, ViT and self-supervised encoders.
