papers.intro:
Visual attention models are trained and evaluated on photographs of natural scenes [26, 24, 5]. Paintings challenge these models in several ways. Their textures, palettes and degrees of abstraction differ from photographs, they span centuries of pictorial conventions, and their content is composed: artists place subjects, lines and contrasts deliberately to organise how a picture is read. Eye tracking has been used to study the viewing of art since Yarbus’ recordings [68, 52, 56, 51, 28], but public data remain scarce. The largest public collection provides aggregated saliency maps for 150 paintings in five styles, without individual scanpaths [44], so scanpath models for paintings have had to rely on domain adaptation from photographs [30, 63, 34]. Two factors explain the gap: recording enough observers per image is costly, and copyright restricts the redistribution of artworks.

papers.title: Matching Tasks to Agents: Mechanism Design for Multi-Agent Contracts
papers.abstract: We study task assignment under adverse selection and moral hazard. In the single-task setting, agents privately know their types, which determine their success probabilities and effort costs. Based on the agents' reported types, the principal selects an agent to perform the task and offers a success-contingent payment. Although optimal Bayesian contract design is generally computationally intractable and Myerson's characterization does not directly extend to settings with hidden actions and multidimensional private information, we show that the single-task problem admits a simple Myerson-style characterization. Our key insight is that incentive constraints depend only on the ratio between effort cost and success probability. We characterize an optimal mechanism and show that it can be computed in polynomial time. We also establish a tight $Θ(1/(NK))$ worst-case bound on the ratio between the optimal profit and the full-information benchmark, where $N$ is the number of agents and $K$ is the number of types per agent. We then extend our analysis to multiple tasks, showing that an optimal mechanism may not exist. Nevertheless, for a constant number of agents, we provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the supremum profit.
papers.intro:
Contract theory studies how a principal can incentivize agents to exert costly, unobservable effort through payments contingent on observable outcomes. In the classical model with a single agent and known action costs and outcome distributions, an optimal contract can be computed by linear programming [20]. Subsequent work has extended this model in several directions to capture more realistic environments. Two main directions are particularly relevant to our work. The first introduces private information, adding adverse selection to moral hazard: an agent can misrepresent its type before choosing an action [13, 23, 3]. The second introduces multiple agents, requiring the principal to make allocation and coordination decisions about how to distribute work and incentives among them [17, 18, 21]. Understanding when these features admit simple, computationally tractable mechanisms is a central challenge for algorithmic contract design.

Understanding when these features admit simple, computationally tractable mechanisms is a central challenge for algorithmic contract design.

Even with a single agent, designing optimal contracts in Bayesian settings is particularly challenging. Indeed, optimizing contracts or menus of deterministic contracts is computationally hard in general [13, 23]. Allowing menus of randomized contracts can restore efficient approximation of the principal’s optimal utility [14], albeit at the cost of greater mechanism complexity. Even when private information is one-dimensional, combining hidden types with hidden actions requires implementability conditions that go beyond the usual monotonicity condition of auction theory [3]. [8] extend the study of Bayesian settings to multi-agent environments and provide algorithms for approximately optimal randomized contracts. Their formulation explicitly represents joint type and action profiles, whose number can grow exponentially with the number of agents. Moreover, the resulting mechanisms are obtained through general optimization procedures rather than a simple characterization of the optimal allocation and payment rules. These limitations motivate the following question: Which structured environments allow the principal to handle private information and multiple agents through a simple optimal mechanism?

In this paper, we focus on the problem of assigning tasks to agents. A firm commissioning a project, for example, may face contractors who differ in their ability to complete it and in the cost of doing so. These characteristics may be privately known, while the effort exerted after the contract is awarded remains unobservable. A successful mechanism must therefore address two distinct incentive problems: it must elicit the information needed to select an agent and induce that agent to work. When several tasks must be assigned, these decisions are further coupled by the requirement that each agent can undertake at most one task.

A firm commissioning a project, for example, may face contractors who differ in their ability to complete it and in the cost of doing so. These characteristics may be privately known, while the effort exerted after the contract is awarded remains unobservable. A successful mechanism must therefore address two distinct incentive problems: it must elicit the information needed to select an agent and induce that agent to work. When several tasks must be assigned, these decisions are further coupled by the requirement that each agent can undertake at most one task.

We study a model of task assignment with binary effort levels and outcomes, which can be seen as a special case of [1], in which only one agent can be assigned to each task. There are NN agents whose types are drawn independently from known finite distributions. For a single task, an agent’s type θi\theta_{i} specifies a success probability pθip_{\theta_{i}} and an effort cost cθic_{\theta_{i}}. The principal commits to a mechanism that maps reported types to an assignment and a payment upon successful completion. A selected agent then decides whether to exert effort. Exerting effort incurs the stated cost and completes the task with the stated probability; exerting no effort produces no reward. The principal receives a unit reward for completion and seeks to maximize expected reward minus payments. In the multi-task extension, each type specifies a success probability and an effort cost for every task, and feasible assignments are matchings between agents and tasks. We seek Bayesian incentive-compatible and individually rational mechanisms which maximize the principal’s utility.

Our results reveal a marked contrast between the single-task and multi-task settings. For a single task, we characterize a simple optimal mechanism and show how to compute it efficiently for an arbitrary number of agents. With multiple tasks, the structure underlying this characterization no longer applies, and an optimal mechanism may not even exist. We therefore take an algorithmic approach and study approximation to the supremum profit when the number of agents is constant.

Our main result is a characterization of an optimal mechanism for a single task and an arbitrary number of agents, together with an efficient algorithm for computing it. The first challenge is that agents’ types are two-dimensional: both effort costs and success probabilities are private information. Our key observation is that, from the perspective of an agent’s incentives, these two parameters can be summarized by a single quantity: the ratio between the cost and the success probability, which we call the critical value. The critical value is the success payment that makes effort individually rational. By rewriting the incentive-compatibility constraints in terms of the critical values, we recover a structure similar to that of procurement and reverse auctions.

papers.title: Investigating Multi-Cultural Value Selection Biases in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) serve users whose cultural identities are multi-layered, yet cultural evaluations commonly reduce identity to one label. In this work, we study LLMs under simultaneous identity cues, with a country persona in the system prompt and a second identity signaled in the user turn, either by naming a country (explicit cue) or through the query language (implicit cue). We test World Values Survey (WVS) multiple-choice probing and open-ended sociopolitical generation. In multiple-choice probing, language cues shift answers about three times more than explicit cues but away from the associated country's distribution, and explicit cues do not consistently move answers toward the named country. Across 1.6 million open-ended responses, naming a country closes 30-44% of the gap to the model's own responses for that country, and explicit cues produce more differentiated value changes than language cues. Our results suggest that country and language cues should be evaluated as distinct signals rather than interchangeable proxies for culture.

papers.intro:
Our world is one of multicultural, complex identities. As of mid-2024, 304 million people (around 3.7% of the global population) live outside their country of birth (United Nations, 2025), many of whom combine multiple cultural identities. Yet, in experiments with large language models (LLMs) and cultural value alignment, most prior work collapses user identity to a single, immutable variable (Zhou et al., 2025b; Adilazuarda et al., 2024), e.g., “You are a person from X”. Social science research though shows that cultural identity is more complex (Brubaker and Cooper, 2000) and that bicultural people switch between cultural frames depending on contextual cues (Hong et al., 2000). Moreover, explicit identity cues can lead to inequitable LLM behavior, e.g., imposing different guardrails for different users (Li et al., 2024). We therefore ask how an LLM responds to a multicultural user who signals ties to two countries at once.

We therefore ask how an LLM responds to a multicultural user who signals ties to two countries at once.

We stress-test LLMs with composite identities (Figure 1), where the model receives two cultural identities through different cues, and measure how far each cue moves its responses. As in a conversational system that stores a user’s identity in its ‘memory’ (OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025a; DeChant, 2025), one country is fixed in the system prompt (persona), and a second identity is signaled in the user prompt, either explicitly by a stated nationality or implicitly through the language of the prompt (§3). The same two cues drive both of our experiments: (1) values selected in World Values Survey (WVS) and (2) values expressed in open-ended generation on sociopolitical topics.

We do not define a “correct” response for a composite identity. In both tasks, we measure how much of the gap between the persona’s baseline and the cued country’s baseline a cue closes (§3). These quantities characterize how the model’s responses change across composite identities, not the values or preferred behavior of genuinely composite-identity individuals. Identity-conditioned behavior is not inherently harmful in value expression, where adaptation may support personalized assistance (Kirk et al., 2024). We therefore compare shifts across countries and languages, because an identity that moves the model much more than others may reflect a bias toward that identity or more distinct values associated with it (§3).

papers.title: Equilibria and Learning in Competitive Market Making
papers.abstract: We propose a market-making game played among $N \ge 2$ strategic market makers and a single non-strategic representative trader. In a continuous quote space, standard finite-game arguments do not apply, while non-convex and discontinuous payoffs rule out classical continuous existence results and complicate learning. Nonetheless, we characterize pure-strategy Nash equilibria (PSNEs) and show that at least one PSNE always exists under minimal assumptions on the underlying asset value distribution, and that the equilibrium bid-ask spread widens strictly with asset value volatility. To obtain a tractable learning framework, we discretize prices and, under an additional regularity condition, show that the time-averaged play of no-internal-regret learners approaches the continuous Nash price envelope as the tick size vanishes. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations.

Classical models of price competition, such as the Bertrand oligopoly model (Bertrand, 1883), elegantly explain why competition may drive prices toward marginal cost. However, applying this one-sided logic directly to financial market making overlooks a fundamental structural feature of liquidity provision: market makers operate simultaneously on both the buy and sell sides of the market, and their quotes actively shape the direction of incoming order flow.

Classical models of price competition, such as the Bertrand oligopoly model (Bertrand, 1883), elegantly explain why competition may drive prices toward marginal cost. However, applying this one-sided logic directly to financial market making overlooks a fundamental structural feature of liquidity provision: market makers operate simultaneously on both the buy and sell sides of the market, and their quotes actively shape the direction of incoming order flow.

This two-sided interaction is particularly prominent in financial markets characterized by inelastic trading demand, such as commodity markets (Bogmans et al., 2024), where overall trading volume does not respond to price changes and market participants simply choose whether to buy or sell. In conventional Bertrand competition, a firm’s price reduction allows it to gain market share at the cost of a lower margin; in contrast, liquidity providers in inelastic markets post bid and ask quotes that establish a market mid-price, which acts as a threshold determining whether buying or selling is advantageous relative to the asset’s fundamental value, ultimately dictating trade direction and, indirectly, execution priority.

To study this mechanism, and how makers learn in it, we model liquidity provision as a static game played among N≥2N\geq 2 strategic market makers and a single non-strategic representative trader. The former simultaneously post bid–ask quotes for a single asset with uncertain fundamental value, while the latter, upon observing the posted quotes, submits either a buy or a sell order according to a fixed decision rule that compares the realized fundamental value of the asset with the market mid-price induced by the quoted prices.

Finally, theoretical predictions and learning dynamics are empirically validated through numerical simulations in Section 5.

Analyzing this market-making game presents distinct theoretical and algorithmic challenges: • Two-Sided Coupling: Updating a quote shifts the implied mid-price, directly coupling execution risk across both sides of the book. As a result, the game cannot be reduced to two independent Bertrand competitions. Indeed, since strategies consist of quote pairs, market makers can execute cross-side deviations (e.g., aggressively lowering the ask while retreating on the bid), thereby expanding the space of potentially profitable strategies in ways that break standard single-side equilibrium arguments. • Continuous vs. Discrete Tension: Payoffs in this game are inherently non-convex and discontinuous. In continuous quote spaces, this rules out standard PSNE existence theorems and complicates learning dynamics. Discretizing prices resolves these hurdles, but it introduces grid-dependent equilibria that obscure the model’s true structure and parameter dependencies.

papers.title: Model Predictive Control of Wind Turbines: A Model-Oriented Review of Prediction Models, Control Objectives, and Nonlinear Aerodynamic Formulations
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) has been applied to wind-turbine regulation with markedly different internal prediction models, ranging from linearized low-order turbine models to nonlinear, aeroelastic, floating, and data-driven predictors. This review organizes the literature primarily by the model propagated by the controller and treats model order, predictor representation, MPC formulation, control objective, and validation plant as separate descriptors. Primary studies show that low-order linear or piecewise-affine predictors are attractive for constrained power and speed regulation, whereas flexible drivetrain, structural, and floating models are needed when drivetrain twist, tower motion, blade loads, or platform dynamics are explicit control quantities. Nonlinear and economic MPC studies further demonstrate coordinated pitch/torque control across broad operating regions, while preview, repetitive, and data-driven formulations address wind prediction, periodic loads, and model mismatch. Particular attention is given to aerodynamic pitch dependence: variable-pitch turbine dynamics can be non-affine with respect to applied pitch, and the term NMPC alone does not prove that the original nonlinear pitch map is retained inside the optimizer. The review therefore adopts a conservative, equation-based classification for direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation. Here, direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation means that the applied pitch at each prediction step is evaluated inside the original nonlinear aerodynamic map, rather than replacing that dependence by a linearized, scheduled, piecewise-affine, or learned surrogate. The literature supports a remaining integration challenge at the intersection of flexible drivetrain prediction, nonlinear aerodynamic pitch treatment, explicit constraints and load objectives, and validated adaptive or learned model correction.

papers.title: Sum-rank analogues of Reed--Muller codes over Abelian Galois extensions
papers.abstract: Let $\mathbb L/\mathbb K$ be a finite Abelian Galois extension with a fixed decomposition $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb L/\mathbb K)=\langleσ_1\rangle\times\cdots\times\langleσ_m\rangle$. We show that the quotient of the multivariate skew polynomial ring $\mathbb L[x_1,\ldots,x_m;σ_1,\ldots,σ_m]$ by suitable central polynomials $H_1(x_1),\ldots,H_m(x_m)$ is isomorphic to a product of $t$ copies of $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb K}(\mathbb L)$, so that one skew polynomial represents all blocks of a sum-rank metric space. The sum-rank weight of an element equals the rank of an associated Dickson matrix and of a generalized Moore matrix. Using this, we define sum-rank Reed--Muller-type codes and show that their dimension and minimum distance are given by the formulas for affine Cartesian codes with side lengths $\mathrm{deg}\,H_1,\ldots,\mathrm{deg}\,H_m$; the same holds for codes supported on lower sets. The family contains as special cases linearized Reed--Solomon codes, Gabidulin codes, rank-metric Reed--Muller codes, and affine Cartesian codes. Over finite fields, every linearized Reed--Muller code of Berardini and Caruso is, after a monomial change of variables, a monomial code in our framework. This gives the dimension of all these codes, and their exact minimum distance in every degree whenever the support is a lower set.

papers.intro:
Polynomial evaluation is a standard method for constructing error-correcting codes. Reed–Solomon codes arise from evaluations of univariate polynomials, and their minimum distance follows from the bound on the number of roots of a nonzero polynomial. Generalized Reed–Muller and affine Cartesian codes use multivariate polynomials evaluated on finite grids [17, 15, 18]. Their dimensions are obtained by counting admissible monomials, while their minimum distances are related to bounds on the number of zeros of a polynomial, including the Alon–Füredi theorem and the Schwartz–Zippel lemma [3, 31, 32, 9, 11].

The rank and sum-rank metrics arise in settings where errors have a matrix structure, notably in network coding. In the rank metric [12, 13, 30], words are matrices over a field 𝕂\mathbb{K}, and the distance between two matrices is the rank of their difference. papers.title: The symmetric skew monoidal structure of Gray-categories
papers.abstract: In previous work, we constructed a closed skew monoidal structure on the category of Gray-categories and Gray-functors whose internal hom Psd(A, B) captures pseudomaps and pseudo-transformations. In the present paper we give a symmetric description of the Gray-category Psd(A,B) and use this to prove that the skew monoidal structure is symmetric skew monoidal.

papers.title: Semi-strict 4-categories as enriched categories
papers.abstract: We introduce several flavours of semi-strict 4-category as enriched categories. This is done using the framework of enrichment over skew monoidal categories of Gray-categories and their associated multicategories, as developed in our previous work. We give the axioms for semi-strict 4-categories in elementary terms and describe a wide range of examples. In particular, we answer the question of what exactly Gray-categories and the higher transformations between them form: namely, a left-sharp 4-category G-Cat$^4$. In addition, we describe examples arising from braided monoidal 2-categories, monoidal Gray-categories (herein defined) and Gray-categories with structure. We use the concepts introduced here and the relationships between them to unify various concepts in the literature, such as Crans' 4-teisi. In the second part of the paper, we investigate homotopical aspects. In particular, we classify the equivalence n-cells in the left-sharp 4-category G-Cat$^4$ for each n. Using this, we show that the left-sharp skew monoidal structure on the category of Gray-categories induces a symmetric monoidal closed structure on the homotopy category of Gray-categories.

papers.intro:
The Gray-tensor product ⊗p\otimes_{p} of 22-categories has many useful features. One of these is that categories enriched in it, called Gray-categories, provide a framework for 33-category theory which is theoretically powerful, sufficiently general and yet sufficiently simple to be amenable to calculations. Let us flesh out the key points which make the theory appealing. (1) (Powerful theory.) The Gray-tensor product forms a symmetric monoidal closed structure (2-𝐂𝐚𝐭,⊗p,1)(2\text{-}\mathbf{Cat},\otimes_{p},1) on the category of 22-categories. This means that the full power of classical enriched category theory [36] — including enriched adjunctions, weighted limits and so on — applies to Gray-categories as a special case. (2) (Sufficient generality.) Each weak 33-category (aka tricategory) is equivalent to a Gray-category, though not necessarily to a strict 33-category [27]. For this reason, Gray-categories are often called semi-strict 33-categories and provide a sufficiently general framework. (3) (Ease of calculation.) Gray-categories are almost strict, involving only a single additional 33-dimensional datum which accounts for the failure of the middle 44-interchange for 22-cells. Since their homs are strict 22-categories, one can use traditional 2-categorical pasting diagrams for calculations. Such calculations can also be carried out using the powerful 33-dimensional graphical calculus [32, 4]. (4) (Natural examples.) Thanks to (1) above, there is a Gray-category of 22-categories, 22-functors, pseudonatural transformations and modifications on which many further examples are based. There is also a close connection between pseudonaturality and braidings, which has the effect that doubly degenerate Gray-categories capture braided strict monoidal categories. More recently it has been shown that 33-dimensional defect TQFT’s lead naturally to Gray-categories with duals [16].

The need for a 44-dimensional analogue of Gray-categories grew out of research on braided monoidal 22-categories in the 1990s. With motivations coming from theoretical physics, braided monoidal 2-categories were first defined by Kapranov and Voevodsky [34]. papers.title: Beyond Global Importance: A Heterogeneity Index for Sensitivity Analysis
papers.abstract: Global sensitivity analysis quantifies how strongly inputs influence a model output, however, input importance often varies across the model space. We introduce a heterogeneity index H to quantify this variation. The index compares normalized regional sensitivity profiles using mean pairwise total-variation distance and its values range from zero to one. We test H on nine benchmark functions and examine its robustness to the number of regions, sample size, and sampling strategy. We further demonstrate it using models of wooden-pallet carbon footprint, flood risk, and steel-structure reliability. Across these cases, H reveals changes in sensitivity that global indices obscure, including inputs whose importance changes substantially across the model space and differences between rare behavioral regimes. The index complements global sensitivity analysis by indicating when a single global sensitivity profile is insufficient. An open-source implementation is provided in the simdec package.
papers.intro:
Environmental and energy models commonly represent complex systems shaped by nonlinear processes, interacting drivers, and interdependent uncertain conditions (Pianosi et al., 2016; Beven and Freer, 2001). Consider a power-system model combining variable renewable generation, electricity demand, storage, and market or network constraints. A global sensitivity analysis may identify electricity demand as the dominant source of output variation overall, while under particular combinations of highly intermittent generation, high demand, or constrained import, other factors such as storage capacity or demand response flexibility may become substantially more influential. Such heterogeneity need not correspond to an explicit threshold or a regime known in advance; it may emerge only when the model is examined across different parts of its input or output space. This matters for decision-making because recommendations based on global importance can overlook the factors that become decisive under particular operating conditions. The term heterogeneity is used in different ways across disciplines. In this study, we define heterogeneity as variation in the overall composition of input importance across the model space.

Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) provides a rigorous framework for quantifying how uncertainty in model inputs contributes to uncertainty in model outputs and has become an established tool for model diagnosis, uncertainty assessment, and decision support (Tarantola et al., 2024). Most commonly used global sensitivity measures, however, summarize importance over the full distributions of the inputs and outputs. This aggregation can conceal variation in sensitivity within the model space. Wei et al. (2013) noted that standard GSA measures input importance over its full range but does not identify how particular ranges contribute to output uncertainty, while Wei et al. (2015) subsequently developed regional extensions of Sobol’ indices to examine how main and total effects change when input ranges are restricted. The same phenomenon has been demonstrated from a temporal perspective. Time-varying sensitivity analysis has shown that dominant model parameters can change substantially with environmental conditions and that these changes may be difficult to anticipate from the model formulation alone (Herman et al., 2013). Related work has therefore developed visualization approaches specifically for exploring changing sensitivity patterns across time and evaluation scales (Massmann et al., 2014). Collectively, these studies show that sensitivity itself can be heterogeneous: the factors that matter, and their relative importance, may change across the domain of a model.

Collectively, these studies show that sensitivity itself can be heterogeneous: the factors that matter, and their relative importance, may change across the domain of a model.

Several branches of sensitivity analysis provide ways to investigate such variation. Regional sensitivity analysis partitions simulations into behavioral and non-behavioral subsets and examines differences between them (Spear and Hornberger, 1980), while later regional approaches investigate contributions from particular portions of the input domain (Wei et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2015). Target and conditional sensitivity analysis focus respectively on the factors driving entry into a critical output domain and on sensitivity within that domain (Marrel and Chabridon, 2021). For temporal or spatial outputs, cluster-based GSA identifies distinct model behaviors and the inputs associated with transitions between them (Roux et al., 2021). Graphical methods such as simulation decomposition (SimDec) provide another route by visualizing how conditional distributions and interactions change across combinations of model inputs, revealing heterogeneous effects that conventional global sensitivity indices may conceal (Kozlova et al., 2024). These approaches differ substantially in their objectives and formulations, but share the recognition that a single global importance measure may provide an incomplete description of model behavior.

What remains difficult to express is the magnitude of heterogeneity itself. Existing approaches can identify sensitivity within particular regions, trace changing indices across time or input ranges, distinguish critical and non-critical domains, or reveal heterogeneous patterns visually. They do not, however, provide a general scalar measure of how much the complete sensitivity profile changes across a partition of the model space. Consequently, there is no direct counterpart to a global sensitivity index for answering a simple diagnostic question: How heterogeneous is the sensitivity structure of this model? Such a measure could complement conventional GSA by indicating when a global sensitivity profile is sufficiently representative and when, instead, more detailed regional investigation is warranted.

In this paper, we propose the heterogeneity index HH to quantify changes in sensitivity profiles across regions of a model. The general index HZH_{Z} is defined from pairwise distances between normalized regional sensitivity profiles, where ZZ denotes the variable used to partition the model space. Regions may be defined by the model output, yielding HYH_{Y}; by an input, yielding HXiH_{X_{i}}; or by an externally specified categorical partition representing application-specific states or behaviors. We first examine the index’s properties using controlled models in which we can systematically introduce heterogeneity. An existing workbench of test functions for sensitivity analysis (Azzini and Rosati, 2022) is then used to investigate the influence of regionalisation and sample size, and to examine the relationship between global input importance and heterogeneity. Finally, three practical cases test whether HH can compactly identify forms of heterogeneous model behaviour previously revealed only through detailed visualisation or regional sensitivity analysis. The method is implemented in the free and open-source simdec package (Roy and Kozlova, 2024; Simulation-Decomposition, 2026) to facilitate its use alongside conventional sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: The Geometry of Meaning in Neural Manifolds
papers.abstract: Just as different languages express the same concept through different words, neural networks express similar functions through incompatible coordinate systems. Different architectures, random initializations, and optimization trajectories produce incompatible parameterizations in extrinsic coordinates, obscuring functional relationships between independently trained models. When models independently solve similar tasks on related data, do their learned representations share exploitable structure despite incompatible coordinates? This thesis shows that semantic correspondence is a fundamental primitive revealing shared geometric structure beneath incompatible parameterizations. By identifying which elements refer to the same semantic content, correspondence breaks the symmetry of arbitrary implementation choices, anchoring incompatible systems to a shared semantic frame and revealing the intrinsic geometry that enables zero-shot transformation between independently trained models. Building on this principle, fourteen contributions explore correspondence-based alignment across zero-shot model stitching, cross-modal translation, policy transfer, activation steering, and neural decoding. They span domains (vision, language, reinforcement learning, neuroscience), architectures (CNNs, Transformers, graph networks), and scales (from small supervised models to billion-parameter generative systems). Each exploits different geometric properties (angular, metric, spectral, sparse, or distributional), yet all instantiate the same principle. It extends beyond artificial systems: fMRI data show that different human brains processing identical stimuli exhibit alignable geometric structure. By revealing intrinsic geometric structure beneath extrinsic parameterization, semantic correspondence transforms model isolation into interoperability.

papers.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) studies how agents learn to make sequential decisions through interaction with an environment, using rewards as feedback to improve future behavior (Sutton and Barto, 2018). Despite strong performance in fixed environments, standard RL methods often require large amounts of data to adapt to new tasks and generalize poorly under environment shifts (Packer et al., 2018; Cobbe et al., 2019). Meta-reinforcement learning addresses this limitation by training agents over a distribution of tasks so they can use past training experience to adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction at meta-test time (Duan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017; Rakelly et al., 2019). A fundamental problem in meta-RL is representing task evidence collected during interaction with the environment (Humplik et al., 2019; Zintgraf et al., 2021). Black-box sequence-based agents learn this representation directly from trajectories using internal dynamics (Duan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Mishra et al., 2018; Alver and Precup, 2021). Latent-context methods instead make task inference more explicit by inferring a task variable or belief from collected experience (Humplik et al., 2019; Rakelly et al., 2019; Zintgraf et al., 2021).

However, standard self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length (Vaswani et al., 2017; Duman Keles et al., 2023), making long adaptation horizons increasingly expensive in online RL settings. papers.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

papers.intro:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which combine language and vision encoders to jointly process images and text, have demonstrated great potential as assistants to ophthalmologists [1, 7, 36, 39, 2, 16]. The visual question-answering (VQA) ability of these models is of particular interest, as it allows users to query a model about the presence of diseases or lesions in an image [32]. However, for such assistants to be trusted in clinical practice, they must not only answer accurately, but also indicate the visual evidence behind each answer. This capability is known as visual grounding, in which a model outputs the spatial location of a queried finding. Without such grounding, a textual answer gives clinicians no way to confirm that a model attended to the relevant pathology rather than exploiting spurious correlations or learned shortcuts [9], or simply hallucinating. This lack of verifiability is a central barrier to clinical adoption [18]. Assessing whether current MLLMs can be trusted therefore requires understanding not only their diagnostic question answering ability but also their capacity to spatially localise the pathology underlying those answers.

Most previous studies focused on evaluating MLLMs in terms of examination performance and diagnosis on real clinical cases [1, 7, 36, 39, 2]. In the former category, frontier models (including GPT-5 [28], Gemini 2.5 Pro [12], Claude Sonnet 4.0 [3], and DeepSeek-V3 [8]) have improved substantially on the Fellowship of the Royal College of Ophthalmologists (FRCOphth) examinations since 2023, with the best-performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, exceeding typical top human candidate scores. However, error analysis still revealed critical reasoning deficits such as premature diagnostic closure and confidently unjustified decisions [1]. On real clinical cases, rather than curated examination questions, the evidence is more mixed: on 50 retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCT-A) cases, GPT-4o diagnosed 62% correctly versus Gemini’s 32% [7]; Med-Gemini surpassed baselines on 18 of 20 medical image classification tasks including ophthalmology [36]; and GPT-4o matched clinicians in differential glaucoma diagnosis on OCT while struggling with primary diagnosis [39], with further evidence of effective few-shot retinal disease diagnosis on OCT [2].

papers.title: Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum: Subexponential Algorithm, Tight Lower Bounds, and Average-Case Analysis
papers.abstract: The Equal Subset Sum problem asks, given n positive integers bounded by M, to find two distinct non-empty subsets with the same sum. We study this problem in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$, where the pigeonhole principle guarantees that a solution exists, and the main challenge is to find one efficiently. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time poly(n).$M$. After a sequence of improvements, the current best algorithm, due to Jin, Williams, and Zhang (ESA 2025), achieves running time poly(n).$M^{1/3}$. In this work, we give the first poly(n).$M^{o(1)}$-time algorithm for Equal Subset Sum in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$. We complement this algorithmic result with a tight conditional lower bound showing that any substantial improvement would require a major breakthrough in approximation algorithms for lattice problems, building on recent techniques of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan (STOC 2025). Finally, we show that our techniques yield an asymptotically faster algorithm for the regime when $M = Θ(2^{n})$: a poly(n)$\cdot 2^{n/4}$-time algorithm in the average case.

Papadimitriou [36] introduced the total variant called the Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum (PESS). In this variant, the sum of the numbers is less than 2n−12^{n}-1, and the goal remains to find distinct subsets A,B⊆SA,B\subseteq S with equal sums. PESS belongs to the class TFNP\mathrm{TFNP} and, more specifically, to PPP\mathrm{PPP}, and it is conjectured to be PPP\mathrm{PPP}-complete [36]. The setting, when the number of collisions is even larger, e.g., the sum of integers is bounded by 2n−12^{n-1}, is called weak-pigeonhole regime and is also an important setting [43]. In that weaker setting, PESS belongs to the class PWPP\mathrm{PWPP} (problems whose totality is proven through the weak pigeonhole principle) [43]. papers.title: The physical and chemical structure of Titan's upper atmosphere: energy balance, photochemistry and Jeans escape
papers.abstract: Titan's upper atmospheric layers provide a unique opportunity to study how photochemistry, photoionisation, haze microphysics and escape processes shape its atmospheric chemical structure, providing a unique benchmark for understanding these processes in exoplanets. Using a 1D first-principles approach, we extend the Kompot model to simulate Titan's upper atmosphere and investigate its thermal and chemical structure, and Jeans escape. We performed self-consistent simulations of Titan's upper atmosphere, above the dense haze layer, over a 1D radial grid by solving the coupled hydrodynamics, thermal and photochemical kinetic, and energy balance equations. We considered heating by stellar X-ray and ultraviolet (XUV) and infrared (IR) radiation, and cooling due to radiative emission of methane (CH4) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). We also included additional nineteen photochemical and 117 thermal reactions to Kompot's standard chemical network. Our modelled atmospheric temperature structures lie within the observed variability of Titan's atmospheric temperature profile. Our simulations reproduce observed nitrogen (N2) and CH4 densities in the upper atmosphere, and abundance of minor chemical species also broadly agree with observationally derived abundances. Near the exobase, our CH4 mixing ratio overlap with Cassini-Huygens results, and our model H2 mixing ratios also exhibit broad agreement with observations. Our simulations suggest no significant thermal loss of CH4, even under the conditions of an early Sun's XUV environment.

papers.title: Adaptive Restart under Unknown KL Geometry in Stochastic Weakly-Convex Optimization
papers.abstract: KL geometry accelerates restart schedules in stochastic weakly-convex optimization, but the schedule depends jointly on an unknown and potentially nonunique geometric description. We introduce CARP-KL, a certified portfolio that adapts over valid KL descriptions while using the same primitive stochastic-subgradient oracle for both optimization and candidate selection. Over declared polynomial parameter ranges, CARP-KL competes with every affordable valid description and preserves the known-description polynomial Moreau-stationarity rate up to logarithmic factors, without objective values, an exact proximal map, direct Moreau-gradient access, or a bounded-domain assumption. Controlled experiments quantify the finite-budget price of this universality. The portfolio repeatedly contains strong candidates, while certification consumes a substantial share of the oracle budget and finite-sample ranking limits their recovery. A common conservative gap bound further reduces the portfolio from $O(\log^3 T)$ to $O(\log^2 T)$ candidates with an explicit scale-mismatch penalty. The theory and diagnostics together establish certified unknown-geometry adaptation and pinpoint selection as the principal practical frontier of the current construction.

papers.title: Adaptive Uncertainty Visualization With jk-Plots
papers.abstract: An important task of uncertainty visualizations is to communicate how the number of available observations influences the precision of estimates, such as a Normal distribution's mean. In this paper, we propose an adaptive approach to visualizing univariate data that produces salient representations while highlighting the uncertainty introduced by the sample size. We introduce jk-plots, inspired by educational material of Bayesian statistics, that combine visualizations of plausible reference models (emulating popular uncertainty visualization idioms) and the observations. We describe a visualization pipeline to create jk-plots, which we implemented in an R package. We demonstrate jk-plots using synthetic datasets of varying size and discuss possible usage scenarios in domain expert interviews.

This kind of uncertainty is often visually conveyed via certainty bounds of a parameter, e.g, confidence intervals or the standard error of the mean. On the other hand, showing the sample as-is, e.g., (Fig. 1, bottom), hides the certainty bounds of a parameter in addition to the reference models, and does not scale to large samples due to overplotting and occlusion. Therefore, popular uncertainty visualizations do not appropriately communicate the sample size’s implications (P1).

papers.title: A New Minimax Theorem for a Class of $C^1$-Functionals
papers.abstract: We establish a new abstract minimax theorem for obtaining ground-state critical points of a class of \(C^{1}\)-functionals. The central feature of this class is that the associated Nehari set is not necessarily a differentiable manifold, but is homeomorphic to a (possibly non-complete) submanifold of the unit sphere. This occurs for functionals whose fibering maps \(t \mapsto I(tu)\) possess a unique global maximum point only when \(u\) belongs to an open cone in the underlying Banach space. A lower semicontinuous boundary barrier, which may be finite, controls minimizing sequences near the boundary of the spherical cone. As a consequence, we provide a general minimax characterization of the ground-state energy level. Elliptic applications complement existing results and include superlinear and quasilinear problems with finite barriers, including thresholds depending on the profile of a first eigenfunction and its gradient.

papers.title: Measuring Research Progress and Linguistic Inclusion in Low-Resource Languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated research on low-resource and multilingual NLP, but their effectiveness in creating an equitable landscape remains unmapped. We analyze 1,158 peer-reviewed open-access papers published between 2020 and 2025, examining research attention to low-resource languages (LRLs) and representation across language and speaker populations. To assess linguistic inclusion beyond publication counts, we introduce the Linguistic Inclusion Framework (LIF), a multidimensional framework that measures linguistic inclusion in four dimensions: research growth, representation expansion, representation continuity, and distributional equity. While annual publications grew from 52 to 415, a 5.4X increase in their ACL Anthology publication share, this growth largely concentrated on represented languages rather than expanding coverage of underrepresented languages. Further analysis shows that languages spoken in Asia account for 64.1% of speakers across LRLs we analyze but receive only 46.7% of the language representation share (0.7X their proportional share), while European languages receive 5.3X their proportional share. At the country level, linguistically diverse regions such as sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia show the lowest language coverage ratios. Applying the framework at the continental level, we find that no region scores well on all four dimensions, showing that research growth alone is not a reliable metric of progress toward equitable and inclusive language technology\footnote{We will release all collected and annotated data for research purposes}.

There are more than 7,000 languages spoken in the world, however only a few languages are represented in the development and use of digital language technology Kornai (2013); Nekoto et al. (2023), public services Nzobonimpa et al. (2026), and workplace tools Brynjolfsson et al. (2025). papers.title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.

Hierarchical retrieval [16, 3, 24, 7] turns evidence gathering into sequential control: an LLM repeatedly selects bb of k≤20k\!\leq\!20 candidate sections and descends into the selected subtrees. The action space is finite and input-dependent, yet deployed systems execute this controller by decoding text. That choice imposes a three-way dilemma. Free-form JSON leaves a protocol surface that dominates the error budget (33–65%65\% of questions fail on syntax, identifiers, or cardinality in our companion interface study). Scoring all kk verified single-token labels in one prefill — the unary shortcut — removes the protocol surface but also the controller’s memory: selection can no longer condition on earlier selections. Grammar-constrained decoding [17, 6] keeps the history-dependent policy and syntactic validity, but pays a serial critical path of bb action tokens plus forced syntax tokens, one model forward each.

Grammar-constrained decoding [17, 6] keeps the history-dependent policy and syntactic validity, but pays a serial critical path of bb action tokens plus forced syntax tokens, one model forward each.

Our central observation is that this dilemma is an artifact of the execution model, not of the controller. A constrained controller with horizon bb has a bounded reachable future: every state it can visit is a prefix over at most bb distinct actions — for greedy control at our deployed horizon of three actions, at most kk states remain once the first is fixed. We therefore compile the action grammar into its prefix tree and evaluate all reachable states at once: one root prefill resolves the first action; one tree-causal probe — a single forward pass over the concatenated prefix continuations, with a block-causal mask and serial position indices — returns every prefix-conditioned action distribution the controller can consult. Because each tree state sees exactly the tokens, positions, and causal ancestry it would see under serial decoding, its logits are the serial controller’s logits, and the greedy chain is recovered arithmetically. papers.title: What Comes Next and Why: Interpretable Next-Event Prediction with Neuro-Symbolic Rules
papers.abstract: In real-world applications, being able to explain why a prediction is made is often as important - if not more so - than achieving high accuracy. However, existing methods for sequential event prediction typically prioritize accuracy at the expense of interpretability. Neuro-symbolic approaches offer a promising direction to improve interpretability by learning symbolic rules, but extending them to next-event prediction is challenging due to the presence of temporal dependencies. We introduce RULES, a neuro-symbolic model that learns sequential rules directly from data, and combine it with a residual network to form RUNES (Rule Network for Event Sequences). RULES accurately recovers ground truth rules from synthetic data and discovers compact, interpretable rule sets on real data. RUNES combines these rules additively with a residual network, achieving competitive accuracy while providing transparent access to active rules and how residuals adjust predictions.

papers.intro:
Next-event prediction is the task of predicting the next categorical element in a temporally ordered sequence. Beyond next-token prediction in language models—where token positions can be seen as discrete event times—next-event prediction arises in many domains, including e-commerce (Nasir and Ezeife, 2023), healthcare (Pishgar et al., 2022; Ramirez-Alcocer et al., 2023), and process log analysis (Tama and Comuzzi, 2019; Bukhsh et al., 2021). Neural sequence models provide accurate predictions across domains and are thus increasingly adopted in practice. However, their internal representations are opaque, making predictions difficult to interpret or justify. This is especially problematic in safety- and regulation-sensitive contexts, where interpretability is key.

However, their internal representations are opaque, making predictions difficult to interpret or justify. This is especially problematic in safety- and regulation-sensitive contexts, where interpretability is key.

Symbolic approaches (Mannila et al., 1997; Fournier-Viger et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2021; Siji et al., 2026) instead focus on describing event dependencies using sequential rules. A sequential rule A⇒BA\Rightarrow B expresses that when the antecedent AA has been observed, the consequent BB is likely to occur later in the sequence. In e-commerce, such a rule might specify that customers who purchased a computer case and a computer processor are likely to subsequently purchase a motherboard or a power supply unit. However, existing rule-discovery methods focus on enumerating frequent or high-confidence rules without a principled way to integrate them into a unified predictive model.

Neuro-symbolic models offer a promising approach to address the accuracy–interpretability tension. For instance, recent neuro-symbolic methods for tabular data use differentiable relaxations to learn interpretable and accurate prediction rules (Qiao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Walter et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). However, their reliance on binarized tabular inputs hinders applicability to sequential data, where temporal structure is central. Naively flattening sequences leads to sparse, high-dimensional representations, limiting both scalability and expressiveness.

For instance, recent neuro-symbolic methods for tabular data use differentiable relaxations to learn interpretable and accurate prediction rules (Qiao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Walter et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). However, their reliance on binarized tabular inputs hinders applicability to sequential data, where temporal structure is central. Naively flattening sequences leads to sparse, high-dimensional representations, limiting both scalability and expressiveness.

To fill this gap, we define a class of sequential rules that incorporate temporal information and can be efficiently integrated into neural network layers for prediction. We then propose Rules, a neuro-symbolic model that learns these rules directly from data, and its extension Runes, which combines Rules with a residual network. Training proceeds in two phases using a self-supervised next-event prediction objective. In the symbolic phase, we train Rules using temperature annealing (Jang et al., 2017) to enable gradient-based rule learning. After annealing, the layers of Rules represent symbolic conditions over events and their relative offsets to the predicted event, yielding meaningful binary representations for sequences. In the predictive phase, we obtain Runes by training a residual network that corrects the predictions of the frozen Rules through additive logit residuals. This phase improves predictive performance while preserving rule-level interpretability.

The residual network enables Runes to achieve competitive accuracy by capturing structure not explained by Rules. Importantly, Runes allows tracing the impact of the residual network, which is mostly used to correct errors of Rules, maintaining interpretability when learned rules are reliable.

papers.title: WildFakeToolBench: Benchmarking AI-Generated Image Detectors with Web-Sourced Image Processing
papers.abstract: As AI generated images are getting popular these days, discussions on such generations are widely existed in current public forums, software repositories, and photography tutorials. Moreover, with the help of LLM-assisted code translation, malicious actors can adopt such information to evade detectors without specialized knowledge or local GPU execution of the resulting tools. To evaluate such risks, we introduce \textsc{WildFakeToolBench}, a benchmark suite of $156$ executable image-processing tools derived from $220$ public sources across $142$ domains. Each tool retains its source evidence and passes syntax, execution, and output-distortion checks without using feedback from the evaluated detectors. On $105$ generated images from five generators, we evaluate six state-of-the-art detectors with images processed by the tools in our collected bench to assess their effectiveness against such in-the-wild risks. The strongest individual tools achieve attack success rates of $25.25\%$--$100\%$ across detectors, exceeding the strongest of six selected image-processing baselines for each detector. Evaluating subsets of an eight-tool pool yields worst-case coverage above $80\%$ for every detector. Effectiveness is sparse and detector-specific: high coverage across candidates does not imply reliable one-shot evasion. These findings not only highlight the potential of such web-sourced risks, but also show the potential on establishing AI-image detector robustness evaluation framework based on those in-the-wild information.

papers.intro:
As AI-generated images become increasingly accessible, more users are discussing them online. However, these images can also be used for malicious purposes, such as spreading misinformation. Although several detectors have been proposed to identify statistical, frequency-domain, or visual-artifact cues, prior work has shown that their robustness against various attacks remains limited [5, 11, 25]. Moreover, malicious actors can draw on publicly accessible web knowledge about photographic appearance, camera artifacts, and detector evasion. With the help of current LLMs, they can translate this knowledge into image-processing operations that make generated images evade detectors. Because these operations can be applied by non-experts with image-processing knowledge using only a CPU, this risk should not be overlooked.

Such knowledge is distributed across forums, software repositories, image-tool sites, and photography tutorials. Some sources explicitly discuss evasion, while others describe ordinary editing or simulated capture effects. Although these sources often provide informal descriptions rather than directly applicable code or software, attackers can use LLMs to translate them into runnable code, reducing the implementation expertise required. Most resulting transformations can also be performed with standard image-processing libraries on CPUs. The relevant question is therefore whether accessible public experience can supply effective robustness tests for current detectors, even without detector-specific attack optimization.

We introduce WildFakeToolBench, a suite of 156156 executable tools with source provenance and a common evaluation protocol. The tools are generated by our WildFake agent framework, which performs text retrieval, method extraction, deduplication, and code generation. They span ten categories, including artifact repair, color adjustment, resampling, and simulated capture effects. To reflect attackers with limited resources, the image-processing operations in our benchmark require no local GPU. Neither tool synthesis nor image-specific parameter proposals use detector feedback. Our contribution is the resulting benchmark resource and its assessment of an accessible processing space, rather than a new detector-specific optimization algorithm.

To measure the robustness of current state-of-the-art AI detectors in our settings, we evaluate six state-of-the-art AI detectors after processing our collected tools on an image set collected across five generators and seven content categories. For each tool and image, we process the tool with five parameter candidates generated by GPT-4o-mini and retain outputs with SSIM at least 0.750.75. Based on the evaluation, we find that every evaluated detector is vulnerable to at least one tool, and the strongest individual tool exceeds the strongest of six selected baselines for each detector. Although most tools cannot effectively affect the prediction of the state-of-the-art detectors, we still find many useful tools for current detectors. For example, the maximum single-tool attack success rate (ASR) for FakeVLM is 45.54%45.54\%, demonstrating substantial weaknesses for current detectors.

papers.title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.

papers.intro:
Proteins constitute the molecular machinery of life, carrying out the catalytic, structural, signaling, and regulatory processes that sustain cells and organisms. A comprehensive understanding of proteins draws on three complementary modalities: (1) amino acid sequences describe molecular identity and evolutionary constraints [1]. (2) 3D structures represent the physical and geometric constraints that govern molecular interactions, thereby revealing the mechanistic basis of protein function [2]. (3) function descriptions capture not only specific protein functions but also the broader body of human knowledge accumulated through biological research [3, 4].

A comprehensive understanding of proteins draws on three complementary modalities: (1) amino acid sequences describe molecular identity and evolutionary constraints [1]. (2) 3D structures represent the physical and geometric constraints that govern molecular interactions, thereby revealing the mechanistic basis of protein function [2]. (3) function descriptions capture not only specific protein functions but also the broader body of human knowledge accumulated through biological research [3, 4].

Importantly, these modalities are not independent views of proteins. We distill protein modeling into six meta-capabilities spanning the directed transformations among sequence, structure, and function: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design. Rather than isolated tasks, these capabilities serve as composable primitives whose combinations give rise to diverse and increasingly complex workflows.

Substantial progress has been made through specialized protein models; in Sec. 2.2, we review these developments and revisit several long-overlooked connections to modern language modeling. Nevertheless, protein modeling remains fragmented across specialized systems and largely disconnected from general-purpose LLMs. We identify two key requirements for next-generation general-purpose protein foundation models: • Unified protein framework. A single model should enable knowledge sharing and mutual reinforcement across tasks, without heavily relying on cross-model interfaces or task-specific adaptation. • Native language capabilities. The model should retain the instruction-following, reasoning, and interactive capabilities native to general-purpose LLMs.

Early attempts explored unifying heterogeneous protein modalities within autoregressive frameworks [5, 6], roughly in parallel with the emergence of unified vision models [7, 8]. Yet these approaches remained limited on structure-intensive tasks such as protein folding. Theoretically, structural contacts do not follow a left-to-right sequence order, so autoregressive generation may commit to early predictions with incomplete context and accumulate errors. Experimentally, existing tri-modal autoregressive models show limited folding performance under single-sample evaluation, leaving open whether the autoregressive paradigm itself provides the right foundation for unified protein modeling.

papers.title: Optimal Search Strategies under Finite Resource Constraints: The Role of Environmental Memory and Directional Information in Informed and Blind Protocols
papers.abstract: Improving the efficiency of a stochastic search often requires to provide the searching agent with resources that modify its dynamics and help it explore space more quickly. Although such resources are often assumed to be unlimited and treated as a cost to mitigate, many realistic search processes operate under a finite resource budget, e.g. in processes with environmental memory in which the searcher deposits long-lasting cues along its path that it can interact with at later times to guide its further search. Here, we address the question of how to allocate a limited budget to maximize search efficiency by investigating a one-dimensional diffusing agent whose access to resources is constrained. We consider three resource models, namely an external force applied by an external controller to pull the searcher towards the target, directional flags deposited by the searcher along its path that redirect its motion towards the target, and self-generated chemorepulsive cues that act as a force field. For all these models, we find that resource usage should be concentrated in narrow regions of space when information about the searcher's current and past positions is available. In contrast, in blind strategies where a predefined time protocol is followed, resources should be used at a steady rate to ensure it to be used at most of its capacity by the time it reaches the target. We further show that blind strategies in non-Markovian processes with environmental memory are significantly less efficient due to the inherent fluctuations in the locations of deposited cues.

papers.intro:
Searching efficiently for a target is a universal task encountered in a broad range of natural and artificial processes, across multiple length and time scales [1]. Examples include, in increasing order of scales, chemical reaction kinetics [2, 3, 4], genetic transcription [5, 6], immune response mechanisms [7, 8, 9, 10], animal and human foraging [11, 12, 13], search-and-rescue missions [14, 15, 16], this list being far from exhaustive. Despite their very different natures, all these examples share the need for the searching agents to reach a target as fast as possible by tuning adjustable parameters, use external resources and develop implementable strategies to increase the rate at which they reach unexplored regions of space and thus increase the probability to locate their target quickly.

Because of this broad relevance, understanding how to optimize search has become a central topic in statistical physics, and many mechanisms to improve search efficiency have been characterized over the past decades. Let us mention e.g. Lévy walks [17], intermittent strategies [18], stochastic resetting [19, 20, 21], persistent motion [22], collective searches [23, 24, 25], trail-leaving walks [26, 27], non-Markovian dynamics [28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33], active particles [34, 35, 36], to name but a few. Many of these approaches require to modify the original dynamics of the searcher, which almost always implies a supply of energy or resources that allow for such modification of the dynamics. Although statistical measures of the overall search time remain the central quantities to optimize in the vast majority of these works, recent studies have sought to identify cost-effective strategies that reduce both the time required to find a target and the cost of implementing the search strategy. For example, resetting a searcher requires mechanical work [37, 38, 39], hiring multiple searchers may cost energetic and material resources [40], or even controlling the protocol itself may be costly [41]. Most of these works assume however that resource availability is infinite: using it may be costly but it can always be done and one tries to minimize a relevant cost function. This is particularly true for non-Markovian search processes where the memory of the process is mediated by cues deposited along the path of the searcher, or by an alteration of the environment that can be sensed and interpreted at later times. This class of processes where agents interact with their own past trajectories has been at the center of recent studies and shown to be efficient search processes [42, 43, 26, 27], but the ability of the searcher to produce environmental memory has always been considered unbounded.

The objective is no longer to minimize a weighted combination of search time and cost, but rather to determine how a limited budget should be allocated in order to minimize the typical search time. This formulation is motivated by many realistic situations in which the available resource is fixed beforehand and cannot be replenished during the search [44, 45, 46]. The objective is no longer to minimize a weighted combination of search time and cost, but rather to determine how a limited budget should be allocated in order to minimize the typical search time. This formulation is motivated by many realistic situations in which the available resource is fixed beforehand and cannot be replenished during the search [44, 45, 46]. Only a few papers made a step towards questioning search strategies with finite resource availability in recent years [47, 48, 49].

The main problem that a finite resource budget raises is the following: how does one make sure that the finite budget is used as much of its full capacity as possible while not spending all of it too fast and searching for most of the remaining time without benefiting from it? In addition, how should one adjust the resource allocation strategy depending on the available information on the current state of the searcher? We therefore distinguish between two classes of processes. First, those where the searcher – or an external agent that controls the resource usage – knows at all times the current position of the walker, which we refer to as informed strategies. It can therefore condition the usage of the resource on it, or on the advancement of the process, and design a spatial protocol: whenever the searcher reaches a certain position for the first time, then it can use a certain pre-determined amount of the resource. In these strategies, resources should be used judiciously to exploit the available budget while minimizing the amount of unused resource remaining when the searcher reaches the target. Second, when neither the searcher nor any external controller knows the searcher’s current position, resource usage must follow a predetermined protocol. For such blind strategies, the optimal protocol should aim to maximize the probability that the resource budget is entirely used by the time the searcher reaches the target, while ensuring that the way it has been allocated does not hinder the search once the budget is exhausted and the search continues without additional resources.

To investigate this optimization problem, we start with a one-dimensional diffusive searcher which we provide with three different types of limited resources to speed up its search performance. First, we start with a reference process in which we apply an external pulling force and constrain the total work that can be expended by it before reaching the target, or equivalently the total heat dissipated. This is the most straightforward type of resource, as it keeps the process Markovian and requires standard techniques to be quantitatively described [50, 51]. However, applying an external force to the searcher requires an external controller, which is not always possible. Consequently, the second model we consider equips the searcher with a supply of directional flags that it can deposit along its path and that act as checkpoints redirecting it towards the target. This makes the process non-Markovian and effectively self-interacting, since the deposited flags alter the subsequent dynamics based on the searcher’s previous positions. Still, this model assumes that the resource carries some information about the location of the target. We therefore consider, as a third model, isotropic chemotactic cues deposited by the searcher along its path which act as an effective repelling force. The search performance of such auto-chemotactic walkers has been recently investigated and found to be efficient [52, 26, 27], but always assuming an infinite supply of cue. In contrast, we consider here a finite supply and investigate how the resulting optimal search strategies are altered.

papers.title: A semiampleness result for hyperkähler fourfolds and smoothings of Lagrangian subvarieties
papers.abstract: We give a geometric proof of the following statement: let $X$ be a smooth hyperkähler fourfold such that the Picard group is generated by a line bundle $L$ that is nef, non-trivial, and not big. If the Kodaira dimension of $L$ is non-negative, some positive multiple defines a Lagrangian fibration. The proof requires a number of tools which are of independent interest, including an analogue of Voisin's unobstructedness result and a smoothing result for singular Lagrangian subvarieties.

papers.title: QUIJOTE scientific results - XII. Characterization of the polarized synchrotron emission at the power spectrum level in the QUIJOTE-MFI wide survey
papers.abstract: We present an analysis of the polarized synchrotron emission at the power-spectrum level in the multipole range $30 < \ell < 130$, using the recent QUIJOTE-MFI wide survey (10-20GHz) in combination with Planck and WMAP data. The EE and BB power spectra are well described by a simple power-law model, with no evidence for the need of additional parameters. The best-fit slopes are $α_{EE} = -3.24 \pm 0.12$ and $α_{BB} = -3.81 \pm 0.34$ for $|b|>20^\circ$, hinting toward a steepening of the BB spectrum relative to EE at the $\sim 1.6σ$ level. The synchrotron frequency spectral indices are found to be $β_s^{EE} = -3.26 \pm 0.05$ and $β_s^{BB} = -3.25 \pm 0.10$ for the same cut, in agreement with earlier real-space analyses. We find no evidence for spatial variations of $β_s$ across different Galactic latitude cuts, within current uncertainties. The synchrotron BB/EE power ratio is approximately 0.2 over the considered multipole range, lower than typical values for thermal dust, and consistent with previous measurements. We also measure a dust-synchrotron spatial correlation in the range 0.1-0.25 over $30 < \ell < 130$. Using these results, we estimate the level of synchrotron contamination in future CMB B-mode measurements, finding an average power in the considered sky masks equivalent to $r \sim 0.003$ at 90GHz and $r \sim 0.0002$ at 150GHz for the relevant angular scales.
