papers.intro:
Cosmic microwave background (CMB) intensity anisotropies have been central to the development of modern cosmology, providing key measurements that have contributed to establishing the standard cosmological model with remarkable accuracy (Smoot et al., 1992; Bennett et al., 2013; Planck Collaboration et al., 2020b). As observational sensitivity has steadily improved, the emphasis has increasingly shifted towards the study of CMB polarization anisotropies, as they enable searches for primordial B modes, whose detection would provide direct evidence for a stochastic background of gravitational waves generated during cosmic inflation (Kamionkowski et al., 1997; Zaldarriaga and Seljak, 1997; Kamionkowski and Kovetz, 2016). Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in constraining the amplitude of such signals, with the most stringent upper limits on the tensor-to-scalar ratio currently provided by the BICEP/Keck experiment (Ade et al., 2021), further strengthened by the inclusion of Planck data (Tristram et al., 2022), to the level of r<0.032r<0.032 at 95 per cent confidence level.

This paper focuses on this third aspect.

The main diffuse polarized contaminants are synchrotron emission (which dominates at frequencies below ∼70\sim 70 GHz) and thermal dust emission (which is the dominant mechanism at high frequencies) (Planck Collaboration et al., 2020e). In addition to synchrotron, two additional foregrounds, anomalous microwave emission (AME) and free-free, emit at low frequencies. AME has been detected in intensity, but no polarization has been measured up to date (Rubiño-Martín et al., 2012a; Draine and Hensley, 2016; Dickinson et al., 2018; Vidal et al., 2026), with current upper limits below the level of one per cent (Génova-Santos et al., 2017; González-González et al., 2025). In addition, theoretical models predict a polarization fraction not larger than a few percent in local specific observation conditions, and lower in the general case (Draine and Hensley, 2016; Lankhaar, 2026). Regarding free-free emission, polarization has not been detected (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016c, see e.g.). According to the concordance model, the peak of the CMB BB-mode power spectrum – or CMB B​BBB power spectrum – is expected to be at intermediate angular scale around multipole ℓ≃80\ell\simeq 80 (Lewis et al., 2000, e.g.). In this range of scales, there is no frequency domain or sky region where the sum of the synchrotron and thermal dust foregrounds is subdominant with respect to a CMB B-mode signal if it has an amplitude of r=10−3r=10^{-3} (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016a; Krachmalnicoff and others, 2018).

Any robust determination of the tensor-to-scalar ratio, rr, will require an accurate separation of the cosmological signal from these Galactic foreground emissions (Remazeilles et al., 2016; Errard and Stompor, 2019). Recent studies have revealed increasing complexity in both the spectral and spatial properties of Galactic dust and synchrotron emissions, posing significant challenges for component separation (Choi and Page, 2015; Planck Collaboration et al., 2017; Krachmalnicoff and others, 2018; Fuskeland et al., 2021; Weiland et al., 2022; de la Hoz et al., 2023). This complexity is particularly relevant in the case of polarized synchrotron emission. Owing to limited sensitivity in the low-frequency channels of Planck and WMAP, polarized synchrotron emission cannot be robustly characterized at intermediate and high Galactic latitudes. As a result, the constraints on the spectral behavior of polarized synchrotron emission in these regions remain limited when using satellite data. In this context, dedicated observations at lower frequencies are required to complement existing satellite data and to improve foreground modeling to the level necessary for future B-mode polarization studies.

This complexity is particularly relevant in the case of polarized synchrotron emission. Owing to limited sensitivity in the low-frequency channels of Planck and WMAP, polarized synchrotron emission cannot be robustly characterized at intermediate and high Galactic latitudes. As a result, the constraints on the spectral behavior of polarized synchrotron emission in these regions remain limited when using satellite data. In this context, dedicated observations at lower frequencies are required to complement existing satellite data and to improve foreground modeling to the level necessary for future B-mode polarization studies.

Recently, three radio surveys are providing key and complementary information in polarization: the S-PASS experiment, which observed the sky from the South hemisphere at 2.3 GHz (Carretti et al., 2019); the C-Band All-Sky Survey (C-BASS) experiment, which will cover the full sky at 5 GHz (Jones and others, 2018), and the QUIJOTE (Q-U-I JOint TEnerife) experiment, a multi-frequency microwave survey carried out at the Teide Observatory, covering the 10–40 GHz frequency range with angular resolutions between 18 arcmin and one degree (Rubiño-Martín et al., 2012b).

Previous studies based on WMAP and Planck data seem to indicate that the polarized synchrotron βs\beta_{\rm s} has a mean value close to −3.15-3.15 (Watts et al., 2024; Fuskeland et al., 2014; Planck Collaboration et al., 2020f). The inclusion of S-PASS data further constrains βs\beta_{\rm s}, leading to a mean index value of βs=−3.22±0.08\beta_{\rm s}=-3.22\pm 0.08, found between 2.3 and 33 GHz (Krachmalnicoff and others, 2018). QUIJOTE results published so far on the polarized synchrotron properties are mostly based on real-space component separation methods. Using a parametric approach on a pixel-by-pixel basis, de la Hoz et al. (2023) found an average value of the synchrotron spectral index of βs=−3.08±0.13\beta_{\rm s}=-3.08\pm 0.13 at two-degree angular scales. This result is consistent with the average synchrotron spectral index measured between the MFI 11 GHz and WMAP 23 GHz channels of βs=−3.09±0.14\beta_{\rm s}=-3.09\pm 0.14 (Rubiño-Martín et al., 2023). More recently, Adak et al. (2026) applied a semi-blind component separation method and obtained an average value of βs=−3.11±0.21\beta_{\rm s}=-3.11\pm 0.21. All these results hint towards spatial variations of the polarized synchrotron spectral index larger than the values reported in current models by a factor of 2–3 (Krachmalnicoff and others, 2018; de la Hoz et al., 2023; Thorne et al., 2017, e.g.). Quantifying the spatial variability of βs\beta_{\rm s} is crucial to estimate the proper amount of synchrotron power at the CMB frequencies observed by current and forthcoming experiments, as intrinsic variability in spectral index leads to higher synchrotron residuals at CMB frequencies.

papers.title: Learning to Incentivise: Using Reinforcement Learning for Sustainable Urban Mobility
papers.abstract: Traffic management has traditionally focused on toll-based and road pricing solutions. However, road pricing often raises concerns about accessibility and public dissatisfaction, leading to its prohibition in some places, such as Finland. This study optimises the dynamic allocation of incentives to drivers, encouraging them to reroute onto alternative (potentially longer) paths to achieve greater societal benefit, reduced total travel time (TTT) and total emissions in the transportation network, contributing to sustainable urban mobility. We employ a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach to dynamically assign incentives to drivers to reduce both TTT and emissions, with travel times estimated using traffic simulation software. We demonstrate that, with an unlimited budget and an objective of minimising travel time, the incentive scheme reduces TTT by 16%, compared to the dynamic User-Equilibrium (UE) with a budget equivalent to about 11% of the UE total time. When the goal is to minimise emissions, a 9% reduction in CO2 emissions is observed under an unlimited budget. We demonstrate a critical trade-off: minimising TTT leads to an increase in emissions, while prioritising emission reductions raises TTT. However, with the right combination of weights in the multi-objective function, both TTT and total emissions are improved beyond the baseline.

papers.intro:
Traffic congestion in large cities is a major contributor to air pollution, with road transport accounting for nearly 26% of the UK’s total emissions in 2021 [1]. Stop-and-go traffic and idling vehicles worsen fuel consumption, increasing pollutants such as nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. Although the Net Zero Emissions scenario projects that 60% of car sales will be electric vehicles by 2030, four out of five cars on the road will still rely on internal combustion engines [2]. To tackle these environmental challenges, urban areas have implemented various traffic management strategies, including congestion pricing, as seen in London [3]. While such schemes help reduce vehicle numbers in specific zones, they often face opposition due to fairness concerns and regulatory barriers. As an alternative, incentive-based approaches have gained attention for their ability to promote voluntary changes in travel behaviour [4, 5].

Incentive schemes have been proposed with the aim of reducing emissions and congestion by influencing travellers’ mode, route, or departure time choices. In the case of route decisions, for instance, if one route is faster but heavily congested, while an alternative is longer but produces fewer emissions, travellers may opt for the latter if compensated appropriately. However, financial constraints limit their widespread implementation, making efficient allocation critical. While an unlimited budget could theoretically optimise traffic flow and emissions reduction, real-world applications require strategic distribution of incentives to achieve the greatest environmental benefits while maintaining smooth traffic movement.

papers.title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
papers.abstract: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.

papers.intro:
Modern language models can write programs, call tools, and act in unfamiliar environments, but only as part of a larger agentic system. In such a system, a symbolic program orchestrates calls to the model, shaping what it observes, what it retains, which actions are available, how it recovers from failure, and how much inference it spends. This surrounding system is commonly termed a harness (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a). A system’s behavior therefore depends on both its harness and its underlying model or models.

In such a system, a symbolic program orchestrates calls to the model, shaping what it observes, what it retains, which actions are available, how it recovers from failure, and how much inference it spends. This surrounding system is commonly termed a harness (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a). A system’s behavior therefore depends on both its harness and its underlying model or models.

This matters for the study of general intelligence, which requires the efficient acquisition of useful new skills in unfamiliar situations (Chollet, 2019). If each novel task requires a human engineer to inspect failures, redesign representations, add tools, and tune control flow, then what improves is not the system’s own capacity to adapt but the engineer’s understanding, transferred into the system by hand. The agent’s learning remains confined to a supplied mechanism whose improvement depends on the engineer. In contrast, humans routinely adapt to unfamiliar situations in everyday life.

ARC-AGI-3 aims to measure general intelligence through agents’ adaptation to novel games. Its main metric, Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines. Harnesses developed under human steering already reach 100 RHAE on the public games with GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 (Lehmann et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b). By contrast, Sol scores 38.3 on the public set in a simple benchmark harness with retained reasoning and compaction enabled (OpenAI, 2026). An off-the-shelf Claude Code baseline scores 42.83 with Opus 4.8/Fable 5 (Zeng et al., 2026). Strong human-steered results make ARC-AGI-3 a revealing test of autonomous improvement: effective harness designs are known to exist for current models. The benchmark lets us examine how reliably models can discover and improve their own designs through experience in unfamiliar interactive environments.

We measure the outcome of updating with a fixed-lineage protocol. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, a model starts from a controlled minimal repository, builds an ARC-AGI-3 harness for the same model profile, receives feedback from five development games, and potentially revises the generated harness twice. papers.title: Stability-Preserving Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneity-Aware Composite Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a flexible mechanism for adapting traffic signal control to heterogeneous traffic and sensing conditions, but directly learned signal actions do not automatically inherit the analytical properties of structured traffic-control methods. This paper proposes Com-MP, a theory-guided RL framework that learns a context-dependent composition of multiple max-pressure (MP) control preferences while retaining decentralized MP phase selection. The learned policy adapts the relative influence of constituent MP formulations according to local traffic and sensing conditions, allowing data-driven adaptation to operate within a structured traffic-control framework. We show that such intersection-specific and time-varying composition preserves strong queue stability for every demand in the strictly stabilizable region under any admissible non-anticipative composition policy, thereby separating the performance-adaptation role of learning from the stability property of the underlying controller. In a representative implementation combining detector-supported queue-based MP and connected-vehicle-supported travel-time MP, experiments on a real-world 45-intersection network show that Com-MP reduces average delay by 15.6\% and 8.6\% relative to the two constituent controllers, respectively, and by about 7.0\% relative to the best fixed composition. The learned composition responds systematically to local traffic and sensing conditions, remains effective under heterogeneous and degraded sensing, and can be transferred without retraining to an unseen network with an average delay only 2.4\% higher than that of a policy trained directly on the target network. These results show how learning-based adaptation can be introduced within a stability-preserving traffic-control structure, providing a theory-guided pathway toward trustworthy learning-enabled traffic signal control.

papers.intro:
Real-time traffic signal control at the network level remains challenging because urban traffic demand is stochastic, spatially coupled, and continuously changing. Centralized control can explicitly optimize network-wide objectives, but it generally requires large-scale prediction and high-dimensional optimization, creating substantial computational, communication, and modeling burdens as the network grows (Yan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2025a). Max-pressure (MP) control offers a fundamentally different approach. Each intersection selects its signal state using traffic information from adjacent movements, while the resulting decentralized policy can strongly stabilize network queues and achieve maximum throughput for demands in the admissible region (Varaiya, 2013). This combination of local implementation, scalability, and network-level stability has made MP an important foundation for large-scale adaptive signal control. Its practical behavior, however, depends critically on how traffic pressure is represented and on the sensing information available to construct that representation.

Centralized control can explicitly optimize network-wide objectives, but it generally requires large-scale prediction and high-dimensional optimization, creating substantial computational, communication, and modeling burdens as the network grows (Yan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2025a). Max-pressure (MP) control offers a fundamentally different approach. Each intersection selects its signal state using traffic information from adjacent movements, while the resulting decentralized policy can strongly stabilize network queues and achieve maximum throughput for demands in the admissible region (Varaiya, 2013). This combination of local implementation, scalability, and network-level stability has made MP an important foundation for large-scale adaptive signal control. Its practical behavior, however, depends critically on how traffic pressure is represented and on the sensing information available to construct that representation.

MP encompasses a family of policies that share the pressure-maximization principle but represent traffic congestion in different ways. Classical queue-based MP uses vehicle accumulation or link occupancy (Varaiya, 2013), while position-weighted formulations account for the spatial distribution of vehicles and downstream storage conditions (Li and Jabari, 2019). Delay- and travel-time-based formulations introduce temporal traffic experience through head-of-line delay, cumulative delay, or vehicle travel time (Wu et al., 2018; Mercader et al., 2020; Liu and Gayah, 2022; Liu and Gayah, 2023; Tan et al., 2026b). Other extensions incorporate switching losses, pedestrian demand, transit priority, and related operational considerations (Wang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025b). These formulations encode different control preferences. Queue-based pressure responds directly to vehicle accumulation and tends to prioritize heavily loaded movements, whereas delay- and travel-time-based states place increasing emphasis on traffic that has accumulated temporal cost. Their relative suitability can therefore change with the local congestion pattern rather than being determined by a single universally preferable pressure definition.

These formulations encode different control preferences. Queue-based pressure responds directly to vehicle accumulation and tends to prioritize heavily loaded movements, whereas delay- and travel-time-based states place increasing emphasis on traffic that has accumulated temporal cost. Their relative suitability can therefore change with the local congestion pattern rather than being determined by a single universally preferable pressure definition.

The usefulness of a pressure formulation also depends on the sensing environment supporting its traffic state. Fixed-location detectors provide persistent aggregate observations at instrumented locations, but practical networks may have incomplete coverage and may experience sensing or communication failures (Klein et al., 2006). Detector-supported states at unmonitored locations consequently rely on reconstruction from available counts, traffic-flow conservation, turning information, or related estimation procedures (Tan et al., 2026a). Connected vehicles (CVs) provide a complementary sensing source by supplying vehicle-level trajectory and travel-time information beyond fixed detector locations (Tan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025b). Their effective observation coverage, however, is penetration-dependent and spatially heterogeneous (Wong et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026a). Consequently, the information supporting a pressure formulation can become more or less representative as detector availability, CV penetration, and local traffic conditions change.

Their effective observation coverage, however, is penetration-dependent and spatially heterogeneous (Wong et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026a). Consequently, the information supporting a pressure formulation can become more or less representative as detector availability, CV penetration, and local traffic conditions change.

Traffic-state heterogeneity and sensing heterogeneity therefore interact. A queue-oriented formulation may be particularly informative under strong local accumulation when reliable queue observations are available, whereas a trajectory-based formulation can contribute complementary temporal information when sufficient vehicle-level observations are present. Their relative usefulness can also vary across intersections because congestion patterns and sensing availability are spatially heterogeneous. Most existing MP studies improve a particular pressure formulation and then apply that formulation with a fixed control preference. Heterogeneous sensing can also be fused to construct a more complete estimate of a chosen traffic state; for example, detector and CV information can be integrated to support travel-time-based pressure estimation (Tan et al., 2026a). Such approaches improve how a particular pressure state is constructed. A different question arises when several valid MP formulations coexist: how should their relative influence be adapted as the local traffic state and sensing environment change?

Traffic-state heterogeneity and sensing heterogeneity therefore interact. A queue-oriented formulation may be particularly informative under strong local accumulation when reliable queue observations are available, whereas a trajectory-based formulation can contribute complementary temporal information when sufficient vehicle-level observations are present. Their relative usefulness can also vary across intersections because congestion patterns and sensing availability are spatially heterogeneous. Most existing MP studies improve a particular pressure formulation and then apply that formulation with a fixed control preference. Heterogeneous sensing can also be fused to construct a more complete estimate of a chosen traffic state; for example, detector and CV information can be integrated to support travel-time-based pressure estimation (Tan et al., 2026a). Such approaches improve how a particular pressure state is constructed. A different question arises when several valid MP formulations coexist: how should their relative influence be adapted as the local traffic state and sensing environment change?

Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a natural mechanism for such adaptation by learning decision rules through repeated interaction with dynamic traffic environments. RL-based traffic signal control has consequently developed into a broad research area spanning direct phase selection, multi-intersection coordination, and network-level control (Noaeen et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2026). Representative approaches learn signal actions or coordination mechanisms directly, with traffic pressure often incorporated into the state, reward, or learning architecture (Wei et al., 2019a; Wei et al., 2019b). At the same time, increasing attention has been given to incorporating transportation structure, reference policies, and operational constraints into learning-based control. Examples include adjusting selected components of an MP controller through learning (Wang et al., 2022), guiding RL using a model-based reference signal policy (Lu et al., 2025), and imposing operational constraints through safe RL formulations (Zhou et al., 2025). More broadly, safe and learning-based control research has emphasized combining data-driven adaptation with explicit control structure or constraints so that desirable system properties are not determined solely by the learned policy (García and Fernández, 2015; Brunke et al., 2022). For traffic signal control, this distinction is particularly relevant to MP: its appeal lies not only in decentralized decision-making but also in its explicit network-level queue-stability properties (Varaiya, 2013). When RL directly determines signal actions, however, the learned policy does not automatically inherit these properties unless they are explicitly retained in the control architecture and established analytically.

papers.title: Notation3: Graph Terms for RDF
papers.abstract: Notation3 Logic was introduced as an extension of RDF allowing the user to express rules on top of triples and to make statements about graphs. The original proposal of the logic only came with an informal specification of its semantics which has been refined later on. While this refinement clarified the meaning of rules and implicitly quantified variables, it left the meaning of graphs used as terms - so-called graph terms - open. In this paper we aim to close this gap. We discuss in detail, how graph terms are used in Notation3, which formal requirements they need to meet, and provide examples to illustrate the difficulties when defining their semantics. We then introduce an abstract syntax for the logic and define its semantics in two steps: similarly to RDF's simple interpretations, we define interpretations and basic entailment for Notation3 which covers plain RDF triples but also triples containing graph terms. N3-entailment is then an extension of basic entailment which assigns meaning to the different special predicates of the logic like for example the implication symbol. N3-entailment is defined in a way that it can be extended whenever a new predicate is added to the logic. As Notation3 Logic is currently under development, we expect many predicates to be added. Our research provides and important step towards the full standardisation of the logic.

Ever since the invention of the Semantic Web, the community saw the need to allow users to make statements about statements. Different approaches like singleton properties [31], the inclusion of named graphs to RDF [30, Section 4], or the integration of RDF-star (formally RDF*) [23, 21] into the upcoming RDF 1.2, are only some indicators for it. And while these proposals and standards to some extend address the problem, they all have some draw-backs: singleton properties and RDF-star only support statements about triples but not about RDF graphs and for named graphs, there is so far no agreement about their semantics [39].

In this paper we focus on another framework which supports statements about statements: Notation3 Logic (N3) [10]. N3 was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee and others to provide a simple syntax for RDF – this resulted in RDF-Turtle [33] – but also as a logical extension for RDF. N3 supports so-called graph terms which are conceptually very similar to RDF-star’s triple terms with the only difference that N3 does not only allow triples as terms but entire graphs. Of course, this comes with challenges: graph terms could stand for themselves or for bigger graphs, scoping of blank nodes is far from trivial, and graph terms are used to express logical constructs. When originally proposed, the semantics of N3 has only been defined informally and different implementations like Cwm [12], EYE [37] or Data-Fu [27] were developed to reason on it. The theoretical works which followed later on to define a model theoretic semantics for N3 did focus on rules [4, 5] and on implicit quantification [6], but did not fully cover the semantics of graph terms as it was originally intended.

In this paper we aim to fill this gap: We analyse the requirements a graph term semantics has to comply with according to the informal specifications and the existing implementations. We then propose an abstract syntax for N3 and define its semantics in two steps: we first specify a base semantics which covers the meaning of graph terms but does not assign any meaning to the built-in predicates of the logic. In that sense our base semantics is very similar to RDF’s simple entailment. In a second step we define N3-semantics which covers the logical predicates in N3’s log-namespace22 2 http://www.w3.org/2000/10/swap/log. Here we mainly focus on logical implication (log:implies) and on graph inclusion (log:includes). Especially the former is crucial for N3 as this predicate enables rule-based reasoning. We furthermore show that our definitions are in-line with the requirements.

papers.title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: the delayed rise of Lyman continuum escape fractions in bursty high-redshift galaxies
papers.abstract: The ionizing radiation that galaxies release into their surroundings depends on whether efficient Lyman continuum (LyC) escape coincides with strong photon production. Stellar feedback can open escape paths as the source population fades, linking the escaping radiation to a galaxy's recent history. We investigate this timing in thirteen high-redshift (z > 3) target haloes from the THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, post-processed with COLT radiative transfer and sampled at ~10 Myr intervals. The clearest delayed relationship links $\text{SFR}_{10}/\text{SFR}_{100}$ to the LyC escape fraction. Selecting the nearest positive cross-correlation peak gives typical lags of ~16 Myr and peak correlations of 0.4-0.6 in massive haloes, with longer and less coherent delays towards lower masses. The fitted delays scale approximately as $M_\star^{-0.19}$ and $M_\text{halo}^{-0.27}$, although the shortest lags approach the native snapshot spacing. Recurrent variations span multiple amplitude-dependent timescales, consistent with repeated episodes of star formation and feedback. Recent star formation closely tracks both intrinsic and escaping photon rates, while the escape fraction reflects the evolving gas transparency. The H$α$-to-UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed association with escape, offering an observable connection between burst phase and leakage. High transparency during a fading phase can nevertheless yield little escaping radiation. The temporal overlap of photon production and transmission therefore shapes both the amount and timing of escaping radiation, informing the interpretation of observed leakers and their contribution to cosmic reionization.

papers.intro:
The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) connects the emergence of the first sustained galaxy population to a fundamental change in the intergalactic medium (IGM), as initially neutral hydrogen became ionized and the mean free path of ionizing radiation grew rapidly (Loeb and Furlanetto, 2013; Wise, 2019; Gnedin and Madau, 2022). The Thomson optical depth constrains the integrated ionization history and is compatible with relatively late reionization, while quasar absorption spectra and Lyα\alpha visibility favour a late and spatially inhomogeneous end to the transition (Fan et al., 2006; Planck Collaboration et al., 2020; Becker et al., 2021; Bosman et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024). Reionization was neither an instantaneous global event nor a simple function of how many ionizing photons galaxies produced. The history depended on where and when galaxies released those photons, and how their radiation propagated through an evolving circumgalactic and intergalactic environment.

Star-forming galaxies are widely considered the main drivers of hydrogen reionization because they are abundant and produce large numbers of Lyman continuum (LyC; h​ν>13.6​eVh\nu>13.6\,\text{eV}) photons (Madau et al., 1999; Robertson et al., 2010; Stark, 2016; Atek et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Pahl et al., 2025). JWST has begun to constrain the abundance, stellar populations, and nebular emission of galaxies well into the EoR, often finding efficient ionizing-photon production among young, low-metallicity systems (Endsley et al., 2023; Endsley et al., 2024; Matthee et al., 2023). Combining the high inferred photon production with escape fractions estimated from the UV-slope relation calibrated on low-redshift leakers can complete reionization earlier than allowed by IGM and cosmological constraints (Chisholm et al., 2022; Muñoz et al., 2024). For example, integrating the fiducial model of Muñoz et al. Absorption by the intervening IGM makes LyC detections increasingly rare with redshift and effectively prevents direct measurements during the EoR (Inoue et al., 2014; Grazian et al., 2017; Bassett et al., 2021; Bassett et al., 2022). Low-redshift LyC leakers constrain the conditions associated with escape (Izotov et al., 2018; Rivera-Thorsen et al., 2019; Flury et al., 2022; Saldana-Lopez et al., 2022; Chisholm et al., 2022; Bait et al., 2024; Leclercq et al., 2024; Carr et al., 2025a; Carr et al., 2025b; Flury et al., 2025; Jaskot, 2025), while Lyα\alpha, ultraviolet absorption, and nebular emission offer indirect diagnostics at higher redshift (Mason et al., 2019; Katz et al., 2022; Choustikov et al., 2024b; Yuan et al., 2024; Jaskot et al., 2024). In a sample of more than 1400 galaxies at 5<z<105<z<10, Giovinazzo et al. (2025) inferred very low escape fractions for most objects but identified a small high-escape subset that raises the population average to approximately the level needed for galaxy-driven reionization. Such a distribution may reflect persistent differences among galaxies, intermittent escape phases, orientation effects, or a combination of all three. Distinguishing these possibilities requires a model for how an individual galaxy moves through observable and high-escape states.

Numerical studies provide the physical context for why LyC escape is strongly anisotropic and time-dependent. Massive stars produce ionizing photons almost immediately after they form, yet their dense birth clouds can absorb most of this radiation. Photoionization, stellar winds, radiation pressure, and supernova explosions subsequently redistribute the gas and open low-density channels. The intrinsic photon-production rate and the transmission of those photons can therefore evolve out of phase, producing order-of-magnitude changes in fescLyCf_{\text{esc}}^{\text{LyC}} over short intervals (Kimm and Cen, 2014; Paardekooper et al., 2015; Cen and Kimm, 2015; Trebitsch et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Barrow et al., 2020; Katz et al., 2023). An observed correlation with fescLyCf_{\text{esc}}^{\text{LyC}} can consequently depend on whether a galaxy is caught during an embedded burst, a feedback-cleared phase, or the re-assembly of its star-forming gas.

papers.title: Unexpected Local Enhancement of Chromospheric Moreton Waves on the Sun
papers.abstract: Solar eruptions often drive shock waves. When propagating in the solar corona, strong shock waves would leave imprints on the solar surface in the chromosphere, which are called Moreton waves. Moreton waves generally decay as they move away. However, to our knowledge, for the first time we report that a Moreton wave is significantly enhanced midway during propagation, as revealed by the spectroscopic observations from China's first solar satellite, the Chinese H$α$ Solar Explorer. Combining magnetic measurements from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we found that the location of the Moreton wave enhancement corresponds to a magnetic null point at an altitude of $\sim$70 Mm in the corona. It is demonstrated that the unexpected local enhancement of the Moreton wave is due to mode conversion around the magnetic null point, i.e., fast-mode waves are converted to slow-mode waves which are trapped locally. It is further revealed that, even for ordinary Moreton wave fronts, the H$α$ Doppler redshift velocity is positively correlated with the height of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points, implying that these low-lying null points, $\sim$1--7 Mm above the solar surface, facilitate mode conversion with different efficiency, thereby accounting for the spatially inhomogeneous Dopplergram of Moreton wave fronts.

papers.title: Robust paths to primordial $B$ modes in the presence of polarised point source contamination
papers.abstract: A detection of primordial $B$ modes in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarisation relies on a robust control and removal of contamination from astrophysical polarised foreground emission. We examine how much polarised extragalactic point sources may contaminate the cosmological signal in ground-based CMB experiments, propagating their impact through component separation to the final parameter constraints. We discuss masking and modelling strategies to ensure that the resulting constraints remain both accurate and precise under this source of contamination. We produce synthetic data containing polarised emission from extragalactic radio sources (ERSs) and dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) following state-of-the-art models for both samples. We find that, while the DSFG contribution is likely too small to cause any significant bias to the cosmological or foreground parameters, the ERS contribution instead, if left unmasked, leads to a bias in the parameters describing the Galactic synchrotron and lensing $B$-mode components. For experiments targeting noise levels of order $σ_P\simeq 1\,μK\,{\rm arcmin}$, we find that masking all ERSs with fluxes above $\sim$0.1 Jy, coupled with a relatively simple model to marginalise over residual point-source contamination, achieves a suitable balance that allows for the robust recovery of unbiased cosmological and foreground parameters at a negligible cost in parameter uncertainties.

papers.title: Light pulse propagation through a dielectric slab. II. Two roads to the same field: numerical cross-validation of local (FDTD-ADE) and non-local (retarded integral-equation) solutions
papers.abstract: Paper I of this series (arXiv:2610.29336) solves, via the retarded Green's functions, the local differential equations governing light propagation in a plane-parallel dielectric slab, obtaining a pair of retarded integral equations that represent, at the continuum level, the microscopic multiple-scattering picture underlying the local formulation. The two formulations are thus proven to be analytically equivalent. The local system of differential equations is then solved numerically with a finite-difference time-domain scheme (FDTD-ADE). This report closes the loop by solving the retarded integral equations directly, without passing through the local formulation, and comparing the result with the FDTD-ADE solution under the same physical and material conditions. The two independently implemented, structurally different numerical schemes agree within 0.02-1.3% for the reported reflected and transmitted energy fractions; the absorbed fraction, computed independently in both schemes from the Lorentz damping term rather than merely inferred from 1-R-T, agrees closely between the two methods, to the precision reported. Both solutions are also compared with an exact reference, the Airy formula weighted over the pulse spectrum: the direct solution reproduces it to within 0.3%, and its Richardson extrapolation to all digits shown. The agreement persists for a few-cycle pulse and for a sub-wavelength slab, where naive fixed-point iteration of the integral equations is not a practical convergent strategy. A complementary set of movie-style, nine-frame visualizations is also presented, illustrating the same equivalence directly in the field rather than only in integrated observables. To the author's knowledge, a direct numerical cross-validation of these two formulations in this genuinely time-dependent regime has not previously been reported.

papers.title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
papers.abstract: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.

papers.title: Consensus-Based Distributed Filtering for Angles-Only Tracking in Cislunar Space
papers.abstract: This paper investigates consensus-based distributed filtering strategies for multi-observer angles-only navigation in the cislunar space. The objective is to estimate the inertial state of a target spacecraft using only line-of-sight measurements collected by a network of observer spacecraft. This problem is particularly relevant for autonomous cislunar navigation, where ground support may be limited, and centralized fusion architectures may be problematic due to communication and computational constraints, and single-point failure risks. Three distributed filtering approaches are considered: the Distributed Extended Kalman Filter, the Information-Weighted Consensus Filter, and the Kalman Consensus Filter. All methods share the same local prediction and measurement-processing steps, but differ in the way information is exchanged and fused across the network. Their performance is evaluated and compared to a centralized Extended Kalman Filter, adopted as benchmark, and independent local filters in a high-fidelity cislunar scenario. Numerical simulations show that the distributed approaches significantly improve estimation accuracy with respect to independent filters. Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses are then conducted to characterize the robustness of the considered methods to finite consensus iterations and prior misalignment among the agents.

papers.title: Donor-acceptor recombination in diamond
papers.abstract: We re-examine several optical systems that have previously been attributed to donor-acceptor (D-A) recombination in diamond, including the broad 2.8 eV and 2.3 eV bands, and the sharp-lined series in the ranges 2.0-2.7 eV and 4.0-5.0 eV. In all cases, internal transitions at one or multiple defect centers provide a more consistent explanation of the experimental observations than the D-A model. The 2.3 eV case is marginal, where the key argument against the D-A recombination is the improbably low probability of tunneling between remote donors and acceptors in diamonds with very low concentrations of impurities (~0.1 ppm). A more realistic model for the 2.3 eV band and the associated phosphorescence and thermoluminescence phenomena is trapping of electrons and holes at nitrogen and boron defects, respectively, followed by recombination at a deep center, which is tentatively assigned to the nearest neighbor B-N pair.

papers.title: Precise Determination of Electric Dipole Polarizabilities of Sr Clock States Using Linear-Response and Equation-of-Motion Relativistic Coupled-Cluster Methods
papers.abstract: We present accurate values of the electric dipole polarizabilities ($α$) of the ground and excited states of Sr using four-component relativistic coupled-cluster (RCC) theory within the linear-response (LR) and equation-of-motion (EOM) frameworks. We first investigated accuracy of the ground-state polarizability using the LR-RCC method in both spherical and Cartesian coordinate representations. Upon obtaining consistent results for the ground state, we determine the polarizabilities of the excited states using the EOM-RCC method within the finite-field approach. The uncertainties in our results are assessed by examining the completeness of the basis set, higher-order relativistic corrections, and contributions from higher-level excitation configurations beyond the truncation in our RCC method. We also discuss various procedures for extrapolating contributions to the complete basis set limit and examine their respective limitations. Our calculated ground-state polarizability is found to be inconsistent with the latest atomic calculation, but agrees with other calculations and experimental value. Using the differential $α$ value from the EOM-RCC method, we estimate the fractional black-body-radiation-induced frequency shift of the Sr $^{1}$S$_{0}$$\rightarrow$$^{3}$P$_{0}$ clock transition to be $-5.40\times10^{-15}$.

papers.title: Can an Agent Debug a Web Corpus? Agentic Auditing of Slovak FineWeb2
papers.abstract: Multilingual pipelines such as FineWeb2 apply one recipe across a thousand languages, leaving the failure modes of individual languages unanticipated. We use an LLM once, as a corpus debugger rather than a classifier: a tool-using agent explores the corpus through a read-only, budgeted API and compiles each finding into an executable test, which a native speaker then validates. On the 26.5M-document Slovak portion of FineWeb2, three runs costing \$2.21-\$2.84 each found seven findings over four phenomena. The largest is a machine-generated content farm of 1,408,437 documents (5.32%) that passed the pipeline's filters, 86.6% of it passing even stricter thresholds. Blinded labels support 6 of the 7 findings (defect rates .53-1.00 against .08 in a random control) and do not support one. The compiled suite scans the full corpus in 0.7 s of wall-clock time without a GPU, against \$12k-\$90k per LLM classification pass. The best static sampling baseline validates more selectors than any agent run, at under half the cost. The agent contributes exact prevalence, a precision estimate checked against sampled documents, an account of why the pipeline missed each slice, and a reusable test. We release the framework, Slovak test suite, validation data and agent trajectories.

papers.title: Active phase separation from concentration-dependent diffusion in chemical networks
papers.abstract: Active phase separation in living systems is ubiquitous, yet the microscopic origins of the non-equilibrium terms in active field theories remain largely unknown. Here, starting from stochastic mass-conserving reaction-diffusion dynamics of two interacting chemical species, we perform a systematic slow-mode reduction and derive the complete Active Model B+ field theory, with all phenomenological coefficients expressed in terms of microscopic parameters. We identify concentration-dependent diffusivities and asymmetric inter-species chemotactic couplings as the minimal microscopic ingredients generating the genuinely non-equilibrium coefficient responsible for microphase separation, cluster phases, and arrested coarsening. Our framework recovers the equilibrium limit consistently and is validated by stochastic numerical simulations. These results establish a direct, bottom-up link between the architecture of chemical reaction networks and the universality class of their emergent large-scale dynamics.

papers.title: Magnetic Activity as a Driver of Low-gravity-like Spectral Morphology in Late-M Dwarfs
papers.abstract: We present a systematic investigation of the connection between magnetic activity and the low-surface-gravity-like near-infrared spectral morphology of late-M dwarfs. Our sample includes TRAPPIST-1 observed with JWST NIRISS/SOSS and 22 late-M dwarfs observed with IRTF/SpeX, together with flare observations from K2, TESS, JWST NIRISS/SOSS, and literature-reported X-ray luminosities. Using one-component PHOENIX/NewEra spectral modeling, we find that all targets are better reproduced by lower-surface-gravity model spectra than by models with the expected high gravities of field late-M dwarfs. The retrieved surface gravities moderately correlate with independently measured gravity-sensitive spectral indices, with the strongest trends seen for FeH$_z$ at 0.998~$μ$m and FeH$_J$ at 1.2~$μ$m, both showing statistically significant Pearson and Spearman correlations with $p<0.005$. They also show strong anti-correlations with flare luminosity and X-ray luminosity: for both relations, Pearson and Spearman coefficients are $<-0.9$, with $p \leq 1.0\times10^{-4}$, indicating that more active stars tend to have spectra favoring lower-gravity morphologies. Time-series spectra of TRAPPIST-1 during two large flares show no clear short-timescale variations in selected photospheric indices, suggesting that persistent small-scale magnetic activity may play a more important role than large flares in modifying the photospheric temperature--pressure structure. A simplified radiative-transfer experiment further shows that activity-associated heating can produce lower-gravity-like spectral features even when the input surface gravity is fixed. Our results suggest that underestimated surface gravities in late-M dwarfs may reflect atmospheres modified by frequent, small-scale magnetic activity, such as microflares, producing emergent spectra that mimic lower-gravity morphology.

papers.title: IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities for Agentic CLI Systems
papers.abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mechanical Engineering: Foundations, Opportunities, Challenges, and Responsibilities
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mechanical engineering (ME), from modeling, simulation, and optimization to diagnostics, design, and technical communication. Drawing on a round-table at the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering (COBEM 2025), this article presents a structured perspective for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than an exhaustive survey, it examines how AI can enhance engineering practice without compromising scientific rigor. We distinguish statistical learning from human cognition and discuss the capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic forms of AI. We then consider industrial adoption, workforce changes, and AI-assisted scientific discovery, alongside the energy and infrastructure demands of AI computation and their implications for sustainability and thermal management. The discussion emphasizes the integration of physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems, particularly in safety-relevant applications. Topics include physics-informed and hybrid learning, physically constrained modeling, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification. We also examine educational, epistemological, and ethical challenges, including curriculum reform, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the preservation of engineering knowledge. We conclude with principles for responsible AI adoption in ME: physical consistency, rigorous validation, explicit treatment of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. AI should complement, not replace, engineering judgment.

papers.title: Muting Tokens: Exploring Token Sparsification for Efficient Audio Transformers
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their reliance on self-attention mechanisms often leads to high computational costs. Token sparsification, which reduces the number of tokens processed in transformer layers, offers a promising solution to maintain performance while improving efficiency. However, although widely studied in the vision and language domains, token sparsification remains underexplored in audio, with existing work often limited to a single method, model size, or dataset. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of token sparsification techniques for audio transformers. We assess a range of token pruning and merging strategies across multiple datasets and model sizes, under both post-training and fine-tuning settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparsification approach that combines attention scores with spectral cues derived from the frequency content of token embeddings. Our experiments show that frequency-aware approaches, particularly those based on spectral flatness and low-frequency energy, consistently outperform attention-only methods. We also find that sparsification based on spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs. These results highlight the value of incorporating frequency-domain and input-specific information into sparsification strategies to enhance performance in audio tasks.

papers.title: Dynamic Active Fleet Sizing of Heterogeneous UAV Relays for Post-Disaster Communication Networks
papers.abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) communication systems are increasingly used to provide temporary connectivity when ground communication infrastructure is damaged by disasters such as hurricanes and wildfires. However, the amount of aerial support required changes as ground networks recover and communication demand evolves. We focus on dynamically adjusting the number and allocation of actively deployed UAVs within a fixed available fleet. We develop a model predictive control (MPC) framework for dynamic fleet sizing of heterogeneous UAV relays during post-disaster communication recovery. The framework accounts for communication demand, ground network recovery, heterogeneous UAV operation, UAV energy availability, and backhaul capacity, which limits how much relayed traffic can be transmitted to the external communication network. The resulting formulation is a convex quadratic program that supports efficient online fleet sizing and deployment decisions. We evaluate the framework using seven historical disaster recovery case studies based on Federal Communications Commission reports, together with four backhaul scenarios and sensitivity analyses. Results show that required active UAV fleet size varies considerably throughout recovery, while backhaul capacity and fleet composition affect communication performance, highlighting the value of adapting active fleet size over time.

authors.name: Jimin Choi
authors.institution: Seoul National University of Science and Technology

papers.title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2π=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.

papers.title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
papers.abstract: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.

authors.name: Gabor Galgoczi
authors.institution: HUN-REN Wigner Research Centre for Physics

papers.title: Matrix Triangle Inequalities: Past, Present, and Future
papers.abstract: This survey provides a concise overview of matrix triangle inequalities. Classical topics, such as inequalities for unitarily invariant norms, are revisited from a different perspective, with a particular emphasis on unitary orbit inequalities and various notions of matrix moduli. The exposition progresses from elementary results to much more recent developments, highlighting the evolution of the subject and its ongoing directions of research.

authors.name: Teng Zhang
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Injectivity and continuity of the intersection form in infinite type
papers.abstract: We study two fundamental properties of the intersection pairing between geodesic currents on infinite-type surfaces which are classical in the finite-type closed setting: injectivity of the marked length spectrum and continuity of the intersection form. We show that geodesic currents on infinite-type surfaces of the first kind are determined by their intersection numbers with closed curves, extending Otal's marked length spectrum rigidity argument from finite-type to infinite-type surfaces. In contrast, we prove that the intersection pairing is not continuous in general for the natural topologies by constructing explicit counterexamples. We then prove sufficient criteria for continuity of intersection numbers for infinite-type surfaces.

papers.title: PriMa-Causa: Causal Prescriptive Maintenance
papers.abstract: Automated manufacturing requires data-driven decisions under uncertainty and sparse observational records, and unplanned downtime is a dominant cost of getting them wrong. Prescriptive maintenance recommends a maintenance action against an impending failure rather than merely predicting it. Established reference architectures couple predictive models with rule- or optimisation-based recommendation logic. Selecting a corrective action, however, requires an interventional quantity: how the line behaviour would change if the action were set. Manufacturing data is observational, so a model fitted to predict the outcome estimates an associational quantity and may misdirect the choice of action without the prediction error revealing it. Causal estimators target the interventional quantity but require an expert-led causal study per case, for which the bounded decision window of operation leaves no room. This dissertation analyses how causal reasoning can be embedded into prescriptive maintenance so that actions are ranked by their estimated interventional effect. The result is PriMa-Causa, built from three components: a causal reasoning layer that integrates the estimate into the PriMa reference model, a parametric simulator that supplies the interventional ground truth absent from manufacturing data, and a graph-conditioned tabular causal foundation model that, pre-trained once on this synthetic production-line prior, answers interventional queries in a single forward pass. PriMa-Causa attains a lower prescription error than associational baselines, with the largest margin under weak overlap and sparse context, and a partially disclosed causal graph reduces this error further. The causal inductive bias of the synthetic prior and the graph conditioning can thus replace per-case estimator fitting, a step toward automating causal inference for autonomous and self-healing maintenance.

papers.title: Beyond Homology: Non-Abelian and Orientability Invariants Sensitivity in Cellular Networks
papers.abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) architectures are typically evaluated on synthetic complex pairs that differ in a target invariant. Yet, whether a model recovers that invariant or an artifact of the chosen discretization is seldom audited. To examine this, we design and test pairs of complexes that look identical to standard homological and local message-passing tests, have the same Hasse graphs, yet differ in the target invariant. We study two beyond-homology regimes: nonAbelian fundamental-group structure and homotopy-matched orientability. For the former, we construct genus-2 pairs that match homology, cell statistics, local incidence profiles, and rank-colored Hasse 1-WL behavior while differing in their fundamental groups. For the latter, we evaluate punctured torus-Klein bottle pairs and show that distance, boundary, cycle, and spectral signals can confound apparent orientability detection, motivating stronger matched controls. Under the tested settings, subcomplex-lifted architectures separate some pairs beyond the matched homological, local-incidence, and Hasse 1-WL controls, while a depth sweep reveals an empirical depth-dependent trend without establishing a general barrier or direct computation of the target invariants. These results show that claims of topological expressivity must be stated relative to the model representation, explicitly controlled information channels, and the precise scope of the benchmark.

papers.title: XALIGN: A Human-centric Visual Analytics Approach to Understanding AI Explanations
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are usually evaluated for technical properties such as faithfulness and robustness. In high-stakes application domains, experts also need to check model predictions against established knowledge. Different explanation methods often disagree, and this disagreement is hard to see when each method is inspected separately. We propose XALIGN, a visual analytics workflow and interface that shows rule-based explanations and several feature attribution methods (TreeSHAP, KernelSHAP, and LIME) side by side for the same Random Forest model. Agreements and contradictions between the methods become visible signals that users can explore and compare with domain knowledge. We apply XALIGN in two case studies: the German Credit dataset and a meteorological dataset, in which events derived from ICON model output and Cloudnet observations are classified. In both, the views reveal discrepancies between the rule-based explanation and the attribution methods that a single method would not show. In an expert evaluation with three specialists, participants found XALIGN useful for identifying influential features and for avoiding over-trust in predictions. Linking rules to attributions was harder for the participant without an XAI background.
