papers.title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.

papers.title: Anomaly Score Preserving Data Poisoning Attacks on Data-Driven Controller Design
papers.abstract: This paper investigates stealthy data poisoning attacks against data-driven controller synthesis and develops an attack generation method. During data collection, an attacker can sequentially manipulate state measurements, while the defender attempts to detect such manipulation using a residual-based anomaly score based on the Mahalanobis distance. Under suitable assumptions on the defender's prior knowledge, we characterize the class of time-varying affine transformations that preserve the anomaly score for arbitrary data and parameterize this class by the orthogonal group. Based on this characterization, we formulate attack design under the stealthiness condition as an optimization problem over the orthogonal group and propose a Riemannian gradient method. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed attack can degrade closed-loop performance while remaining stealthy.

papers.title: Obstructions to deforming space curves lying on a complete intersection of quadrics
papers.abstract: Let $S=S_{2,\ldots,2}\subset\mathbb P^{n+2}$ be a smooth complete intersection of $n$ quadrics containing a line $E$, where $n\geq 3$, and set $D=(n-1)\mathbf h+E$, where $\mathbf h=[\mathcal O_S(1)]$. We study the deformations of smooth curves $C\in |mD|$ and their obstructions. The linear system $|D|$ defines a birational morphism $f:S\to\overline S$ that contracts $E$ to a point and realizes an unprojection in the sense of Papadakis--Reid. When $n=3$, the surface $S=S_{2,2,2}\subset\mathbb P^5$ is a $K3$ surface and $E$ is a $(-2)$-curve. We prove that the complementary open surface $S\setminus E$ admits first-order infinitesimal deformations in $\mathbb P^5\setminus E$ that are obstructed at the second order. Using these obstructions, we show that, for every sufficiently large $m$ with $\operatorname{char} k\nmid m$, there exists a generically non-reduced irreducible component $W_m$ of the Hilbert scheme $\operatorname{Hilb}^{sc}\mathbb P^5$ of smooth connected curves in $\mathbb P^5$. Its general member $C$ lies on a complete intersection $S_{2,2,2}$ of three quadrics, satisfies $C\sim mD$, and has $h^0(N_{C/\mathbb P^5})-\dim_{[C]}\operatorname{Hilb}^{sc}\mathbb P^5=3$. In contrast, when $n>3$, we prove that, for every sufficiently large $m$ with $\operatorname{char} k\nmid m$, the corresponding family of curves in $|mD|$ gives rise to a generically smooth irreducible component of $\operatorname{Hilb}^{sc}\mathbb P^{n+2}$.

papers.title: Uniformity of the minimal exponent on the GIT boundary of projective hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a non-stable (in the sense of GIT) hypersurface of degree $d \ge 3$ in the projective space $\mathbb{P}^{n}$. S. G. Park proved that the global minimal exponent of $X$ satisfies the inequality $\widetildeα(X) \le \frac{n+1}{d}$. In this paper, we establish the uniform sharpness of this inequality: we prove that $\widetildeα(X) = \frac{n+1}{d}$ holds for a general member $X$ of every irreducible component of the strictly semistable locus. Moreover, a general point of each irreducible component of the GIT boundary $\partial M^{\mathrm{GIT}}$ admits a strictly semistable zero-weight representative with this minimal exponent. By the lower semicontinuity of the minimal exponent on the affine cone and a theorem of Mustaţă--Popa for general linear combinations of monomials, the problem is reduced to computing the log canonical thresholds, at the cone vertex, of the monomial ideals associated with the maximal strictly semistable supports with respect to a maximal torus and their weight-zero parts. Since the barycenter of the degree-$d$ simplex lies in the convex hull of each of these supports, Howald's formula forces these thresholds to be uniformly equal to $\frac{n+1}{d}$.

papers.title: From Venus to the Parking Lot: A Flexible Stellar Interferometry Experiment
papers.abstract: We describe a simple extension of our earlier Venus interferometry demonstration that can be performed indoors or outdoors, independent of planetary visibility or atmospheric seeing. A small flashlight is placed 15-50 meters away from a telescope and covered with a circular aperture mask (hole diameter 2-6~mm). A small telescope fitted with an opaque mask bearing two 2~mm holes, spaced between 5 and 20~mm apart, is then used to observe interference fringes from this artificial extended source. By varying the hole separation and observing the fringes students can estimate the angular diameter of the source and verify their result directly by simple geometry, a check not possible with astronomical targets. The experiment requires no telescope tracking, no dark skies, and no special equipment beyond materials described in the original paper. It serves equally well as a pre-lab to build intuition before observing Venus, a standalone indoor daytime or outdoor nighttime activity, or a quantitative test of the interferometric method itself.

papers.title: Supercritical magnetic ray transforms in hyperbolic space: the complexification method from the transport-twistor lens
papers.abstract: We present new inversion formulas for the unattenuated and attenuated magnetic ray transforms in the Poincaré disk, in the case of a constant, supercritical magnetic field. Our approach mirrors earlier complexification approaches by Novikov (Ark. Mat., 2002) and Bal (J. Math. Pures Appl., 2005), and a second feature of this article is to connect the approach with the Transport Twistor framework recently introduced by Bohr-Paternain (J. Éc. polytech. Math., 2023; arXiv:2606.25173).

papers.title: Same Events, Weaker Bound: Model Dependence in Magellanic Microlensing Limits on Primordial Black Holes
papers.abstract: OGLE microlensing of the Magellanic Clouds sets the leading bounds on primordial black holes (PBHs) as dark matter from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{3}\,M_\odot$. Holding the detected events and survey efficiencies fixed, we show that changes to the Milky Way halo, the stellar lens populations and the Large Magellanic Cloud halo, each motivated by recent data, weaken the published strict 20-year bound by up to $\simeq6$, and by over an order of magnitude in an extreme stress test. With primordial clustering, the planetary-mass bound weakens by a factor $3.4$--$6$. We strongly recommend that compact-object dark matter limits be quoted together with their modeling assumptions and, generally, be derived under conservative assumptions.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Generative Reward Models
papers.abstract: We study generative reward models (GenRMs) as online preference providers for policy optimization in creative writing. Across Qwen3 reward-model sizes from 0.6B to 14B, Thinking judges trained with GRPO have higher static Gold-label accuracy than Answer-Only judges trained with SFT. This ranking often reverses when the judges train policies through online DPO: Answer-Only rewarders yield higher peak and top-five-average policy Elo in seven of eight matched settings under a fixed, learned 32B Gold evaluator. Intermediate Thinking-judge checkpoints can also outperform later, more statically accurate checkpoints as rewarders. Sweeps over rewarder size, policy size, training duration and DPO regularization show substantial benefits from reward-model capacity, including judges larger than the policy. We analyze trajectories with evaluator-specific Elo arenas, conditional match-resampling intervals and descriptive scaling fits. These results demonstrate an evaluator-rewarder gap in the studied pipelines: fixed-distribution judging accuracy does not determine downstream optimization quality. The comparison changes judge-training objective as well as response format, and the main ranking is conditional on its learned reference rather than a universal human-quality result. A limited follow-up using a different learned judge is inconclusive overall.

papers.title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
papers.abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

papers.title: UniGuard: Multi-View Guardrail Learning for Cross-Interface Safety Generalization
papers.abstract: Guardrail models are increasingly used as safety layers for LLMs and agentic systems, but most are trained on fixed prompt or response interfaces and become unreliable when the same safety case appears as a conversation, agent trajectory, multi-agent trace, or policy-conditioned input. We propose UniGuard, a training framework that learns interface-invariant safety representations from multiple semantically aligned views of the same safety case. We also construct the UniGuard-FT dataset by transforming 1,000 public safety cases into prompt, response, multi-turn conversation, agent-trace, and multi-agent-trace views, and train UniGuard-0.6B with classification, supervised contrastive learning, and asymmetric confidence calibration losses. Across unseen-interface benchmarks ATBench, PolicyGuardBench, and DynaBench, UniGuard-0.6B improves over its pretrained guardrail by 45.12 F1 points on average and reduces expected calibration error by 35.41 points, while remaining competitive with much larger guardrails such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.2 - despite being a 0.6B model and trained only with synthetic data.

authors.name: Viet-Thanh Pham
authors.institution: Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City

papers.title: Explicit Measurable Counterexamples to Finite-Difference Operators
papers.abstract: Let \[ D(f,h)=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k f(b_kh) \] be a finite-difference operator, where the coefficients may be complex and the nodes are real. We study the asymptotic implication \[ D(f,h)=o(h)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(h)=o(h) \] for Lebesgue measurable functions. In 2017, Ash, Catoiu, and Csörnyei \cite{ACC} showed that this implication holds for every measurable function precisely for operators belonging to a very restricted class of finite differences. To establish that every operator outside the exceptional class admits a counterexample, Ash, Catoiu, and Csörnyei analyze an infinite system of linear equations. Their argument is therefore existential in nature and does not provide an explicit description of the counterexamples. By contrast, we give a substantially simpler and elementary construction based on zeros of finite Laurent polynomials and multiplicative characters on finitely generated multiplicative subgroups. This provides a direct recipe for constructing measurable functions \(f\) such that \[ D(f,h)=0\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb C, \] while, in fact, \[ f(h)\not=o(1)\qquad\text{as }h\to0. \]

papers.title: Bounded symbols and one-component geometry
papers.abstract: We prove that every bounded truncated Toeplitz operator on a Hardy model space admits a bounded symbol if and only if its defining inner function is one-component, meaning that it has a connected sublevel set at some level in $(0,1)$. This resolves the bounded symbol conjecture of Baranov, Chalendar, Fricain, Mashreghi and Timotin and, through known equivalences, the embedding and weak factorization conjecture of Baranov, Bessonov and Kapustin. A uniform bound $R$ for the ratio of least bounded symbol norm to operator norm on the rank-one family associated with point evaluation in the disk already forces this geometry. The corresponding bound for all bounded truncated Toeplitz operators is at most $CR\log(e+R)$, where $C$ is absolute, and the logarithmic factor is optimal. In a nonzero de Branges space, the same geometric condition characterizes when every sufficiently small equivalent change of norm preserving the de Branges structure is represented exactly by reweighting the original integral with a positive density bounded above and away from zero. This characterization remains valid when the norm changes are restricted to discrete sampling norms. Outside the one-component class, every model space admits self-adjoint trace class truncated Toeplitz operators without bounded symbols, with arbitrarily small norm and singular values satisfying any prescribed positive upper bounds.

papers.title: The reverse Ritz inclusion: computable bounds on the pseudospectra of an operator by those of a finite-rank compression
papers.abstract: We consider a bounded operator on a separable complex Hilbert space, reached only through its action on vectors and that of its adjoint, and split it along a subspace of finite dimension into a compression, a far block acting on the complement, and the two couplings between them. Given upper bounds on the norms of the couplings and of the far block, we show that outside a disc a pseudospectrum of the operator lies in a pseudospectrum of the compression, with an explicit loss in the level; this reverses the classical inclusion of the Ritz values in a pseudospectrum of the operator. The same bounds, with the smallest singular value of the shifted compression, bound the resolvent of the operator, count its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity inside every contour outside the disc on which a computed inequality holds, and enclose its spectral projector; no normality, self-adjointness or positivity is used.

authors.name: Isaia Nisoli
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro

papers.title: The Penrose Correspondence over a Non-Archimedean Field
papers.abstract: Let \(K\) be a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic different from \(2\), and let \(V\) have dimension four over \(K\). The Drinfeld upper half-spaces of \(V\) and \(Λ^2V\) define compatible open analytic subsets of \(\Pp(V)\), \(\Gr(2,V)\), and \(\Flag(1,2;V)\). Both restricted incidence projections are smooth and surjective. For every torsion-free discrete subgroup of \(\PGL(V)(K)\), the three actions are free and properly discontinuous, and the incidence correspondence descends to smooth analytic quotients. These domains contain an explicit flag defined over an unramified extension of degree seven. A symplectic form on \(V\) equips the projective domain with a contact structure and places the Grassmannian domain in \(\Sp_4/(\Sp_2\times\Sp_2)\). For torsion-free discrete symplectic groups, this contact structure descends to the quotient. Free discrete symplectic groups of every finite rank at least two give contact threefolds whose underlying Berkovich spaces have the homotopy type of a bouquet of circles. Every quotient of the projective domain by a torsion-free discrete group preserving the contact distribution is noncompact. For every torsion-free discrete projective linear group, the flag quotient and all fibers of its two incidence projections are noncompact; both projections are nonproper.

papers.title: Generalized Images for Brownian First Passage to Monomial Boundaries
papers.abstract: We study the first passage of Brownian motion to a monomial moving boundary. For every integer degree at least two, we construct a time-independent signed image measure whose heat potential is the killed Brownian transition density on a nonzero interval of the natural Brownian time scale. The image density is determined by a second-kind Volterra equation in the image coordinate, not by the classical Volterra equations in time for the hitting density. Its kernel is an explicit Wright function, and the first-passage density is recovered afterwards from the boundary flux. Exponential bounds establish convergence, while a beta-moment transform connects the Wright kernel with the finite-order differential hierarchy previously obtained from transported moving zeros. A cubic numerical experiment independently checks the resulting density against simulated Brownian paths.

papers.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
papers.abstract: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

papers.title: aggmetrics: Aggregating Classification Performance Measures for Machine Learning
papers.abstract: aggmetrics is a Python package that extends any binary performance measure expressed in the four confusion-matrix counts to multiclass, multilabel, ordinal, cost-sensitive, soft-label and cross-validation settings, by substituting one of four aggregation operators for what libraries usually expose as an average switch. The package also stores, for every measure, the structural properties that decide which identities apply to it, can infer those properties from a user-supplied formula, and uses them to warn when a measure is used where it does not behave as commonly assumed. Its test suite encodes the results of the companion theory as executable tests. The package is BSD-3 licensed, depends only on NumPy, and is available at https://github.com/rcprati/aggmetrics; documentation at https://aggmetrics.readthedocs.io.

papers.title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Regularized lattice Boltzmann methods improve numerical stability by projecting the nonequilibrium distribution onto its hydrodynamic second-order Hermite sector and filtering the remaining kinetic modes. We introduce a separate relaxation time for the complete complementary kinetic subspace. The resulting extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method (E-RLBM) interpolates continuously between the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and regularized collision operators while retaining a two-rate implementation. A Chapman-Enskog expansion shows that the isothermal Navier-Stokes equations are recovered with kinematic viscosity $ν=c_s^2(τ-Δt/2)$, independently of the kinetic relaxation time $τ_{\rm nh}$, whereas $τ_{\rm nh}$ changes higher-order truncation errors. For linear transverse shear, its first effect is a fourth-derivative term whose coefficient depends on the direction of propagation relative to the lattice. This fourth-order coefficient is affine in $τ_{\rm nh}$. For linear shear on D2Q9 and $τ_{\rm nh}$ between $τ$ and $Δt$, it lies between the corresponding BGK and RLBM values in every propagation direction. Stability maps for the decaying Taylor-Green vortex and flow past a rectangular obstacle show that an appropriate kinetic relaxation substantially enlarges the stable parameter domain. In a Taylor-Green convergence test with consistent initialization, all three operators converge at second order, and their error differences follow the hyperviscous coefficient for diagonal shear waves: the E-RLBM error is about 6% above the BGK error and about 40% below the RLBM error; in a double shear layer at Re = 80000, the E-RLBM follows the RLBM convergence curve. The proposed collision operator therefore provides a low-cost means of controlling nonhydrodynamic modes without introducing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.

papers.title: Post-Hoc Feature Selection Layer for Neural Networks Interpretability
papers.abstract: The interpretability of complex neural networks remains a critical challenge, especially for models already deployed in high-stakes domains. To address this, we adapted the Feature Selection Layer (FSL) to optimize feature weights post-training, a variant we term post-hoc FSL. Our approach reframes the FSL as a lightweight, trainable module that integrates with already frozen pre-trained models on tabular datasets to highlight the features the original model considers most important. This post-hoc FSL learns feature relevance by fine-tuning its weights based on the original model's learned outputs. Crucially, this process is non-invasive, operating without altering the original model's architecture or its learned parameters. We conducted our experiments using both statistical and visual metrics, including accuracy, F1 score, recall, precision, weighted t-SNE and silhouette score, and also analyzed the stability of the post-hoc FSL on high-dimensional synthetic and real-world tabular datasets. We compared the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method using these metrics against the original embedded FSL and other post-hoc interpretability methods, such as Integrated Gradients, Noise Tunnel, DeepLIFT, Gradient SHAP, and Feature Ablation. Experimental results demonstrate that the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method successfully identified relevant features across the different datasets, maintaining the predictive power of the original neural network while enhancing its interpretability.

papers.title: QuaNAS: Uncertainty-Aware Reuse of Earlier Searches for Query-Efficient Neural Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) on a new dataset often affords only tens of short training runs, so what the search knows before its first evaluation decides its efficiency. Yet most NAS methods start from scratch, guided at best by zero-cost proxies that are unreliable across tasks. QuaNAS treats a library of earlier searches in the same search space as explicit knowledge of uncertain reliability. Main effects of design decisions learned from this library and, secondarily, zero-cost proxies become priors over candidate architectures without any label of the new dataset. A Gaussian process starts at the prior optimum and re-estimates after every evaluation how far each prior is trusted. Under a protocol frozen before any confirmation data were seen, QuaNAS was evaluated once on 12 new image, time-series, text and tabular datasets. It lowered anytime regret on the short-training objective 2.7- to 3.9-fold relative to five pre-specified NAS baselines that start from scratch (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012 each). Its final models matched (non-inferiority margin 0.5 pp) or exceeded matched-recipe reference models on nine datasets, as did the prior optimum, selected without a single evaluation. Post-hoc comparisons with established transfer methods given the same library trace the gain to the library: without it, the same Gaussian process had over twice the regret. They also show where each transfer mechanism works best: the pooled main effects of QuaNAS for weakly transferable tabular tasks, per-task surrogates for image, time-series and text tasks and for small or mismatched libraries. Finally, the main effects make the transferred knowledge inspectable.

papers.title: Class-Grounded Batik Captioning under Scarce Text Annotation: Label Retention and Source-Specific Error Propagation
papers.abstract: Class labels offer compact supervision for describing cultural-heritage images when expert text annotations are scarce. We investigate a batik-captioning cascade that integrates a LoRA-adapted DINOv2 classifier with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, adapted using LoRA and loaded in 4-bit NF4. A $3\times2$ evaluation combines three captioner conditions with two inference prompts to examine adaptation and predicted-class injection. Across 150 caption-evaluation images, all three injected conditions achieve a ground-truth class-label mention rate of 0.9067. The classifier's separate test yields 96.10% pooled accuracy, with 98.33% on 300 public-source images and 75.76% on 33 local images. Supported-class macro-F1 and balanced accuracy on the local subset are 0.8493 and 0.8302, respectively. The classifier and captioner use separate partitions, and their training--evaluation overlap remains unquantified. Differences in label semantics and training support also affect interpretation of the source-specific accuracy gap. Reference-based caption metrics and image--text compatibility scores produce different model rankings. Qualitative examples show both retention of correctly predicted identities and propagation of classification errors into fluent descriptions. These findings characterize how class conditioning preserves label information and transfers upstream errors into batik captions under scarce text annotation.

papers.title: Optical and near-infrared s-process abundance scales in the Galactic disc
papers.abstract: A discrepancy has recently emerged between optical and near-infrared (NIR) s-process abundance scales, particularly for Neodymium (Nd). We investigated this issue using a direct cross-match between the optical Gaia-ESO Survey (DR5) and NIR SDSS-V/MWM (DR19). While atmospheric parameters and Cerium (Ce) abundances exhibit robust 1:1 correlations, Nd displays a systematic X-shaped vertical stretching. Our analysis reveals that the SDSS-V pipeline expands intrinsic Nd variations by a scaling factor of 5.54 relative to the stable optical baseline. This phenomenon is driven by baseline compression in the APOGEE H-band, where the growth of the molecular forest (CN and CO) at high metallicities depresses the local continuum. This forces the chi^2 minimisation engine in the NIR abundance determination to inflate derived abundances to reach mathematical convergence. We provide an empirical calibration framework to reconcile these disparate regimes. This correction effectively eliminates the contradictory negative radial [Nd/Fe] gradient of -0.052 dex/kpc reported in recent NIR surveys, bringing them into alignment with the rising trends established by the optical high-resolution Gaia-ESO survey. These results demonstrate that the observed scale expansion is a spectroscopic artefact of line-blanketing rather than a physical Galactic trend.

papers.title: Short curves in homogeneous spaces of the unitary group for unitarily invariant norms
papers.abstract: Let A be a unital *-subalgebra of $M_n(C)$ and let $M = U(n)/U(A)$, with the quotient Finsler metric induced by a unitarily invariant norm on $u(n)$, normalized so that $||iP|| = 1$ for rank-one projections $P$. This family contains the unitary orbits of Hermitian matrices, in particular flag manifolds and Grassmann manifolds. We prove that if $z_0$ is a minimal lifting of a tangent vector $X$ with $||X||_{\infty} < π/2$, then the one-parameter group $t \mapsto e^{t z_0}\cdot o$ has minimal length among all piecewise smooth curves in $M$ joining its endpoints. The same holds in manifolds $N=SU(n)/(SU(n) \cap A)$ for every Ad-invariant Finsler norm on $su(n)$, not necessarily symmetric (i.e. the unit sphere does not need to be balanced). The proof relies on the convexity of the distance from the identity along geodesic segments, valid for all these norms. We also prove that the ball of radius $π/2$ around the identity, for the spectral norm, is convex along one-parameter segments. This extends known results for the p-Schatten norms with p even, and gives a new proof for the operator norm, where the result is due to Duran, Mata-Lorenzo and Recht.

papers.title: Almost simple subgroups of the space Cremona group
papers.abstract: We prove that every finite almost simple subgroup that is not simple of the group of birational automorphisms of the three-dimensional complex projective space is isomorphic to one of the following: $\mathfrak{S}_5$, $\mathfrak{S}_6$, $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7)$ or $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$. We also prove that the group of birational automorphisms of the three-dimensional complex projective space contains unique (up to conjugation) subgroups isomorphic to $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7)$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$.

papers.title: Weighted boundedness of maximal operator associated with invertible linear transformations on variable Lebesgue spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the boundedness of $M_{A^{-1}}$, the maximal operator involves an invertible matrix, on the weighted variable spaces $L^{p(\cdot)}(w)$, where the weights are in an appropriate class. In general, we obtain the necessary conditions for the weight classes and exponents. However, for certain types of invertible matrices, we characterize the weights such that the boundedness holds.

papers.title: Exceptional points and cusp singularities in relativistic stellar oscillations with causal bulk relaxation
papers.abstract: Causal relativistic hydrodynamics introduces relaxation degrees of freedom that elevate a quadratic oscillation problem to a cubic non-Hermitian spectral pencil. We study its exceptional-point (EP2) curves and an $A_3$ cusp, and construct an exactly solvable radiating wave--relaxation problem with a Pöschl--Teller potential and an Israel--Stewart channel. Using hyperboloidal coordinates, outgoing Siegert conditions become endpoint conditions. For the aligned transport profile and away from discrete resonant couplings, we prove that the complete quasinormal point spectrum decomposes into a tower of sector cubics, with radiative damping rates determined by the boundary-value problem. The resulting EP2 and cusp geometry is therefore realized by genuine quasinormal eigenvalues. Multiprecision bordered-Newton calculations certify the degeneracies and their square-root and cubic-root splitting laws. Under a controlled parity-preserving deformation of the viscosity profile, the fundamental EP2 survives over a finite parameter window before annihilating with a partner and moving into complexified parameters; the cusp also persists. For dense matter, we derive a criterion independent of the relaxation time: $(v_{\rm FR}/v_β)^2 \ge 1+Θ(γ)$, where $Θ(γ)$ is the minimum coupling ratio along the EP2 locus. For weakly radiating compressive modes, $Θ\simeq 8$, requiring $v_{\rm FR}\gtrsim 3v_β$. Internally consistent nucleonic Urca matter misses this threshold by more than two orders of magnitude. Exotic-matter comparisons are indicative benchmarks rather than same-equation-of-state exclusions. The radiating model is not a relativistic TOV-star perturbation; establishing the mechanism in a realistic star remains open.

papers.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

papers.title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
papers.abstract: This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

papers.title: Assortment optimization under the perception-adjusted Luce model
papers.abstract: The Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM) introduced by by Echenique et al. (2018) is a sequential choice model that can accommodate violations of regularity and choice overload, behaviors not captured by the utility-maximization framework. Flores et al. (2019) studied the assortment problem under the PALM and proved that, for the case of two levels, there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. They also conjectured that revenue-ordered by levels remain optimal for the general PALM with any number of levels. We resolve this question in the affirmative by showing that every PALM instance admits an optimal assortment that includes, within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold. The proof involves first showing how the conjecture which deals with a discrete optimization problem, can be reduced to proving certain property of a related continuous optimization problem. Specifically, we study a continuous refinement of the assortment decision under the same PALM choice rule. Although the refinement permits partial utility selections, we prove it always has an optimum that selects complete revenue tiers. This allows us to show that the assortment problem is polynomial-time solvable when the number of levels is fixed.

papers.title: Norm-Euclideanity in cyclic fields
papers.abstract: Consider a cyclic number field of prime degree $p$. For a fixed degree, there are only finitely many such fields which are norm-Euclidean. When $p=2$ or $3$, these have been completely determined. If instead $p>3$, one can bound the discriminant of such fields from above. We substantially sharpen these upper bounds via an explicit Burgess-type criterion and describe a method for completely resolving other small prime cases.

papers.title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
papers.abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

papers.title: Journal Basket: Supporting Cross-Disciplinary Literature Searching and Methodological Transparency
papers.abstract: Business students beginning a research project must learn how to identify relevant scholarly publications, distinguish disciplinary sources, construct database searches, and report the decisions behind their literature reviews. These tasks can be difficult because journal classification systems and bibliographic databases organize scholarly information differently. This paper introduces Journal Basket, a browser-based tool developed to help business students conduct journal-bounded literature searches and currently available in beta. Journal Basket enables users to construct journal collections from the Australian Business Deans Council (ABDC) Journal Quality List, choose from 42 business discipline presets, entire ABDC fields or the Financial Times FT50 list, apply journal rating thresholds, and generate search expressions for Scopus, Web of Science and Business Source. Users can also inspect and modify journal collections, download journal inventories, and generate methodological descriptions and deterministic identifiers for journal selections. Companion learning resources use explanations, examples and interactive activities to teach review methods, database choice, referencing and the use of contemporary AI tools. Drawing on the journal-basket concept used by Litbaskets.io, I describe the educational motivation, design rationale, technical architecture, and practical workflow of Journal Basket. I distinguish reproducing a journal collection from reproducing an entire database search and discuss the limitations of journal rankings as search boundaries. The paper addresses scholarly information retrieval through a workflow for defining journal boundaries, generating database-specific queries and documenting search decisions.

papers.title: Probabilistic and game thresholds
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a finite set and $\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^X$ a non-trivial increasing property. We show that the bias-threshold $b(\mathcal{F})$ for the Picker-Chooser $\mathcal{F}$-game satisfies $b(\mathcal{F}) \ge α/ p_c(\mathcal{F})$, where $p_c(\mathcal{F})$ is the threshold for the property $\mathcal{F}$ and $α> 0$ is an absolute constant. This proves that Picker-Chooser games satisfy one-sided ``probabilistic intuition''. The proof is based on the notion of influence from the theory of boolean functions.

papers.title: A note on functional non-central limit theorem for periodic regime-switching stable-like processes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a functional non-central limit theorem for regime-switching stable-like processes with periodic coefficients. Our approach relies on stochastic analysis methods, in particular semimartingale characteristics, combined with the ergodic theory of Markov processes. If the set on which the order function achieves its minimum value $\underlineα$ has positive Lebesgue measure, then the limit is a rotationally invariant $\underlineα$-stable Lévy process. Otherwise, the limit is the zero process.

They have been used as mathematical models in problems related to signal processing, biological and ecological systems, queuing networks, financial engineering, and other fields (see, e.g., [31] and [33]). The main characteristic of these processes is the interaction between the dynamics of the system and discrete events that provide information about its current regime. This feature enables such systems to describe complex phenomena involving inherent uncertainty and environmental randomness.

papers.title: Isogenies of Oriented Elliptic Curves
papers.abstract: We construct and describe the moduli stack $\mathrm{Isog}$ of isogenies between oriented elliptic curves. We show that $\mathrm{Isog}$ is a spectral Deligne-Mumford stack and a relative spectral algebraic space over $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{or}}$, and give a fiber product decomposition of $\mathrm{Isog}$ corresponding to a connected-étale factorization on oriented elliptic curves. In the process of proving these results, we construct a theory of duality and quotients for spectral abelian varieties, prove a higher-algebraic version of Nakayama's lemma, and lift the rigidity theorem for morphisms of elliptic curves to the setting of spectral algebraic geometry.
papers.intro:
The contemporary study of elliptic cohomology is largely based on Lurie’s theory of oriented elliptic curves. An oriented elliptic curve is the analogue of an elliptic curve in spectral algebraic geometry, together with the additional data of an orientation: an equivalence between the formal completion E^\widehat{E} of the curve and the spectral Quillen formal group 𝔾^AQ\widehat{\mathbb{G}}_{A}^{Q} of the base ring. The moduli stack ℳellor\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{or}} of such curves shares an underlying topos with the classical moduli stack of elliptic curves, and its structure sheaf coincides with the presheaf of 𝔼∞\mathbb{E}_{\infty}-rings given by the Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem. In particular, the global sections of this stack is T​M​FTMF.

The purpose of this text is to develop an algebreo-geometric foundation for the analogous theory in elliptic cohomology, namely the theory of Hecke operators. These have been studied by Baker ([1]), Ganter ([3]) Rezk ([16], Zhu ([19]), and others; the state of the art when it comes to the algebreo-geometric approach is probably Jack Davies’s paper Hecke operators on topological modular forms ([2]), which in particular shows that stable Hecke operators cannot be defined on non-twisted T​M​FTMF without localizing at their corresponding primes. My own motivation for studying these operators comes partially from a result of Hopkins–Mahowald–Sadofsky (Proposition 2.1 of [8]) which can be interpreted as an Artin reciprocity isomorphism for the maximal unramified abelian extension of the K⁡(1)K(1)-local sphere. A height-22 analogue of this result would likely involve eigenvalues of Hecke operators on elliptic cohomology, and would serve as the basis for a theory of topological modular Galois representations. This is one of a few observations that serve as basis for my chromatic Langlands program, of which this paper is a part. The next step, which will be carried out in the sequel, is the construction of the Hecke operators themselves.

In the classical setting, Hecke operators are constructed by a pull-push operation on the source and target morphisms from ℳ0​(p)\mathcal{M}_{0}(p) to ℳell\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}. Effectively, this is a sum over all the operations induced by isogenies whose kernel has rank pp, which is classically computed as a double-coset formula. In our setting, we similarly need to understand such moduli of isogenies. There is a major problem, however: unless pp is inverted, such isogenies will not all be étale, and so they cannot be orientation-preserving, even up to an automorphism of the base. Accordingly, the study of these operations requires that we understand the theory of all isogenies of oriented elliptic curves, including those which are ramified. Because the usual tools of spectral deformation theory (see below) are most suited to describing deformations of étale objects, we instead work directly with the spectral isogenies and their spectral moduli stack, ultimately reducing the problem to pieces which can be understood deformation-theoretically.

papers.title: Fefferman--Chang-type atomic decompositions for product Hardy spaces associated with Schrödinger operators
papers.abstract: We establish a geometric (Fefferman--Chang-type) atomic characterization of the two-parameter Hardy space associated with a pair of Schrödinger operators $L_i=-Δ+V_i$ on $\mathbb R^{n_i}$, $i=1,2$. The space is defined by the product conical square function. We assume comparability of neighbouring covering cubes, a local bound on the potentials, and decay of the semigroup mass at large scales. We prove that the Hardy norm is equivalent to a sum of classical local product Hardy norms at scales determined by the adapted coverings. This localization formula yields an atomic decomposition whose atoms satisfy size and partial cancellation conditions, with cancellation required only below the corresponding local scales. Both the atoms and their rectangular components remain supported inside fixed enlargements of the covering rectangles. The proof combines one-parameter Schrödinger Hardy space characterizations with standard vector-valued arguments and a localized product atomic decomposition with uniform control of scales and supports. The assumptions cover the model case of reverse Hölder potentials $V\in RH_q$, $q>n/2$, as well as potentials outside every $RH_q$ class, $q>1$, including half-space indicators and exponential potentials.

More recently, Deng and Guedjiba [5, Definition 3.5 and Theorem 4.1] established atomic characterizations for product Hardy spaces associated with nonnegative self-adjoint operators satisfying Davies–Gaffney estimates. Their rectangular components are represented through powers of the underlying operators. Here we obtain atoms defined by support, size, and ordinary partial cancellation conditions, with the dependence on the Schrödinger operators encoded by the adapted coverings and their local scales.

The local product theory of Ding, Lu, and Zhu [6] provides the classical two-parameter model for our construction. Geometric atomic descriptions of local Hardy spaces also occur in the multi-norm setting studied in by the author, Nagel, and Ricci in [14]. In that setting, the geometry is specified by families of dilations. In the present paper, the local scales vary with the spatial location through coverings adapted to the Schrödinger potentials.

papers.title: A Study in Solution Models for SAT using the PBNF-transform
papers.abstract: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described earlier in two articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a statement of conjunctions of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations, inverting the problem by \emph{multiplying} letters (literals) in the transferred clauses, now phrases: $pqrs\cdots s_{\ell}$, and using a binary iterated composition based on \emph{adding polynomials} for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value $1\mapsto 0$(T). To find a solution, we look for repeating literals in the clauses to factor out. With reversed literal repetition, we can even reduce the CNF to the sum of the transformed clauses.

papers.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
papers.abstract: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.

We apply the temporal-liquidity crossing framework to Ethereum through a Temporal Crossing Mechanism for EIP-1559. Transactions submit bids or offers according to their temporal-liquidity roles: a consumer signs a positive temporal authorization as its bid for earlier service, while a provider’s below-floor fee fields determine a shortfall, the minimum monetary offer required for accepting later service. In this framework, these correspond to the consumer’s Δu\Delta_{u} and provider’s Δf\Delta_{f}. Settlement uses a pool rather than a direct transfer: selected consumers pay their bids into it, the pool covers funded provider offers, and what it does not spend is burned. Here, “earlier” means completion within a defined early region of the block, while “later” means execution outside that region. The formal rule ranks qualifying consumers by authorization per unit of realized gas while retaining builder discretion over opt-out transactions and all ordering not expressly constrained.

papers.title: Radial Schur multipliers on trees and quantitative Fourier--Schur separation
papers.abstract: We study ordinary and completely bounded norms of radial Schur multipliers on trees. On the homogeneous tree of countably infinite degree, we show that boundedness implies complete boundedness. The argument realizes arbitrary matrix amplifications of a shifted Toeplitz symbol inside rectangular corners of the original multiplier. It also applies to some locally finite trees of unbounded degree. Consequently, the completely bounded radial multiplier theorem of González-Pérez, Parcet, Pérez García and Wang has no general counterpart with ordinary norms. We also determine the optimal order of the comparison constant for positive definite even symbols. For each $1 < p < \infty$ with $p \neq 2$, we construct radial symbols on finitely generated nonabelian free groups, supported in the ball of radius $N$, whose completely bounded Herz--Schur norms remain bounded as $N \to \infty$, whereas their ordinary Fourier multiplier norms grow at least like $N^{|1-\frac{2}{p}|}$. For each fixed $0 < \vartheta < π$, we also determine the exact order $t^{-|1-\frac{2}{p}|}$ of both the ordinary and completely bounded Fourier multiplier norms of the damped radial phases $s \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{(-t+\mathrm{i}\vartheta)|s|}$ as $t \to 0$. Finally, we compute the local amenability modulus of free balls, we bound the Fourier--Schur ratio of free balls from above and below in terms of this modulus, and we show that its restriction to radial symbols grows polynomially in the radius.

papers.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs
papers.abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.

papers.title: Irrationality Exponents of Real CM Elliptic Periods and Powers of the Lemniscate Period
papers.abstract: We give a determinant proof that every nonzero real period of a nonsingular elliptic curve over $\mathbb Q$ with complex multiplication, measured with a specified nonzero rational invariant differential, has irrationality exponent two. The proof uses an integral origin chart, matched local lengths, an actual compactification and weighted packet map, and arithmetic and analytic estimates for the same selected minor on a rectangular sublattice of the full CM period lattice. For the integral-defined lemniscate period $Ω=2\int_0^1(1-t^4)^{-1/2}\,dt$, we also give the uniform bound $μ(Ω^n)=O(n\log(2n))$ for integers $n\geq1$. Its new arithmetic ingredient clears integration denominators prime by prime while retaining the coefficient order; a one-root norm argument and an analytic estimate at algebraic centers complete the power proof. The two arguments are presented with their different charts and exact dependencies. Lean verifies the new CM determinant argument and rational normalization relative to explicit classical uniformization, CM-lifting and theta inputs; the lemniscate-power endpoint is also verified. The formalization record states the exact classical boundary and theorem references.

papers.title: Ultra-hard-edge universality under deterministic preconditioning
papers.abstract: Let $A_n$ be an $n\times n$ real matrix with iid entries distributed as a fixed centered, variance-one, symmetric subgaussian random variable. For deterministic invertible $M_n$, set $h_n=\|M_n^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$ and $B_n=M_n^{-1}/h_n$. We prove $\mathbb{P}(s_{\min}(M_nA_n)\le\varepsilon/h_n) =(1+o(1))\varepsilonΘ_n(B_n)$ as $n\to\infty$, uniformly over $M_n$ and $e^{-cn}\le\varepsilon\le n^{-C}$. Here $Θ_n(B)=\mathbb{E}\sqrt{nU^\top BB^\top U}$, where $U$ is uniform on $S^{n-1}$. The constants $c>0$ and $C>1$ depend only on the entry law. No condition-number bound or effective-rank assumption is required. The coefficient tends to one for diffuse inverse profiles. For convergent concentrated or spiked profiles, its limit is an explicit Gaussian expectation. The proof combines the submicroscopic comparison of Sah, Sahasrabudhe, and Sawhney with signed-permutation averaging and a weighted comparison for random hyperplane normals. Applications include inverse amplification, square sample covariance matrices with arbitrary deterministic positive-definite population matrices, and independent random environments.

papers.title: Superintelligent Software Engineering: Governance That Scales with Capability
papers.abstract: Software agents are being trained to exceed human engineers; we argue that capability alone does not produce better software engineering. We define superintelligent software engineering as the discipline of building and evolving software with agents whose capability exceeds that of human engineers, in which governance (gates, contracts, decisions and decay control) scales with capability. The argument rests on three claims. First, correctness in a project rests on decisions and contracts that the code does not carry. Second, knowledge decays. Third, once an agent outpaces its reviewers, reading catches a shrinking share of the changes built on stale knowledge. A simple model shows that, past a fixed review capacity, escaping changes grow linearly with throughput while the share that reading catches falls toward zero; governance can lower the slope, capability alone cannot. An exploratory snapshot of 452 of the most-starred public GitHub repositories finds a root-level or .github agent context file in 48.67% (95% confidence interval 44.1 to 53.3); in the median file that names repository paths, 9.5% to 22% of those paths do not resolve, depending on how a reference is read. We then present OSTEON, a discipline for the regime, archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23436020 as a plugin for Claude Code. In OSTEON, each project gets a governed knowledge repository of decisions and contracts, every change is checked mechanically against it, and the knowledge itself is checked for decay at every session start; planning is gated, and sessions record what they learn without writing rules. We report no measured effect of OSTEON, mark claims about its mechanisms as opinion and the author's practice heuristics as design rationale, and state the questions that would falsify the thesis.

papers.intro:
Coding agents now resolve real issues in real repositories, and benchmarks such as SWE-bench [1] track how often they succeed. One route to better software engineering is to train more capable agents; we call it the training route, and it now states its goal plainly. Self-play SWE-RL trains a single agent to inject and repair bugs of rising difficulty in real codebases, with no human-labelled issues or tests, and presents itself as a first step toward training superintelligent software agents [2]. If that route succeeds, the agents that work in a codebase will, on much of the work, exceed the engineers who are responsible for it. Fig. 1 summarises the argument of this paper.

This paper asks what engineering discipline that regime requires. Our answer is that capability is necessary and not sufficient. Software engineering has never been only the production of code that passes its tests. It is the production of code that is correct with respect to what a project has decided: the trade-offs it accepted, the contracts it holds with its neighbours, and the state of the system it actually runs. Most of that knowledge lives outside the code. It changes, and parts of it go stale without anyone noticing. In a snapshot of 452 of the most-starred public GitHub repositories, 48.67% carry a root-level or .github file written to brief coding agents. In the median such file that names repository paths, between 9.5% and 22% of those paths do not resolve, depending on how a path reference is read (Section IV). An unresolved path is a mismatch between a file and its tree, not shown to be a wrong instruction; it is one observable form of the drift this paper is about. An agent that consults stale knowledge may build the wrong change, and cannot tell that it has. We expect a more capable agent to build it faster, at larger scope, and to defend it better. [Opinion]

papers.title: An asymptotic $Γ$-BMT inequality
papers.abstract: We refine a bound of Cheng-Feyzbakhsh to prove an asymptotic $Γ$-Bayer-Macrì-Toda ($Γ$-BMT) inequality on every smooth polarized complex threefold. The proof relies on a reduction to small tilt stability parameters. Using this inequality we verify Feyzbakhsh-Thomas's condition $(wBG)$ whenever $K_{X}$ is numerically proportional to the polarization. For polarized Calabi-Yau threefolds, this yields a reduction of positive rank generalized Donaldson-Thomas (DT) invariants to those counting sheaves pure in codimension one. We further express these invariants in terms of rank one generalized DT invariants. Thus, the rank reductions of Feyzbakhsh-Thomas hold without assuming the BMT conjecture.

papers.title: Local heights for nef toric compactified divisors
papers.abstract: We present a definition of a local height of nef toric divisors in the sense of Yuan and Zhang by approximating a height for canonical divisors and then using the local energy to extend to other metrics on the same geometric divisor.

papers.intro:
Heights are a tool in diophantine geometry to estimate the algebraic complexity of numbers and can, for example, be used to control the number of rational points on a variety.

Heights are a tool in diophantine geometry to estimate the algebraic complexity of numbers and can, for example, be used to control the number of rational points on a variety.

From the perspective of Arakelov theory, heights can be viewed as an arithmetic analogue of the intersection number associated to a collection of line bundles. The original theory of arithmetic intersections introduced by Arakelov in [Ara74] for arithmetic surfaces and extended by Gillet and Soulé in [GS90] works with divisors on smooth projective arithmetic varieties defined over the ring of integers 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} of a number field kk that are compactified in a suitable sense by adding to each divisor smooth metrics at all places at infinity. Then, Zhang in [Zha95] developed an approach that furnishes the line bundles with continuous metrics on the Berkovich analytification coming from an algebraic model at every place vv in kk, unifying the treatment of archimedean and non-archimedean places. This leads to a definition of the local height h⁡(X,D¯0,…,D¯d)h(X;\overline{D}_{0},\ldots,\overline{D}_{d}) of a dd-dimensional proper variety XX over a valued field kk with respect to metrized divisors D¯0,…,D¯d\overline{D}_{0},\ldots,\overline{D}_{d}, where the metrics can be differences of semipositive metrics. Here, a metric is called semipositive if it is a uniform limit of metrics coming from algebraic models.

papers.title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
papers.abstract: Coding agents can be guided with instruction files in a repository. We examine this emerging practice through a census of 22,854 popular, active GitHub repositories in thirteen languages, treating each repository's root 'AGENTS$.$md' and 'CLAUDE$.$md' as one instruction set. Agent instructions appear in 26.3% of repositories and 59.6% of the most-starred; where both files exist, 'CLAUDE$.$md' usually points to 'AGENTS$.$md'. We analyse 341,852 statements using model-assisted annotation and human review. The annotations reveal a practical mix of project knowledge and rules about code, building and workflow. Collaboration rules name concrete requirements, from test plans to commit formats, yet 74.0% of directives give no reason. Projects disagree on AI attribution: commit-message rules more often prohibit it than require it, while pull-request rules more often require disclosure. A third of instruction sets have a generator-associated signature, a tool-inserted block, shared text or an AI-marked creation commit; four in five are edited after creation. Prespecified tests associate repository popularity with rules on pull requests and AI contributions. Exploratory analyses link activity to process-oriented content and show that LLM and agent projects are over-represented among adopters. The models agree much more closely with each other than with the human reviewer's topic assignments, a caution for automated annotation. We release the annotations, taxonomies and pointers to the analysed file versions.
papers.intro:
Human contributors learn a project’s norms through review: which commands to run, what a pull request must contain, when a change is done. Coding agents, which now work in open-source repositories at scale [Robbes et al., 2026a, Li et al., 2026], often start a task without that history, so projects write the norms down for them, mostly in two root files: AGENTS.md, an open format that calls itself a README for agents [AGENTS.md, 2026], and CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code reads [Anthropic, 2026b]. Whether such files help agents is contested [Gloaguen et al., 2026, Lulla et al., 2026], so it matters what projects put in them. Existing studies characterise them on repositories already tied to agent use [Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2026] or screen broad samples under other definitions, with adoption estimates from 5% of mature repositories [Mohsenimofidi et al., 2026] to 21.7% of agent-using ones [Díaz et al., 2026]. What popular projects write, statement by statement, where that text comes from and what it varies with is not known.

We answer these questions with a census of 22,854 public GitHub repositories returned by GitHub’s search API in thirteen languages with at least 1,000 stars and recent activity, and treat each repository’s AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md as one instruction set. We ask who has agent instructions (RQ1), what they contain (RQ2), how instructions are expressed (RQ3), where their content comes from (RQ4) and what it varies with (RQ5). Analysing the files together, down to individual statements, lets us examine both the requirements projects give their agents and the traces of generators, tools and shared text in those requirements. We combine this account with adoption and file-history measurements, prespecified hypothesis tests and exploratory associations with project characteristics. We release file-version pointers, annotations, taxonomies and aggregate results, without redistributing the corpus texts.

papers.title: Chemistry-resolved disagreement between Materials Project-compatible PBE(+U) and r2SCAN stability verdicts in the GNoME materials database
papers.abstract: GNoME's stability labels rest on a Materials Project-compatible GGA/GGA+U workflow. Its authors report that 84% of discovered binaries and ternaries retain a negative decomposition energy under r2SCAN and 86.8% of tested quaternaries remain stable on the r2SCAN hull. We resolve that aggregate by chemistry over the 139,541 GNoME materials released with r2SCAN recomputations, a subset the dataset authors selected rather than sampled, using cluster bootstrap intervals over 8,429 structural-prototype proxy clusters. The aggregate conceals a 26.7-point spread at fixed element count, from 4.0% [3.3, 4.7] for plain quaternary intermetallics (no lanthanide, no 3d metal) to 30.7% [27.7, 33.8] for lanthanide-free 3d-containing quaternary oxides, a pair identified post hoc against a prospectively fixed threshold. Under our reading of the release's "All" reference set the two cells sit at 14.5% and 37.4%, preserving a 22.9-point spread. Presence of a Materials Project Hubbard-U-list element is strongly associated with disagreement, conditional on the other covariates, in a model over all 139,541 materials (cluster-robust odds ratio 3.45 [3.13, 3.80]). Neither selective U application nor hull proximity explains the association away: disagreement stays elevated outside the U-treated regime, and a natural cubic spline in the continuous PBE decomposition energy moves the odds ratio in the 117,018-material model only from 3.53 to 3.43 [3.07, 3.83]. For allocating a verification budget, composition supplements hull proximity rather than replacing it: over held-out cluster splits at a 20% budget, the two together surface 45.8% of disagreements against 40.4% for hull distance alone. An exploratory comparison against previously catalogued materials changes direction between populations. We measure disagreement between two workflows, not accuracy.

papers.intro:
Computational materials discovery has shifted from enumerating candidates to generating them. GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration) reported 381,000 new entries on the convex hull, the surface of lowest formation energy below which a composition has no cheaper decomposition into competing phases, for a total of 421,000 stable crystals (Merchant et al., 2023); subsequent releases, which widened the release criterion from the documented on-hull tolerance of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} eV/atom to within 1 meV/atom of the hull (Google DeepMind, 2023), brought the public summary file to 554,054 entries (our row count). Generative models such as MatterGen (Zeni et al., 2025) and expanded databases such as Alexandria have followed, the latter’s PBEsol/SCAN subset (Schmidt et al., 2022) using PBEsol geometries with SCAN energies rather than PBE. GNoME’s own stability verdicts, which are what this paper analyses, rest on density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) level (Perdew et al., 1996), executed in VASP (Kresse and Furthmüller, 1996) with Materials Project (MP)-compatible settings (Jain et al., 2013), including a Hubbard UU for eight transition metals in oxides and fluorides and the Materials Project 2020 (MP2020) correction scheme’s empirical anion and GGA/GGA+UU mixing corrections (Wang et al., 2021). The functional and correction choices differ across MatterGen, Alexandria and GNoME, so the question we ask of GNoME does not transfer to the others unchanged.

GGA formation energies carry errors of order 0.1 eV/atom (Kirklin et al., 2015), but formation-energy errors do not directly determine stability-verdict disagreement, because a decomposition energy compares a material against composition-conserving combinations of competing phases rather than against an elemental reference. We therefore analyse the released decomposition-energy outcomes directly. The need for chemistry resolution is practical: a laboratory choosing which predicted compound to attempt cannot act on an aggregate error rate, a database maintainer deciding where to spend a finite recomputation budget faces the same problem at scale, and aggregate benchmark scores against PBE-derived labels (Riebesell et al., 2025) do not show how sensitivity to the workflow varies across chemistry.

GNoME’s authors anticipated the question. They recomputed a subset with the r2SCAN meta-GGA, the regularised-restored form of the SCAN functional (Furness et al., 2020), and reported that 84% of discovered binaries and ternaries retain negative phase-separation energies (their term for the decomposition energy), with 86.8% of tested quaternaries remaining stable on the r2SCAN hull (Merchant et al., 2023). Supplementary Note 2 of that paper observes that the discrepancy concentrates near the hull and that the same effect appears in the Materials Project and the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD), but gives no breakdown by chemistry. The authors released the underlying r2SCAN data with the statement that it is provided “expectantly serving as a foundation for analysing discrepancies between functional choices.”

We measure disagreement between two computational methods: a material released as stable at the PBE level whose r2SCAN decomposition energy is positive (defined precisely in Section 3.4). We do not establish which functional is closer to the truth for any material, and we say nothing about whether these compounds are stable in reality. We therefore use the term flip throughout and avoid calling flipped labels “incorrect”. Where we discuss practical consequences the operative quantity is the share of labels a higher-fidelity recomputation would revise, which is a statement about what the expensive calculation would say, not about nature. This constrains every claim that follows, including the budget model of Section 4.12, whose payoff is measured in disagreements surfaced rather than errors corrected.

Our contributions are: (i) a chemistry- and element-resolved map of stability-verdict disagreement between the two workflows on GNoME; (ii) stratified comparisons showing that a lanthanide-pooled form of the composition contrast is present within every populated hull-distance band, that the 3dd-associated excess is present within every band-gap bin, and that the contrast persists with cell size as a covariate, under inverse-probability weighting (IPW) for recomputation selection (Section 4.8), and outside the Hubbard-UU-treated regime; (iii) the observation that the binary verdict change reflects a chemistry-dependent sign in the underlying energy displacement; (iv) an exploratory matched comparison against previously catalogued materials whose direction varies with composition; (v) a verification-budget evaluation over repeated cluster-wise splits showing that composition supplements rather than replaces proximity to the hull; and (vi) the observation that the compositional regime GNoME advertises most prominently is recomputed at the meta-GGA level too sparsely for stratified analysis.

papers.title: Cohomological change of coefficients for noncocommutative Hopf algebras
papers.abstract: Let $A$ be a finite Hopf algebra over a Noetherian commutative ring $R$. For any map $f : R \to k$ where $k$ is a field, there is a natural map on the cohomology of $A$ under this change of coefficients $H^\ast(f): H^\ast(A, R) \otimes_R k \to H^\ast(A_k, k)$. In this paper we examine this map for $R = \mathbb Z[ζ]$ the cyclotomic integers with $ζ$ an $\ell$th root of unity. We show that under a finite generation assumption, the induced map gives a homeomorphism on the spectra of the two cohomology rings. Finally, we turn to small quantum groups defined over $\mathbb Z[ζ]$ and show that, with mild restrictions on $\ell$, every fiber map whose residue field has a good prime characteristic induces an isomorphism on cohomology.

We study when a change in coefficients preserves the spectrum, i.e. when the induced map Spec⁡H∗​(f)\operatorname{Spec}H^{\ast}(f) is a homeomorphism. Etingof and Ostrik conjecture that cohomology rings of finite-dimensional Hopf algebras over a field are always finitely generated [12]. In the cocommutative setting, this is known to be true by a celebrated theorem of Friedlander and Suslin [13]. In [26], van der Kallen extends this result to finite group schemes (equivalently, finite cocommutative Hopf algebras) over a Noetherian ring. Cohomological finite generation is still open for finite noncocommutative Hopf algebras.

Essential to the proof in [7] is the second half of van der Kallen’s theorem. This further states that the cohomology rings of finite cocommutative Hopf algebras over Noetherian rings are entirely torsion in positive degrees, i.e. there exists a positive integer which annihilates H>0​(A,R)H^{>0}(A,R) [26]. In the noncocommutative setting, cohomology rings can look drastically different. In many known cases, the cohomology ring is entirely free, or has a significant free component. The goal of this paper is to determine to what extent the proof from [7] extends to finite noncocommutative Hopf algebras.
